note: Both songs are built on a long list of Ganapati's food offerings (fruits, appam, sugarcane, dal, sesame, puffed rice, tender coconut). In 2 the list is the god's own table; in 4 it is what the worshipper sets before him with sit-ups and ear-holding.
audit_text_issue: 2 has a corrupt glyph in தன஧முலம்; 4 in செற஧முளை.

note: Thiruppugazh 1 says that Ganapati, dwelling in the minds of devotees like the kalpaka tree (அடியவர் புத்தியில் உறைபவ கற்பகம்), makes deeds leave quickly (வினை கடிதேகும்). Tirumanthiram 1695 says the same of Siva: when the Lord takes his place in a pure mind (இறைவன் இடங்கொண்ட போதே), deeds strong as weeds go (வினையது போக). Both make the god's dwelling in the mind, not the rite, the thing that drives deeds out.

Thiruppugazh 3 praises Ganapati as the one who won the fruit by going round his father (தந்தைவலத்தால் அருள் கைக்கனியோனே). Thiruppugazh 176 tells the loser's side: Hara gave the fruit to the elephant-faced one (அந்தப் பலனைக் கரிமுகன் வசம் அருளும்) while Murugan circled the golden mountain, and Murugan, angry, went to Palani. The same contest is a title of honour in the one song and the origin of a shrine in the other.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 176 has a corrupt syllable in line 2 (தன஧முவ).

note: Thiruppugazh 3 names Ganapati by the circling of his father that won him the fruit. Thiruppugazh 153 sets the two circlings side by side: the elephant-faced one runs round Hara (ஆனைமுகர் அரனை ஓடி வலம்வரு முன்) while Murugan's peacock goes round the sea-girt world (உலகை வலமாக வரு துரக மயில்வீரா). Read together, the two songs give both halves of the contest that 3 compresses into one epithet.

Thiruppugazh 4 lays out the offerings to the single-tusked elephant face (fruit, appam, aval, sesame, puffed rice, plantains, tender coconut) and asks that it give a mind that thinks of Murugan's feet, vel and peacock (நினது திருவடி சத்தி மயிற்கொடி நினைவு கருதிடு புத்தி). Thiruppugazh 1002 lists nearly the same offerings (கடலை பயறொடு துவரை ... அவல் பொரி ... கதலி) and then names Murugan as the one who comes after (பிறகு வருமொரு முருக), confessing failure to bow to him. Both make Ganapati's worship the step before Murugan's; 1002 turns that order into the poet's fault.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 4 has a corrupt glyph (செற஧முளை).

note: Thiruppugazh 6 says Murugan taught the three-eyed Lord what comes before the Veda (முக்கட் பரமற்குச் சுருதியின் முற்பட்டது கற்பித்து) without naming it. Thiruppugazh 176 names it: the child guru spoke the secret of the pranava into Siva's golden ear (பொற்செவியுட் பிரணவ ரகசியம் ... உரைசெய் குழந்தைக் குருநாதா) so that his mind was made clear. 176 confirms the reading of 6 as Om.
audit_text_issue: 176 has a corrupt glyph (தன஧முவ).

note: Thiruppugazh 6 calls Murugan the one seed of release (முத்திக்கொரு வித்து) and the guru who taught Siva what precedes the Veda, taken as Om. Tirumanthiram 2676 says the omkara holds the one word, form and the formless, and is itself bright release and attainment (ஓம்எனும் ஓங்காரம் ஒண்முத்தி சித்தியே). If the teaching in 6 is Om, the Tirumanthiram gives the reason its teacher is called release's seed; that reading of 6 is the tradition's, not the song's words.

Both set the Lord against Death's messengers at the hour of death. Tirumular says those who think of the Lord will not be harmed by them; 8 is the prayer of one who has not done the thinking and asks Murugan to come anyway, on the peacock, at that moment.

The Kural says the heart melts at the thought of begging; 15 confesses the act, a poet praising patrons as Tamil's refuge 'with a wounded heart', and asks to trade that service for service at Murugan's feet.
Both describe women who want a man for his wealth and whose sweet invitations harm him; the Kural warns, 19 confesses to having trusted them.
Both make Murugan Siva's teacher: in 6 he teaches what precedes the Veda, in 12 he punishes Brahma and gives the knowledge to Siva.
audit_text_issue: 12 has one corrupt glyph in the praise.

note: Thiruppugazh 7 describes lovemaking at length and asks only whether he will ever give up delighting in it (கனகலவியை மகிழ்வது தவிர்வேனோ), so that giving it up is the condition of grace. Thiruppugazh 153 describes the same scene, bird-cries of the throat included, and says that even if he falls into that river of pleasure (அநுபோக நதியினிடை வீழுகினும) he will not forget the feet for a moment. On the reading that 7 makes renunciation the way to Murugan, 153 holds that devotion can survive the pleasure without it.

Tirumanthiram 163 compresses a life into three numbers: the egg born in three hundred days, marriage at twelve, ruin at seventy (கெட்டது எழுபதில் கேடறியீரே). Thiruppugazh 9 runs the same course stage by stage, ten months in the womb (கருவடைந்து பத்துற்ற திங்கள்), nursing, crawling, ornaments, youth, women and wandering in disease. The song spells out what the Tirumanthiram's count leaves implicit, and both end in decay that the person does not see coming.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 163 has an underscore in முந்_று (முந்நூறு).

note: Kural 918 says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an afflicting spirit to those without discerning understanding. Thiruppugazh 10 shows that embrace from the inside: the kohl eyes, the smile, the net of talk, 'come in' (மனைக்கு எழுந்திரும்), the bed, and then the plea to be freed from the sorrow of these poisonous girls (நஞ்சன சிறுமிகள் துயரற). The song is the experience the Kural's verdict describes.

Kural 329 says those whose work is killing (கொலைவினையர்) are base in their work (புலைவினையர்) to those who discern. Thiruppugazh 11, asking Murugan to end his birth today, names himself small, base, a killer (சிறியன் புலையன் கொலையன்), setting புலையன் beside கொலையன் as the Kural joins them. The poet passes on himself the judgment the Kural passes on killers.

Thiruppugazh 13 asks whether, no longer agitated in the chain of bonds, he will call 'Kanda' again and again (கந்தனென் றென்றுற்று), see him and love him. Tirumanthiram 278 says men call the Lord 'our father, our Lord' (எந்தை பிரானென்று) inside their wants and do not seek him with longing (நச்சியே ... நாடுகிலாரே). The Tirumanthiram adds the condition the song's plea implies: the repeated name counts only when it carries love rather than want.

Naladiyar 44 refuses to be moved by blind, petty men (கண்ணில் புன்மாக்கள்) who call eyes lilies, carp and spears. Thiruppugazh 16 gives those men's praise in full, eyes like carp (கயல் ஒக்கும் பருத்தகண்), hair like darkness, breasts like golden pots, and says the young men worship the women (இளைஞோர்கள் துதித்து முன் கும்பிட்டு), then calls himself a madman caught by them. The Naladiyar's speaker stands outside the comparisons; the poet confesses being inside them.

Thiruppugazh 17 speaks of women who take a man's wealth and pick a quarrel (பொருட்கவர்ந்து ஒன்றிய பிணக்கிடும் சண்டிகள்) and asks what he gains by wearing out his body after them. Naladiyar 372 shows the quarrel's pretext: the woman who swore to leap from the peak with him found, when he had no gold, a pain in her feet (காற்கால்நோய் காட்டி) and stayed behind. Both tie the courtesan's company to the money and her excuse to its running out.

Tirumanthiram 371 says the Lord rose bearing bones and a skull, and that without his bearing them they would have fallen to dust; whose bones they are it leaves to tradition. Thiruppugazh 18 names Siva as the one who wears the boar's tusk, the tortoise shell, serpents and the old bones of the gods (சுரர்கள் பண்டை என்பு அங்கம் அணிபவர்). The song states plainly the reading the Tirumanthiram's nuance can only attribute to tradition: the bones are the gods' own.

Thiruppugazh 19 calls himself the small fool who trusted the false minds of the courtesans (கணிகையர் தமதுபொய் மனத்தை நம்பிய சிறியனை) while they seized his wealth. Naladiyar 377 says those fooled into thinking such a woman's love their own (ஏமாந்து எமதென்று இருந்தார்), while she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many. The fault in both is the trust, not only the women's greed.

Thiruppugazh 20 says that, overcome by women, he perishes like cotton caught in fire (எரிப்படும் பஞ்சு போல மிகக்கெடும் தொண்டனேனும்). Tirumanthiram 117 uses the same cotton for the opposite: the sunstone burns the surrounding cotton only in the sun's presence, as the malas end before the Lord. In the song the self is the cotton that burns; in the Tirumanthiram the impurity is, and its burning is release.
audit_text_issue: One corrupt glyph in 20 (புண்ட஡ணகம்).

note: Thiruppugazh 20 asks for Murugan's lotus feet so that he may reach the shore of the sea of bonds (தொந்த வாரி கரையேற). Tirumanthiram 1498 says the rare shore is the shade of the Lord's feet (அருங்கரை யாவது அவ்வடி நீழல்), the one shore for all souls coming toward it. Both make the feet the shore of a sea; the song names the sea as bonds, which the Tirumanthiram leaves unnamed.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 20 has a corrupt word (புண்ட஡ணகம், for புண்டரீகம்).

note: Both hear the funeral drum over the corpse while kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still marries and seeks joy; 23 draws a different lesson, that one should share even a grain before the summons comes.
The Kural makes sharing one's food the chief of all duties; 23 arrives at the same act, sharing even a millet grain, through fear of death rather than compassion.

Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as a man's money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and in 33 the woman who melted him while wealth lasted beats him from the door when it ends.
audit_text_issue: 33 has a garbled word in the praise (மண்டுநநருர்).

note: Both turn desire away by showing the desired woman old. The Naladiyar gives one picture, the woman bent on her mother's staff; 34 takes each charm the songs praise, hair, eyes, breasts, and shows its ruin, then names a different remedy, service at the Lord's feet.
Both see the living body as a stinking corpse: the Naladiyar's cart torn by vultures once its axle breaks, and 30's body that already stinks, rots and rattles with worms and bones.
Both pray at the hour of death: 8 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's men strike, 28 that Death not call him while his body fails and his mother weeps, and that he reach the feet.

Both make evening the hour when love's sickness deepens; the Kural's woman says it bewilders the whole town, while in 24 a mother names the crescent, the south wind and the anril bird as what wears her daughter down.

Thiruppugazh 21 gives the courtesans' own street talk: what you gave before is not enough, give today, come to my house (பண்டு தந்தது போதாதோ மேல் இன்று தந்து ... இங்கு நின்றது என் வீடே வாரீர்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love, bring harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The song stages exactly the இன்சொல் the Kural warns of, and lets the demand for money show through it.
audit_text_issue: Two words in the second half are garbled (வா஡ணர், நநடுர் கேர்டுர்).

note: Thiruppugazh 22 asks for the day when his mind loosens and dissolves, his speech ends and his own action perishes (சிந்தையும் அவிழ்ந்து அழிந்து உரையொழித்து என்செயல் அழிந்து) so that he sees Murugan. Tirumanthiram 1896 says silence is speech and mind both stilled, and that speech alone falling silent is mere muteness (வாக்கு மனமும் இரண்டும் மவுனமாம் ... மூங்கையாம்). The song asks for the end of mind as well as speech, which is the silence the Tirumanthiram counts as true.

Thiruppugazh 23 draws from the picture of Death's summons one remedy: without the delusion 'this is ours', share even half a kunri seed or a grain of millet, not putting it off to today or that day (எமதுபொருள் எனுமருளை இன்றி ... பங்கிட்டு உண்கை ... இன்றைக்கு அன்றைக்கு என நாடாது). Tirumanthiram 250 gives the same rule as commands: give to all without saying this one or that one, look out for others before eating, do not hoard old goods (ஆர்க்கும் இடுமின் அவரிவர் என்னன்மின் ... பழம்பொருள் போற்றன்மின்). The song supplies the reason the Tirumanthiram leaves unstated: the hour of death makes 'ours' a delusion.

Thiruppugazh 25, after calling his bathing in women's play an abhisheka, asks that he be given fine words in his heart to sing Murugan's paired feet and live (உன் இணையடிகள் பாடி வாழ எனெஞ்சில் செஞ்சொல் தருவாயே). Thiruppugazh 2 says he will not forget the grace by which Murugan told him to sing the Thiruppugazh (திருப்புகழ் விருப்பமொடு செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை மறவேனே). The plea in 25 asks for the gift that the book's opening song says was given: song as the way out of the life it confesses.

Thiruppugazh 26 asks not to end in the false play of women's embraces but to think on the feet with birth ended, and its praise tells of the one who conquered with fire the Kama whose flower arrows frightened even ascetics (துறவினரும் தோற்று அஞ்சத் தனிமலர் அஞ்சு ஆர் புங்கத்து அமராடி ... தழலெழ வென்றார்). Tirumanthiram 346 reads the burning of Kama at Korukkai as inner restraint: settling the mind and destroying Kama's work is the yoga of tapas (காமன் செயலழித்து அங்கண் அருந்தவ யோகம்). Paired, the myth in the song's praise answers its plea: the conquest of Kama is the discipline the poet asks for. The reading of the praise is tentative.

Thiruppugazh 27 asks to see clearly how to leave the embrace of women (மகளிர் தோதக இன்பின் முயங்குதல் ஒழியுமாறு தெளிந்து) and to be given the feet held in mind by those who melt in the jnana of Sivayoga (சிவயோகத்து உருகு ஞான பரம்பர தந்திர அறிவினோர்). Tirumanthiram 831 says that only those who have reached the five-nazhigai paryanka yoga may embrace the woman with sandal on her breasts (பரியங்க யோகத்துப் பஞ்ச கடிகை ... அடைந்தவர்க்கு அல்லது ... தழுவ ஒருவற்கு ஒண்ணாதே). On the reading that the Tirumanthiram makes union itself a yoga for the adept, the two disagree about whether the yogi's path leaves the embrace or masters it.

Thiruppugazh 28 asks that Death not call him while his mind fails, speech goes and eyes roll (அறிவழிய மயல்பெருக உரையும் அற விழிசுழல), and asks now for the boon of drawing near the feet. Kural 335 says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). Both fix the moment when speech is lost as the deadline; the Kural asks for good deeds before it, the song for the Lord's feet.

Thiruppugazh 29 asks whether he will gain grace if Murugan calls him and gives him his sandals (விளித்து உன் பாதுகை நீதர நானருள் பெறுவேனோ), just after naming Rama, the uncle, in the praise. Thiruppugazh 1187, after a funeral, asks to be set holding Murugan's two sandals (இருபாதுகையைப் பற்றி நிற்க வைத்தெனை அருளாதோ). Only these two songs ask for the sandals rather than the feet, a humbler refuge; in 29 the image may borrow from the sandals Rama left as a sign of rule.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1187: end of the hunter-girl line corrupt.

note: Thiruppugazh 31 asks not to wander night and day thinking of a woman but to bathe in the sea of Murugan's compassion and be given the love that knows him within (உனை எனதுள் அறியும் அன்பைத் தருவாயே). Tirumanthiram 270 says love and Siva are not two, and that those who know it rest as love that is Siva (அன்பே சிவமாய் அமர்ந்திருந்தாரே). The song asks for love as the means of knowing the Lord inside; the Tirumanthiram takes the step further and makes the love and the Lord one.

Thiruppugazh 32, after describing lovemaking with women scented with sandal and kumkum, asks about the முகடி, the goddess of ill fortune, of mingling with them (அரிவையருடன் கலந்திடு முகடியும் நலம்பிறந்திட அருள்வாயே). Kural 936 calls gambling a முகடி that covers those it swallows (சூதென்னும் முகடியான் மூடப்பட்டார்). Both name a vice as the ill-fortune goddess herself; Kural 920 already sets women, liquor and dice together. The sense of the song's line is uncertain.
audit_text_issue: Song 32's முகடி line is of uncertain division.

note: Thiruppugazh 33 calls the courtesan's bed a one-sided union (ஒருதலை மருவு புணர்ச்சித் தூர்த்தர்கள்), where she melts a man only while his wealth lasts. Kural 1196, in a woman's voice, says love is painful on one side only and sweet on both, like the load of a carrying pole (ஒருதலையான் இன்னாது காமம் காப்போல இருதலையானும் இனிது). The song takes the akam term for unreturned longing and turns it on paid love, where only the man loves.
audit_text_issue: 33's praise has a garbled word (மண்டுநநருர்).

note: Thiruppugazh 35 speaks of women who talk tenderly, snatch coins and whose hearts are weighed exactly to the coin (உருக்கம் பேசிய நீலியர் ... காசளவே மனம் உறைக்கும் தூரிகள்). Kural 912 tells one to weigh and avoid women who weigh the gain and then speak of their goodness (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் பண்பின் மகளிர்). Both describe the same weighing, tender speech measured by the money.
Both bring a corpse into the courtesan's bed: in the Kural the man embracing her is embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; in 43 it is she who would embrace even a corpse for money.

Both list the body's insides, guts, blood, bone, sinews and skin, almost word for word (குடர், குருதி, என்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்). The Naladiyar turns the list on the desired woman; 48 turns it on the poet's own body, which he still fondles.

Both follow the drums of a funeral to the moment the body is left: the Naladiyar ends with the dying carrying the dead; 38 ends with the mourners leaving it on the road, and calls the whole scene mithya, a false life to escape.
Both ask Murugan to come on the peacock at the hour when Death's men arrive with the noose; 46 adds the kin following to the burning ground and asks above all to see his form.

Thiruppugazh 36 calls himself, among other names, one who has not written a single leaf, wholly ignorant (ஏடெழுதா முழு ஏழையை), and asks Murugan not to scorn him but to give him his cool feet. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the one of pure knowledge (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). The Kural makes the feet the end that learning serves; the song asks for the same feet without the learning. The reading of ஏடெழுதா as 'unlettered' is not certain.

Thiruppugazh 38 pictures the corpse carried on the bier with great drums beating in order and the children following, rolling on the ground (கட்டணம் எடுத்துச் சுமந்தும் பெரும்பறைகள் முறையோடே ... மக்கள் ஒருமிக்கத் தொடர்ந்தும்). Tirumanthiram 153 shows the land's lord mounting the burning ground's palanquin, people following behind and drums beating in front (காட்டுச் சிவிகையொன்று ஏறி ... நாட்டார்கள் பின்செல்ல முன்னே பறைகொட்ட). The same procession; the Tirumanthiram lets it stand as irony, while the song names the whole of it மித்தை, a false life to escape.

Thiruppugazh 39 asks to mix with loving devotees of good mind who sing the Lord's praise and so gain their nature (பண்புடைய சிந்தை அன்பர் தங்களினுடன் கலந்து பண்புபெற). Naladiyar 139 says even the unlearned gain good sense by keeping company with the learned, as a new pot gives its water the scent of pathiri flowers (கற்றாரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகின் நல்லறிவு நாளும் தலைப்படுவர்). The same logic, that one takes on the nature of one's company, is applied in the Naladiyar to learning and in the song to devotion.

Thiruppugazh 40 asks to reach a pure mind, learn virtue, wealth and pleasure fully, and having left them, know grace itself (அமலமாகிய சிந்தை அடைந்து ... அறம்பொருள் இன்பமும் அடைய ஓதி உணர்ந்து தணந்தபின் அருள்தானே அறியுமாறு). Kural 34 says spotlessness of mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). For the Kural the pure mind completes aram; for the song it is the first step, after which aram itself is learnt and passed beyond into grace, if தணந்த is read as leaving the three aims.

Thiruppugazh 41's praise names Murugan as the one who gives the virtue of the head and of the hands, of the kadamba garland, of Siva and of austerity (சிரப்பண்பும் கரப்பண்பும் ... சிவப்பண்பும் தவப்பண்பும் தருவோனே). Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a sense that cannot sense (எண்குணத்தான் தாளை வணங்காத் தலை). The Kural judges the unbowed head; the song makes the bowing head a gift of the Lord. The division of the chiming line is uncertain.
audit_text_issue: 41's chiming syllables make the divisions uncertain.

note: Thiruppugazh 42 asks Murugan to break the prison of the body given by birth and give the joy of his feet (பிறப்பங்கம் சிறைப்பங்கம் சிதைத்து உன்றன் பதத்தின்பம் தருவாயே). Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body has not found a home of its own (புக்கில் அமைந்தின்று கொல்லோ உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு). The Kural calls the body a temporary lodging; the song goes further and calls it a prison to be broken, and names the feet as the home.

Thiruppugazh 43 describes courtesans who lead moneyless youths astray and leave them spent, and who melt in bed when they get great wealth (பொருளில் இளைஞரை ... தளர விடுபவர் ... பெருகு பொருள்பெறில் அமளியில் இதமொடு குழைவோடே). Naladiyar 374 says to such women men without money are poison, and even an oil-presser with earned wealth is sugar (காணமிலாதார் கடுவனையர் ... செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம் அன்னார்). Both set the moneyless man and the rich one side by side to show love following only the money.

Thiruppugazh 44 describes women born to quote a price who join with seeming love, friendship and kindness (பிறந்து விலைகூறி ... அன்பு நண்பு பண்பு முடனாகப் புணர்ந்து). Kural 917 says those without a firm heart touch the shoulders of women who join while tending other things in their hearts (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணிப் புணர்பவர் தோள்). The song names what the Kural leaves unspecified in பிற: the price, under the show of love.

Thiruppugazh 45 speaks of women who bargain so that a man's wealth runs out and make him trust them (நன்றுபொருள் தீர என்று விலைபேசி நம்பவிடு மாதர்), and of himself wasting like a frog that has eaten poison. Naladiyar 377 says those who trust as their own the love of the woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands and then turns away will be laughed at (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு ... எமது என்று இருந்தார்). Both make the man's trust the trap that lets the wealth be taken.

Thiruppugazh 46 asks that Murugan come on the peacock before Death's messengers drag him off and before loving sons and mothers follow wailing to the burning ground (காதலார் மைந்தரும் தாயராரும் சுடுங்கானமே பின்தொடர்ந்து அலறாமுன்). Tirumanthiram 145 shows the town wailing aloud, calling him a corpse, burning him and bathing to forget him (ஊரெலாம் கூடி ஒலிக்க அழுதிட்டு ... சூரையங் காட்டிடைக் கொண்டுபோய்). The same wailing procession: the Tirumanthiram ends on the mourners forgetting, the song asks for the Lord's sight before it begins.

Thiruppugazh 47 asks Murugan gently to bring to shore one who drowns in a sea of pleasure among women, and to give his golden anklets (இன்பக் கடலூடே அமிழுவேனை மெத்தென ஒரு கரைசேர்த்து அம்பொற் றண்டைக் கழல்தாராய்). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர் ... இறைவன் அடிசேராதார்). The song turns the sea of births into the sea of pleasure, and like the Kural makes the feet the way across.

Thiruppugazh 48 calls his body a rough hut of guts, fat, bone, filth, blood, pus and flesh wrapped in skin, carried about with fondness (குடர்நிணம் என்பு ... சீயூன் பொதிதோல் குலவு குரம்பை), and asks to be rid of that nature. Tirumanthiram 725 says he once held the body a thing of shame, then saw the Highest had made it his temple, and now cherishes it (உடம்பினை முன்னம் இழுக்கென்று இருந்தேன் ... உத்தமன் கோயில் கொண்டான்). The song holds the view of the body that the Tirumanthiram says it held first and then gave up.

Thiruppugazh 49 asks not to wander toiling in the sorrowful pot of the body, eating and enjoying until the body-lump grows fat (சுகப்பண்டம் சுகித்து உண்டுண்டு உடற்பிண்டம் பருத்து). Tirumanthiram 724 says that since life and true knowledge perish with the body, he learned the means of nurturing the body and so nurtured life (உடம்பை வளர்க்கும் உபாயம் அறிந்தே உடம்பை வளர்த்தேன்). Both speak of growing the body; the Tirumanthiram limits it to the means (உபாயம) that serve knowledge, which excludes the feasting the song condemns.
The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, to be free of all other clinging; 54 asks, after confessing his infatuation, to attain clinging to Murugan (நின் பற்று அடைவேனோ).

Both name the Lord the eight-qualitied (எண்குணத்தான், எண்குணன்): the Kural makes the head that does not bow to his feet useless; in 52 the eight-qualitied Siva is himself the one who bows, worshipping Murugan.
audit_text_issue: 52 has unclear words in the first half (செஞ்செநீடும், அண்டுஞ்சகன்).

note: Both list the conventional comparisons for a woman's eyes, the carp, the lily, the spear. The Naladiyar names them as the talk of blind petty men to be ignored; 57 piles them up as the delusion that holds the poet, then asks to be freed of it.

The two songs are built alike: a confession that catalogues women's adornments, then a praise made of a chain of epithets ending -க்கார, each naming one role of Murugan. Read together they show the formula at work.
Tirumular warns against withering in praise of petty men for their wealth and bids one praise the Lord instead; 60 asks to give up praising impure men and to worship Murugan's feet.
Both quote the patron's flattery, the giver called a cloud and a lord of red or lotus hands. In 15 the poet confesses having begged so; in 55 he asks to keep such names for Murugan alone.

64 scorns poets who sing a girl's love-sickness, with Kama's arrows, the south wind and the crescent, without naming Thiruchendur; 24 uses the same devices, but for a girl in love with the lord of Senthil. The scorn falls on poems that leave out the shrine, not on the akam convention itself.
46 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's messengers drag the poet off; 63 asks further that he speak to Death and claim the man as his own devotee.

51 asks Murugan to place his feet on the poet's head (என்றன் தலையில் சந்தப் பதம் வைத்தருள்வாயே) instead of his being entangled with women. Tirumular tells that gesture as done (திருவடி வைத்தென் சிரத்து), Nandi seen in the guru's form so that the way to the womb was drained. The pairing shows what the Thiruppugazh plea asks for: the guru's initiation by the feet.

The Kural says that letting no day fall idle (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) by doing good blocks the road of further births; 53 asks to sing the நமோநம praise daily and worship so as not to waste days (வீணாள் படாது). Both make the unwasted day the unit of the good life; the Thiruppugazh fills it with worship where the Kural fills it with good deeds.

56 asks, in one line, that Guha come with the splendour of his own form (நின் சொரூப ப்ரகாசம் கொடே வந்து) and rule the poet. 62 makes that plea its whole song: anklets, kadamba, faces and vel before his eyes so that they are cooled (கண்குளிர என்றன்முன் சந்தியாவோ). The pair shows the vision-plea in brief and at length.
audit_text_issue: 56's நின்செர்ரு பம் appears garbled for சொரூபம்.

note: The Naladiyar says that to women with loveless hearts (ஆணமில் நெஞ்சத்து) a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser with wealth is sugar. 58 names the same motive in the women it adorns with sandal and musk: great desire seeking money (மிக்காசை கொண்டு பொருள் தேடு மதி) with cruel, deceitful hearts, while their glance feigns longing.

59 asks why some waste away in the body of maya and in பசு பாசம், without loving the feet the Vedas proclaim. Tirumular states the doctrine behind the question: pasu and pasam cannot of themselves reach Pati (பதியினைச் சென்றணுகா), but when Pati draws near they do not remain. Read together, 59's question is answered by the grace it praises.
audit_text_issue: 59 has a stray glyph (நீலக் ஡ணபக), an encoding glitch

note: The Kural says the ills perish when the names of desire, anger and delusion (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்) perish; 59 names the same triad in Sanskrit form, காம க்ரோத லோப, as what souls waste away in. The Thiruppugazh's third term is greed where the Kural's is delusion.

Both call the body a perishing hut: 61 the false hut of earth, water, fire, wind and sky (வண் காயம் பொய்க் குடில்) that comes apart and goes to the burning ground, Tirumular the hut that does not stay (நில்லாக் குரம்பை) which the unlearned think permanent. Tirumular warns that the Lord is not seen by those who so mistake it; 61 asks for the feet before the hut falls.

62 asks that Murugan, who dances before him at Senthil, appear so that the poet's eyes are cooled (கண்குளிர). Tirumular says what such seeing does: for those who see the joyous dance, tears of grace drip, the heart melts and bliss wells up (திருக்கூத்துக் கண்டவர்க்கு). The Thiruppugazh song asks for the sight whose effect the Tirumanthiram describes.

63 lists the kin who gather at death with their claims and debts (கடனுதவு மந்த வரிசைமொழி) and asks Murugan to come and claim the man from Death as 'our devotee'. Tirumular shows the kin's limit: the town wails, calls him a corpse, burns him, bathes and stops thinking of him (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). The pairing explains why 63 turns from the kin to a single claimant who will not forget.

Both end with Murugan bowing to Valli: in 65 he sees her feet, cries 'refuge' and stands behind her and bows (தஞ்சம் எனும்படி ... கும்பிடும் இளையோனே); in 71 he joins his red hands and bows to her in the millet field (செங்கரம் குவித்துக் கும்பிடும்). In 65 the image mirrors the plea, where the poet asks to cry தஞ்சம் at the Lord's feet.

Both picture old age with speech failing, teeth gone and a staff in hand. The Naladiyar's old man still keeps his eyes on desire; in 68 the women laugh at him, and the poet turns the scene into a prayer for Murugan to come at the hour of death.
The Kural holds nothing more degrading to the tongue than asking; 69 confesses a tongue put to exactly that use, poems of praise carried from one patron's door to another.

Both list the poet's genres, கோவை, உலா, மடல் and the rest. In 69 they are tools for begging at patrons' doors; in 76 they are titles of honour and the source of the poet's pride, which he asks to have removed.
Both draw Death on his buffalo with noose and club and ask Murugan to come on the peacock at that hour; 75 grounds the claim in hereditary service, 8 in the confession that he has not served.
The Kural calls the embrace of deceiving women an அணங்கு, a possessing spirit; 73 gives the deceit a literal form, the love-pellets and the charm hidden in the betel.
audit_text_issue: 73's opening phrase is hard to divide.

note: The Naladiyar likens the harlot's love to lamplight that goes out when the oil runs out, and her love when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 66 stages the same course with a real lamp: she takes him upstairs by lamplight (விளக்கெடுத்து), coaxes coins, strips his hands of jewels and drives him out exhausted (இளைக்க விட்டுத் துரத்துவார்).

The Naladiyar says such women would bow and dismiss even red-eyed Mal if he came with nothing in his hand to give (விடுப்பர் தங்கையால் தொழுது). 67 gives the dismissal in the woman's own words once the man is spent: 'you are finished, go today' (அற்றனை என இன்று ஓட்டு).
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 67's dense opening lines divide uncertainly.

note: The Naladiyar says learning has no shore and the learner's days are few, so one should choose what is fit, like the bird drinking the milk from the water. 70 asks that before the body ages in seeking endless crores of books (நூல் அனந்த கோடி தேடி) he be given the books of knowledge in which the Lord is mingled (நீ கலந்துள ஞான நூல்). Both set limited life against unlimited books; 70 names the choice as the jnana books.

Both quote the flattery a poet gives a patron by borrowing the god's names: in 55 'you are the noble Vel' (துங்கவேள்), in 71 'Kandan for beauty' (நிறத்திற் கந்தன்), along with Kubera and Indra. 55 asks to keep those names for Murugan; 71 confesses the hunger (பெரும் பசிக்குத் தஞ்சமென்று) that drove him to give them away.

The Kural calls the petty knowledge that takes the impermanent for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்) the lowest. 72 opens with that error made personal, taking the impermanent thing for oneself (நிலையாப் பொருளை உடலாக் கருதி), and follows it with what results: wasted days, deafness, blindness and the bed of filth.

The Kural calls birth a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை) that true knowledge removes by seeing the true thing. 74 places the courtesans within that larger condition, the darkness of defiled birth and its bonds (பங்கமேவும் பிறப்பு அந்தகாரம் ... பந்தபாசம்), and asks for the feet as the way out.

The Kural names them பொருட்பெண்டிர், women of wealth, whose false embrace is like a hired man clasping a stranger's corpse in a dark room. 77 uses the same name, பொருளின் மகளிர், after a full description of the embrace, and asks whether he will not give up their 'love' (அன்புப் பண்பு); the description the Kural refuses, 77 gives in full before refusing it.

Both make a woman's eyes a weapon: the Kural's eyes eat the life of those who see them and are at war (அமர்த்தன) with her gentleness; 78's eye-corners are whetted as weapon upon weapon (படையம் படையென அந்திக்கும் கண்கடை). The Kural's lover is held in wonder; 78 names the same look the source of his bewilderment (மறுகிடு மருளன்) and asks for grace.

Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). 79 asks for the same gift: Tamil words that string together the meaning of his golden feet (அப்பொருள் தங்கத் தொடுக்கும் சொல் தமிழ் தந்து). Both make Tamil verse the purpose for which the poet is given.
audit_text_issue: 79: dense rhythm makes the first half uncertain.

note: The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring ruin. 80 gives the sweet words, the cuckoo voice saying 'come home' (வாரும் வீடே), and their show of love on the bed, 'as if loving' (அன்புளார் போல்), and asks whether union with them is fitting.
The Kural puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of those Fortune has abandoned; 88 joins two of the three in one figure, the courtesan who herself drinks palm toddy.
Both describe the yogi who binds the breath and tastes the nectar of bliss from the moon; Tirumular sets it against the liquor of fools, 94 against a life of delusion and the elements' illusions.
Both catalogue old age through the failing senses, cough and phlegm before death; 68 adds the mocking women and the family, 93 asks for more than rescue, the removal of Death's very principle.
Both confess wandering from door to door of worthless patrons with poems; 91 adds that Murugan himself is the true owner of the Tamil garlands the poet wasted.
76 asks to be rid of the poet's titles and honours as pride; 83 asks for the poet's title and fame, but only so that his service and song to Murugan may flourish.

The Tirumanthiram verse tells how Brahma and Vishnu sought Siva's foot and crown and did not see them (அடிகண்டிலேன், with Brahma lying முடிகண்டேன்). The song names the same gods, with Indra, as wandering in search (திரிய) of a thing it calls only ஒன்றை, and asks that this be given (தரவேணும்); what the gods failed to find by searching is asked for as a gift.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 81's opening epithets divide uncertainly.

note: Tirumular says that if both gazes are set on the middle of the nose (நாட்டமும் இரண்டும் நடுமூக்கில் வைத்திடில்) there is no self and no seeking, and one becomes Siva (தானில்லை ... சிவனவ நாமே). The song asks for the same practice, both eyes on the nose (நாசியின் மீது இரண்டு விழிபாய), with the 'I' broken (யானெனும் மேதை விண்டு), as the cure for infatuation: the two texts tie the gaze to the end of the self.
audit_text_issue: 82 has a garbled word in line 9 (காலுட லுடி).

note: The Kural says that one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு அறுப்பான்) enters a world above the gods'. The song asks that the 'I' break (யானெனும் மேதை விண்டு) and gives a method for it, breath and gaze held and body, speech and heart made one (காயமும் நாவும் நெஞ்சும் ஓர்வழியாக), turning the Kural's renunciation into a yogic practice.

Tirumular describes the town wailing, the name taken away and replaced by 'corpse', the body burned on the burning ground and the mourners bathing and forgetting (நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). The song runs through the same sequence, kin wailing (வந்து கதற), the body in the fire and what is left cast into water (விண்டு புனலில் ... விழ), but where Tirumular ends on the mourners forgetting, the song turns to the feet it asks to worship.

The Kural's lover says blue lilies, if they could see, would hang their heads, saying they cannot match her eyes (குவளை கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்). The song's blazon uses the same conceit, eyes that cast shame on arrow, carp, bee and lotus (கணை அம் கயல் வண்டு புண்டரிகங்களையும் பழி சிந்து பார்வை), but the whole catalogue ends in the question whether to trust these deceivers (செயல் வஞ்சரை நம்புவேனோ): the Kural's praise is turned into evidence against the women.

The Kural says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow (நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்). The song calls the poet's own trade, begging by singing Tamil (இசைக்கும் செந்தமிழ்க் கொண்டு அங்கு இரக்கும் புன்தொழில்), base, and asks for its disgrace to end: the tongue that sings Tamil is the tongue the Kural says begging shames.
audit_text_issue: 86: opening lines hard to divide.

note: Tirumular says the poor in sense, seeing that even their own shadow does not help them, still sit saying 'this wealth is mine' (என்னது மாடென்று இருப்பர்கள்). The song lists house, gold, sons, wife, rank and kin and calls taking the pleasure of this passing dream as 'mine' (மாயக் கனவுநிலை இன்பம் அதனை எனது என்று கருதி) the error, then follows it to the womb (கருவில் விழுகின்றது): both locate the fault in the claim of 'mine'.

The Naladiyar compares a harlot's love to lamp-light: as the light ends when the oil is gone, their love ends when the hand is empty (அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Among the song's charges is the same: the women coldly drop, with love gone, those who have no money (காசிலாதவர் தங்களை அன்பற ... நெகிழ்ந்த), so the song's catalogue contains the Naladiyar's whole verse as one item.

The Kural warns that the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth rather than love bring harm. The song shows the order exactly: on the bed they say 'first give the gold coins' (பொற்பணம் முதல் நீ தா), and once paid they speak as sweet as milk and honey (ஈந்தால் ... ஆன்பால் தேன் போல செப்பிடும்); the sweet speech is the receipt for the gold.
audit_text_issue: 89 heavy rhythmic splitting; praise uncertain

note: The Naladiyar says household women cannot dress up their womanliness the way maids do, while the other kind, like a fresh flood, show their charms themselves (புதுப்பெருக்கம் போலத் தம் பெண்ணீர்மை காட்டி). The song is built on the same verb, காட்டி repeated for hair, brow, smile, eyes, breasts and hips, ending in women who show their practised arts (தொழில் அதிகம் காட்டு மடமாதர்): beauty as display is the shared mark of the women both texts set apart.

The Naladiyar says that those with aching hearts who stand begging at the gates of great houses (நெடுங்கடை நின்றுழல்வது) do so as the fruit of former deeds (முன்னை வினையாய் விடும்). The song confesses the same wandering at the doors of fools (முஞ்சர் மனை வாசல் தேடித் தேடி உழலாதே) and asks that the former deeds go (முந்தைவினை ஏவராமல் போக): what the Naladiyar states as fixed consequence, the song asks Murugan to remove.

In 22 the poet asks that his mind melt and his own agency be undone again and again (என் செயல் அழிந்து அழிந்து அழிய) so that he may see Murugan. Here, following women, he fears wandering with his agency undone (செயல் அழிந்து உழன்று திரிவேனோ): the same loss of one's own doing is the goal in one song and the ruin in the other, depending on what undoes it.

The Naladiyar pictures the old whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth, and says that those who still turn to desire have no path to safety (ஏம நெறிபடருமாறு இல்லையே). The song gives the same decay, hearing gone, acts faltering, harsh voice (செவி கேட்பற்று ... செயல் தடுமாறி), and asks at that very stage for the golden feet and a little grace (சற்றருள்): it allows a way the Naladiyar closes, on condition of grace.

Both put a woman's eye to a doubting question with Death among the answers. The Kural asks whether it is Death, an eye or a doe and finds all three; 103 lengthens the list to poison, fish, Kama's arrow and Yama's messengers, and turns the doubt into the poet's own confusion before he asks for Murugan's feet.

The Naladiyar says that one who sees kin wailing in crowds (சுற்றத்தார் கல்லென்று அலற) as a corpse is carried to the burning ground and still marries believing there is joy is answered by the funeral drum. The song gives the wife, sons and evening kin crowding and wailing (மண்டிக் கதறிடு) and the worm-body as food for the fire (புழுவுடல் அங்கிக்கு இரை), and asks for the feet on that day: the household is shown helpless at death in both.

The Naladiyar tells the heart that it will not let go of attachment to the house (மனைப்பாசம்) and pines for its children, and asks how many ages it expects to live. The song lists the crawling, crying child, the house of golden halls and the wife taken as refuge (தஞ்சம் என்று), then names the time when these fade (மங்கு காலம்) and asks for the feet instead: the same house and children, with the feet put where the Naladiyar puts good deeds.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). The song names the bond of desire for women and children (மடமாதர் மக ஆசை தொந்தம்) and asks not for release from it but for love of the two feet (இருதாளின் அன்பு தருவாயே): the Kural's principle in the form of a prayer.

Tirumular says the Lord stands having cut off the birth that comes through maya's bond and through union with women of flowered hair (மாயஞ்செய் பாசத்தும் கொந்தார் குழலியர் கூடிய கூட்டத்தும்). The song asks whether the dark sorrow and delusion of maya (இருளாய துன்ப மருள் மாயை) that come through such women will never end: the same pairing of maya and women, as complaint in the song and as what the Lord cuts in Tirumular.
audit_text_issue: 405: variant last line reverses the sense.

note: Tirumular's verse, uncertain in sense, likens the guru to the swan parting milk from water and speaks of seeds that have touched the fire for seven births (ஏழ் பிறப்பு எரி சார்ந்த வித்து), seeds that will not sprout again. The song says the body came from seed and has burned a crore of times (விந்ததின் ஊறி வந்தது காயம் வெந்தது கோடி) and still comes again: burning the body does not end birth, while Tirumular's fire falls on the seed itself.

The Kural's woman says that when her lover is away evening comes like enemies to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல வரும்). For the love-sick hill girl of the song the gentle things turn hostile in the same way: the moon burns like the sun (இந்து வெயில்காய) and the soft breeze comes like fire (மிதவாடை வந்து தழல்போல), with gossiping women's blame added (வசைகூற).

The Naladiyar says that to loveless women men without wealth are poison, while even an oil-presser who has earned wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார்) is sugar. The song shows a man acting on that rule, going for wealth as far as Bengal and China (பொருள்தேடி வங்காளம் சோனம் சீனம் போய்) to join such women's shoulders, and asks whether he must suffer such hard pain (வன்பே துன்பப் படலாமோ).

Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums while the kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still believes in household joy; 115 adds the mourners washing and letting go of the bond, and asks Murugan to come before that day.

Both say the paid embrace is false. The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse in the dark; 111 shows it from inside, the price bargained, the tight embrace and the man melting like wax, and calls it a madness from which only release frees him.

The Naladiyar says those set on the right path will not embrace such women; 108 says their laughter makes even renouncers weaken. If 108's துறவினர் சோர is taken literally, it doubts the Naladiyar's confidence; it may be only the poet's hyperbole.

Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan: the moon that burns like the sun, Kama's arrows and the blaming women torment her, and the speaker asks him to come to her. 101 asks for his garland, 116 for his embrace on the peacock that is Om.

Both confess begging from patrons by praising them in Tamil. In 15 the plea is to trade that service for service at Murugan's feet; in 117 the begging is tied to desire for women and to the ruined body, and the fear is another birth.
Both identify Murugan with the Tamil saint who sent the Jains to the stakes at Madurai; 104 adds the cure of the king's fever, holy ash and Pugali, the details of Sambandar's story.
Both run a life in one breath from infancy to youth and desire for women. 9 begins in the womb and ends in disease; 110 stops at sixteen and names the omission, never praising the devotees' feet.

Thiruppugazh 104 opens with the poet calling himself the witless one who keeps company, without shame, with the followers of the six sects (சட்சமயிகளொடு வெட்காது அட்கிடும் அறிவிலி), and turns to Murugan's feet at Palani. Tirumanthiram 1533 gives the reason such company is folly: those who saw the six sects did not see him, and he is not what they hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). The song's self-reproach rests on the claim the Tirumanthiram states; the split of அட்கிடும் is not certain.

Thiruppugazh 105 asks for grace to leave the sea of births and reach the high good state (பிறவிக் கடல் விட்டு உயர் நற்கதியைப் பெறுதற்கு அருளைத் தரவேணும்). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song, beaten by Kama's arrows, asks for what the Kural names as the only crossing, and asks it of grace rather than of effort.

Thiruppugazh 106 makes Murugan the one tradition that fills the worlds, the elements and the tattvas down to the atom within the atom (அணுவில் அணு எனநிறைந்திட்டு நின்றது). Tirumanthiram 2008 calls the First Lord the atom within the atom (அணுவில் அணுவினை ஆதிப் பிரானை) and says only those who divide it a thousandfold can approach him. The same phrase serves the song as a sign of pervasion and the Tirumanthiram as a sign of subtlety to be approached.

Thiruppugazh 107 asks whether, through the meaning of the mantra of instruction (உபதேச மந்திரப் பொருளாலே), he will think of Murugan and gain grace, and names him the true guru who gave the rosary (ஜெபமாலை தந்த சற்குருநாதா). Tirumanthiram 2429 reports the gift as received: the Lord told him the mantra that cannot be spoken (உரைசெய்யா மந்திரம் சொன்னான்) and he stands wearing his feet. What the song asks for, the Tirumanthiram speaks of as done.

Thiruppugazh 108 spends its first half on the courtesan's toilet, turmeric bath, saris, combed hair, camphor dot, agil and musk paste on the breasts (அகில்புழுகு ஆரச் சேறு தனத்திட்டு), and asks for the feet to end the desire it rouses. Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands (படுசாந்தும் கோதையும்) have not seen vultures tear the stinking cart once its axle breaks. The Naladiyar supplies the end of the body the song only adorns.

Thiruppugazh 109 asks that, instead of thinking real (மெய் என மனம் நினைவது) the wife, kin, children, rich land and town, he be given the work of worship. Kural 345 says that for those set on ending births even the body is excess, so what of other ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). The song lets go of the household; the Kural extends the same letting go to the body itself.

Thiruppugazh 110 confesses that from birth to sixteen he never praised the feet of the devotees who recite the Siva texts, Agamas and Vedas (மறை ஓதும் அன்பர் திருவடிகளே நினைந்து துதியாமல்). Tirumanthiram 547 says the poet entered the Lord's city by going with the devotees of the Lord's devotees (உடையான் அடியார் அடியாருடன் போய்). What the song regrets omitting is, in the Tirumanthiram, the very way in.

Thiruppugazh 113 describes women who swear oaths, rouse desire and then make a man's wealth in hand run out (கைப்பொருள் மாள) before quarrelling and bewildering him. Naladiyar 377 says those who think theirs the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then turns away will be laughed at. Both name the same sequence, a show of love, the hand's wealth taken, then the turn.

Thiruppugazh 114 speaks of devotees who wear holy ash (பூதி) chanting Arumugam, take as their aid the feet of those who wear the feet of great ascetics, and say 'Guha who rides the peacock, my Lord' (ஏறுமயில் வாகன குகா ... எனது ஈச). Tirumanthiram 2111 says those who wear the ash crying 'you who ride the bull, our Lord, our master' (ஏறுடையாய் இறைவா எம்பிரான்) are devotees, and those who wear the feet have no deeds left. The two verses share the cry, the ash and the worn feet, with the mount changed from bull to peacock, and the song's vel that ends evil deeds matches the Tirumanthiram's வினையில்லை.

Thiruppugazh 115 follows a life to the pyre and ends with those who embraced him bathing in water and leaving the bond (நீரில் படிந்து விடு பாசத்து அகன்று). Tirumanthiram 145 ends the same way: they burn him, bathe in water and stop thinking of him (நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both make the bath, not the burning, the moment the living let go.

Thiruppugazh 115 and 895 both tell the funeral rite by rite, drums, pyre and the mourners' bath, and both end the mourners' grief at the water (115: நீரில் படிந்து விடு பாசத்து அகன்று; 895: மருவு புனல் முழுகி மனை புக்குத் துக்கமறு). 895 adds that Kama then takes the mourners again, so the bath that ends grief begins desire; 115 instead asks Murugan to come before that ending.
audit_text_issue: 895's line உறவுநிலை சுட்டுச் சுட்டி is hard to divide.

note: In Thiruppugazh 116 the sounds of the night, the sea's drum, the flute and the bull's bell, pierce the lovesick girl's ears like an iron spike (வேயோசை ... இருசெவியின் நாராசம் உறுவதென). In Kural 1228 the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) is the burning evening's messenger and a weapon that kills. Both turn the pastoral flute, sweet in itself, into a weapon against the separated woman.

Thiruppugazh 117 confesses that he praised as equal to the five heavenly trees men who never gave a single coin (ஒரு காசே கொடாதவரை ஐந்து தருவை நிகரே யாக) and begged daily in great Tamil without finding a footing. Kural 1067 begs all beggars not to beg of those who hide what they have (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). The song is the Kural's warning lived out: the poet begged of exactly those the Kural names, and found no footing.
audit_text_issue: 117 flagged uncertain; நிலைகாணா may describe the body rather than the begging.

note: Thiruppugazh 118 and 831 are near-repeats in the same metre: both open with breasts like a pair of caskets, round and thrilling (இருசெப்பென ... வட்டமும் ஒத்து இளகிப் புளகித்து), both ask whether, struggling and embracing (சருவிச் சருவி), he must wander without tapas (தவமற்று உழல), and both name Murugan the kinsman of Vishnu's son and the cock-bannered fighter of the asuras. The praise differs at the close: 118 has Murugan tell Siva the good meaning, 831 has him speak the three Tamils to those who love him.

Both turn on a courtesan's vow never to part: the Naladiyar woman who promised to be like the gem on its thread turns like a ram's horn, and 121's women who swear union until death strip the man and go to meet the next. The Naladiyar asks the heart to leave; 121 asks Murugan to come.

The Kural cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe; 126 claims the eyes have beaten the deer into the forest and trampled Yama himself. The same comparisons, but the Kural's lover wonders and the poet of 126 fears to fall.
audit_text_issue: Several lines of 126's first half are compressed and hard to split; the marker flags uncertainty.

note: Both set Murugan against Death's buffalo and noose at the hour of death; 8 asks him to come on the peacock, 129 asks that Death not come near at all and adds the jackals and fire that claim the corpse.
Both are confessions of worship never done, built as a list of negatives (தொழுதிலன், சேவித்தறியேனே); 8 ends at the hour of death, 123 at the wish to end birth.
Both give Murugan the impaling of the Jains, the Madurai story told of Sambandar: 17 names the Tamil mouth that set them on stakes, 132 has him settle at Palani after seeing them there.
12 praises Murugan for giving the knowledge to Siva; 133 asks whether the poet, as a servant, will receive the same teaching of the Veda's meaning.
audit_text_issue: 12 has a corrupt glyph in கி஡ணவ (likely கிரீவ).

note: Thiruppugazh 120 asks whether he must die with the thought of the women settled in his heart (அவர் குடிபுகுந்த நினைவொடும் இறந்துபடலாமோ). Tirumanthiram 2102 tells the reader to think of the Lord even at the time of dying (இறந்தொழி காலத்தும் ஈசனை உள்கும்). The song fears the failure of the Tirumanthiram's rule: the thought held at death is the women's, not the Lord's.

Thiruppugazh 121 describes courtesans who swear an oath (சூள் உரைத்து) that until the body's nest is left (உயிர்க்கூடு விடுமளவும்) they will never slacken in union, then wipe out a man's wealth and go to meet the next. Naladiyar 372 recalls a woman who swore she would leap with him from the high peak, then, since he had no gold, showed a pain in her feet and would not go. Both oaths are vows to the death, and both end where the money ends.

Thiruppugazh 122 names the world's ties of pasu and pasam (உலக பசு பாச தொந்தம்), kin, parents, house and children, and asks for grace so that his mind's balance is not destroyed by them. Tirumanthiram 115 says pasu and pasam cannot reach Pati, but when Pati draws near they do not remain (பதியணுகிற் பசு பாசம் நில்லாவே). The song's plea for grace (அருள் தாராய்) is the request for the approach the Tirumanthiram says the bound soul cannot make itself.

Thiruppugazh 123 confesses he never sought the rare life and asks whether, thinking to end birth, he will not give up the burden of desire (பிறவியற நினைகுவன் என் ஆசைப்பாடைத் தவிரேனோ). Kural 362 says that if one must want, want not to be born, and that comes by wanting not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). Both tie the end of birth to the end of desire.

Thiruppugazh 123 and 1023 close with the same chain of epithets in -kara: the plunderer of the asuras (நிருதர் புர சூறைக் கார / நிருதர்பதி சூறைக் கார), the guardian (அடியர் காவற் கார / அமரர்பதி காவற் கார), the generous delighter (விதரண விநோதக் கார / விதரண உதாரக் கார), and the bodyguard of the hunters' girl (வேளைக் காரப் பெருமாளே). In 123 the guarding is of his worshipping devotees, in 1023 of the gods' king, and in both the chain ends with the Lord as Valli's sworn servant.

Thiruppugazh 124 opens with the sect-disputers who cannot recognise one another's truth (ஒருவரை ஒருவர் தேறி அறிகிலர் மதவிசாரர்) and end in hell and rebirth. Tirumanthiram 1558 says the six sects are six roads to one city, and those who say 'this is good, that is bad' are like a dog barking at a hill (குன்று குரைத்தெழு நாயை). Both make the quarrel itself the fault; the song asks for ash and the feet instead of a better doctrine.

Thiruppugazh 124 begins with the sect-disputers who cannot recognise one another's truth (மதவிசாரர்), and 951 asks to leave the rites and quarrels of the six sects who divide and clamour (சட்சமயிகள் பங்கிட்டுக் கலகலெனும்) with the arts of disputation. 124 asks for the knowledge that leads to Siva (பரம ஞான சிவகதி), 951 for the knowledge that cannot be pointed to (குறியாத அறிவை); both set a given knowledge against sectarian argument.

Thiruppugazh 126 makes the women's eyes defeat every standard of comparison, branding the bee, sending the carp into the pond, putting the spear in fire and trampling Yama (யமப் ப்ரபுவைத் துகைவித்து). Thiruppugazh 1023 runs the same conceit more briefly: the kohl eyes chase Kama's arrow, the bee, the spear and the carp and overcome Yama (யமனை அட மீறி). Both turn the stock comparisons for eyes into defeated rivals, with Death the last of them.

Thiruppugazh 128 says that even though (ஆகிலும்) he is anxious with infatuation for women, he will not forget (மறவேனே) Murugan's golden body, six faces, vel and lotus feet. Kural 1125 has the lover say he would recall her qualities if he forgot, but he does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்). The lover's vow of unforgetting is turned in the song to the Lord's form, set against the very desire the Kural's lover feels.

Thiruppugazh 130 puts the lover's praise as questions: is the hair a black cloud or darkness, are the eyes arrows or a vel (மேகமதோ இருளோ ... கணைகொலோ அயில் வேலதுவோ), and seeks women like golden peacocks. Kural 1081 is the first such doubt: is she a goddess, a peahen or a woman (அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ ... மாதர்கொல்). The Kural's bewildered question becomes in the song the infatuated man's whole way of seeing, which he then calls worthless (கசடன்).

Thiruppugazh 130 and 887 are built the same way: the hair a cloud or darkness (கரிய மேகமதோ இருளோ குழல் / சொரியு மாமுகிலோ இருளோ குழல்), the eyes arrows or does, the breasts mountain or pots, all put as questions. 130 ends asking that after a hundred years his life reach Murugan's feet; 887 asks to reach the praise the jnanis sing, which is release. The near-repeat shows the question form as a fixed device of the book.

Thiruppugazh 133 names its own book: Murugan defeats want and enmity for those who recite and read the Thiruppugazh (திருப்புகழை உரைப்பவர்கள் படிப்பவர்கள் மிடிப்பகைமை செயித்தருளும்). Thiruppugazh 242 says those who read the Thiruppugazh with love have their affliction cut (திருப்புகழ் விருப்பொடு படிப்பவர் இடுக்கினை அறுத்திடும்). The two are the book's claim for itself, in nearly the same words.

Both confess begging from patrons: 15 praises them in Tamil with a wounded heart, 134 stands without shame at the gates of those who give food. 134 sets the begging at the end of a life that runs from the womb through women.

Both reject the poets' comparisons for a woman's eyes as carp, spear and the like: the Naladiyar ascetic answers them with the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit, 135 asks not to drown in their maya and turns to studying Murugan's poems.
audit_text_issue: 135 line 4 has corrupt characters (பா஡ண, இ஧ல்முழ்).

note: Tirumular says that if one knows how to reach the inner light there is no quarrel at all; 138 lists the clamouring schools and asks for the teaching and vision of knowledge that would end the dispute for him.
Both open with the sects that cannot agree and ask Murugan for knowledge and his feet instead; 124 adds the ash, 138 names the schools one by one.

The Kural's பொதுநலத்தார், women whose favours are common to all, are 141's women who set a price so that all may take their pleasure; the Kural says the wise will not touch them, 141 confesses that he did.
The Kural calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire in which base men sink; 144 confesses to desiring those golden shoulders and sinking low (தாழ்வடைந்து).

Both list the body's contents, guts, fat, blood, bone and flesh. The Naladiyar asks where among them the garlanded woman is; 145 applies the list to the body the poet himself lives in, and answers with the Lord's grace.
Both give Murugan a deed of Sambandar: 132 the impaling of the Jains, 137 the milk of Parvati given to the child who then sang Tamil.

The Naladiyar sees people with aching hearts begging at the gates of great houses in sight of all (நெடுங்கடை நின்றுழல்வது) and calls it former deeds. 134 confesses the same daily standing at the gateways of those who give food (மனைகள் தலைவாசல் நின்று அநுதினமும் நாணமின்றி) as the end of a life of desire. The pairing shows the shame the Naladiyar observes in others spoken in the first person.

The Kural's lover cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). 135 lists the same kind of question about a woman's eyes, vel or carp (வாள்விழி வேலோ சேலோ), but as the trap of the eyes' maya (இருகண் மாயையில் மூழ்காதே). The doubting simile the Kural uses for wonder the song repeats in order to refuse it.
audit_text_issue: 135 has corrupt glyphs (மாயையி ஧ல்முழ், பா஡ண).

note: The Kural says the sweet words of braceleted women who desire wealth, not love, bring disgrace (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). 136 names courtesans who speak ever so sweetly (கனியக் கனியவுமே மொழி பேசிய விலைமாதர்) and asks not to wander thinking their union sweet. Both locate the danger in the sweetness of the speech.

Tirumular says the guru set his holy feet on his head (திருவடி வைத்தென் சிரத்து) and he saw Nandi in the guru's form. 139 calls Murugan the guru (குருநாதா) who grants his feet on the poet's head (எனது தலையில் பதங்கள் அருள்வோனே). Both make the feet on the head the guru's gift to the disciple.

The Naladiyar says those who mean to reach the right path will not embrace the large breasts of women who go their own way (செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென்பார் ... தடமுலை சேராரே). 140 describes women who seize a man's wealth (பொருள்பறி) and asks whether he will give up the pleasure of the base path (புலையவர் வழி இன்பைத் தவிர்வேனோ). Both set the courtesan's embrace against the path, as a rule in one and a confession in the other.

The Naladiyar says men fooled into thinking a courtesan's love theirs, after she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). 142 confesses he is like a fool to be laughed at (இடக்கன் எனச் சிரிக்க) for his melting infatuation (அனற்குள் மெழுக்கென). The Naladiyar's ridicule from outside is what the poet fears for himself.
audit_text_issue: 142's word splits in its packed metre are uncertain.

note: The Kural says good deeds must be done quickly, before the hiccup comes that stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 143 has the hiccup rise in the man wasted by women (விக்கலுமே எழுந்து) and asks whether, leaving that disease, he will yet praise Murugan. The same sign of the end of life makes the urgency of the Kural's counsel the poet's own late plea.

Tirumular says the Lord set his foot on his head so that his bonds were cut again and again and the confusion of his deluded heart was cut (கால்கொண்டென் சென்னியிற் கட்டறக் கட்டற, மயக்கிற் றுயக்கற). 146 asks Murugan to place his feet on his head (எனது தலை பதம் அருள்வாயே) so that grief ends, deeds scatter (வினைகள் சிதறிட) and infatuation goes. The song asks for what the Tirumanthiram reports as done.

Tirumular says he once held the body base but, seeing the Lord had made it his temple, now cherishes it (உடம்பினை யானிருந் தோம்புகின்றேனே). 146 calls the body a house of blood, filth, worms and diseases (மலசலம் ஒழுகு ... புழுவது நெளியும் உடல்) and confesses cherishing it (இதை அடல் பேணி) as a fault. On the reading that 146 condemns care of the body as such, it holds the view Tirumular says he gave up.

The Kural says the two kinds of deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who love the Lord's true praise (இருவினையும் சேரா). 147 plays on கழல: for those who bow at his anklets, deeds come loose (கழல் பணிய வினை கழல்). Both make worship the thing deeds cannot hold to.
audit_text_issue: 147's yamakam splits are partly uncertain.

note: Tirumular has the Brahmins enter the Pranava and see the Lord who is the end of sound, Veda and knowing (வேதாந்த போதாந்த நாதனை). 148 calls Murugan the one whose form is A, M and U at the end of the ancient Veda (பழைய மறையின் முடிவில் அகர மகர உகர படிவ வடிவம்). Both place the Lord in the syllable at the Veda's end.

Both name Seypathi (Vayalur) as the place where Murugan acted on the poet: in 149 he stopped him and made him his servant, in 152 he gave him the love of singing Thiruppugazh daily. Read together they are the book's account of its own beginning.

Both hear the funeral drums and see the body covered and the fire taken up. The Naladiyar ends in irony, the dying carrying the dead; 157 asks for release before that hour comes, while the hut of the body still stands.

Both take the body apart into blood, bone, nerves, skin and flesh. The Naladiyar asks which part is the woman one desires; 158 turns the list on the poet's own body and confesses that, knowing this, he still desires women.

Both place the soul's bondage at conception: Tirumular has maya join the soul in the womb, turiya broken and karma take hold; 160 has the form grow in the womb from seed and breath, divided by the three gunas and covered in deceit, and contrasts it with the turiya state of the liberated.

The Kural's first line makes A the first of letters as the Lord is first of the world; 163 borrows the words (அகர முதல்) and asks for the meaning that is first in that way, the secret that 173 says Murugan told Siva.

Both credit Murugan with Sambandar's victory over the Jains of Madurai: 149 with the impaling and the word set into fire and water (கனற்புனலிற் கனத்த சொலைப் பதித்து), 150 with the impaling, the leaf that went against the river (உரை நதி எதிர்பட) and the poem that raised a girl from her bones. Together they show the book's consistent identification of Murugan with the Tamil saint.
audit_text_issue: 150's rhythmic runs split uncertainly.

note: The Kural's lover asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman (அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ ... மாதர்கொல்). 151 strings the same doubting questions on each feature, hair darkness or cloud, brow bow or crescent (இருளோ புயலோ, சிலையோ பிறையோ). The Kural's figure of wonder becomes in the song the catalogue the poet sets against the feet he would rather think on.

Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he might make the Lord well in Tamil (என்னை நன்றாக இறைவன் படைத்தனன் தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யுமாறே). 152 says the love of singing Thiruppugazh daily was given him by Murugan at Seypathi (திருப்புகழ் நித்தம் பாடும் அன்பது செய்ப்பதியிற் தந்தவன் நீயே). Both poets say the work of praise was the Lord's gift.

The Naladiyar says those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth yet keep their eyes on desire have no way to safety (சொல்தளர்ந்து கோல்ஊன்றி). 154 runs from the women's embrace to stammering speech and the staff (சொற் குளறிட்டுத் தடிதொட்டு), disease, the sickbed and the pyre. The song extends the Naladiyar's picture of desire outliving the body to its end in the burning ground.

The Kural likens the false embrace of women for wealth to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room (ஏதில் பிணந்தழீஇ அற்று). 154 moves from the women's embrace (கொளுமாதர் சுகமுற்று) straight to the burning of his own body and asks whether he will become a corpse (சடமாமோ). The corpse the Kural sets inside the embrace the song sets at its end.

The Naladiyar says courtesans would send away even Vishnu with joined hands if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன் றில்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). 155 describes priced women who snatch gold (பொன்பறி விலைமாதர்) and shut the front door when the man pleads (கெஞ்சிட முன்றலை வாயில் அடைத்து). Both show the welcome ending where the money ends.

Tirumular defines the Siva-guru as one who tests with pure teaching so that fault is removed (சுத்த வுரையால் துரிசறச் சோதித்து) and shows the real and the unreal. 156 opens with Murugan as the guru who spoke the instructing mantra into Siva's ears (உபதேச மந்த்ரம்) and asks him to come to one lost in base illusion (அவமாயை) and give grace-knowledge so that understanding grows and trouble ends. The song applies the Tirumanthiram's account of the guru's work to the poet's own need.

Tirumular has the whole town wail, rename the man a corpse, burn him in the cremation ground and then bathe and forget (சுட்டிட்டு நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). 157 has kin wail and babble, burn the body and be told to plunge in the sea (சுடலைதனில் இடு கனலை ... திரைகடலில் முழுகென). The same funeral sequence moves Tirumular to the forgetting and the song to a plea for release before the hut goes (படிக்குடிலை ஒழியாதே).

Tirumular addresses those who feel the perishing hut lasting (நில்லாக் குரம்பை நிலையென்று உணர்வீர்காள்). 158 confesses cherishing as lasting the body that stinks once life leaves it (உடம்பு பேணி நிலையென்று). The error Tirumular charges to the unlearned the poet admits in himself.

Tirumular cherishes the body because the Lord has made it his temple (உத்தமன் கோயில்கொண்டான் ... ஓம்புகின்றேனே). 158 lists the body as pus, blood, worms and bone, food for jackals and crows, and makes cherishing it (பேணி) part of his ruin. The conflict holds if 158 condemns cherishing the body as such; if only cherishing it as lasting (நிலையென்று), the two can stand together.

Tirumular enters the Lord's city in the company of the devotees of the Lord's devotees (உடையான் அடியார் அடியாருடன்போய்). 159, after calling himself fool, liar and rubbish (கூளன்), asks only to be joined with Murugan's devotees (உனடியரொடு கூடும் வகைமை). Both seek the way in through the company of devotees rather than by their own worth.

Tirumular says Nandi taught him that knowledge is his form, and he remained as knowledge (அறிவு வடிவென்று அருள்செய்தான் நந்தி). 161 asks, after taking the love-treatise for scripture (மதனூலே சுருதியென), to know knowledge by knowledge and become full (அறிவை அறிவால் அறிந்து நிறைவாகி). The goal the song asks for is the state Tirumular reports.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 2357: last word அருந்திருந்தானே looks corrupt.

note: Tirumular's khechari verse raises the tongue, drinks the honey-water and says Sivaya nama (தேனீர் பருகிச் சிவாய நமவென்று). 162 asks to climb the mountain of Namasivaya and let the tongue's bliss fall like a waterfall (நமசிவாய வரையேறி நாவின்ப ரசமதான ஆநந்த அருவி பாய). The song's yogic ascent uses the Tirumanthiram's joining of the five syllables with the nectar of the tongue.

Both are love-laments in the same short metre over a lovesick girl, worn down by Kama's arrows, the sea or south wind, and evening; both name Murugan as the one who spoke a word to Siva. 24 is plainly the mother's voice; 164 asks Murugan for his garland for the girl.

Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons for gifts. 15 regrets it with a wounded heart and asks for service instead; 175 adds the patrons' contempt and asks whether men who do not think of Murugan deserve to be sung at all.
Both credit Murugan with Sambandar's victory over the Jains, who are impaled, and with the holy ash: in 149 the ash is spread through the town, in 171 a pinch of it cures the Pandya king.
audit_text_issue: 171's confession lines are partly unclear.

note: 153 alludes to the race round the world in one line; 176 tells the whole story, including Murugan's anger at losing the fruit, and makes it the reason he dwells at Palani.
audit_text_issue: 176 line 2 has corrupt characters (தன஧முவ).

note: The Kural warns of women who weigh the profit and then speak of their goodness; 172 describes the same pretence from inside, women who take every possession 'with great friendship'.
Both make a man's welcome depend on what he brings: the Naladiyar's courtesans find a moneyed oil-presser sugar, and 178's women question at the door those who come with property and carry it off.

The Kural's woman says that with her lover away the evening comes like enemies to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல வரும்). 164 lines up Kama's bow, the roaring sea and the hour when the light fades (ஒளிமட்கு மிகைப் பொழுதாலே) as attackers through which the creeper-girl's life grows faint (உயிர் எய்த்த). The song carries the Kural's hostile evening into a plea to the god for his garland.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 164's first lines divide uncertainly.

note: 165 asks that when kin, house, wealth and power become strangers (அயலாக) before Death's rope, Murugan's feet end his loneliness (எனது தனிமை கழிய). The Tirumanthiram names the Lord as the one whom those without kin take as kin (சுற்றற்றவர் சுற்றுக் கருதிய). The song asks for exactly the kinship the Tirumanthiram says the Lord gives the kinless.

The Tirumanthiram's kin rise wailing but turn back at the edge of the town (ஊர்த்துறைக் காலே ஒழிவர்) and then light the pyre. 165 says that at Death's coming kin, friends and house all turn into strangers (தமரும் அமரும் மனையும் ... அயலாக). Both see the bonds of kin end at death; the song draws from it a plea for the feet.

The Tirumanthiram's dying man is let go by the physician after the pulse is felt (கைவிட்டு நாடி) while wife and wealth stay behind. 166 asks to be spared both the diseases and physicians who name remedies, turn deaf and ask payment for failing age (சரியும் வயதுக்கு ஏது தாரீர்). Both make the physician the figure who fails at the end.

The Tirumanthiram says the great medicine (மாமருந்து), like mantra and the pure path, is the Lord's pair of feet. 166 lists headache, jaundice, fever and colic and the physicians' useless cures, and asks instead for the two feet that sages hold in their hearts (இருபாதம் உளமது தரித்தே). The song applies the Tirumanthiram's claim to a catalogue of real illness.

Tirumular asks why people seek a later birth when they do no tapas beforehand, and says the Lord made him to render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). 167 confesses he has no tapas or japa (தவமிலி, செபமிலி) and asks first that he may sing good Tamil (நற்றமிழ் பாட), then reach the feet and be rid of both deeds. The song takes the Tirumanthiram's way out, Tamil in place of the missing tapas, as its own plea.

Both songs build the poet's self-portrait from privative names: 167 with -இலி (திடமிலி, தவமிலி, கொடையிலி), 320 with -இலன் (தவமிலன், புகலிலன், பொறையிலன், கலையிலன்). 167 asks to sing Tamil; 320 lacks the art of learning Murugan's praise. The same device in distant chapters makes the lack of song itself part of the confession.

The Tirumanthiram says that one born of two who sought pleasure and grown in painful bondage can still, once born, seek the Ancient and chant (தொன்புற நாடிநின்று ஓதலுமாமே). 168 accepts that Murugan may leave him in birth (செனனம் அதனில் விடுவாயேல்) and asks only for a whole body, family and knowledge, and to be taken into service. Both treat birth not as the end of hope but as a place from which service is still possible.

Tirumular took on servitude to the servants of the Lord's servants and the Lord took him, saying this one is my servant (அடியான் இவன் என்று அடிமைகொண்டானே). 169 quotes his oath to women, I will be your slave (யான் அடிமையாவேன்), confesses he never joined the Lord's devotees (அடியாரோடு கூடுகிலன்), and asks that this servant be redeemed (யானடிமை ஈடேறவே). The pairing shows the same அடிமை offered to the wrong master and the right one.

The Kural says an unlearned man's standing wilts once he meets others and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்). 171 says the court poets' learning, decked with titles and regalia, breaks and changes colour when tested (முடிவில் அவை ஒன்றும் அற்று வேறொரு நிறமாகி முறியும்). Both make the test of speech the place where false learning collapses.
audit_text_issue: 171: some lines of the confession are unclear.

note: The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from men's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks. 172's women take every possession under the guise of friendship (பொருட்கள் யாவையும் மெத்தவும் நட்பொடு பறித்து) and invent new tricks daily. Both locate the fraud in affection used as the instrument of taking.

The Tirumanthiram says even one guilty of the five great sins (அதிபஞ்ச பாதகன்) escapes hell if he gives to the Lord, the guru and those free of desire and learns from them. 174 calls himself guilty of the five great sins (பஞ்ச பாதகன்) and also a miser (லோபியன்) headed for hell, who never joined the devotees. The Tirumanthiram names the condition of rescue, giving, and 174 confesses lacking exactly that.

The Kural calls the man who parades useless words not a man but chaff among men (மக்கட் பதடி). 177 names himself chaff in understanding (அறிவிற் பதடி), a fool made helpless by daily embraces, and asks for one word of grace. The rare word பதடி carries the Kural's contempt into the poet's self-judgement.

Both say the courtesan's sweet talk serves her wish for wealth, not love. The Kural states it as a warning; 180 shows the sequence, talk, trust, then the wealth snatched, and asks for the Lord's love in its place.

Both raise the breath from the root through the channel between ida and pingala to the head and arrive at the Lord's feet. Tirumular states the method; 188 asks for it as a gift, and hears the goal as the anklet sound of the dancing foot.
audit_text_issue: 188's நாலங்குலம் and சிகாரம் lines are obscure.

note: 27 asks to see how to leave the embrace and gain the feet; 190 describes the same embrace and vows not to forget the feet even there. Read as a vow, 190 allows a remembrance inside desire that 27 seeks by leaving it.

The Tirumanthiram's verse is a chain of the Goddess's names, Tripura, Sundari, Narani, Manonmani, by which the one stands as many. 179 ends its namo-nama litany with the same names for Uma (மாதா மநோமணி ஆயி சுந்தரி தாயான நாரணி அபிராமி) as Murugan's mother. Worship by naming the Goddess is shared, and 179 sets it inside a hymn to her son.

Tirumular says people see the times of child, youth and old man pass (பாலன் இளையன் விருத்தன்) and still do not understand, and lies at the Lord's feet. 181 tells that life in stages, from being sent by Brahma to eat deeds through the breast and childhood to the grown man in common women's houses, and asks when he will worship the feet. The song fills in the Tirumanthiram's three stages with its own history.
audit_text_issue: Song 181 செறிவுடன் றிந்து looks damaged.

note: The Tirumanthiram says the Veda and the Agama are both the true Lord's scripture and not different for the great. 182 asks to live in service without straying from the Manu texts, seeking the meaning the Vedas hold and following the Agamas in order (மிகுத்த பொருள் ஆகமங்கள் முறையாலே). The song turns the Tirumanthiram's doctrine of the two scriptures into a rule of conduct.

The Kural's lover says the girl's shoulders are made of nectar because each touch makes his life sprout anew (உயிர்தளிர்ப்ப ... அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்). 185 drinks the nectar of women's smiles (நகையமுதம்) and perishes by it (அழியும்), and asks to drink instead the nectar of the Lord's feet (இருதாளின் அமுது). On the plain reading the same nectar of love gives life in the Kural and death in the song.

The Naladiyar's renunciant refuses men who call eyes water-lilies, warring carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேல்) and sees the eye as a scooped palm fruit. 186 uses the same conceit of eyes outdoing deer, mango slice and carp (முதிய கயல்கள்) to describe the women whose eyes forced him into bondage. The figure the Naladiyar dismisses is the snare the song confesses.

The Tirumanthiram compares women who smile and display their breasts to the etti tree, fine in leaf and fruit but not to be eaten, and tells the heart to turn away. 187 lists a woman's ornaments in detail, then her sweet words, coral lips and poisonous eyes (நச்சுக்கண்), and asks whether he must go on wandering caught by them. Both set an adorned surface over harm.

The Tirumanthiram says no tapas is needed to make the mind Siva for one who has kinship with those whose minds have joined Siva's bliss (சிவானந்தம் சேர்ந்தோர் உறவு). 189 lists the mantra, giving, silence and jnana he lacks and asks for the keenness to join those of knowing heart (ஞான நெஞ்சினர் பால் இணங்கிடு கூர்மை). The song asks for the one remedy the Tirumanthiram says replaces the missing disciplines.
