The Kural asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the soft arms of the beloved (மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்). 190 describes the same embrace and says that even sleeping on that bed (அமளி மலரணையின் மிசை துயிலுகினும்) he will not forget the lotus feet. The song keeps the Kural's sleep in love but refuses to let it displace the god.

The Naladiyar scorns blind, petty men who call women's eyes lilies, carp or spears. 191 confesses he was such a poet, describing hair as cloud, breasts as lotus buds, face as moon (உருவக உரைசெய்து), and melted like wax in a furnace in the union that followed. The song indicts its own craft in the terms the Naladiyar uses against the praisers.

The Naladiyar says bright-browed women hide harmful intent behind words spoken to be believed and belong to no one but their own bodies. 193 abuses women who talk of love without knowing friendship, never melt despite sweet words (இன்சொல் புரிந்து உருகாத) and attend only to the act of union. Both find the courtesan's speech a performance that hides an unmoved heart.

Both set the Lord above the alchemist's work. Tirumular makes the five-letter mantra the alchemist's pill that turns the body to gold; 194 says mercury and the nine metals end as charcoal, while knowing Murugan as the gem brings everything.
Both tell the poet's life as one arc from the womb and the breast to the houses of women. 181 adds Brahma sending the soul out to eat its deeds; 195 adds the age of sixteen and the wealth lost.
Both make weeping the sign of devotion: Tirumular melts in love and cries day and night, and 199 asks to wear the feet on his head and weep and weep for grace.
Both songs of Avinankudi call Murugan the giver of போதகம், the teaching: 179 opens by hailing him as such, and 200 ends with Siva bowing to receive it.

Thiruppugazh 195 runs a single life from the womb (வனிதையுடல் காய நின்று உதிரமதிலே உருண்டு) through youth to ruin in women's nets and only then asks for grace. Tirumanthiram 487 says that one born of two who met for pleasure and grown in painful bondage (துன்புறு பாசத்தில் தோன்றி வளர்ந்தபின்) can still seek the Ancient and chant him. The mantra states as a general possibility what the song enacts as one man's late plea (உன்றன் அருள்தாராய்).

Thiruppugazh 196 names the ninety-six tattvas as agents crowding the body (தத்துவகாரர் தொண்ணூற்றறுவர்) and calls the body a thieving, false hut (சோரம் பொய்க்குடில்). Tirumanthiram 154 counts the same ninety-six as dwellers in a walled temple (முப்பதும் முப்பதும் முப்பத்தறுவரும்) who all run off once it falls. Both picture the tattvas as tenants of a house that does not last: the mantra as a temple that falls, the song as a false hut.

Both songs open with a physician's list of the body's diseases: 196 has வாதம் பித்தம் ... ஈளைகள் ... மூல வியாதிகள், 894 has வாதமொடு பித்த மூல ... ஈளை. 196 then calls the body a false hut (பொய்க்குடில்) and 894 a ruined body (பாழுடல்) Brahma built, and both ask not to waste life carrying it. The two songs, far apart in the book, are near-repeats of one complaint.

Thiruppugazh 197 opens by likening a woman's breasts to an elephant (வாரணந்தனை நேரான மாமுலை) and goes on to ask that he see her whole charm as great maya in form (மாமாயையே வடிவாக நின்றது). Kural 1087 has the lover compare the cloth over her firm breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேல் கட்படாம்). The same elephant figure is the Kural lover's wonder and, in the song, the first item of an inventory the poet asks to see through.

Thiruppugazh 198 describes women whose breasts seek battle and whose eye-nets delude all, and asks that his mind not wither under them (எனது சிந்தையும் வாடிவிடாவகை) but be ruled by the feet. Tirumanthiram 2141 says desire rising at the waist and a mind sunk at the breast (முலைவாய நெஞ்சத்து மூழ்கும்) send one wandering, while a mind made firm as stone stands before Siva (சிலையாய சித்தம் சிவமுன்). Both set the mind drowned in the woman's body against the mind held before the Lord; the mantra states as a rule what the song asks for.
audit_text_issue: 2141 line 4 is obscure.

note: Thiruppugazh 199 asks to wear the anklet feet on his head and, weeping and weeping, long for grace (அழுதழுது உன் அருள் விரும்பி). Tirumanthiram 43 says the Lord fills and gives his feet to those who speak of Hara's feet crying and weeping (அரற்றி அழுது) and meditate daily on them. Both make tears joined to the feet the way to grace; the song asks for the very state the mantra promises.
audit_text_issue: 43's உரன் அடி / நிரன் அடி are obscure.

note: Thiruppugazh 200, after a life wasted on women, asks only to pour Ganges water on the two lotus feet, bow and do some little puja (பூசையும் சிலவே புரிந்திட). Tirumanthiram 252 says that anyone can give God a green leaf (யாவர்க்குமாம் இறைவற்கு ஒரு பச்சிலை). Both set the measure of worship low: water and a leaf are enough, and the song's modest plea fits the mantra's claim that such worship is within everyone's reach.

Tirumular teaches breath held on the left so that the body does not decay; 211 asks to be rid of the anxious yoga that turns back the breath because it will not accept that the body must go, and seeks silence instead. The conflict holds if 211's participles describe the yoga it rejects, which is the likelier reading.
audit_text_issue: Two corrupt glyphs in 211 (அனலு஡தி, புண்ட஡ணகம்)

note: Both use the string-puppet for a life with no inner agency: in the Kural the man without shame only seems alive, in 207 the poet dances on the strings of his two deeds.
Tirumular says the knowers perceive Siva within the soul 'like a painting'; 212's obscure plea for the end 'in the painting' may ask for the same still perception.
audit_text_issue: 212's ஓவியத்தில் அந்தம் and தூமமேய்க் கணிந்த are obscure, possibly corrupt.

note: Both complain of the poet's life at patrons' gates: 210 of the men who slip away once praised in song, 220 of genres wasted on fools who toss a coin; both turn to the Lord's feet instead.

Thiruppugazh 201 confesses that, deluded by craving for women, he never once thought of the name Sivaya (சிவாயவெனுநாமம் ஒருகாலும் நினையாத). Tirumanthiram 905 teaches the way: chant சிவாயநம, நமசிவாயநம and no birth follows. The song is the confession of one who neglected the mantra Tirumular prescribes, and asks Murugan to call him from that darkness.

Thiruppugazh 202 asks that one day Murugan set his lotus feet as a crown on the poet's head (உன் வாரிஜபதங்கள் நாயடியேன் முடிபுனைந்து) and rule him with a word of teaching (போதக வாசகம்). Tirumanthiram 1597 tells how Nandi placed his holy feet on his head (திருவடி வைத்தென் சிரத்து) and was seen in the form of the guru. The song asks for the initiation, feet on the head and the guru's word, that the mantra records as received.

Thiruppugazh 203 asks when, the darkness of great maya gone (மாமாய இருள்), he will reach the light beyond the thirty-six (ஆறாறின் அதிகம்). Tirumanthiram 617 says the devotees went beyond the thirty-six (ஆறாறு அகன்று) and, shattering dense maya by grace (செறிவான மாயை சிதைத்து அருளாலே), knew the state of unparted grace. The two use the same Siddhanta count and the same two steps, past the tattvas and through maya; the song asks for what the mantra describes as attained.

Thiruppugazh 204 says that at Swamimalai the ascetics' jnana makes deeds flee like straw before fire (துரால் மிக தீ முன்). Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas end before the guru-sun as cotton round a sunstone burns only in the sun's presence (சூழ்பஞ்சைச் சுட்டிடா ... சந்நிதியிற் சுடும்). Both picture bondage as dry fibre burned by knowledge; the mantra adds that the burning waits on the presence of the sun, the guru.

Thiruppugazh 205 asks that, the two deeds broken and the dark of impurity cleared, he and the six faces mingle so that the two become one without difference (பேதம் இலை என இரண்டு பேரும்). Tirumanthiram 1441 reports reaching the state where He and I are not two (தானென்று நானென் றிரண்டிலாத் தற்பதம்), so that he can no longer speak of He and I. The song's plea for union without difference is the state the mantra speaks from.

Thiruppugazh 207 says that, driven by his two deeds (இருவினை), he danced like a puppet on strings (பாவை துன்றிடுங் கயிறுவிதம் என மருவி ஆடி). Tirumanthiram 2344 says the Lord makes the elements dance as deeds make a false puppet dance (பொய்க்கரி யாட்டும் வினையென), and calls this Hara's grace. In both the puppet is moved by deeds; the song feels it as torment, while the mantra places even that motion under grace.
audit_text_issue: 2344's பொய்க்கரி is uncertain.

note: Thiruppugazh 208 sets life beside the wealth that misers gather without giving (இடாது பல தேடும் கிராதர் பொருள் போல்): neither stays. Naladiyar 10 says those who give nothing and hoard will lose it (கொடாஅது வைத்தீட்டினார் இழப்பர்), as the honey bee's store shows. The hoard that is lost is the Naladiyar's lesson about giving, and in the song it becomes a figure for life itself.

Thiruppugazh 209 asks whether he must suffer lodged in a body like a nest in a bush (செடிநேர் உடற் குடம்பை). Kural 338 likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The same word names the body: the Kural stresses how lightly life leaves it, the song how mean a lodging it is.

Thiruppugazh 209 credits Murugan with teaching Keeran grammar and, by grace, giving verse whose alliteration fits (அடிமோனை சொற்கிணங்க ... உன் அருளால் அளிக்கு), and asks grace on his own poor words. Tirumanthiram 81 says the Lord made him well so that he would render him well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யுமாறே). Both poets see their Tamil verse as the Lord's doing and given for his praise.

Thiruppugazh 210 asks whether he must go night and day to the gates of powerful men who slip away once praised in song (நழுவிய ப்ரசண்டர் வாசல் இரவுபகல் சென்று வாடி). Naladiyar 107 says that people with aching hearts standing at the long gates of great houses (நெடுங்கடை நின்றுழல்வது) in everyone's sight are paying for former deeds. The same wilting figure at the rich man's gate is a plea for release in the song and an explanation by karma in the Naladiyar.

Thiruppugazh 211 asks to leave a yoga of breath and fire and enter the full silence beyond qualities so as to reach release (மோன நிர்க்குணம் அது பொருந்தி வீடுற). Tirumanthiram 1611 says that for those to whom silence has come, release comes too (மோனங்கை வந்தோர்க்கு முத்தியும் கைகூடும்). Both tie release to silence, though the song sets silence against breath-yoga while the mantra also lists powers among its fruits.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 211 has corrupt glyphs (அனலு஡தி, புண்ட஡ணகம்).

note: Thiruppugazh 212 asks not to waste away in desires (காமியத்து அழுந்தி) but, with love for the letter Om welling up (ஓமெழுத்தில் அன்பு மிகவூறி), to be given the end. Tirumanthiram 2436 says that, having driven off lust, anger and delusion (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் இவைகடிந்து), he reached the abode within the sound Om. Both pass from desire to Om; the short song asks for the path the mantra reports as travelled.

Thiruppugazh 213 describes women who seize their lovers' belongings (உடைமை மனமுடனே பறிப்பவர்கள்) and calls himself the fool who became their slave (அசடன்). Naladiyar 377 says those who take as their own the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks are laughed at by many. Both make the man who takes this for love the fool; the song confesses it in the first person.

Tirumanthiram 967 promises that to one who begins the holy name and does not tire of it, the Lord comes to remove the grief of clinging deeds (சார்ந்த வினைத்துயர் போக). Thiruppugazh 214 is a litany of names chanted daily (அநுதினம் உனையோதும்) by devotees still crushed by cruel deeds, ending 'do you not hear their cry for refuge?' (அபயமிடுகுரல் அறியாயோ). The song sets beside the promise the devotee's experience of waiting for it to be kept.

Thiruppugazh 215 describes courtesans who embrace to snatch coins (காசு பறிக்க மறித்து முயக்கிகள்) and act out a learned art of deceit (தோதக வித்தை). Kural 913 says the false embrace of women who love wealth (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both name the embrace itself as false because it is for money; the Kural adds the image of revulsion.

Thiruppugazh 216 asks, without embarrassment, for wealth, yoga and a great life together with Siva-jnana, mukti and the supreme state (சகலசெல்வ யோக ... சிவஞான முத்தி பரகதியும் நீ கொடுத்து). Tirumanthiram 1714 says Sadasiva remains giving enjoyment and release, understanding and powers (போகமும் முத்தியும் புத்தியும் சித்தியும்). Both treat worldly enjoyment and release as gifts from the same giver, not as rivals.

The Naladiyar gives one picture, a pot of filth leaking from nine openings under a dark skin; 217 takes the body apart organ by organ and disease by disease, and adds the hut of five elements taken up birth after birth.
audit_text_issue: 217 has garbled words (சங்முளை, வங்க்முடே).

note: The Kural finds the body's joy in touching one's children; 218 asks for that very joy with the Lord as the child on the lap, and puns the child's kiss (முத்தி) into release.
Both are songs of a girl lovesick for Murugan, voiced by someone near her, with the evening moon and Kama's arrows; 221 adds the street's gossip.
Tirumular counts the Agamas twenty-eight, heard from Siva; 223 asks for the release that runs through the same twenty-eight, so the plea rests on the Siddhanta canon.
Both call the courtesan's embrace false (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், பொய்க்கலவி) because it is for wealth; the Kural likens it to a corpse in a dark room, 227 adds poison and wealth snatched.

Tirumular lists the body's constituents, இரதம் உதிரம் இறைச்சி தோல் மேதை ... அத்தி ... மச்சை ... சுக்கிலம், and calls them பாழாம் உபாதி, a perishing adjunct. 217 runs the same inventory, நரம்பு, எலும்பு, தசை, இரத்தம், சுக்கிலம், to call the body a குடில் of five elements taken up birth after birth. The same catalogue serves Tirumular's analysis of tattvas and the song's disgust at rebirth.
audit_text_issue: 217 has garbled words (சங்முளை, வங்க்முடே).

note: Tirumular's women cling like grass in a storm (புயலுறும் புல்லின் புணர்ந்தவரேயினும்) and say 'stay near' (சார இரும் என்பார்), then talk with others and are gone. 219's women say they have no wish for money (பணத்தில் ஆசையிலை), lie close like a wife for all time, then seize legs and hair in a quarrel. Both make the profession of attachment itself the trap.

The Naladiyar's man of worth, even when fortune leaves him, will not stand with bowed neck behind fools who hoard wealth (அருத்தம் செறிக்கும் அறிவிலார் பின்சென்று எருத்திறைஞ்சி). 220 confesses doing exactly that: making envoy poems and verse garlands for patrons, walking to fools (மடையரிடமே நடந்து) and being tossed a coin with 'come another time'. The song turns the Naladiyar's rule into a poet's confession and a plea to sing for the Lord instead.

The Kural says no help exceeds good company and nothing brings more affliction than bad (நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). 222 asks not to be worn out mingling at the doors of the wicked (நாசர் தம் கடையதனில் விரவி) and sinking, but to speak the words of those who praise Murugan. The song applies the Kural's choice of company to devotion.

Tirumular says that on nearing him there is no difference such as 'I' and 'you' (நானென நீயென வேறில்லை), like flesh and its life. 223 asks for union in which neither the Lord says 'you are other' nor the poet 'I am other' (நீவேறெனாதிருக்க நான்வேறெனாதிருக்க). The song asks for, as the fruit of the Agamas' jnana, the non-difference Tirumular states.

858 ends its long account of a miser's life by asking for the supreme bliss where 'you and I' become one enjoyment (ஏக போகமாய் நீயு நானுமாய்). 223 asks for the same goal in doctrinal terms, non-difference from both sides after the Agamas' four ways. Read together they show the book's goal of release is union, not only reaching the feet.

Tirumular's first mother (ஆதி முதல்வி) stands with her power as the Veda, the moving and unmoving, the five elements (ஐம்பூதம்) and the many lives. 224's praise names Uma as the single source (ஒருமுதலாகி நின்ற உமை) of the seven worlds, the gods' worlds, Kailasa, the golden mountain, lives and the five elements. The praise half of a courtesan song carries Tirumular's doctrine of Shakti as first cause.
audit_text_issue: மதனு஡லின் is garbled in the source.

note: Tirumular names the Shakti of the Tripura chakra திரிபுரை, சுந்தரி, ... நாரணி, Manonmani, and says she stands as many. 226's praise names Murugan's mother டாகினி திரிபுரை நாரணி, the light on Siva's left side. The song draws its names of Uma from the same list of the Goddess that Tirumular gives as the forms of one power.

Tirumular tells his hearers to praise the lord of Kailasa and stand telling the nature of the one who kicked Death (கூற்றுதைத்தான் தன்மை கூறிநின்று உய்ம்மினே). 228 asks that Death not come near him (காலன் எனை அணுகாமல்) but that he worship at Murugan's holy feet (திருகாலில் வழிபட). The song makes the son's feet the refuge from Death that Tirumular finds in the father's.

Tirumular says the women who once desired him like sugarcane juice now find him bitter as the kaanjiram fruit (கரும்பொத்துக் காஞ்சிரங் காயுமொத்தேனே). 229 asks for the feet before the women scorn him (இகழ) as his hair whitens and youth hides away. Both argue against desire from the women's own turning away in old age, not from their deceit.

Tirumular says the Lord, like a parent who sees both the ways and the faults of the sons he begot, does without anger what fits each soul (பெற்ற புதல்வர்போல் ... குற்றமுங் கண்டு ... செற்றமிலாச் செய்கை). 230 asks Murugan to bear with his faults (பிழையே பொறுத்து) after a life deluded by Kama's Agama. Tirumular's teaching is the ground for the song's plea for forgiveness rather than reward.

On the reading that அவன் is the devotee, Tirumular says those who draw near him and love him can draw near Siva too (அவன்பால் அணுகியே அன்புசெய் வார்கள் சிவன்பால் அணுகுதல் செய்யவும் வல்லன்). 231 asks to become one with the devotees who melt beside themselves (உருகு தொண்டருடன் அதாகி) and to be given servanthood that grows from love. Both make the company of devotees the way to the Lord.

The Kural says one who neither gives nor enjoys has nothing however rich; 239 is the confession of such a man, who kept his wealth for his hands and youth and shared nothing with the hungry, and finds it at the funeral.
Both set sharing food against the funeral drum and the wailing kin: 23 resolves to share even a grain before the summons, 239 confesses that he never did.

The Naladiyar says leprosy rots the fingers when the old deed (பழவினை) of breaking crabs' legs and eating them comes home. 232 calls its many diseases பாதகவியாதி, diseases of sin, and says through them he has drunk sin like liquor. Both read disease as the fruit of one's own fault, the Naladiyar of a past deed, the song of present lust.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 232: a word in line 12 is corrupt.

note: The Naladiyar says those who, with failing speech, staff and fallen teeth, still stay at home with eyes set on desire (காம நெறிபடரும் கண்ணினார்க்கு) have no way to safety. 233 confesses growing old (வயதாகி) while wandering after kohl-eyed women and seeking wealth for their ornaments, and asks whether he must go on wandering. The song is the Naladiyar's old man speaking of himself.

The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then turns away, and those who think her love theirs are laughed at. 235's dancers draw a man close, dose him (மருத்திட்டு ஆட்டி) and snatch his wealth (சீர்பொருள் பறி), and the song asks whether a bond with these false dancers can be right. Both describe a seeming affection that ends in taking the man's wealth.

In the Naladiyar the jewelled woman who swore to leap from the peak together shows a pain in her feet at the brink because the man had no gold (காணம் இன்மையான் மேவாதொழிந்தாள்). 238's women agree to deceitful play once red gold is spread as the price (விலையாக மிக்க செம்பொன் வரவே பரப்பி) and quarrel after a few days. The two show the same bond from either side: it begins with gold and fails without it.

The Naladiyar tells the man of great wealth to give it away, since none escapes Death and tomorrow the funeral drum will sound (நாளைத் தழீஇம் தழீஇம் தண்ணம் படும்). 239 confesses refusing to share food with the hungry and keeping wealth for himself until kin surround him weeping and drums beat (தமர்சுற்றியழப் பறைகொட்டியிட) as Death takes the life. The song is the Naladiyar's warning spoken as regret.

858 traces the miser who sends the begging ascetic from door to door and ends with kin wailing, drums and the fire. 239 compresses the same life into refusing food to the hungry (பசியுற்றவருக்கு அமுதைப் பகிர்தற்கு இசையாதே) and the funeral drum. The two songs, far apart in the book, make refusal to give the sin that the funeral exposes.

Both put the courtesan's embrace for money in a dark room (இருட்டறை). The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse; 252 keeps the room and the seized wealth but not the corpse, and confesses the pull instead of warning.

Both take the body apart into bone, blood, fat and entrails to break desire. The Naladiyar asks which part is the garlanded woman; 248 turns the inventory on the poet's own body, a house he still longs to carry.
Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons in Tamil for gifts; 245 adds the rebuff, 'come tomorrow' and the turned face, and asks, like 15, for the feet instead.
Both are catalogues of diseases set as the plea; 232 ties them to sin and women, while 243 asks to be spared them in every birth.
audit_text_issue: 232 has a corrupt word in line 12 (வெற஧முடி).

note: Both name the Thiruppugazh within itself as a means of grace: 242 says reading it cuts affliction, 249 asks to live among those who sing it.

Tirumular says the eaters of flesh are seized by Yama's messengers and thrown into hell; 247 counts the daily eating of killed flesh among the bonds and asks for release from them, without the threat.
audit_text_issue: 247 has garbled readings (த்ததகுரு, encoding glitch in கொலு஡னை).

note: The Tirumanthiram's adept takes the teaching that is Om (பிரணவமாம் உபதேசத்தை) into a true heart and stands as servant of the Father (அத்தற்கு அடிமை). 240 tells the same Om-teaching with the roles turned: the son, as guru, speaks the end of the one word Om (ஒருமொழி பிரணவ முடிவதை) into the ear of the Father, Siva (பரமன திருசெவி களிகூர). The pairing shows the pranava upadesa running downward from Siva in one book and upward to him in the other.

The Kural likens death to falling asleep and birth to waking (உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு ... விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு). 241 asks whether he must again gain this birth that slips past in a blink, lying down and rising (இமைப்பினிற் சடக்கெனப் படுத்தெழச் சறுக்கும் இப்பிறப்பு). The song takes the Kural's calm image of sleep and waking and makes it the speed with which a birth is lost.

The Tirumanthiram says those who rise in the morning and recite Mulan's three thousand Tamil verses knowing their meaning (கருத்தறிந்து ஓதிடின்) will reach the Lord of the world. 242 recalls that those who read the Thiruppugazh with love (திருப்புகழ் விருப்பொடு படிப்பவர்) have their affliction cut. Both books promise a fruit for reciting the book itself, one asking for understanding, the other for love.

The Tirumanthiram says he is awareness and life, the senses and union, yet cannot be reached by thought (உணர்வும் அவனே உயிரும் அவனே ... எண்ணலும் ஆகான்). 244 traces the same light of knowledge through life and awareness (உயிரினூடு ... உணர்வினூடு) and on through the elements to turiya, then asks only for some means of touching it (தொடும் உபாயம் ஏதோ). The song takes the pervasion the Tirumanthiram states and turns its 'cannot be thought' into a plea for a way.
audit_text_issue: 244 has several garbled glyphs (஡ for ஊ in ஊடு).

note: The Naladiyar ranks as the lowest life following, for desire of wealth, people who do not recognise one's worth (பொருள்நசையால் தம்மை உணரார்பின் சென்று நிலை). 245 confesses exactly that life: seeking out who the rich were, singing them quick verses (ஆசு கவிபாடி), and walking back and forth until they said 'come tomorrow' and turned their faces (நாளை நடவுமென ... முகம்வேறாய்). The song gives the scene of humiliation that the Naladiyar's ranking only names.

The Kural says that grace is not killing and its absence is killing, and eating that flesh is not right (அவ்வூன் தினல் பொருளல்லது). 247 lists among the bonds that keep him from release the daily satisfying of hunger with killed flesh (கொலூனை நித்தம் பசியாறல்), set against mukti (முத்தம்) and bondage (பெத்தம்). The pairing shows the Kural's ethical rule placed by the song inside the Siddhanta scheme of bondage and release.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 247 has corrupt glyphs (கொலு஡னை, த்ததகுரு); Kural 254's Tamil has lost its initial அ (ருளல்லது for அருளல்லது).

note: The Kural asks whether the life that lodges in the body as a temporary shelter (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has found no home of its own. 248 calls the body a house (வீடு) of bones, blood, filth and worms, full of conspiring tattvas, and asks whether he must desire and carry that house and wander (வீடதை நத்தி எடுத்து இவண் உழல்வேனோ). Both use the image of the body as a dwelling the soul does not truly own; the song adds the disgust and the tenants.

The Naladiyar says that even the unlearned who keep company with the learned gain good sense day by day (கற்றாரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகின் நல்லறிவு நாளுந் தலைப்படுவர்), like water taking the scent of pathiri flowers. 249 asks to live among those who speak of Murugan daily through the Thiruppugazh (உரைத்திடுவார் தங்குழி மேவி) and never to part from the knowledge they impart (உணர்த்திய போதந் தனைப் பிரியாது). The pairing shows the Naladiyar's rule of learning by company applied to the company of devotees.
audit_text_issue: 249: குளிமேவி is likely குழு மேவி; the praise lines (வேள் கொன்றவன்) are uncertain.

note: The Naladiyar rebukes the heart that will not let go of the bond of home and pines for children (மனைப்பாசம் கைவிடாய் மக்கட்கென்று ஏங்கி), as though it would live for ages. 250 asks not to die with his mind clouded by thoughts of house, wife and children (மனைகள் பெண்டிர் மக்கள் தமை நினைந்து ... மடியாதே), and for release now. Both name house and children as the attachment that holds at the end; the Naladiyar's remedy is good deeds, the song's is Murugan's coming today.

251 argues that a father does not let a son run crying before him and leave him to cry (அப்பன்முன் மைந்தனோடிப் ... அழ பார்விடுப்பர்களோ), so Murugan, as father and mother, must take him. The Tirumanthiram also makes the Lord a parent of sons, but one who has seen their tendencies and faults (நாற்றமும் குற்றமுங் கண்டு) and deals with each by its nature, without anger (உயிரது பான்மைக்குச் செற்றமிலாச் செய்கை). The pairing adds a condition to the song's claim: the father's care is fitted to the child's nature, not only drawn by its crying.

The Naladiyar mocks those who think theirs the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), saying many will laugh at them. 253 describes women who take the wealth in a man's hand (கைப்பொருள் கவர்தரு) and calls himself a slave of desire and a fool (அறிவிலி) for melting before them. The song speaks in the first person the folly the Naladiyar sees in others, with the same word for the taking.

Both say the six sects lead back to birth: in Tirumular they perish where they stand, not knowing the way to leave the earth, and in 257 the sectarians who install many gods wander only to enter the womb again.
audit_text_issue: TM 1535 'முண்ணின் றழியு' looks corrupt (perhaps உண்ணின்று).

note: Both call the body a pot to turn the mind from women. The Naladiyar's pot is the woman's body seeping filth; 258 turns the image on the poet's own body, a false pot of flesh, skin and semen, and asks not just to leave desire but to have that birth cut off.

Both make the town's gossip feed love's sickness: the Kural's woman calls it the manure of her disease, and in 262 the women's talk is one of the torments, with cuckoo, moon and sea, that waste the girl's arm.
Both laments end by asking Murugan to give the wasting girl his garland; 265 calls it a garland of compassion, so the love token becomes grace.
The same formula of the courtesan's love that lasts as long as the money: in 33 the man is beaten from the door when it ends, in 266 he is left groaning there.
audit_text_issue: 266: ஡ணங்கிசை corrupt; 33: மண்டுநநருர் garbled.

note: Both identify Murugan with Sambandar defeating the Jains: 261 tells the cure of the Pandyan and the crushing of the Jains, 263 the impaling.
audit_text_issue: 261: கடலு஡டே has corrupt glyph.

note: The Tirumanthiram defines the servant's path as temple work, lighting lamps, gathering flowers, sweeping and bathing the image (தளிதொழில் செய்வது தான் தாசமார்க்கமே). 255 asks that, free of deceitful women, he may become Murugan's servant and live at his shrine (உனக்கு அடிமையுற்று உன் தலத்தினில் இருக்கும்படி). The pairing shows the song's hope of servanthood at the shrine as the path the Tirumanthiram lays out in detail.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1502: opening words are garbled ('தீப miடல்').

note: The Naladiyar says that to women without their lover the clouds thundering in every direction sound like the funeral drum (நெய்தல் அறைந்தன்ன). 259 asks whether a girl should waste away under the roaring, swelling dark sea (கனைத்து அதிர்க்கும் இப் பொங்கு கார்க்கடல்) and a moon risen red as fire. In both the loud sound of nature, cloud or sea, becomes a torment for the one who is parted.

The Naladiyar says that to loveless courtesans a man without money is poison, while even an oil-press driver with earned wealth is sugar. 260 describes courtesans who embrace whoever gives the most as if he were an old friend (அதிகமா ஒரு பொருள்தருபவரொடு பழைய பேரென இதமுற அணைபவர்). Both make the same charge, that the courtesan's affection is ranked by payment, not by the man.

The Kural says that as water changes with the soil, a person's understanding takes the nature of their company (இனத்தியல்பதாகும் அறிவு). 261 confesses that, having joined liars, sense-followers, blind fools, thieves and sectarian disputants (செறிதலுற்று), he knows nothing at all (அறிவேதும் அறிதலற்று) and sinks in the sea of the womb. The song shows the Kural's rule at work in one life, and asks for the feet as the way out of bad company.

The Tirumanthiram says those who bathed at the Kanni ford have no thought of bathing in it, and that with that thought there would be no further birth (கன்னித் துறைபடிந்து ... பின்னைப் பிறவி பிறிதில்லை). 263 asks not to bathe at Kumari with a grieving mind (குமரி கலித்துறை முழுகி மனத்துயர்) and be mocked as a diseased wretch, but to be given the praise that dwells in the feet. Both treat the outward bath at Kumari as not enough to end birth; the Tirumanthiram asks for the inner intent, the song for the feet and the Thiruppugazh.

The Kural says those who do austerity do their own work, while the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). 264 asks whether it is fit to be kin to the women who kindle infatuation and, feeding desire, destroy austerity (மயற் புகட்டி தவத்து அழிப்பவர்க்கு உறவாமோ). Both set தவம் against desire; the song names the women as the means by which desire undoes it.

The Naladiyar compares a courtesan's love to a lamp's light: the light ends when the oil runs out, the love when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 266 describes courtesans who speak desire for many days to get money and, when the money ends, leave the man groaning at the door (பொருள்தீரில் ஏங்கியிடக் கடையில் தளிவைப்பவர்). The song gives the scene that the Naladiyar's lamp image compresses.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 266 has a corrupt glyph in line 3 (஡ணங்கிசை).

note: The Kural's lover says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse (ஏமம் மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). 268 ends by making Murugan himself the lover who painted Valli's feet, arms, face and breasts on the madal (மடலிடை எழுதிய பெருமாளே). The Kural's last resort of a suffering man is, in the song, a mark of the god's love for Valli.

The Tirumanthiram praises the mantra raised with Om as spreading to all lives, granting boons, driving away surrounding enemies and giving strength (வரந்தரு மந்திரம் ... துரந்திடு மந்திரம் சூழ்பகை போக). 269 claims the same powers for the Thiruppugazh: fire to enemies and their clans (பகைத்தவர் குடிக்கும் ... நெருப்பு), granting what one thinks (நினைத்ததும் அளிக்கும்), and cutting birth. The pairing shows the song giving its own praise the powers the Tirumanthiram gives the mantra.
The Kural makes the Lord's feet the way across the great sea of births; 284 makes them a raft (புணை) and adds two more seas to cross, desire for women and the arts of learning.
Both say learning without knowledge of the Lord leaves one a fool; 279 confesses it in the first person, having read Vedas and Puranas and mocked the silent knowers as dumb.
Both measure the Lord by breadth and length and find no measure: Tirumular asks who knows them, and 279 names the reality whose breadth and length cannot be told, which the poet's learning scorned.
Both take the body apart as a false pot, a bellows and a home of diseases, and both ask not for health but for the end of the birth that brings such a body.
Both make the Thiruppugazh itself what saves: 269 gives it the power to end birth, and 277 asks that devotees live speaking it without forgetting.

The Tirumanthiram says the soul is born and dies again through much folly (பிறந்தும் இறந்தும் பல் பேதைமையாலே) until, renouncing, Siva's grace becomes its light. 270 counts the same round, how many bodies, how many times Death took his life (எத்தனை ... நமன் உயிர் பறிகொள்வது அளவேதோ), and names himself the fool whose mind is ruined (மசகனை ... மதியழி விரகனை). Both put the cause of the endless births in folly, and look to grace to end it.
audit_text_issue: 270's opening (சினத்திலத்தினை) is hard to divide.

note: 271 renounces the poets who liken base patrons to the pouring cloud, Kubera's padma treasure, the wish-cow and the wish-tree (சொரியு முகிலைப் பதும நிதியைச் சுரபி தருவை). 292 confesses having done this himself, comparing poor men to the cloud, the sun and the divine tree (முகிலும் இரவியும் ... தெய்வதரு நிகரென). The two songs quote the same list of a patron-poem, once as satire of others and once as the poet's own begging (இரவு).

The Kural makes the rain cloud (மாரி) the figure of a giver who seeks no return: what does the world give back to it? 271 mocks poets who call a base patron the pouring cloud (சொரியு முகில்). The Kural's image of true giving is the stock flattery the song refuses to sing.

The Tirumanthiram tells of going with the devotees of the Lord's devotees (அடியார் அடியாருடன் போய்) into his city, where the gatekeepers announce him and the Lord says 'let him come'. 272, after heaping abuse on himself, asks whether there is no state to be gained by going with the devotees (அடியாரொடு போய்ப் பெறுகைக்கு இலையோ கதி). The song's hope is the arrival the Tirumanthiram describes: the unworthy man is admitted in the company of devotees.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 272: தவ்முழ்குந் looks damaged.

note: 274 asks for the grace that எத்தார் and the showy (வித்தாரத்தே) cannot reach (கிட்டா எட்டா அருள்); 275 closes on the Lord hard for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise in Tamil (எத்திடார்க்கு அரிய ... எத்தினார்க்கு எளிய). If எத்தார் is read as ஏத்தார், those who do not praise, rather than cheats, the two neighbouring songs make the same rule about who can reach the Lord.
audit_text_issue: 274's clipped syllables make the opening lines hard to divide.

note: 275 and 298 end on the same line: the Lord hard for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise him with pure Tamil verse (எத்திடார்க்கு அரிய முத்தபாத் தமிழ்கொடு எத்தினார்க்கு எளிய பெருமாளே). The repeat is a near-identical refrain; 275 sets it after a plea for the loathsome body to fall, 298 after a plea to let go of the household before Death.

The Tirumanthiram says that by grace the five states cease to work and the five malas leave like evening darkness before a flame (சுடர்முனம் அந்தி இருள்போலும் ஐம்மலம் மாறுமே). 276 asks for the day when the states and tattvas perish (அவத்தை தத்துவம் அழிபட), the darkness is driven off and a single light spreads (இருளறை விலக்கு வித்தொரு சுடரொளி பரவ). The song's plea uses the Tirumanthiram's doctrine and its image of darkness ended by a flame.

276 asks that the tattvas perish (தத்துவம் அழிபட); 278 asks that he not perish in the great tattvas (கனத்த தத்துவம் உற்று அழியாமல்). The two neighbouring songs use the same verb with the tattvas in opposite directions: the bonds are to be destroyed so that the soul is not destroyed by them.

The Tirumanthiram calls the Lord companion on the way and medicine (வழித்துணையாய் மருந்தாய் இருந்தார்). 277 names the poet a servant who seeks Murugan as companion (உனைத் துணைதேடும் அடியேனை) and calls Murugan physician of the disease of birth (பவரோக வயித்திய நாத), against the sickness of becoming (பவநோய்) in the plea. Both join the two roles, companion and cure, in the one Lord.

The Tirumanthiram calls the body a bag (காயப்பை) of the senses and the bound inner faculties, which the Lord ties and unties. 280 calls it this bag of disease bound by the three humours and the senses (முக்குற்றத் தொடைப் புலனாலும் பிணித்த இப்பிணிப்பை) and asks for the purpose that cuts off its birth. The same bag, tied by the senses, is described by one as the Lord's work and by the other as something to be ended.

The Tirumanthiram says that seeking the Lord's feet without fault, the eight great siddhis are not hard for him (அரியது எனக்கில்லை அட்டமா சித்தி) because the Lord cut off his birth. 281 asks to be set at the red-gold feet by which all powers and the eight siddhis become easy (அகில சத்தியும் எட்டுறு சித்தியும் எளிதென). Both make the siddhis follow from the feet rather than be sought for themselves.

The Tirumanthiram says clarity is seeing the guru's form, saying his name, hearing his holy words (குருவின் திருவார்த்தை கேட்டல்) and thinking on him. 282 calls himself the evil man who has lost the guru's word and so abandoned the way of release (குருமொழி அற்றுக் கதிதனை விட்டிட்டிடு தீயக் கயவன்). The song shows the Tirumanthiram's rule from the other side: without the guru's word, desire takes the place of clarity.

The Kural's lover says the girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும்). 283 makes women's eyes a sharpened sword that rushes to the ears, cuts and pierces (வடிகூர் வாள் போல ... வெட்டித் தொளைத்து), and the Lord a rescuer from the prison of women's eyes (மாதர்கள் கண் சிறை). The killing eye the Kural admires the song asks to be saved from.

The Kural's lovesick woman says the sea of desire certainly exists and the safe raft to cross it does not (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). 284 names the seas of desire, birth and learning (ப்ரியக்கடல், கருக்கடல், கலைக்கடல்) and asks for a raft, the anklet-bright feet (கழற்புணை). The song answers the Kural's despair with a raft, on condition it is the Lord's.

The Naladiyar says learning has no shore (கல்வி கரையில) while the learner's days are few, so one must choose what is fitting, like the bird that leaves the water and drinks the milk. 284 puts the sea of the many arts (அநேகங் கலைக்கடல்) beside the seas of desire and birth as one more sea to whirl in. The Naladiyar's shoreless learning becomes in the song something to be crossed, not sifted.
audit_text_issue: 284 has broken characters (ப்ரியக்கடல் லு஡டும்).

note: Both are laments for a girl in love with Murugan, with the moon, the south wind and Kama's arrows as what wears her down; 24 is a mother's grief, 286 adds the town's women quarrelling in the street and asks for the god's garland.
Both confess begging praise of patrons in the language of gods and clouds; 292 goes further, quoting the poet comparing a poor patron to the six-faced Murugan himself, the god he should have praised.

Tirumular says the women and children who ate from the house do not follow the dead; 298 asks for that knowledge in advance, that wife, children, mother and goods become alien to the mind before the buffalo comes.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood, knowing grey hair will come; 296 is the prayer of one who did not, asking even when his hair is grey and his body ripens and falls to be taken into the supreme light.
The Kural makes women of divided heart the company of those whom Fortune has left; 299 lives the sequence, infatuation, all money given away, then hunger burning in the belly.

The Kural's woman says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). 285 shows a girl melted and helpless under Kama's arrows and asks that her chastity not perish (கற்பழியாதே) while she is given back her senses. The song prays for the girl to be spared what the Kural says desire does.

The Kural's woman says her sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure (ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக) and her mother's words as water. 286 lists among the things that have left the girl sleepless and helpless the women in the street who quarrel angrily over her (தெருவிற் பெண்கள் மிகக் கறுவிச் சண்டையிட), beside Kama's arrow, the south wind and the moon. Both count the town's talk as a cause of the love-sickness, not just a result.

The Kural warns against women who weigh the profit and then speak of their own virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). 287 says the courtesans babble bird-call arts precisely so that the money in a man's hand passes to them (கைப்பொருள் புக்கிடவே தான் புட்குரல் விச்சை பிதற்றும்). Both see the sweet speech as calculated for gain.

The Kural asks what learning is for if one does not worship the good feet of the pure knower (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). 288 confesses he has not left the babble of books (புத்தகப் பிதற்றை விட்டு) to praise Murugan, nor learned to melt praising the golden feet. The song is the Kural's question answered in the first person.

The Naladiyar says that studying worldly books while leaving the books of wisdom is only clamour (கலகல கூஉந் துணை) and does not remove confusion. 288 calls book-learning babble (புத்தகப் பிதற்று) that keeps him from praise and from a mind free of trouble (கலக்கமற்று). Both name the noise of reading that does not end bewilderment.

The Tirumanthiram tells of entering the Lord's city with the devotees of his devotees and being welcomed. 289, after calling himself proud, a miser and one who never bows at the shrine, asks to be given the assembly of those dear to Murugan (உனக்கு இனியார் தம் சபை தாராய்). The song asks for the company that, in the Tirumanthiram, brings even the unworthy to the Lord.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 289 has a corrupt word வன்பில஧முகன்.

note: The Kural's lover says that the jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). 290 calls the drooping in union (கலவியில் துவள் பிணி) an incurable disease (பிணி தீரா) and asks instead for a place in the Lord's refuge. On the reading that the பிணி is union itself, the Kural makes union the remedy and the song makes it the illness.

The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which gets there first whatever other way one devises (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள). 291 asks for the one thing that comes to erase what Brahma wrote (விதித்தன் எழுத்தினை தரவரும் ஒருபொருள்). If Brahma's writing is read as fate, the song claims there is something stronger than fate, which the Kural denies.
audit_text_issue: தரவரும் is odd for 'erase'; perhaps தறவரும்/தடுக்கவரும் — the sense 'counter' is likely but not secure.

note: The Kural's woman says the pleasure of love is a sea (இன்பம் கடல்) and its pain greater than the sea. 295 describes union's pleasure as waves on a shoreless sea (கலவி கரை அழி இன்ப அலை) and asks for the Lord's love so that the care of being tossed on it ends. Both make love's pleasure a sea; the song finds the trouble in the pleasure itself, the Kural in the pain that follows.

The Kural's woman asks whether Kama, who works on one side only, does not see her misery and grief (பருவரலும் பைதலும் காணான்கொல் காமன்). 297 tells of Kama, firm in deceit, loosing his five arrows on a lonely girl and asks the Lord whether he will not think of her wasting loneliness (பொன்றும் தனிமையை நினையாயோ). Both turn the love-sickness into a question to one who should see it.
audit_text_issue: 297's closing lines are garbled (லதனு஡டே, மலாணனும்).

note: The Kural says that for those set on cutting off birth even the body is too much, so why any further ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). 298 lists wife, children, old mother, town, garden, house and wealth and asks that all become alien to him before Death's men come, so that he may reach release (முத்தி வீடு அணுக). The song turns the Kural's rule into a plea, naming the ties one by one.
Both close by naming the poet's own work at Thanigai: 299 has Murugan delight in the Tamil garland of Arunagirinathan, and 301 has Thanigai as the place where those who chant Thiruppugazh gather.
audit_text_issue: 301's battle line has a garble (புநக்முள).

note: Thiruppugazh 300 lists the street women's carp eyes (சேல் உற்று எழு நேர்விழி) and cuckoo speech and says he who lacks ஞானமுடன் கல்வி will fade in மயல் and die. Naladiyar 44 is the knowledge he says he lacks at work: it refuses those who call eyes கயல் and வேல், having seen an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The pairing sets the poet's admitted want beside the renunciant's remedy.

Thiruppugazh 301 asks not to fall face down into every womb-pit (கருக்குழி தோறும் கவிழாதே) after sinking among women. Tirumanthiram 185 uses the same word: after harsh Death places them in the womb-pit (காலன் கருக்குழி வைத்தபின்) the base fall into it again, bewildered. Both make rebirth a repeated fall into a pit; the song asks to be spared it, the verse blames those who do not reflect.
audit_text_issue: 301's battle line has a garbled word (புநக்முள).

note: Both renounce the poet's trade of praising patrons; 292 quotes the comparisons he made, and 306 names the misers and the bards' claim that they are Pari and Kari, and asks instead for one word from Murugan.

The Kural begs those who beg not to beg of those who hide what they have; 306 confesses doing exactly that, praising misers as generous, and its answer is not to choose better patrons but to give patrons up for Murugan.
Both make Murugan the Tamil poet who sent the Jains to the stake, i.e. Sambandar; 299 adds the woman's husband brought back, 306 the Pandya's hunch and fever cured by the holy ash.
audit_text_issue: 299 has மிக்முள, probably மிக்குள.

note: Tirumular teaches that bindu and nada, raised in the body, join in samadhi; 305 uses the same terms but says the state cannot be reached even by jnanis and silent sages, and asks Murugan to come and give it.

Thiruppugazh 302 borrows the lovesick girl's afflictions, Kama's arrows, the moon, and the many women who learned slander (வசை கற்ற பல தத்தையர்), and asks for பத்தி and முத்தி as the cure. Kural 1147 has the girl say the town's gossip (ஊரவர் கெளவை) is manure and her mother's words water for this sickness. The song takes over the Kural's alar convention, where slander feeds the love it attacks, and turns the lover's sickness into the devotee's.
audit_text_issue: 302's இசைபட்ட திகிரி is unclear.

note: Kural 353 says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) heaven is nearer than earth. Thiruppugazh 303 asks Murugan to dwell in the heart with compassion so that troubles and doubts are scattered (இடர் சங்கைகள் கலங்க அருள்வாயே). The Kural makes the clearing of doubt the seeker's attainment; the song adds that it comes as grace from within the heart.

Kural 1183 has the woman say her lover took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor (நோயும் பசலையும்) in exchange. Thiruppugazh 304 sets one such line inside a praise song: is it fitting that the girl who bows to Murugan's flower feet should droop with pallor and infatuation (பசலை மயல்கொடு தளர்வது அழகோ)? The akam complaint against the absent lover is addressed to the god.

Thiruppugazh 307 calls the courtesans women who speak many flattering words (நிதமொழி பலகூறிகள்), sell their arts for a price (கலைபகர் விலைமாதர்கள்) and ruin the families of young men (இளைஞர்கள் குடிகேடிகள்). Kural 911 locates the harm in the same place: the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth, not love, bring disgrace. Both make the trade and the speech, not desire alone, the charge.
audit_text_issue: 307 line 4 'நி முடனை' appears to have lost a syllable.

note: Both confess the poet's begging trade, praising patrons as wishing trees and clouds; 310 adds the name of the Sangam giver Kumanan and calls the flattery a blind theft of the words owed to the Lord.
Tirumular says the Lord is not the thing the six sects hold; 314 makes him the truth hard for the six sects who quarrel daily, and yet the common ground (பொது) that holds all.

Both set the Lord who is one with everything yet apart against the confusion of the six sects; 257 mocks their images and wealth, 314 their angry argument, and asks to teach the truth in every direction.
Both see through the bubble: the Naladiyar's body is a bubble in the rain that forms and bursts, while 316 sees the whole world (ப்ரபஞ்சம்) as a bubble, and asks for the ripeness to reach the Lord.

Both picture the old man with failing speech or senses, leaning on a stick, staggering, teeth gone; the Naladiyar's still has eyes for desire, while 319 adds the disgust of his kin and wife and asks for the feet before that day.
Both picture the poet's old age with stick, white hair and loose teeth while others mock; 68 asks Murugan to come at the hour of death, 319 to reach the feet before that despised birth.

Thiruppugazh 308 names Murugan the young one who gave the holy padhigams (ஆன திருப்பதிகம் அருள் இளையோனே), a short song's single allusion. Thiruppugazh 837 tells the whole Sambandar story as Murugan's: the Kauniya brahmin child who drank Uma's milk, a poet beyond all singers, the disputants impaled and the Pandya's hunch straightened. Read together, 837 shows what the brief epithet in 308 carries: Murugan identified with the child poet of the Thevaram.

Thiruppugazh 309 tells Daksha's sacrifice by its details: the god of the discus and Brahma struck in fear, the sun's teeth knocked out (கதிரவன் பல் குற்றி), the bird's wings cut, Daksha disgraced; and then Siva, who raged that day, worships Murugan at Kachi. Tirumanthiram 358 lists the same maimed gods, Hari, Brahma, Daksha, the sun, and says they fell without Hara's grace (அரனருள் இன்றி). The same story serves Tirumular to show Siva's grace as decisive and the song to set even that angry Siva among Murugan's worshippers.

Kural 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு) than begging, even water for a cow. Thiruppugazh 310 shows the poet's tongue in that disgrace: he learned the poetry owed to Murugan, then flattered patrons as the wishing tree and as Kumanan, blind with begging (இரவான குருடு), stealing every word (சத்தம் அனைத்தும் திருடி) to fit them. The song applies the Kural's verdict to a bard's trade, where the begging also misuses the words.

Thiruppugazh 311 builds the body from bones, blood and bound nerves (அத்தி ... இரத்தம் செறி நரம்பிட்டுக் கட்டிய சட்டம்), a prison of deeds and a raft in the sea of birth. Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, linking sinews and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman. The same anatomical catalogue serves the Naladiyar against desire and the song against embodiment and birth.

Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்) has not found a home of its own (புக்கில்). Thiruppugazh 311 calls the body by that very word, a hollow dwelling the instruments move into (கரணாதி குடிபுகும் பொக்கப் புக்கில்). Where the Kural denies the life a புக்கில், the song grants the body the name only to call it hollow.

Thiruppugazh 312 asks whether, with clinging gone (பசை ஒழிந்து), he will gain the one meaning enclosed in every object (பொருள்தொறும் பொத்தப்பட்டது ஒர் அத்தம்). Tirumanthiram 440 gives the image for such a meaning: one clay becomes many good vessels, and the Lord is one in all the wombs. The verse states the pervasion the song asks to come to know.
audit_text_issue: 312 plea lines obscure

note: Thiruppugazh 314 names the Lord the common ground that holds all the tattvas and stands free of them (சகலமும் பற்றிப் பற்றற நிற்கும் பொது). Thiruppugazh 313 turns the same phrase onto the devotee: the high vow by which those who reach the supreme state, held in rapture, stand free of attachment (பரவசம் பற்றிப் பற்றற நிற்கும் பரவ்ரதம்), which the poet confesses he lacks. The formula describes the Lord in one song and the devotee's goal in the other.
audit_text_issue: 313's Goddess litany hard to divide.

note: Thiruppugazh 315 names Murugan the thief who hides in the mind (சித்தத்துக்குள் ஒளிக்கும் கரவடன்). Tirumanthiram 1531 calls the Lord the one hidden within the heart (உள்ளத்துளே தான் கரந்து) and the thief-chief (கள்ளத் தலைவன்) who enters and leaves the hut of the body, unknown to those who quarrel. Both give the indwelling Lord a thief's secrecy: he is in the heart and is not seen there.

Kural 151 calls bearing with those who scorn you the highest thing, like the earth that holds up those who dig into it. Thiruppugazh 318 asks what words could match the forbearance (பொறை) by which Murugan bore the poet's faults (பிழையுடன் பட்டு) and set him among devotees. The virtue the Kural asks of a man is praised in the god, with the poet in the digger's place.

Thiruppugazh 319 pictures the old man with teeth fallen, scorned by others, his descendants and his own wife (அரிவையும் துத்துத் துத்து என). Tirumanthiram 180 has the speaker say the women who once desired him like cane juice now find him like the bitter kaanjiram fruit. Both measure old age by the turning away of those who once desired one; the song asks for the feet before that despised birth comes.

Kural 350 commands: cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging (பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை), so as to let clinging go. Thiruppugazh 320 lists among the poet's faults that he has not the least bond (பற்றுச் சற்றும் இல்) to the one who holds all and stands free of clinging (பற்றற நிற்கும் பொருள்). The song names as its lack the very attachment the Kural prescribes.

Kural 338 likens the body-life bond to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழிய). Thiruppugazh 321 calls the body a great hut (பெருங்குடில்) and a rag given by father and mother, from which Death drives out the breath and drags it away alone (தனியில் இழுக்கப்படும்). Both picture death as the life leaving its shelter, the Kural with the body left alone and the song with the life taken alone.
audit_text_issue: 321's praise lines hard to divide.

note: Kural 236 says: if you are born, be born with renown (தோன்றின் புகழொடு தோன்றுக). Thiruppugazh 322 asks for just such a birth (சனனம் பெறாதோ) in which many poets honour him as a true poet, a master of the tattvas and a man of virtue, and the world calls him forbearing and a renunciate. The song turns the Kural's renown into a devotee's, asked as the road to the supreme.
Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, wounded by Kama's flower arrows and a burning moon, and ask him to come with his garland; 337 adds that the moon rose with the poison of the sea.

Both are laments for a lovesick girl in another's voice, with the classical torments of the evening world: 24 the anril bird, south wind and crescent, 334 the roaring sea and the crescent seized by the serpent.

The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; 329 asks for the clinging that does not suffer, set against the clinging to food and wealth, if its line is divided so.
Both have the heirs at the deathbed thinking of property: in 68 the young sons ask about debts and goods, in 324 the kin cry 'a little for me, a little for you' over the wealth and gold plate.
Both confess worshipping patrons for gold; 310 tells the flattery at length, 331 sets the patrons' feet (தருவோர் தாள்) against the Lord's in a few beats.
audit_text_issue: 331's doubled syllables make the first lines' division uncertain.

note: The Thiruppugazh song lists the body by its parts, எலுப்பு, சுக்கிலம், அத்தம், தடி, தொக்கு (bone, semen, blood, fat, skin), and calls it a pot (கடம்) it does not want to wander tending. The Naladiyar verse runs the same kind of list, குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும் ... தோலும் ... தடியும், and asks which of these is the garlanded woman. The Naladiyar turns the catalogue on the desired woman's body, the song on the poet's own, both to undo the desire named beside it.
audit_text_issue: 323's third line is too dense to divide.

note: In 324 எனக்குச் சற்று உனக்குச் சற்று ('a little for me, a little for you') is the heirs squabbling over the dead man's gold plate. In 325 the same words name the poet's own craving (எனக்குச் சற்று உனக்குச் சற்று எனும் ஆசைச் சிறை), a prison he lives in. Read together, the heirs' greed at the deathbed is the same grasping the living man already has.

The Thiruppugazh song builds the body as a house: walls plastered with flesh and blood (இறைச்சிப் பற்று இரத்தத்து இட்டு ... சுவர் கோலி) on a frame of bone (எலுப்புக் கட்டளை). The Tirumanthiram verse also makes the body a hut, with two posts, a ridge beam and thirty-two rafters (காலும் இரண்டு முகட்டலகு ஒன்று), whose roof comes apart so the life cannot re-enter. The Tirumanthiram stresses the house's collapse, the song the prison of craving lived in while it stands.

The Thiruppugazh song tells the funeral in quick verbs: the corpse is carried, the drums beat (எடுத்துக் கொட்டிட), it is laid on the logs and the fire set (கட்டைப்பட ... அனல் ... கொளுத்தி), and the kin let go and leave. The Naladiyar verse counts the funeral drum's beats (முக்காலைக் கொட்டினுள்) until the corpse is covered and the fire taken up, the dying carrying the dead. The song uses the scene as the deadline before which it asks to sing the feet in Tamil, the Naladiyar as a call to see that the bearers are next.

The Thiruppugazh song ends a life with the kin who burn the false corpse and go home (பொய்ப் பிணத்தைச் சுட்டு அகத்திற் புக்கு அனைவோரும்). The Tirumanthiram verse has the town wail, rename him a corpse (பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு), burn him, bathe and stop thinking of him (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both make the same point, that the kin's mourning ends at the pyre; the song then asks that the clinging of birth itself end.

The Thiruppugazh song pictures women who bind young men by the neck and unite on gold-adorned beds, and asks to avoid such unions (புணர் மாதர் பொருத்தத்தைத் தவிர்த்து) and gain the golden feet. The Naladiyar verse says those who mean to reach the right path (செந்நெறிச் சேர்தும் என்பார்) do not embrace the breasts of such women. Both make giving up that embrace the condition of reaching the goal, the Naladiyar as a rule, the song as a plea.

The short Thiruppugazh song praises the holy feet fit to be set on the round flower (வட்டப் புட்பத் தலம் மீதே வைக்கத் தக்க திருபாதா) and asks the Lord to take hold of one whirling through every birth. The Kural speaks of the great feet of the one who moved upon the flower (மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் மாணடி) and promises long life to those who reach them. The flower that bears the feet is shared; if it is the heart's lotus, as the song's nuance suggests, both place the feet there.

Two songs of the same chapter make the same plea in nearly the same words: 332 fears not joining the pure devotees of pure mind (சுத்தச் சித்தத்து ... பத்தர்க்கு) and being trapped by women who bring sickness (பிணிமாதர்), and 335 asks to join the pure devotees of pure mind (சுத்தச் சித்தத்துப் பத்திப் பத்தர்க்கு ஒத்து) instead of whirling in grief over women. A near-repeat: the company of devotees is set against the company of women in both.

The Kural says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). The Thiruppugazh song shows the tongue already failing in old age, coughing and stammering (திக்கித் திக்கிக் குளறி), and asks to speak pure Tamil with conviction (சுத்தச் சித்தித் தமிழைத் திட்டத்துக்குப் புகல). It applies the Kural's deadline to speech itself: what must be done before the tongue fails is to praise.

The Thiruppugazh song calls the body a hollow bag of skin (பொக்குப் பை ... தொக்குப் பை), a false hut the poet keeps tending. The Naladiyar verse calls it a skin bag (தோற்பை) in which a dancer works until he leaves, after which it does not matter what is done with it. The same skin bag serves the Naladiyar to show the body's worthlessness once the life goes, and the song to show the folly of tending it while alive.

The Thiruppugazh song describes women's eyes as vel, fish and poison (அயில் அப்புக் கயல் ... நச்சுக் கண்) and confesses that the poet staggers, loses sleep and work, and whirls for them. The Naladiyar verse names the same figures, darting carp and spears (பொருகயல் வேல்), refuses to give way to them, and sees the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The song is the man who gave way, the Naladiyar the one who will not.
Both picture old age by teeth lost and a body bent on a stick. The Naladiyar uses it against the old man who still desires; 341 carries the picture on to the corpse burned and the kin going home.

Both are laments in another voice for a girl lovesick for Murugan, worn down by the night's sights and sounds: in 24 the crescent, the south wind and the anril bird, in 344 the stained moon and the roaring sea.
The Kural warns that women who desire a man for his wealth bring him harm; 345 tells the harm from inside, the wealth given away and a poverty that burns like the undersea fire.

The Tirumanthiram verse says Vedanta is where craving ends (வேதாந்தமாவது வேட்கை ஒழிந்திடம்). The Thiruppugazh song asks to give up the experience of infatuation with a woman (மால்கூர்ந்திடும் அநுபோகம் இனிவிட) and be given the feet that are the substance of the Vedantic house of supreme bliss (வேதாந்த பரமசுக வீடாம் பொருள்). The song places the end of craving and the Vedantic goal together as the Tirumanthiram does, and names the feet as that goal.

The Thiruppugazh song sets aside the quarrelsome sectarians (கலக காரண துற்குண சமயிகள்) who find no single way (ஒருகதி காணாது) among their many texts. The Tirumanthiram verse says the six sects are six roads to one city, and those who call this one good and that one bad are like a dog barking at a hill (குன்று குரைத்தெழு நாய்). Both reject the sects' quarrel; the Tirumanthiram grants the roads a common end, while the song asks to be told the silent truth beyond them.

The Thiruppugazh song's praise hails Uma as the lady who kept her grace on the poet and ruled him (எனையருள் வைத்திட்டு ஆண்ட நாயகி), the maiden (குமரி), Sivakami. The Tirumanthiram verse hails the mother who stands within the poet's own strength (என் ஆற்றலுள் நிற்கும்), the girl of rare penance (அருந்தவப் பெண்பிள்ளை). Both address the Goddess as a young girl and as the poet's personal ruler, not only as Siva's consort.

The Thiruppugazh song gives the death as the kin's wailing heard: 'he is dead, I am ruined' (செத்தார் கெட்டேன் அஆ உஉ), then they burn and leave. The Naladiyar verse gives it as the people's quick report: he stood, sat, lay down, and with his kin wailing he was gone (நின்றான் இருந்தான் கிடந்தான் தன் கேள் அலறச் சென்றான்). The Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good now, the song asks whether the bewilderment will not end.

The short Thiruppugazh song asks for a heart of devotion so that it may sing (பாடப் பத்திச் சித்தம் எனக்குத் தரவேணும்). The Tirumanthiram verse says the Lord is within the devotion of those who make verse (பாவினையாளர் தம் பாகவத்துள்ளவன்). The song asks for the devotion that the Tirumanthiram finds the Lord dwelling in, in those who sing; the Tirumanthiram line is uncertain in sense.

The Tirumanthiram verse says fools take Siva's burning of the three cities literally; the three cities are the work of the three impurities (முப்புரமாவது மும்மல காரியம்). The Thiruppugazh song speaks of burning the forest of the three cities to ash and uprooting the sheath of sleep (முப்புரக் காடு நீறெழச் சாடி நித்திரைக் கோசம் வேரற) as the poet's own inner attainment of jivanmukti. The song applies the Tirumanthiram's inner reading to the devotee, who can burn the three cities and still slip back.

The Thiruppugazh song, spoken for a lovesick girl, names the stained moon that the poisonous serpent seeks (நச்சரவம் ... நச்சுமிழ் களங்க மதி) among her torments. The Kural's woman says the gossip from one day's meeting has spread like the serpent seizing the moon (திங்களைப் பாம்பு கொண்டற்று). Both akam voices use the eclipse: the Kural for scandal swallowing the lovers, the song for the moon itself as a wounded tormentor.

The Naladiyar verse says a courtesan's love, like a lamp's flame, ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). The Thiruppugazh song tells the result from the man's side: he gave much real wealth to quick-talking women until his life withered (மெய்ப்பொருள் பல கொடுத்து அற உயிர் வாடா), and now lives in poverty that burns like the undersea fire (மிடியெனப் பெரு வடவை). The song is the Naladiyar's emptied hand, lived.

The Thiruppugazh song describes women who talk money, send go-betweens and want many men's leavings (பலர் எச்சிற்கு ஆசைக் காரிகள்), and asks whether such company befits him (சந்தமாமோ). The Kural says those of refined understanding will not plunge into the base charms of women whose goodness is common to all (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம்). Both rest the refusal on the women being shared by many.

The Thiruppugazh song asks for That which is hard to tell people (மக்கட்குக் கூறரிதானது), cannot be held in the chain of tattvas (தத்வத்திற் கோவைபடாதது) and is the cause of release. The Tirumanthiram verse speaks of the tattva hard to tell (சாற்றரிதாகிய தத்துவம்) whose attainment brings the senses to rest and union with the Supreme. Both name the goal first as what cannot be spoken; the song piles up such negations, the Tirumanthiram says what follows its attainment.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 347: வெருபம் in the praise looks garbled.

note: The Thiruppugazh song lists the woman's deer-like eyes and spear-like eyes (மறிபோலுகின்ற விழி, அயிலே நிகர்ந்த விழி) among what destroys the poet's understanding (அறிவே அழிந்து). The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ), finding all three in it. The doe's softness and the deadly weapon are joined in both; the Kural is wonder, the song a plea not to swoon.

The Thiruppugazh song names the women outright as priced (விலைமாதர்), cheats whose way of life brings sickness of mind and sores. The Naladiyar verse says such women find a moneyless man poison and even an oil-presser sugar if he has wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம்). Both make price the whole of the bond; the song adds what it costs the man in body and mind.

The Tirumanthiram verse says that if one knows how to reach the light standing within, there is no quarrel at all (பிணக்கொன்றும் இல்லை). The Thiruppugazh song praises those who leave the wave-loud, quarrelsome sects and their hard learning, and by grace, free of attachment, know the Lord, melt and reach his feet, and asks a place among them. The song shows the people the Tirumanthiram describes, those past the sects' quarrel by inner knowing.

In 501 the poet was drawn to women like a needle to a magnet (காந்தமொடு ஊசியென மடவார்பால்), the image of compulsion. In 351 the magnet and needle (காந்தக் கல்லும் ஊசியுமே) are named in the praise as what was sung in Tamil at Kanchi, while the plea vows not to forget the one word despite the women's eyes. The same figure stands for the pull of women in one song and appears in the Lord's praise in the other; the division of 351's line is uncertain.
audit_text_issue: 351 several lines garbled (பொலாய்ந்துப்பாணி)

note: Both songs confess the poet's trade: in 352 he made poems praising senseless, ungrateful men who never bow to the Lord (அவலர் மேல் சொற்கள் கொண்டு கவிகள் ஆக்கி) and spent the gain on women, in 310 he flattered patrons as the wishing tree and Kumanan and stole all words of meaning to suit them (சத்தம் அனைத்தும் திருடி). A near-repeat of the confession across the Kanchi songs; 352 adds where the money went.

Tirumular, by Nandi's command, promises that breath tied fast keeps the body for thousands of years; 355 calls the yogi who holds the breath to make the impermanent flesh last a fool. The conflict holds if 722 is read as bodily longevity sought for its own sake and 355 as rejecting that practice, not only its misuse.
Both say the courtesan desires the wealth and not the man; 357 sharpens it into a measure, the desire acted exactly as far as the gold goes.
Both confess the poet's trade of praising unworthy patrons for gold: 352 tells it in summary, 358 quotes the begging speech itself, the boast of prosody and the call for jewels.
Both take the body apart into entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin. The Naladiyar asks which part is the desired woman; 362 makes the inventory the hut in which the poet's own senses run wild.
Both speak of the Absolute by what cannot reach it: 347 by learning, the mind, the tattvas and the Vedas, 359 by chariyai, kiriyai and the turiya state.

The Kural warns that the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of bangled women who want wealth, not love, bring harm. Among the courtesans' arts 353 lists binding men with idle talk (வம்புரை கூறி வளைத்து இணக்கவும்) and taking their wealth without anyone blaming them (நிந்தை செய்யாது பொருட்பறிக்கவும்). The song shows the Kural's point at work: the talk is the tool and the wealth is the aim, and the harm goes unblamed.

The Kural says a head that does not bow at the feet of the Lord is as useless as a sense organ that cannot sense (கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே). 354 asks whether he must perish without having sung with love on his tongue (அன்புடன் நாவிற் பா) and without worship of the feet by his hand (பாதமும் அங்கையின் நானிற் பூசையும் அணியாமல்). Both measure the bodily organs by whether they serve the feet: the Kural names the head, the song the tongue and the hand.

In the Kural the lover says he once had shame and manliness, and now has only the palmyra horse that the lustful ride (காமுற்றார் ஏறும் மடல்). 356 says the breasts of these women make even renouncers ride the madal of desire (துறவோரை ஆசைமடல் ஊர்வித்து ஆளும்). The song carries the Kural's figure past the lover to the ascetic: the madal now marks the fall of a renouncer, not only of a man's pride.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 356 has a corrupt glyph in உ஡ர்வித்.

note: The Tirumanthiram calls dull (ஊமர்) those who disregard the body as filth (மலமென்று உடம்பை மதியாத), and says that holding it as good grasps the cosmos in it. 357 calls his own body a worm-filled cave of filth he has built as a house (புழுக்கொள் மலக் குகை வீடு கட்டி இருக்கும் எனக்கு). On the reading that மலம் in the Tirumanthiram means filth, the song takes exactly the stance the Tirumanthiram rejects.

The Tirumanthiram places the jnani and the silent one above those of chariyai and kiriyai (தானிக் குலத்தோர் சரியை கிரியையே). 359 describes the One that those who practise chariyai and kiriyai cannot tell (ஓது சரியை க்ரியையும் புணர்ந்தவர் எவராலும் ஓத அரிய), beyond turiya, seen only by those with Siva-knowledge (சிவஞானம் சால உடையவர் கண்டுகொண்டது). Both rank the first two stages below knowledge; the song states it from the side of the goal, the Tirumanthiram from the side of the seeker.

The Tirumanthiram teaches that kin is one and God is one (ஒன்றே குலமும் ஒருவனே தேவனும்). Among the marks of the Absolute, 359 says it has neither caste nor clan (சாதி குலமும் இலது). The Tirumanthiram makes one clan of all people under one God; the song carries the same denial of division into the nature of God itself.

The Kural says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is a deadly அணங்கு to those who lack discerning knowledge (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு). 360 says the courtesans take as a sacrifice the lives of the lustful who do not know the higher path (பரநெறி உணரா அக்காமுகர் உயிர்பலி கொளும்). Both find the danger in the man's want of knowledge, and both make it a matter of life and death.

The Tirumanthiram's speaker, having driven off lust, anger and delusion (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் இவைகடிந்து), reaches the abode within the sound Om. 361 calls himself the sinner in whom lust, anger and greed are not destroyed (காமக் க்ரோத லோப ... இவை சிதையாத பாவி) and asks for the path of knowledge, yoga, japa and tapas. The two verses stand on either side of the same condition: the Tirumanthiram speaks after the inner enemies are driven off, the song before, asking for the means.
audit_text_issue: Song 361's fourth vice (மப) is garbled.

note: 355, in the same chapter, refuses to be a foolish yogi who holds the breath so it does not leave the nostrils (நாசி அடைதல் அந வாயு ஓடாத வகை சாதித்து) thinking the flesh will last. 361 asks to love the path of knowledge praised by those who make the breath circle (வாயு வலம்வர லாலிப்பார்கள்), and yoga, japa and tapas. Read together, 355 does not reject breath practice as such but its use to keep the impermanent body (அனித்தமான ஊன் நாளும் இருப்பதாகவே).

The Tirumanthiram says five elephants live in the forest (அஞ்சுள ஆனை அடவியுள் வாழ்வன) and the five letters are their goad. 362 says the five senses run into the forest (ஐம்புல அடவியில் ஓடும்) and drive him to the five great sins, so that he never tries worship or meditation. Both place the five senses in a forest; the Tirumanthiram supplies the goad whose absence the song confesses.

358 names Murugan who at Tamil Madurai put the palm leaf into fire and water against the Jains (அனற்கே புனற்கே வரைந்த ஏடு) and won the name of father of dharma. 363 asks to be given the wise life of Madurai of mansions (மாடக் கூடற் பதி ஞான வாழ்வை). Read beside 358, the short song's 'wisdom at Madurai' may point to that same contest of Sambandar, whom the songs identify with Murugan.

The Naladiyar says that even if he were Mal whom the gods worship, women tender as young shoots would send away a man with nothing in his hand, bowing with folded hands (விடுப்பர் தங்கையால் தொழுது). Among the courtesans' traits 366 lists that they gently put out those without money (காசற்றாரை இதத்தில் ஒழிச்சிகள்). Both stress that the dismissal is courteous: the politeness is part of the trade.

The Tirumanthiram says that after knowing the knowledge that knows 'this' (ஈதென்று அறியும் அறிவை அறிந்தபின்) one is of the nature that knows. 367 says Murugan, in prattling speech, taught Siva that the meaning is to know the knower (அறிவை அறிவது பொருளென அருளிய). The song gives as the content of the child's teaching to Siva the same knowing of knowledge that the Tirumanthiram names as the final state.

Both see the sects as people wandering off, each crying its own 'this is supreme'. Tirumular's remedy is to go the ordained way and seek the King; 369's is to melt in devotion and drop 'mine', when the reality the Vedas proclaim is easily gained.

Both use the Kural's word for courtesans (வரைவிலா, வரைவில்) and picture their pleasure as something a man sinks into: the Kural's mire (அளறு), 370's sea of pleasure, which 370 sets against a second sea, the bliss of Siva.
Both make the courtesan a woman who weighs: in the Kural she weighs the profit and speaks of her virtue to match, in 373 she measures her heart to the money (திரவியம் அளவளவு அளவியர்).

Both end the plea with the same vow, not to forget the word and the two feet given at Arunai; 371 confesses every pleasure first, 373 every deceit of the women, and both keep the vow inside the confession.

The Kural's lover discovers that Death has a woman's eyes, half in wonder; 374 extends the discovery to every charm, breasts as Yama and the pearls on them as Yama's rope, and turns it into a reason to turn away.
Both open the hour of death with the same formula, Yama casting his thick-handed noose (பரியகைப் பாசம் விட்டு எறியும்); 376 asks for the life to be saved, 378 for the fault to be forgiven.
Both count the flute among the torments of the lovesick woman: the Kural's herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills, and 380's sweet lone flute is one of four things she asks to survive.

The Tirumanthiram says that wealth which seemed lasting is like writing on water (நீள்பொருள் நீர்மேல் எழுத்துஒத்து) and urges conquest of the senses. 368 says 'enough, enough' to births like letters on water (சலில லிபியன சனனமும் அலமலம்). The same figure of impermanence is applied by the Tirumanthiram to wealth and by the song to birth itself.

941 says 'enough, enough' (அலமலம்) to the quarrels of the faiths, to worship for gain and even to the mantra lore of the Saiva texts, and asks for the highest state. 368 uses the same refrain against lovemaking, the poet's flattery, perverse sects and births, and asks for the feet and silence. The two songs, in distant chapters, use one refusal formula; 941 extends it even to Siva's own scriptures.
audit_text_issue: 941 has encoding damage (சுக் ¡£பர், வயலு¡ரா).

note: 358 confesses the court poet's begging speech, offering a patron a madal or kovai and calling him without equal on earth. Among the things 368 sweeps away with அலமலம் is the learning that likens men of the world to the wish-tree (உலகோரைத் தருவை நிகரிடு புலமையும் அலமலம்). The later song renounces in one phrase the trade the earlier one dramatises.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. 369 ends its chain of conditions with the casting off of the impurity called 'mine' (எனதெனும் மலம் அறில்), after which the reality without rising or death is easily gained in knowledge. Both make the end of 'mine' the condition of the highest state; the song calls it a மலம்.

The Tirumanthiram says that when knower, known and even the mark of knowledge subside, the clear silence becomes Siva's bliss (தேறிய மோனம் சிவானந்தமாமே). 370 asks when his life, tossing in the sea of pleasure the courtesans give (வரைவில் அரிவையர் தருசுக சலதி), will plunge into the sea of silent Siva-bliss (மவுன சிவசுக சலதி). Both identify silence with Siva's bliss; the song sets it against the women's pleasure as one sea against another.

The Kural says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard or strength but the madal (ஏமம் மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). 371 ends with Murugan, mad with longing for the doe of the millet field, writing a lone madal (மயல்கொடு தனிமடல் எழுதிய). The lover's last resort in the Kural is given in the song to the god, who takes the desperate lover's part for Valli.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 has a garbled word (நிற்முசும்).

note: 372 asks not to spend days praising women in set comparisons, hair as darkness, face as moon, eyes as arrows, breasts as lotus buds (குழலென ... முகமென ... கணைவிழி ... முலையென). 374 takes the same comparisons and denies each (முகிலல, அமுதல, மடுவல), replacing it with a danger: the breasts are Yama, the woman a form built of deeds. 372 renounces the similes; 374 inverts them into teaching.
audit_text_issue: 372 has garbled glyphs in its first lines.
