note: 1231 sets beside the women who sell love the poets who learn to make verses on their limbs (அவயவங்களைப் பாடு கவி தெரிந்து கற்பார்கள்), and offers his song to the feet instead. 372 asks not to praise women's bodies in set comparisons day and night but to think of Murugan's procession on the peacock. Both songs, in distant chapters, name love poetry on women's bodies as a fault and turn the poet's art to the Lord.
audit_text_issue: 372 has garbled glyphs in the opening lines

note: The Tirumanthiram says people do not know what head and foot are (தலைஅடி யாவது அறியார்) and places them in the body, at the crown and the root. 373 calls the poet one who knows neither foot nor crown (அடிமுடி அறிகிலன்), yet who will not forget the silent word and the two feet given at Arunai. Both use not knowing foot and crown for the soul's ignorance; the Tirumanthiram answers it with knowledge of the body, the song with the remembered feet.

The Tirumanthiram tells of those who married with sweet talk, lived with the husband till their love was sated, then laid him on the bier and wept as was fitting (ஆசந்தி மேல்வைத்து அமைய அழுதிட்டு). 376 pictures the wife wailing 'husband, I am ruined' (கணவ கெட்டேன்) and the sons crying 'father' round the bier (பாடையில்). The Tirumanthiram reads the wife's weeping as measured custom; the song lets it be heard and turns from it to Murugan as the only protection at the noose.

The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). 377 asks whether he will worship the two feet that are a raft for the life (உயிர்ப் புணை இணைத் தாள்). The song makes the feet themselves the float by which the Kural's sea is crossed.

The Tirumanthiram tells how the town wails, names the man a corpse, burns him in the thorny ground, then bathes in water and forgets him (நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). 378 imagines Death's noose, the kin no longer holding on (பற்றாது), the body left to the spreading fire and parted in the waves (படரெரிக் கூடுவிட்டு அலைநீரிற் பிரியும்). Both follow the dead through fire and water to the kin's letting go; the song then asks to hear Murugan say 'I have forgiven your fault'.

In the Kural the woman says her sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure (ஊரவர் கெளவை எருவாக). 379, in a lovesick woman's voice, names the excess blame the women of the town speak (வருணமட மாதர் கற்ற வசையின் மிகை பேச) among the things, with moon and Kama's arrows, that wear her life away. The song keeps the akam rule that gossip feeds the sickness, now with the god as the absent lover.

A near-repeat: both songs set the full moon born of the submarine fire (வடவாமுகத்தின் எழுகனலிலே பிறக்கும் முழுமதி; வடவை அனலூடு புக்கு முழுகி எழு மாமதி), the sweet music and Kama against the lovesick girl and ask Murugan to come on his peacock (மயிலில் ஏறி ... வரவேணும்), and both name him the guru who taught Siva. 380 speaks in the girl's own voice; 381 speaks of her, adding the wailing sea.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 381 has a corrupt glyph (வடவையனலு஡டு).

note: The Kural says good deeds must be hastened to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 382 asks whether, before he dies with his old deeds unshed (ஊழ்வினை விடாமல் சாவதன் முனே), Murugan will take him into service (ஏவற் கொண்டிடாயோ). Both set the deadline at death's approach; the Kural asks the man to act, the song asks the Lord to claim him.
Both quote the courtesan's invitation, 'come to my house' (21's இங்கு நின்றது என் வீடே, 384's அருகு வீடு இதுதான் அதில் வாரும்); 384 adds that it is spoken to men of wealth and sworn on oaths.
audit_text_issue: 21 has garbled words (வா஡ண, நநடுர் கேர்டுர்).

note: Both give a woman's eyes the power to eat the life of those who look: the Kural's lover says it of one girl with wonder, 386 of women's eyes in general, likened to Siva's throat-poison and Murugan's vel.
Both liken women's eyes to poison and end with Murugan hiding his own form to follow the hunter girl; 387 takes the simile further, to the poison of the churned sea that cracked the cosmic egg.
Both stage the death-bed with wife and sons weeping before Yama comes; 376 asks for the life to be saved, 388 for knowledge to clear his troubles so that he can think of the feet.
audit_text_issue: 388's opening (இரவியு மதியுந் தெரிவுற எழுமம் புவி) is of uncertain sense.

note: Both set the uproar of the sects (கோலாகலச் சமயம், கலக விபரித பர சமயிகள்) against a knowledge they cannot reach: 369's reality without birth or death, 394's seal of silence.
audit_text_issue: 394 line 1 garbled (தொழுத்மு டூடு, கடலு஡டுற்).

note: Both make the town's talk feed the girl's love-sickness: in the Kural gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water, in 397 the town reproaches her alongside the north wind.

The song's women are அமுதம் ஊறு சொல் ஆகிய தோகையர் who call பொருளுளாரை, men of wealth, with 'என் ஆணை உன் ஆணை, my house is near'; the Kural says the இன்சொல் of women who want பொருள், not love (அன்பின் விழையார்), brings harm. The pairing shows Arunagiri dramatising the Kural's 'sweet words' as an actual street invitation sealed with an oath.

The song calls the women கரவது ஆம் மன மாதர்கள், women whose hearts hide, and the poet a fool who fell into their நீள்வலை not knowing true love (நேசமது அறியாத). Naladiyar 379 says such women hide a harmful heart (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் உள்ளடக்கி) and that those who trust their words and call them 'ours' are deceived. Both put the danger in the concealed heart behind the speech.

The song says the women's eyes are the churning-poison itself, eye-nets that take lovers' lives as sacrifice (காமுகர் உயிர்பலி கவர்வுறு ... விழிவலை). The Kural's man asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both fuse the eye with a killer, the Kural in wonder, the song in alarm.

The song pictures the deathbed with wife and fine sons weeping, hearts melting (மாதும் எழில் புதல்வரும் நின்று அழுது உளம் உருகும்), as Yama comes, and asks to think of the feet first. Tirumanthiram 157 follows the same kin, wives and children (சுற்றமும் பெண்டிரும் மக்களும்) to the town's edge, where they turn back and leave him to the fire. Together they show why the song asks for a refuge other than the weeping family.

The song has Death coming by fate's way, saying today is the day to take the life (இன்று உயிர்கொளும் நெறி இன்று என), and asks to worship the feet before (வருமுன்) that tumult of weeping kin. Naladiyar 20 says merciless Death roams looking for his people (ஆட்பார்த்து உழலும் அருளில் கூற்று), so take provisions in good time. Both press for action before Death's appointed hour; the provision in the song is worship of the feet.

The song lists the moon, the small south wind that comes like fire (எரியென வரு சிறு தென்றல்) and Kama's arrows as attackers of the girl alone on her flower bed. The Kural's woman says evening comes like strangers to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல). Both turn the hours and breezes of love-poetry into armed assailants of the lone woman.

The song asks to enter the shade of the feet, which are a raft of lotus (சததள மலர் வார் புணை நின கழல்), out of a life worn down in the world by the body. The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). The song makes the Kural's feet into the raft (புணை) that does the swimming.

The song asks not to be born into the sea of misery by cultivating the friendship of the wicked (கருக்காரர் நட்பைப் பெருக்கு ஆசரித்துக் கலிச்சாகரத்தில் பிறவாதே). The Kural says nothing brings more affliction than bad company (தீயினத்தின் அல்லல் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). The song stretches the Kural's affliction into the next birth.
audit_text_issue: 392's opening phrase is hard to construe.

note: The song follows a life spent on women's breasts until the body bends, he walks coughing, speech goes (உரைபோய்) and feeling ends, and asks for the feet to escape fire-mouthed hell. Naladiyar 13 describes men whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth (சொல்தளர்ந்து கோல்ஊன்றி), yet still keep their eyes on desire, and says they have no safe way. The song is the Naladiyar's old man speaking for himself and asking for that way.

The song fears falling, a mere bubble, into the whirlpool of the sea of birth (புற்புதமாய பிறவி வாராகரச் சுழி). Naladiyar 27 calls the body a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts again and again (படுமழை மொக்குளின் பல்காலும் தோன்றிக் கெடும்). The Naladiyar's bubble is the body; the song makes each whole birth the bubble.
audit_text_issue: Opening line garbled (தொழுத்மு டூடு, கடலு஡டுற்).

note: The song seeks the seal of silence (மோன முத்திரை) that the noisy sects cannot know, as the way out of births. Tirumanthiram 1611 says that for those to whom silence has come (மோனம் கை வந்தோர்க்கு), release and the powers come too. The Tirumanthiram states the reward the song is reaching for.
audit_text_issue: 394 line 1 garbled ('தொழுத்மு டூடு', 'கடலு஡டு').

note: The song's women bewitch anyone at all for the love of wealth (ஆசை பொருட்டு ஆரையும் எத்தாக மயக்கிடும்) and send go-betweens to snatch money. Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser is sugar if he has wealth. Both make wealth the only thing the women see in a man.

The lovesick woman in the song says the small wind of the end (இறுதிச் சிறுகால்), the moon and the sea make her life droop (உயிர் துவள). The Kural's woman tells evening it is not evening but an hour that eats the life of the wed (உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). Both make the natural hour a devourer of the separated woman's life.

Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as the money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and 398's women of magic arts cling only as far as the wealth goes (பொருளது அளவும் மருவுறு).

Both call the body a pot (கும்பம்) of filth: the Naladiyar's pot seeps through nine openings under its dark skin, 402's is a pot where stench and liquor pool. The Naladiyar turns the image on the desired woman; 402 turns it on the poet's own body.

Both describe the embrace in full and then refuse to forget the feet within it: 403 says 'even then I will never forget', 420 asks 'even in union, will I forget your golden feet?'. Unlike most of the book, they ask for remembrance, not escape.
Both use the evening torments of love, the moon and Kama's arrows, for a girl in love with Murugan. In 24 her mother speaks; in 404 the girl herself asks him to come before she dies.

Both describe the same yoga: kindling the fire and raising it until the nectar of the moon is drunk. Tirumular calls those who do it Siva-yogis; 405 confesses that the poet has not done it and wanders after women instead.
Both list the foods Ganapati takes, gram or dal, sesame, plantains and other fruits; in 2 they lead into the poet's call to sing, in 409 into pure praise.
audit_text_issue: 2 has a corrupt word in the offering list (தன஧முலம்).

note: Both show the old man with failing speech and a staff. The Naladiyar's still keeps his eyes on desire; 412 follows the man spent on courtesans to the end, deaf and on a mat, while his own wife, children and kin call him a curse.

The poet, who speaks the threefold Tamil night and day (இயல் இசை முத் தமிழ் கூறி), asks only for firmness (திரம்) and grace. Tirumulan says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). Both see their Tamil as the work grace gave them, and the song asks for that work to stand firm.

The song names Murugan the supreme guru who moves within the atom (அணுவில் அசைவாய) and is every form. Tirumanthiram 2008 calls the First Lord the atom within the atom (அணுவில் அணு), reached only by those who can divide it a thousandfold. The song's brief epithet is the Tirumanthiram's whole verse.

The song asks Murugan to appear so that the two deeds take fright and the dark disease fades (இருவினை அஞ்ச ... இருள்பிணி மங்க). The Kural says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who love the Lord's true praise (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும் சேரா). Both pair darkness with the two deeds and make the Lord's presence or praise the release from both.

The song names the body, among other vessels, a குடம்பை and a hut (குரம்பை) that heart and life move out of (நெஞ்சொடு உயிர் குடிபோம்). The Kural says the bond of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The song uses the Kural's own word and gives the soul the same departure.

The girl says the flute's music comes like the sun to take her life (இரவி எனது உயிர் கவர வரு குழல் இசை). The Kural's woman says the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). In both the flute, not the lover's absence alone, is the killer.

The voice asks whether the girl should suffer from the moon, the rumour spread by the blaming women (மலந்தைமார் சொல் வதந்தி) and the south wind. The Kural's woman says the town's gossip is the manure of her sickness and her mother's words its water. Both count other people's talk among the forces that feed the lovesick girl's pain.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 406: மலந்தைமார் is an unusual word.

note: The song lays out a woman's beauty from face to gait and ends by asking whether one should be kin to those who coax and snatch wealth (குனகி பொருள் பறிபவர்க்கு உறவாமோ). The Kural says to avoid women who weigh the profit and then speak of goodness (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The song's catalogue is the 'speaking of goodness' the Kural warns against, and the last line names the weighing.

The song closes with the true guru made manifest (மெய்ப்ரத்யக்ஷ நற்சற்குருபர) who appeared at Arunai and gave the poet clarity (எனக்குத் தெளிவருள்). Tirumanthiram 139 says clarity is seeing the guru's form, saying his name, hearing his words and thinking of him (தெளிவு குருவின் திருமேனி காண்டல்). The song reports as experience what the Tirumanthiram defines.
audit_text_issue: 408's first half dense; some comparisons unclear.

note: The song lists what women's eyes do: they meet arrows, wage war on the young (இளையோர் முன் செருவை) and wring out men's lives. The Kural's man says he never knew Death before and now knows it as the eyes that make great war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both see the eye as a warrior that kills.

In the song the girl who is modesty itself (நாணான தோகை) wilts as the townsfolk revile her and slanders pile up (நாடோர்கள் ஏச ... நானா பவாதம்). The Kural's woman asks how she can be ashamed of gossip (அலர்நாண) now that he who said 'fear not' has left her. Both join the girl's shame to the town's talk; the Kural's woman has passed beyond the shame the song's girl still suffers.

The song ends with kin, wife and children crowding round the decayed man saying 'chi, this curse won't go' (சீசீ சிச்சிசி போகா நற்சனியன்). Tirumanthiram 150 says the wife marries with sweet talk, lives till love is sated, then weeps as is fitting (அமைய அழுதிட்டு) at the bier. Both show the household's love worn out before the man is gone, the song saying it aloud.

Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, tormented by Kama's five flower arrows, and ask him to come with his garland; 101 is spoken for her, 413 by her, and adds that one night feels like an age.
Both run a life from the embryo in the womb through birth, nursing and crawling to desire for women. 9 ends in disease; 423 counts learning among the stages, calling it empty knowledge.
audit_text_issue: 423's praise has a garbled name (likely Vibhishana)

note: Tirumular lists the rotations of the five-letter mantra in order from SI: சிவயநம, மசிவயந, நமசிவய, யநமசிவ, வயநமசி. 425 chants the same rotations in the same order, each joined to the name of Arunachala, making a teaching of the mantra into a hymn to the hill.

Both make Murugan the Tamil saint who sent the Jains of Madurai to the stakes. 104 adds Pugali and the cure of the king's fever; 426 adds the milk the mountain's daughter gave, the other mark of Sambandar's story.

Both show vultures tearing at the body. The Naladiyar's stinking cart is shown to men who praise sandal and garlands; 422 sees the poet's own body as the feast of dogs, jackals, vultures and worms, and turns from it to the company of devotees.

The Kural's woman says the long nights now passing are crueller than the cruel man himself (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள் நெடிய கழியும் இரா). 413's girl, struck by Kama's five flower arrows on her bed, says one night has come on like an old aeon (பழைய பேருகம் விளைந்ததென ஓரிரவு). Both make the lengthened night, not the absent lover, the torment of separation.

414 names Murugan only as the one who spoke a single word into the First One's ear (ஆதியர் காது ஒருச்சொல் அருள்வோனே). 176 tells the same act and names the word: the secret of the pranava spoken into Siva's golden ear (பொற்செவியுட் பிரணவ ரகசியம்). The fuller song supplies what 414's 'one word' is.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 176 has a corrupt glyph (தன஧முவ) and a garbled line.

note: The Naladiyar says those who think the love of a worthless woman their own, while she licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). 415 confesses the same end from inside: wealth, youth, learning and mind spent on such women (பொருள் இளமை கலை மனமும் ஏகப் போக்கிய), until the world reviles him as an outcast (புலையன் இவன் என உலகம் ஏச). The quatrain's warning is the song's confession.

The Tirumanthiram says people see the times called child, youth and old man pass and still do not understand (பாலன் இளையன் விருத்தன் ... கண்டும் அறிகிலார்). 416 runs the same stages, infant, youth, householder, bent old man, to the body made dust with the firewood, and says of itself that it never knew this (மறியாதாய்). Both turn from the passing of ages to the feet or home that does not pass.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate: devise another way and it is there first (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள). 417 names fate as a cause of its ruin, deeds of fate bent on harm (ஊழ்வினையினால் மிகுத்த கேடுறுகவே நினைக்கும் வினை), yet asks Murugan to come with the vel to rule him and grant release (வீடுதவி ஆள). On the reading that the plea expects grace to override what fate decreed, the song sets a limit to the Kural's 'no greater strength'.

The Tirumanthiram orders it: praise and sing the Pure One's form, turn back the five senses, then pour the Lord into the heart (போற்றிசைத்து ... நாதனை ஊற்றுக உள்ளத்து). 419 asks Murugan to come daily on the peacock into the minds of those who sing the kadamba with full devotion (நீபமலர் பத்தி மெத்த ஓதுமவர் சித்தம்). In both, singing praise is the way the Lord comes to dwell in the heart.

The Kural names quarrelling, making up and union as the fruits of those who love (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல் இவைகாமம் கூடியார் பெற்ற பயன்). 420 tells exactly that course, the sulk (புலவி மிகுத்திட்டு), bowing at her flower feet until love returns (அநுராகம்), and union, then asks whether even in union he would forget the golden feet (புணரினும் நிற் பொற்பதங்கள் நெஞ்சினுள் மறவேனோ). The song keeps the Kural's sequence but holds the feet above its fruit.

The Tirumanthiram describes the one made one with the Supreme (பரத்துடன் ஏகமாய்), stilled like clear water after waves, who has fully tasted the rare nectar (ஆரமுது ஒக்க உணர்ந்துளோன்). 421 asks for the same end in a devotee's words: hunger stilled by the nectar of Siva-knowledge (சிவஞான அமுதே பசியாறி) and the two becoming one form (இருவோர் ஒரு ரூபமதாய்). Union and nectar go together in both.
audit_text_issue: 421 line 3 has a lost letter (ஒ ரு பமதாய்).

note: The Tirumanthiram's poet entered the Lord's city by going with the devotees of the Lord's devotees (உடையான் அடியார் அடியாருடன் போய்). 422, after seeing his body as carrion between the nets of birth and death, asks for a share with the loving servants (அன்புறும் தொண்டர் பங்குறுக) and to delight in union with the devotees (அன்பரோடே கலவி நலம் மருவி). Both reach the Lord in company, not alone.

The Tirumanthiram says the form grows ten bright months, comes into the world in its season, and grows mingled with maya (ஒண்டிங்கள் பத்திற் ... மருவி வளர்ந்திடு மாயையினாலே). 423 traces the same: seed and blood in the womb, birth in the tenth month (மதி சொற்ற பத்தின்), then growth into empty learning and bathing in infatuation (மயலிற் குளித்து). The song fills in the life the verse compresses.

The Naladiyar mocks the untaught petty men who babble that smiles are jasmine buds and pearls (முல்லை முகைமுறுவல் முத்தென்று இவைபிதற்றும் கல்லாப்புன் மாக்கள்), having seen the teeth in the burning ground. 424 quotes such flattery in its own mouth, teeth like rows of pearls (பந்தித் தரளம்), lips sweeter than fruit, and names the speaker a dull-witted fool (மந்தப் புந்திக் கசடன்). The quatrain's mocked praiser is the poet's self-portrait.
audit_text_issue: Naladiyar 45 ends with a stray '3' (ஒழுகுவேன3).

note: 420 asks whether even in union he would forget the golden feet in his heart (புணரினும் நிற் பொற்பதங்கள் நெஞ்சினுள் மறவேனோ). 427, after a long list of women's charms, seems to make the same vow, that even sporting with them in bed (அமளியின் ஆடினும்) he will keep to the lotus feet with their anklets (பூங்கமலம் சரண்). On that reading the two songs hold the feet in mind within the embrace, where most of the book flees it.
audit_text_issue: 427's line 16 is corrupt; அன்தகையேனே is uncertain.

note: The Kural says neither the shaved head nor long matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 428 confesses to both marks, the shaved head and the grown locks, with the condemned conduct, the hunt for gold, kept underneath.
Tirumular says the false garb is worn for the sake of eating; in 428 the poet confesses to wearing it to make gold, and asks for pity rather than claiming the garb.

Both list the same diseases (scrofula, the great belly, phlegm, colic, urinary flux). 243 asks that they not afflict him through his births; 441 gives up on the body and asks instead for Siva-knowledge and the power to sing the Thiruppugazh.

429 abuses the courtesans as cheats who scour brass ornaments with ash and wear them in their ears (பித்தளையிற் பணி மிக நீறால் விளக்கியே குழையிட்ட புரட்டிகள்). 1317 has the same picture, tarnished brass ornaments polished with ash to shine (மாசுற்றேறிய பித்தளையிற் பணி நீறிட்டே ஒளி பற்ற விளக்கிகள்). In both the false gold stands for the false love of a priced trade.

The Kural's man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). 430's girl is burned by cool moonlight (சீதநிலா எறிக்கும் அனலாலே), and the cure asked is that the god come and embrace her. Both turn coolness and fire inside out in love-sickness, with nearness as the only cooling.

431 asks that diseases, colic, fever, wind and bile (சூலை வெப்பு அடர்ந்த வாத பித்தம்), not come near, and then asks for the gift of fine song (பாடல் மிக்க செஞ்சொல் தரவேணும்). 441 lists wind, bile, colic and many more, says it can no longer carry the body, and asks for the power to praise Thiruppugazh on its tongue (திருப்புகழை எனுநாவினிற் புகழ). In both songs the remedy asked for after disease is song itself.

The Kural says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with the bar of shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). 432's woman says the cuckoo's call destroys her modesty (நாணம் அழிய உரைக்குங் குயிலாலே) as she wastes in longing. Both make shame the last barrier that love-sickness breaks.

The Naladiyar calls the body a paltry lodging (நொய்யதோர் புக்கில்) whose covering of skin, if torn, brings the crows. 433 names it a hut bound by the noose, made of skin, wind and flesh and stained (தோலாலே காலாலே ஊனாலே சூழ் பாசக் குடில் மாசு). Both set the body as a frail dwelling of skin against the sweet speech of women.

The Tirumanthiram tells how Nandi took body, wealth and life with water (உடல்பொருள் ஆவி உதகத்தாற் கொண்டு), the disciple's whole self given to the guru, and ended birth. 434 makes the same gift in its own words, counting heart, gold, life and goods as Murugan's (அகம் பொன் ஆவி பொருள் என நினைந்து). The pairing shows the song's offering as the old formula of surrender.

The Kural commands: cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). 435, after heaping names on itself, does not ask that desire end but that he think of the feet daily with a longing not let go (நினது தாளை நாடோறு மனதில் ஆசை வீடாமல் நினையுமாறு). Both turn attachment toward the Lord instead of ending it.

436 describes poets who liken the rich to the kalpaka tree, the rain cloud and Pari and make thieving poems for money (திருட்டுக் கவிகள் பாடி). 271 renounces poets who liken base patrons to the pouring cloud and the wish-tree and who steal and twist old verses (பழைய மொழியைத் திருடி நெருடிக் கவிபாடி). Both name patron-praise as theft; 436 adds that the gold so earned goes to the courtesans.

424 quotes the poet's flattery of women, breasts like pots, teeth like pearls, peacock, Lakshmi of the lotus, as he coaxes them and worships their feet (அவர் தாடொழு). 436 quotes the flattery of patrons, kalpaka tree, cloud, Pari, made to end poverty (மிடிபோக). The same stock comparisons serve desire in one song and begging in the other, and 436 joins the two trades when the patron's gold goes to the women.

The Naladiyar's renunciant will not be moved by petty men who call eyes water-lilies, darting carp or spears (தெண்ணீர்க் குவளை பொருகயல் வேலென்று), having seen an eye is a scooped palm fruit. 437 lists the same likenings, deer, poison, carp, arrow, vel, sword, blue lily (கயல் மீனை ... வடிவேலை ... உற்பலத்தினை), then names the body an oozing filth and a bloated corpse (ஊதும் பிணம்). The song confesses being caught by the comparisons the quatrain sees through, and asks that the delusion clear (இப்ரமை தெளியாதோ).

The Naladiyar likens a harlot's love to a lamp: the light ends when the oil runs out, and her love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 438 lists the courtesans who for love of coin sell their breasts to many (காசாசையில் முலை பலர்க்கும் விற்பவர்) and the low-priced (விலைச்சிறுக்கிகள்). Both make money the whole measure of the love.

The Kural warns that the sweet words of bangled women who desire wealth, not love, bring harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). 439 shows such women crying the price of their breasts in the street (முலை விலைகூறி), luring with deceitful play and snatching life (உயிரே பறிப்பவர்கள்), and asks whether they can be kin (உறவாமோ). The song's scene is the Kural's sale and harm made visible.

In the Naladiyar, to women without their companion the thunder of rain sounds like the funeral drum beaten in every direction (நெய்தல் அறைந்தன்ன). In 440 the roaring sea that bends and cries out (வளைந்து அரற்று கடல்) and the moon rising with poison torment the separated girl. Both turn a sound of nature into the separated woman's affliction; 440 then asks for mukti as the end of it.

The Kural names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom Fortune has cast off (இருமனப் பெண்டிரும் கள்ளும் கவறும்). 442 gives the women a hundred thousand minds (நூறாயிர மனமுடை மாபாவிகள்) and calls itself the clown reviled by earth and sky who is wholly in their thrall. The Kural's two minds become the song's hundred thousand.

Tirumular says the form grows ten months, comes into the world in its season and grows mingled with maya, and asks who knows how. 444 follows that same growth month by month to birth in the tenth, and then on past it to the pyre.
audit_text_issue: 444's embryo passage is hard to divide.

note: Both hear the funeral drum while kin wail over the corpse; the Naladiyar's drum mocks the living, while 444 notes that the kin weep each for their own share.
audit_text_issue: 444's embryo and battle passages are hard to divide.

note: The song asks to reach the feet by speaking of them in old Tamil set to music (முதிய மா தமிழ் இசையதாகவே மொழிசெய்தே நினைந்திடுமாறு). Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யுமாறே). Both poets treat making the god in Tamil as their own way to him, Tirumular as the purpose of his birth, Arunagiri as the remedy for a life misspent.

The song ends its life-story with the kin weeping each for their share (சந்தித்து அவரவர் பங்குக்கு அழுது), the drum, and the burning that leaves not a handful of ash. Tirumular's verse has the whole town wail (ஊரெலாம் கூடி ஒலிக்க அழுதிட்டு), rename the man a corpse, burn him and bathe and forget. Both close on the mourners rather than the dead man, and the song adds a motive Tirumular leaves out: the weeping is for the share.

The song asks for the feet that are Jnana-Siva (ஞானசிவமான பதம்), against the fool who took what he sought for the goal (நாடியதுவே கதி எனா). Tirumular says knowledge of the holy feet makes one Siva and is itself release (திருவடி ஞானம் சிவமாக்குவிக்கும் ... திருவடி ஞானமே திண்சித்தி முத்தியே). The song's compound names in one phrase what the Tirumanthiram verse unfolds line by line: the feet, knowledge and Siva as one goal.

Both end the cherished body as carrion: the Naladiyar's vultures tear the stinking cart once its axle breaks, and 446 lays the householder in a pit for vultures and dogs. The Naladiyar's target is the praise of perfumes and garlands; 446's is family life.
audit_text_issue: 446's opening (சரக்கேறித் தப்பதி, பரிக்காயம், குரக்கோணம்) is obscure.

note: The Kural says what is called virtue is household life itself (அறன் எனப்பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை). The song confesses that very life, wearied in samsara, delighting in kin and cherishing the family (சமுசாரம், சுற்றத்தவரோடு இன்பத் தழைத்து, குடிபேணி), as what leads him straight to the grave pit, and asks for the roots of the world's maya to be dried. On the reading that the song counts householding itself, not its excess, as the fault, the two judge the same life oppositely.

The song asks that, not aiming at the attachments of worldly men (செகத்தோர் பற்றைக் குறியாதே), the Lord set his peerless flower feet on him and rule him (மலர்த்தாள் வைத்து எத்தனை ஆள்வாய்), with சிரத்தானம் possibly naming the head. Tirumular says the Lord set his foot on his head so that his bonds were cut (கால்கொண்டு என் சென்னியிற் கட்டறக் கட்டற) and his heart's delusion ended. Tirumular reports as done what the song asks for, and names its effect: the feet on the head end the attachment.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 447: the split of சிரத்தானத்திற் பணியாதே is uncertain.

note: The song says the human form is the five gathered and massed together (பஞ்சவர் கூடித் திரண்டது ஓர் நர உரு) in the cosmos Brahma creates. Tirumular's creation verse has the five crowd together and become the five elements from which the worlds take form (ஐந்தும் செறிந்து ஐந்து பூதமாய்). The same assembling of five that builds the world builds the body the song finds frail, disease-covered and in need of an unshaken mind.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 385: கான் and தேன் may be corrupt.

note: Both give the courtesan's course in one sequence: the Naladiyar's woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hands and then balks like an ox; 458's coaxes, takes gold until the wealth is gone, then drives him off with deceitful words.
Both carry the courtesan song past the bed to the diseases it leaves, sores with pus and festering; 456 follows them into Death's city, 461 to the onlookers who cover their eyes.

Both songs are litanies in which every line ends 'behold the Lord' (பெருமாள்காண்), with no plea at all. At Chidambaram Murugan is 'my own guru' (எனது குருநாத); at Kathirkamam he is the guru of the pure Siva (அமலர் குருநாதப் பெருமாள்காண்). Read together, the form is a fixed praise-litany carried from shrine to shrine, and the guru title moves between the poet's teacher and Siva's.

The litany names Murugan the guru of the Lord of Sivakami (கத்தர் குருநாதப் பெருமாள்காண்) and pure Siva-knowledge itself (சுத்த சிவஞானப் பெருமாள்), without telling a story. Song 458, in the same Chidambaram set, tells the act: he poured the true meaning into Siva's ear (சிவனார்தம் செவிக்குச் செம்பொருள் கற்கப் புகட்டி). The title in 450 is the event in 458.

The song asks not to roam with the heart in the seven hells (எழுநரகில் உழலும் நெஞ்சு) and calls Murugan easy to reach for those who practise the path of compassion (கருணைநெறி புரியும் அன்பர்க்கு எளியோன்). The Kural says those whose hearts are joined with grace will not enter the dark world of pain (அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க்கு இல்லை இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் புகல்). Both make compassion, not worship alone, the way out of hell, the song adding that it also brings the god near.

The song asks for Siva's nectar to well up on the tongue (சிவ அமுது ஊறுக) and to reach the space with neither day nor night (பகலும் இரவும் இலா வெளி) as the supreme state. Tirumular speaks of the place without night and day (இராப்பகல் அற்ற இடத்தே) where one drinks the nectar of bliss (ஆனந்தத் தேறல்), in the joy of the twin feet. Both join the same two images, the nectar and the dayless, nightless space, for the state beyond waking and sleep.
audit_text_issue: 331: last line (இராப்பகல் மாயை இரண்டிடத் தேனே) is obscure.

note: In 453 the poet asks to serve Murugan's devotees (உன் அன்பருக்குச் செயல் தொண்டுபட்டு) instead of the women who take his money. In 454 he names his life with the women as servitude itself and asks when it will end (ஊழியம் செய்வது என்று போமோ). Together the two songs set service against service: the bondage to the courtesans is undone not by freedom but by a different servitude.

The Kural says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன் நல்வினை). The song pictures the man who did not: eyes and ears failing (கண் செவியும் சுகங்கள் திரும்பி), he asks whether he must lie with the wrongs he did before and die (முன்செய்த வஞ்சினங்களுடன் கிடந்து உடல் அழிவேனோ). The song is the deathbed the Kural's warning looks ahead to.

The Kural says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not the man bring harm (பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார் இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The song shows those sweet words at work, the courtesan speaking as if she knew the man already (நீர் எந்த ஊர் அறிந்தவர் போல ... இன்சொல் கூறி) and joining whoever shows gold in his hand, and then the harm: sores, worms, colic and death. The song gives the scene and the consequence the Kural compresses into இழுக்கு.

The song says the poet has come again and again, sprouting from seed (வந்து வந்து வித்தூறி), his life worn in the forest of his own deceits (எந்தன் வஞ்சனைக் காடு). The Kural calls craving the seed that yields unceasing birth (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). Both see rebirth as a seed sprouting; the Kural names the seed as craving, the song lets it grow into a forest the Lord must scatter.

The song describes women who snatch a man's wages in a moment and embrace him on soft beds, and asks whether such women can be kin (பஞ்சணை மீது அணை மாதர்கள் உறவாமோ). The Kural likens the false embrace of women of wealth to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room (இருட்டறையில் ஏதில் பிணம் தழீஇ அற்று). Both deny that the bedroom embrace makes a relation: the song's உறவு and the Kural's ஏதில், 'a stranger', answer each other.

The song's courtesans set their terms as money in the hand in advance (முற்பணம் கைக்கொடும் தாரும்) and cling until the man's debts cover him. The Naladiyar says such women would send away even red-eyed Mal, worshipped by the gods, with joined hands if he had nothing in his hand to give (தம் கைக்குக் கொடுப்பது ஒன்று இல்லாரை). Both make the hand with gold in it the whole condition of the courtesan's welcome.

Both pleas are built almost wholly of epithets for courtesans in -இகள், each a separate insult: 462 has திருடிகள், நடுவிகள், சிதடிகள், குருடிகள், 438 has முகத்துலக்கிகள், விலைச்சிறுக்கிகள், செகத்தில் எத்திகள். The pairing shows the abuse-catalogue as a fixed form Arunagiri uses at Arunai and Chidambaram alike; 462 closes by asking whether such women can be kin (உறவாமோ), 438 by asking when he will reach the feet.
audit_text_issue: Several epithets in 462 (சிதடிகள், சங்க்ய சங்கிகள்) are doubtful.

note: The song lists a woman's beauties from hair to breasts like an elephant's temples and then asks whether his mind should be one that clutches at such women (கவண்டிய சிந்தையாமோ). Tirumular says that as the etti fruit is not to be eaten however good its leaves and clusters, the heart should turn from women who smile and show their breasts (விலகுறு நெஞ்சினை வெய்துகொள்ளீரே). Both concede the beauty and refuse the heart's grip on it; Tirumular gives the reason in one image where the song gives only the catalogue and the question.

Both see the body as a bubble that forms and bursts; the Naladiyar praises the firm who resolve from this to end their wandering, and 469 asks from it for the one release complete in wisdom, silence and bliss.
The Kural makes the letter A first of letters as the Lord is first of the world; 467 takes the letter itself as a name of the Goddess, calling Sivakami the அகரம் and the life of all.

Both ask not to leave the bed but to hold the Lord there: 468 vows to keep the twelve eyes and twelve arms even while sporting with women, and 467 asks for the moon faces and feet in the same embrace.
Both make poverty the end of the courtesan's love: the Naladiyar's flood ends when the income ends, and 477's women first show delusion and then show poverty.

The song calls the poet a wretch suffering the bond of the five senses (ஐந்திந்த்ரிய பந்தம் தரும் துன்பம் படும் ஏழை), with no steadiness, fickle (சலன்). Tirumular confesses the same failure in his own voice: வெல்லகில்லேன் புலன் ஐந்துடன் தன்னையும், he is like a horse that bolts. Both are first-person admissions, not instructions; the song adds the remedy Tirumular leaves unsaid, that the Lord recognise him as his old servant (உன்றன் பழந்தொண்டு).

The song's women destroy men with a charmed powder (மந்த்ர பொடிகொண்டு அழிக்கும் வஞ்சர்), and the praise answers with Murugan who sends Siva's five syllables first into battle (சிவம் அஞ்செழுத்தை முந்த விடுவோனே). Tirumular says that once the truth of the five letters is known there is no deceit (வஞ்சகம் இல்லை) and no ruin to the house. Together they set the five syllables against வஞ்சம, the holy spell against the deceivers' spell.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 980: அஞ்சுக is ambiguous (fear / five).

note: The song asks that, doubt cast off and understanding (விடுசங்கையற்று உணர்ந்து), the poet circle Murugan, praise him and receive his golden feet. The Kural says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. The song makes the Kural's step a plea within worship: the shedding of doubt is what lets the circling and the praise reach the feet.

After its heap of self-abuse the song hails the Lord as the one who became the highest state by being seen (தெரிசன பரகதி யானாய் நமோநம). Tirumular makes clarity itself consist in seeing the guru's holy form (தெளிவு குருவின் திருமேனி காண்டல்). The pairing shows the litany's title as the Saiva teaching that the sight of the Lord or guru is itself the gift; the reading of தெரிசன பரகதி as 'the goal given by sight' is the one this depends on.

The song calls Murugan the guru who spoke into an ear that did not know the eight and two (எட்டிரண்டும் அறியாத என்செவியில்) and said 'this is the lingam'. Tirumular's verse turns on the same phrase and almost the same words: எட்டும் இரண்டும் அறியாத ஏழையர் miss that the eight and two are the step of the Siddhanta path. The song places itself among Tirumular's ignorant and names the guru's whispered teaching as what cured it; what the eight and two stand for is unsettled in both.

The song turns from deceitful talebearers with poisoned minds to the Lord and says, the burden is yours, for who is my helper (உன்றனக்கே பரமும் என்றனக்கு ஆர் துணைவர்). Tirumular runs துணை four times: make Nandi your close support (உறுதுணை), and he stands as support. Both make the Lord the only துணை; the song speaks it as a complaint that the Lord has not yet come.

Tirumular commands the hearer to melt his own love (என் அன்புருக்கி ... முன் அன்புருக்கி) before seeking the Lord, after which the Lord's love answers. The short song, wavering over women, cannot do this itself and asks for it as grace: அன்புருக அருள்வாயே. The pairing shows the melting of love that Tirumular sets as the devotee's work turned into the Lord's gift.

The song catalogues a woman's beauty from hair to waist and then calls such women without good nature (இயல் குணமிலாத), a net in which he will perish. Tirumular says the ripe etti fruit cannot be eaten however good its leaves and clusters, so the heart must hold back from women who smile and display their breasts (முலைநலம் கொண்டு முறுவல் செய்வார்). Both set the beauty on show against what lies under it.

The song tastes the woman's lips like jackfruit segments (பலாசுளையின் சுவை கண்டு இதழ் உண்டு) and ends by asking whether he must fall like a dog with his body wasting. The Kural's lover finds the water at his beloved's teeth like milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன் கலந்தற்றே). The same image of the mouth's sweetness is joy in the Kural's love and the prelude to ruin in the song.

The song lists learning (கல்வி) with father, mother, house, gold, silver and kin as a trouble (அல்லல்) to be shed before he can sing the Lord. The Kural calls learning the one imperishable wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி), other things not wealth. The conflict holds on the reading that the song counts learning itself as a bond; if அத்து பண்ணு கல்வி means only learning pursued for gain, it narrows to a qualification.

The song says the women, after their show of beauty, plunder gold like skilled raiders (வல்லவர்கள் போல பொற்சூறை கொண்டார்கள்) and asks whether infatuation with them is fitting. The Naladiyar's woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from the man's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and turns away, and those who thought her love theirs are laughed at. Both name the taking of wealth as the purpose behind the display.

Both join the catalogue of the body's diseases to the ninety-six tattvas living off the body; 487 adds the house-building and desire for wealth that keep the poet from the space where the peacock dances.
Tirumular counts the ninety-six as tenants of a walled temple who run off when it falls; 487 makes the same ninety-six the eaters of the body, a picture of consumption rather than desertion.
audit_text_issue: 487 has the corrupt glyph ஡ in லு஡சல்.

note: Both turn the body into a dwelling whose real occupants are diseases, listed at length; 485 names the fault as taking that dwelling for permanent.

Tirumular's Siva-jnanis go about as dead while their senses and body remain; 490 asks for exactly this, the goal won by dying in the mind before the body is carried to the burning ground, but offers the Lord the alternative of living on in understanding.

The Naladiyar says it matters nothing whether the body is dragged, buried or thrown away once its dweller has left; 493 lists the same receivers of the corpse, vultures, jackals, fire and earth, but as weary claimants, so that the repetition across countless births is itself the burden.

Both are laments for a girl sick with love for Murugan, told by another voice, with the wind, the birds and the signs of evening wearing her down; 24 is the mother's, and 488 asks Murugan for his garland.
audit_text_issue: 488's வருகொவே looks corrupt (வருகோவே).

note: Both make the courtesan's only question whose money there is: the Naladiyar's women find even an oil-presser sweet if he has wealth, and 481's women, with hearts dry as cane waste, think only whose wealth it will be.

The song's women coax with feigned love and then pick a quarrel (பசப்பிப் பின் பிணக்கைக் கூறிய வீணிகள்) once the money is asked and given. The Naladiyar's women seem sweet while a man is infatuated and turn harsh as a ram's horn once they are full (தாம் ஆர்ந்த போதே தகர்கோடாம்), and those who would reach the right path avoid them. Both mark the same turn from coaxing to coldness; the Naladiyar ties it to the path, the song to the plea for the feet.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 479's plea line (பரத்துற் றண்பதத்துப் போதக் மீதென) is garbled.

note: The song makes the body a walled hut where the tricksters of the senses (பொறி விரகாளர்) dwell and where craving for women and land gathers (ஆசை பெணாசை மணாசைகள் தொக்கு), and asks for release. The Naladiyar names the five senses as five mouths of craving (ஐவாய வேட்கை அவா) and promises release to one who can guard them. The song confesses that it cannot do this guarding and asks the Lord for the release the Naladiyar ties to it.

The song calls the women's long eyes a net like the spears in the hands of Death's messengers (காலத் தூதர் கை வேலெனு நீள்விழி). The Kural's lover asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both draw the woman's look and Death together; in the Kural it is the lover's wonder, in the song a warning against the trade.

The song's praise shows Murugan walking through the hunters' forest for love of Valli until his fragrant feet reddened (வேடக் கானகத்து வாசத்தாள் சிவப்ப வருவோனே). The Naladiyar's mother asks whether her daughter's feet, which drew back even from red dye on soft cotton, have borne the stony forest path (பரற்கானம்) of her elopement. Both measure love by tender feet on the wild path; the song gives the god the part of the eloping lover.

The song's women pain the heart while seeming close and hide enmity within (உள்ள நோவைத்தே உறவாடியர் ... உள்விரோதக்காரிகள்). The Naladiyar's women keep a heart that does harm hidden inside (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் தம் உள்ளடக்கி) and speak words to be trusted, yet belong to no one but their bodies. Both locate the deceit in the concealed heart behind the closeness.

Sinking daily in the sea of lust the women give, the song asks for its remedy in company: to join the Lord's devotees, the silent jnanis (உனது அடியாராகிய மோன ஞானிகளுடனே சேரவும்). The Kural says there is no greater support than good company (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை) and nothing that brings more trouble than bad. The song applies the Kural's rule to the spiritual life, setting the devotees against the women.

The song catalogues the body's filth and diseases and names the fault as taking this flawed dwelling for lasting (குடிப்புக்கு ஊனம் இதே சதமாம் என). Tirumular addresses those who feel that the hut that does not stay is permanent (நில்லாக் குரம்பை நிலையென்று உணர்வீர்காள்) and says the Lord cannot be seen in their hearts. Both make the error not the body's frailty but the belief in its permanence.

The song calls itself the fool who, loving women for a price (விலைமாதர்), drowns in ruinous deeds and sinks into the seven hells (ஏழ்நரகு ஆழும் மூடனை). The Kural calls the soft shoulders of women who set no limit the அளறு, hell and mire at once, in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). The shared verb ஆழ் shows the song taking the Kural's hell literally and multiplying it to seven.
audit_text_issue: 486's plea line காரிர் பாருமை யாசி வாபத is garbled.

note: Among the things that torment the lovesick girl the song names the bell of the bull coming home at evening (அடைந்திட்ட விடைமேவு மணியாலும). The Kural's woman calls the herdsman's flute a messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). Both turn the gentle pastoral sound of the herds' return into evening's weapon against the parted lover.

The song's women will not call a man back unless he pays the sum they name (பலஞ் செப்பித் தர மீள அழையாதவர்). The Naladiyar says that even if he were Mal whom the gods worship, they would dismiss with joined hands a man with nothing to give (கொடுப்பதொன்றில்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). Both make payment the only thing that keeps a man welcome; the Naladiyar's god makes the point by exaggeration.

The song's women talk with betel-red mouths, play at intimacy and state their wage (சம்பளம் ஈது என ஓதி) before the bed. The Kural says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song shows the sweet talk ending in the named wage, the motive the Kural names.

The song names women cheats (எத்திகள்) in every part and act and asks, as a dog wandering with them, for the anklet of wondrous wisdom by the Lord's own act (உன் செயலால் அற்புத ஞானத்தின் கழல்). The Kural says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an அணங்கு to those without discerning understanding. The song accepts the Kural's diagnosis, lack of understanding, and asks for the wisdom from the Lord rather than from his own effort.
audit_text_issue: 492 has a garbled word (சுக்முழ் கிப்).

note: The song counts births beyond the sands of the seven seas and says the servant is the Lord's servant (அடிமை உன் அடிமை), so his protection is the Lord's debt (கடன் உனது அபயம்). Tirumular says a deed of servitude to Siva (ஆவணம்) was written for him, his mother and father across seven times seven births. The song presses the bond Tirumular records as a legal claim on the Lord.

The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 497 asks to be spared ochre, matted hair, forest wandering and fasting and to be given instead the inner knowledge in which the self subsides. Both set the ascetic's outward marks aside, the Kural for conduct, 497 for grace and knowledge.
Both run a life from the womb through infancy and youth to women and then decline without pause; 9 ends in disease, 508 in Death's arrival, and both ask for release from the cycle.

The song asks to be spared the turmoil of the six sects quarrelling in turn (அறுவகை சமய முறைமுறை சருவி) and of reciting shastras, and to be given the one real object (வடிவுள பொருள்). Tirumanthiram 1558 says the six sects are six roads to one city (ஒன்றது பேரூர் வழியாறு), and those who say 'this is good, that is bad' are dogs barking at a hill. The verse supplies the reason the song's quarrel is futile: the roads lead to the same place.
audit_text_issue: 494 line அலைபடு தநல்முச் சினையாகும் may be corrupt.

note: The song lays out a woman from head to foot, her smile nectar and gems (அமுர்த மாணிக்க நகை), and only at the end asks to be given another thought (வேறு சிந்தனையைத் தந்து ஆள்வாய்). Naladiyar 45 refuses exactly such talk of smiles as jasmine buds and pearls (முல்லை முகை முறுவல் முத்து), because the speaker has seen the teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground. The pairing shows what the song's 'different thought' looks like in practice.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 495 line 'இணைசொல்க்஡ண' is garbled; Naladiyar 45 ends with a stray '3' (வேன3).

note: The song asks for the place where nectar wells like a falling stream (அருவி பாய இனமுதம் ஊற) as impurity leaves and the light at the root shines. Tirumanthiram 2535 puts the same welling stream (ஊறும் அருவி) on a high summit, a tank that fills without a river. Both use the spring on the height for the nectar of yogic ascent.

The song links the flow of nectar to the leaving of impurity (மலம் ஒழியவே ... அமுதம் ஊற). Tirumanthiram 800 says that when the sky-river is let into the tank, the one who looks up is free of dirt (அழுக்கற்ற வாறே). Both make the inner flood the cleansing itself.

The song asks not to wander wearing ochre and matted hair, but to see the lamp of knowledge that comes when self and elements subside (சீவனொடுக்கம் பூதவொடுக்கம்). Tirumanthiram 1660 grants that any garb, false or true, saves only those who have understood (உய்வேடமாகும் உணர்ந்தறிந்தோர்க்கே). The verse names the condition under which the song's rejected marks would still have worth.

The song's women gather asking 'will money come?' (பொருள் வருமோ) and join with many at once. Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison, while even an oil-presser who has earned wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார்) is sugar. Both make money the only question these women ask of a man.

The song pictures the pomp of wealth, a palanquin under umbrellas (குடை சூழ் சிவிகை) with armies (பலபடை) and music, and calls it a false show that vanishes in a moment (நொடி மறையும் பொய்ப் பவுஷு). Naladiyar 3 shows men who rode under the umbrella at the head of armies (குடைநிழற்கீழ்ச் சேனைத் தலைவராய்) fallen when their deeds run out. Same emblems, same verdict.

The song's pomp is a palanquin (சிவிகை) with attendants, which it says vanishes in a moment. Tirumanthiram 149 shows a man who gained a palanquin and rode it in the square (சிவிகைபெற்றேறினான்), and did not turn back when the cry came that he had gone. Both use the palanquin as the sign of a status that does not last.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 499 விருமஞ்சித் திரமமா does not split cleanly.

note: The song's wealth is a procession of drums, veena and conch that vanishes in a moment. Kural 332 compares great wealth to the crowd gathering at a dance hall (கூத்தாட்டு அவைக் குழாத்து) and its going to that crowd dispersing. The Kural gives the reason the song's noisy show is the right image for wealth: it is a gathered audience.

Against the perfumed body of the confession, the song asks to wear the bright ash (ஒண்பொடி அணிந்து) and bathe in bliss like ascetics (தவசர் சந்தம் போலும்). Tirumanthiram 1662 names wearing ash (பூதி அணிவது) as the first emblem of the Siva-yogi. The song takes the ascetic's first emblem as its sign of turning.

The song's praise names Siva dancing before the serpent-form sage and the tiger-footed one (பாம்புருவான முநி, வாம்புலியான பதன்) at Puliyur. Tirumanthiram 67 lists Patanjali and Vyaghra who worshipped at the hall (மன்று தொழுத பதஞ்சலி வியாக்ரமர்) among the masters who received Nandi's grace. The two sages of the Chidambaram dance are named by their marks in the song and by name in Tirumular.

Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினை) do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise. The song asks Murugan to come so that his servant's two deeds turn to ash (அடியன் இருவினை நீறுபட) while the gods sing of the wonder. The song turns the Kural's 'do not cling' into a burning away at the god's coming.

The song's women, once both have drowned in infatuation (மயல் மூழ்கிய பின்), pawn his jewels and loot what he has (ஆபரணம் வைத்து அடகு தேடு பொருள் சூறைகொளுவார்). Naladiyar 377 says such a woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hand (கைப்பொருள் கொண்டு), then lies down like a balking ox. Both put the taking after the fondness.
audit_text_issue: 503 has a garbled glyph in னு஡றல்.

note: The song's client ends coughing and hiccuping like a howling dog (ஊளை நாயென) while people say 'chi chi'. Naladiyar 375 calls the men who embrace women of double conduct dull-witted like beasts (விலங்கன்ன வெள்ளறிவினார்). Both turn the client, not the woman, into an animal.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 504: Achyuta phrase corrupt.

note: The song cries 'will birth never end?' (பிறப்பு முடியாதோ) and asks for the unfading flower of the feet (வாடா மலர்ப்பதவி). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song is the Kural's claim spoken as a cry from inside the sea.

The song climbs from the root lotus (மூலகமலம்) through the nadis and mantras to drink the gods' nectar (வானவமுதத்தை உண்டு) and reach the hall of the dance. Tirumanthiram 2989 tells the seeker to pass through the lotus of the flesh (ஊனார் கமலத்தின் ஊடு) and beyond, and then drink honey to the full. Both are the same ascent from the body's lotus to a drink of sweetness.
audit_text_issue: 506 has a corrupt glyph (இந்துவினூடு).

note: At the top of the song's ascent bindu and nada sound like a conch (சங்கொலி விந்துநாதம்). Tirumanthiram 731 names bindu, the mantra and the abiding nada (மன்னிய நாதம்) as the yogi's path. The song uses Tirumular's terms for the same stages.
audit_text_issue: 506 has a corrupt word.

note: The song asks whether the poet must wander daily at the women's command (கட்டளையாக ... நித்தமும் உழல்வேனோ) instead of holding the feet with true knowledge. Kural 909 says virtue, wealth and other aims are absent in those who do a woman's bidding (பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்). The Kural speaks of the husband and the wife; the song moves the same servitude to the courtesan and its loss to release.

The song runs from the womb to falling into the pit of women (மாதர்க் குழி விழுவார்) and to Death, and asks whether this sorrow of illusion (மாயத்துயர்) will never end. Tirumanthiram 185 says that after Death sets the base in the pit of the womb (கருக்குழி) they fall into it again, their bewilderment unending (திகைப்பொழியாரே). The two pits, of women and of the womb, are the same circle.

Both picture the body as food for scavengers: Naladiyar 48 has vultures tearing the stinking cart once its axle breaks, 510 the ghoul, the dog and the fly. The Naladiyar uses it to shame those who praise the body; 510 asks to be taken out of it into release.

Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums (பறை), and both make the funeral a lesson: Naladiyar 24 notes that the dying carry the dead; 512 sets the funeral at the end of a life spent on courtesans.

Both speakers address their own mind (நெஞ்சே, மனமே) and urge it to set out with them on the good path. Naladiyar 55 gives the reason as youth wasted and old age coming; 513 gives only the Lord, who cuts the root of impurity.

The song asks for the day it will be taught what Siva's emblems mean, the skull-bowl, the ash, the konrai, the axe and the deer (இவையிவை என உபதேசம்). Tirumanthiram 521 says no one knows the meaning of the darkened throat (கண்டங் கறுத்த கருத்து) and that the unknowing say merely that he drank poison. Tirumular gives the kind of reading of an emblem the song asks to receive.

Both songs credit Murugan with Sambandar's victory over the Jains: here the sage with the sword of knowledge who changed the hair-plucking Jains (தலைபறி அமணர் சமூகம் மாற்றிய தவமுனி), there the one who came in the form of the Kaundinya lord of Brahmapuram when the Buddhists and Jains were ruined (புத்தர் அமணர்கள் மிகவே கெடவே). Song 913 gives the story's details (the ash, the leaf in the fire) that 509 only points to.
audit_text_issue: 509 has one corrupt word (ஊற லு஡ட்டியும்).

note: The song calls the body a vessel (பாத்ரம்) of flesh, blood, bile and urine and asks to be moved from this pot to that one (இக்கடத்தை நீக்கி அக்கடத்துள் ஆக்கி). Naladiyar 47 calls the body a pot (கும்பம்) seeping filth from nine openings that the fool admires for its skin. Both make the body a filthy pot; the song alone asks for another pot.

The song sets the letters na, ma, si, va, ya (நகர, மகர, சிகர, வகர, யகர) at their places among the elements of the body. Tirumanthiram 890 says the ground at the root is நமசிவாய and that, spoken, it becomes the yoga of the breath (வாசி). Both place the five letters inside the yogic body rather than on the lips.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are obscure; 890's syntax is uncertain.

note: The song ends its man's life with the corpse dressed and named (பிணம் ஒப்பித்துப் பெயரிட்டு), drums beaten, kin wailing, and the body fed to the fire in the burning ground. Tirumanthiram 145 has the town wail, take away his name and call him a corpse (பேரினை நீக்கிப் பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு), burn him and bathe. The renaming as 'corpse' is the shared point.

Naladiyar 25 mocks the man who sees kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground and still marries, believing there is joy here. The song shows the cost in full: the courtesans' trade (முலைவிலை உரைசெய்து) runs without pause through old age to the same funeral. The song extends the Naladiyar's warning from marriage to lust.

In Kural 1241 the woman asks her heart to think and tell her a medicine (நினைத்தொன்று சொல்லாயோ நெஞ்சே) for love's sickness. The song reverses the roles: the poet tells his mind what is good for it (மனமே உனக்கு உறுதி புகல்வேன்), to worship the god who cuts the root of impurity. The form of the love poem's talk with the heart is turned to worship.

The song's women seize a man's wealth and call in another (பொருள் பற்றி வேறு அழைத்திடுவார்). Tirumanthiram 206 says such women, though they cling and say even the gods would be bewitched, turn to talk with strangers and are gone (அயலுறப் பேசி அகன்றொழிந்தாரே). Both name the turning to the next man as the end of the women's fondness.

The song names the Lord exalted in the space of light where there is no day or night (பகலிரவில்லாத ஒளிவெளி). Tirumanthiram 331 speaks of the place without night and day (இராப்பகல் அற்ற இடம்) where the bliss of the twin feet is drunk. Both put the goal outside the day-and-night of the world.

Both songs are litanies with no plea in which every line closes on பெருமாள் காண், 'see, the Lord', and both name the Lord as guru (பரமகுரு நாத; அமலர் குருநாதப் பெருமாள்). Song 636 points at Murugan of Kathirkamam; 515 points at the dancer of the golden hall. The rare refrain makes the two a pair across the book.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 515 has a corrupt word (கருவுதனி லு஡று).

note: The song's women carry crores of deceit gathered in their hearts (வஞ்சமே கோடி கோடிகள் நெஞ்சமே சேர) while they coo. Naladiyar 379 says such women hide a harmful heart (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் உள்ளடக்கி) behind words meant to be believed. Both place the danger in the concealed heart behind the sweet speech.

Both begin the life with a drop like dew (பனிபோல், பனியின் விந்துளி) and follow it head down out of the womb to the crawling child; 508 goes on to women and Death, 520 to past deeds and a ruined mind.

Thiruppugazh 517 begins its ascent with காலின் இருவழி அடைபட்டு, the breath's two ways shut, before going by the path of Siva to the one beyond. Tirumanthiram 795 names the harm of the breath that runs இடம் வலம், left and right, without keeping to the middle, and says joy comes when it is led as it should go. Read together, the song's two closed ways are the Tirumanthiram's left and right channels, and both make stopping them the first step.

Thiruppugazh 518 asks that the soul, its deeds powdered, come to know itself as Siva's form (சீவன் சிவச்சொருபம் என தேறி). Tirumanthiram 2017 says there is no difference between சீவன் and சிவன, and that once souls know Siva they remain as Siva. Both make the change a matter of knowing (தேறி, அறிந்தபின்), not of becoming something new.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 518's opening line is corrupt (பழ஧த்தசிவ ...... ம ளுறத்).

note: Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of யான் எனது, I and mine, enters a world higher than the gods'. Thiruppugazh 518 asks for நானென்பது அற்று, the 'I' gone, together with the flesh, and places the goal in the light of nada and Brahman where knowledge wells up as bliss. The song takes the Kural's renunciation of 'I' and names what lies past it in the language of union rather than of a higher world.
audit_text_issue: 518: the opening's last words are corrupt.

note: Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which worthless men sink (ஆழும்). Thiruppugazh 519 lists the laughter, stares, threats and acting of thieving women who gather a man's wealth, and asks whether he must fall (விழுவேனோ) into their deluding net. Both make the courtesan's embrace a place one falls into; the song gives the arts that set the trap, the Kural the verdict on who sinks.

Kural 1020 likens the movements of the shameless to a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) that feigns life by its string (நாணால்). Thiruppugazh 520 makes the newborn body of nine gates a doll (பதுமையின் செயல் போலவே) dancing on a rope of breath (வளிகயிறினுடன் ஆடி). The Kural uses the puppet for a man without inner shame; the song extends it to every embodied life, whose string is the breath itself.

Tirumanthiram 487 says one born of two who met in pleasure and grown within painful bondage (துன்புறு பாசத்தில்) can, once in the world, still seek the Ancient. Thiruppugazh 520 tells the life from the drop in the womb through birth and a ruined youth and then turns with இனி, now, to ask for the feet. Both set the turn to the Lord after a birth and growth told as bondage, and both hold it still possible.

Thiruppugazh 521 asks Murugan for the gift of singing immortal poems like the wise one of Pugali (புகலியில் வித்தகர்), Sambandar. Thiruppugazh 1282 says Murugan himself, as Sambandar (சம்பந்தனென), filled the land with Tamil. Read together, the poet in 521 asks for Sambandar's gift from the one the book elsewhere names as Sambandar.

Naladiyar 377 says the worthless woman licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from a man's hands (நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), and those fooled (ஏமாந்து) into thinking her love theirs are laughed at. Thiruppugazh 522 has the courtesans deceive (எத்தி மழுப்பி), snatch goods (பொருட்பறித்து) and give kisses and embraces, and the poet fears perishing daily for them. Both tie the caress directly to the taking of wealth; the Naladiyar ends in ridicule, the song in daily ruin.

Tirumanthiram 2178 says the countless tattvas are contained in தொண்ணூறோடு ஆறு, ninety-six, and those in twenty-five. Thiruppugazh 523 asks to know ஒருபது இருபது அறுபது உடன் அறு and then seek the feet within. If the song's numbers are read as summing to ninety-six, it takes the Tirumanthiram's count as the knowledge to be had before the inward turn; the pairing depends on that reading, since the song does not name the tattvas.

Kural 997 says those without human quality are like trees (மரம்போல்வர்) even if sharp as a file. Thiruppugazh 523 asks not to wander like a tree in the street (தெருவினில் மரமென) talking with everyone in idle work, but to see the six-faced Lord within. In both the tree is a person with an outward faculty, sharpness or speech, who lacks the inner one that makes it count.

Both look ahead to grey hair and the staff and draw the lesson that one should act before they come: the Naladiyar praises those who renounced in childhood, 524 asks to serve the Lord's servants before the body ripens.
The two songs end with the same two lines, Murugan dwelling on the Venkatam hill and giving his devotees whatever they ask when they ask it; a formula of this shrine.

524 lists old age part by part and asks to take up service உடம்பு பழுத்திடுமுன், before the body ripens. Tirumanthiram 179 says the same about timing: youth and strength are spent (தேய்ந்தற்று ஒழிந்த இளமை), so hold to Nandi உயிருள்ள போதே, while life is still there. Together they place the turn to devotion before decline, not at death.

525 chants the six-syllable formula and then widens its plea from itself to all creatures, that the sufferings of those born on the sea-girt earth (கடலுலகினில் வரும் உயிர்படும் அவதிகள்) cease. Tirumanthiram 85 makes the same widening, யான்பெற்ற இன்பம் பெறுக இவ்வையகம், and ties it to a mantra held within. Both turn a mantra-practice into a wish for the whole world.

525 asks that birth and death end (சனனமரணமதை ஒழிவுற) for one who chants and melts in Tamil (தமிழினில் உருகிய அடியவர்). Tirumanthiram 81 asks why anyone should be born again and says the Lord made him to render him well in Tamil (தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). Both set Tamil praise against rebirth.

527 asks not to die in women's union and fall into hell (நெறியில் மாண்டு இங்ஙனே நரகில் வீழ்ந்து அலையாமல்), hell coming after death. Kural 919 makes the women's soft shoulders themselves the அளறு, hell and mire, in which base men sink. The Kural puts in the present embrace the hell the song fears after it.

528 trusted worldly people as his help (உலகர் தாம் துணையாவர்) and now asks whether it is right that he go alone (யான் தனி போய்விடுவது) into Death's hands. Tirumanthiram 144 says the women and children who ate from the house do not follow (பின்செலார்); only vows and knowledge go with the dead. The pairing names what the song's lonely departure lacks.

529 asks for the feet so that what is mine and what is theirs (எனதாம் தனதானவை) fall away along with the frenzy of lust. Kural 346 says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. The song places that 'mine' beneath its desire for women.

Both see the body as a bag full of holes (Naladiyar தொளைபலவாய், 534 தொள்ளைப் புலாற்பை). The Naladiyar tells the lover to look at the desired body as a bag turned inside out; 534 turns the image on the poet's own body and asks to be rid of it.
Both take the poet's body apart as a list of containers, pot, bellows and bag in 280, a dozen kinds of bag in 534, and both ask for the end of that body rather than its health.
audit_text_issue: 534's bag-words (ஞெள்ளற்பை, துராற்பை) and praise are obscure.

note: Both songs call the body கள்வைத்த தோற்பை, a skin bag holding toddy, a formula the poet reuses. In 534 it is one of a dozen bags; 536 sets it against the formless form seen by the inner eye.
audit_text_issue: 536 has மொழிக்தரு, probably corrupt.

note: Both set the sect-disputers' learning aside: 124 opens with sectarians who cannot see one another's truth, 535 asks not to be tossed in the wrangling of the six sects' logicians. 535's reading rests on one clear line in a dense song.
audit_text_issue: 535 is dense rhythmic text whose word division is largely conjectural.

note: Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, tormented by the moon and the breeze, and ask him for his garland as the cure; 537 adds a plea that he not blame her old karma.

530 sees home and the young ones slowly becoming strangers (இல்லும் இளையோரும் மெல்ல அயலாக) as Yama on his buffalo comes to take his life. Tirumanthiram 157 has the wailing kin, wives and children turn back at the town's edge (ஊர்த்துறைக் காலே ஒழிவர்). Both show the family stopping short of the dying man's road.

531 counts the swamp of many books of means (உபாயப் பலநூலின் அள்ளல்) among his bonds and names yoga as the way the soul is saved. 709, in a distant chapter, sets the read books and argued creeds (வாசித்த நூல் மதங்கள்) against the bindu-light and yogic samadhi. Both place learning on the side of bondage and yoga on the side of release.

532 asks Murugan to tell the one thing by which the mind dies within (உள்ளத்தின் மாய்வது ஒன்றை மொழியாயோ) and never droops again; the reading of the uncertain line is the link's basis. Tirumanthiram 2956 says that when the mind's maya itself dies (மனமாயை தான்மாய) nothing else remains to die. Tirumular states as doctrine what the song only asks for.

533 begins wilting before jasmine (முல்லை) and women's teeth (பல்லுக்கும் வாடி) and ends with the body burned in the brands and dropped in the pit. Naladiyar 45 refuses the men who call smiles jasmine buds and sets against them teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground (புறங்காட்டு உதிர்ந்துக்க பல்லென்பு). The same jasmine-teeth figure leads both to the cremation ground, in the Naladiyar as the cure for desire, in the song as its end.

535 asks whether he must wander in the learned wrangling of the stubborn logicians of the six sects (சமயமாறின் ... வல்லர்க்கர் மூர்க்கர் கல்விக் கலாத்து). Tirumanthiram 1558 says the six sects are six roads to one city and those who argue 'this is good, that bad' are dogs barking at a hill. Both treat the sectarian quarrel itself as the fault.

536 asks for the knowledge that sees with the inner eye (உள்ளக்கண் நோக்கும் அறிவு) the one thing at the end of the ages, after refusing the body of five elements. Tirumanthiram 2944 says fools see with the eyes in their faces, and seeing with the eye within (அகத்திற் கண்கொண்டு) is bliss. Both make the inner eye the organ of the real.

537 praises Murugan as the poet who reached the shore of all learning (கல்விகரை கண்ட புலவோனே). Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore (கல்வி கரையில) and a short life must choose what to learn. Read literally, the song claims for the god a shore the Naladiyar denies exists for the learner; the conflict holds only if the god is measured by the human limit.

538 took mother, wife, children, family and wealth as all that was needed (குலம்வாய்த்த நல்ல தனம்வாய்த்தது) until Yama comes and he is burned at the இடுகாடு. Naladiyar 25 has the man who sees corpses carried yet marries and says 'there is, there is' (உண்டு உண்டு உண்டு) answered by the funeral drum. Both set household gain against the burning ground.

539 ends with the god who stood and worshipped the hunter girl's lotus feet (குறமங்கை பங்கயம் வரநின்று கும்பிடும்). 209, at Swamimalai, has him bow his cool crown daily on her golden feet (பொன்னடிமீது நித்தமும் தண்முடி). The reversal of worship, god to devotee, recurs far apart in the book.

540 opens with வரைவில் பொய் மங்கையர், false women without bounds, and describes their embrace. Kural 919 calls the shoulders of women who draw no line (வரைவிலா மாணிழையார்) the hell in which base men sink. The song's word is the Kural's chapter word, though the song names no price.

Both picture a man who clings to house and desire into a failing old age. The Naladiyar's old man, toothless on his staff, still has his eyes on desire and so has no path to safety; 541's clings to children and gold until he is grey and breathless, and asks for grace before Yama's rope catches him.

543 asks whether, sunk in the sea of birth (பவசாகரம்), his heart will think of the six syllables and cry குகா குகா. Tirumanthiram 916 repeats அரகர என்ன four times and ends அறும்பிறப்பு, birth is cut off. Both make the repeated name, in doubled form, the way out of birth.
audit_text_issue: Two corrupt words in 543 (வி஡ணர் வி஡ணரென, நிணங்கள்ழு ழுவென).

note: 544 praises Murugan for teaching the six syllables within the one syllable (ஓரெழுத்தில் ஆறெழுத்தை ஓதுவித்த) to the Lord who taught the gods, and asks to be told the wisdom to love him. 1124 asks to be taught sweetly the silent mantra (மவுன மந்த்ரம்) Murugan gave Siva and fills in what it holds. The short song's guru story is expanded there into a plea for the same teaching.

545 lists the woman part by part, hair, moon face, banyan-leaf navel, carp eyes, breasts, each with its comparison, and the poet wanders blind (அந்தனாகி மயல்). Naladiyar 46 lists the body's parts as entrails, fat, blood, bone and sinew and asks which of them is the garlanded woman. The same part-by-part method dissolves the figure the song is caught by.

Both open with a riddle of what a woman's eye is, a string of 'or's of weapons, poison and fish. In 103 Yama's messengers are one of the answers; 546 keeps them out of the list and sets them, with club and noose, at the end of the plea.

546 opens with the lover's riddle about the eye, கோலோ வாளோ வேலோ சேலோ மீனோ மானோ. Naladiyar 44 refuses the eyeless men who call eyes lilies, carp and spears (குவளை பொருகயல் வேல்) and sees a scooped-out palm fruit. The song voices the very comparisons the Naladiyar rejects, and then confesses where they led.

546 uses மயல் for the poet's lust and again for Murugan, who in love fell at the hunter girl's feet (மயல்கொண்டு உலாய் அவள் தாள்மீதே வீழ்). 309, at Kanchi, also gives the god's infatuation (அடிபணிந்திட்டப் பட்டு மயற்கொண்டு அயர்பவன்) while asking that the poet's own desire be quenched. Both set the god's praised mayal beside the poet's confessed one.

Both make the courtesan's welcome depend on the gift in hand. The Naladiyar's women would send away even Vishnu with folded hands if he brought nothing; 550's will not speak to a man on the day he brings no gold.

Both picture the courtesan's double dealing as a body turned to more than one man at once: the Naladiyar's eel shows its head to the snake and its tail to the fish; 553 gives the eyes to one man, the breasts to another, the hands to a third.
audit_text_issue: 553 has a corrupt glyph in வயலு஡ரா.

note: Both show Yama's servants binding the soul with ropes and driving it into fire. Tirumular gives the punishment to those who urged killing; 558 names no sin, and lists the tortures at length only to ask Murugan to end them.
audit_text_issue: 558 has the corrupt glyph ஡ in அனலு஡டே.

note: Both describe the Lord as beyond speech and conduct: Tirumular's great one is beyond speech, word and feeling (பேசா உரையுணர்வற்ற); 561's Reality cannot be read, worshipped or spoken (வாய்விட்டுப் பேசொணாதது).
audit_text_issue: 561 reads போசொணாதது for பேசொணாதது, and வயலு஡ரத்தில் has a corrupt glyph.

note: The song's courtesans act out a false love and deal with a man only as far as his coins go (அன்பு போற் பொய் நடித்துக் காசளவு உறவாடி). The Kural describes women who weigh the gain first and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). Both put the measuring of money before the show of affection; the song adds that the show is a studied art (இன்ப சாஸ்த்ரம், பண்டு இராப்பகல் கற்று).
audit_text_issue: 547: அங் மாய்ப்பரி has lost a letter.

note: The Naladiyar says the body appears like mist on a hill and goes, so its owners should take the fruit it can yield while they have it (யாக்கையால் ஆய பயன்கொள்க). The song tells the mind not to trust the body, a string-worked contraption Brahma locked (நம் ஆக்கையை நம்பாதே), and names the use to make of it now: to belong to the vel-bearer under his deed of possession (இனிமேல் நாம் ... வேலவனார்க்கு இயல் அங்கு ஆகுவம்). The song fills in what the Naladiyar's 'fruit' should be.
audit_text_issue: Many splits in 548's middle lines are uncertain.

note: In 686 the poet asks for grace before the world laughs at him as a madman reciting Kama's arts (உலகோர்கள் ... நகைகள் கூறி விடுவதன்முன்). In 549 he asks whether a lecher should be left to be mocked (பகடியிடும்படி தூர்த்தனை விடலாமோ), and sets against that public shame a public grace: the guru came on the peacock and took him so that the world knew it (ஆட்கொளல் சகமறியும்படி காட்டிய குருநாதா). The pair shows the same public that mocks being made witness to the claiming.

Tirumular says Nandi subdued him who would not be subdued, set his foot on him and placed him in supreme bliss (அடங்காத என்னை அடக்கி அடிவைத்து). The song names Murugan the guru who came on the peacock and took the poet as his own (வந்தெனை ஆட்கொளல்). Both speak of the guru's taking of an unruly self as a done act, told in the first person.
audit_text_issue: TM 2741 has a garbled word (பரானநத்தத்தே).

note: Tirumular says the Lord is not in the mansion, the hall or the temple, but stands within the hearts of those who have given up craving (வேட்கைவிட்டார் நெஞ்சில்). The song places Siva's dance in the hall that is the heart of unfailing devotees (தளர்வறும் அன்பர்க்கு உளமெனும் மன்றில்), and its plea is for the love that scorns union (கலவியை நிந்தித்து). The song asks for exactly the condition Tirumular sets for the Lord's dwelling in the heart.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 551: திநட்முழ்குங் is corrupt.

note: The Naladiyar's courtesan licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hand and turns away, and those who think her love theirs are laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). In the song the greed for money is presented by the woman's kin as affection (சுற்றம் பரிவென வைக்கும் பணவாசை), and the poet calls himself mocked and deluded (பகிடி மருட்கொண்டு). Both name a feigned tenderness that covers the taking of money, and the ridicule that follows the one who believes it.

The Kural says men without a firm heart embrace women who join with them while tending other things in their hearts (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணிப் புணர்பவர்). The song spells this out as a division among many men: eyes to one, breasts to another, thoughts to a third (ஒருவரொடு சிந்தை ஒருவரொடு நிந்தை), and confesses the delusion that the love is real (அன்பு பெருகவுளதென்று மனநினையும் இந்த மருள்). The song's six-fold ஒருவரொடு is a list of what the Kural compresses into பிறநெஞ்சு.
audit_text_issue: வயலு஡ரா has a corrupt glyph (஡ for ஊ).
