note: The Naladiyar says to loveless women a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser with wealth is sugar (செக்கூர்ந்து கொண்டாரும் செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம்). The song's women demand money before the cloth is touched (உடைதொடாப் பணம்). Both make money the only test applied to the man.
audit_text_issue: 554's invitation line is corrupt (ஓ஡ணர் பா஡ணர் வா஡ணர்).

note: Tirumular strings the Goddess's names, Tripura, Sundari, Antari, Narani, Manonmani, and says by these the one great power stands as many (வருபலவாய் நிற்கும்). The song's praise is the same kind of litany, with திரிபுரை, சுந்தரி, குண்டலி, நிரஞ்சனி, சமய நாயகி among the names, ending in the mother who bore Murugan. The shared names show the song drawing on the Shakta naming that Tirumular records.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 555: மதனு஡லின் has a corrupt glyph.

note: In 556 the namo-nama litany is quoted as the song the poet failed to sing: he never took up the devotion that sings it (என்றுபாடும் பத்தி பூணாமலே) and fell like a stray bull on women's breasts. In 567 he asks for that very thing, to hold to Murugan with devotion and sing his Thiruppugazh again and again until freed (பத்தியால் ... மா திருப்புகழ் பாடி முத்தனாமாறு). Read together, the confession of 556 is answered by the plea of 567.

Tirumular says Nandi taught that the guru is Siva, and that people do not grasp it (குருவே சிவமெனக் கூறினன் நந்தி). The song asks Murugan for the secret knowledge that makes clear the Lord is the guru (பதி குருவெனத் தெளி போத ரகசியம்). Tirumular states the doctrine; the song asks for it as a secret to be told, which matches Tirumular's 'they do not grasp it' (குறித்தோரார்).
audit_text_issue: 557's shrine word சகசிரகிப் has probably lost a syllable.

note: The Kural groups double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The song calls the courtesans goddesses of misfortune who make men poor (மிடியர் ஆக்கு மூதேவிகள்) and drinkers of liquor (பேய்நீர் ஊணிகள்). Where the Kural says such company follows the loss of Fortune, the song makes the women themselves the bringers of misfortune.
audit_text_issue: 559 க்஡ணடா பீடிகள் and பொலர்மு தேவிகள் corrupt

note: The Kural names the courtesans women who draw no line (வரைவிலா மாணிழையார்), whose shoulders are the mire base men sink in. The song charges that they couple even with outcastes without refusing (புலையர் மாட்டும் மறாதே கூடிகள்) and fall on many (பலர் மேல் வீழ்). The song's charge is a concrete case of the Kural's வரைவிலா.
audit_text_issue: 559 'க்஡ணடா' is corrupt, as the marker notes

note: The Kural warns of the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார்). The song's whole charge is in its first words, women whose minds are set on seizing wealth (பொருள்கவர் சிந்தை அரிவையர்), and it asks to stop wandering in that passion and praise the feet with a melting heart. Both define the courtesan by where her desire is aimed.

The Naladiyar says a harlot's love is like a lamp's light: it ends when the hand is empty as the light ends when the oil runs out (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). The song's women look with disgust on a man once the wealth is gone (விரவிய திரவியம் இலரானால் வெறுத்து நோக்கிகள்). The song sets against that love, which ends with the money, a vow that does not end: he will not forget the feet in dream or waking (கனவிலும் நனவிலும் மறவேனே).
audit_text_issue: Song: க்ருஷிபணு தடத்து is hard to split.

note: Both measure women's charms by their effect on ascetics: in 108 their laughter makes renouncers weaken (துறவினர் சோர), in 563 their breasts make the ascetics of the great principle faint (தத்துவத்துத் தவர் சோர), the same verb.

Both list the tortures Yama's messengers inflict, binding, dragging, burning. 558 lists them without a reason; 564 gives them one, an account of the poet's deeds opened and totalled, with the torture matched to the sum.
audit_text_issue: 558 has corrupt glyph in அனலு஡டே; 564's opening splits are uncertain.

note: The Kural likens the cloth on a girl's unfallen breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேல் கட்படாம்). The song's breasts chase off the elephant (களிற்றைத் துரத்தி) and make even ascetics faint (தவர் சோர). Both pair the breast with the must elephant as a dangerous force; the Kural's lover sees it held in by the cloth, while the song's confessing poet sees it overpower all.

The Kural's lover asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). The song's eyes rival the carp and match the doe (கயலைச் சருவிப் பிணையொத்து), and through them the poet has lost goodness, knowledge and feeling (நலமற்று அறிவற்று உணர்வற்றனன்). The song counts the cost of the கூற்றம் the Kural only glimpses in the look.

Tirumular confesses he cannot conquer the five senses and himself and is like a horse that bolts (வெல்லகில்லேன் புலன் ஐந்துடன் தன்னையும்). The song names the senses as five cheats who play their falsehood of sound, touch, smell, form and taste (சூதர் ஐவர் சத்த பரிசான மண ரூப ரசம்) while Death draws near. Both are first-person confessions of defeat by the five.

The Naladiyar calls the body a pot seeping filth from nine openings, which the fool praises as a woman because of its dark skin. The song calls the poet's own body a basket that knows no cleanness (சுத்தமறியாத பறி காயம்) and recoils from its smell (சீசி இது நாற உடல்) as he seeks women's houses. The Naladiyar turns the disgust on the desired body, the song on the desiring one's own.

Tirumular teaches that when the two deeds balance, the sweet power of grace comes as the guru and the three impurities end (இருவினை நேரொப்பில் இன்னருட் சத்தி குருவென வந்து). The song names Murugan as that descent (ஞானசத்தி நிபாதா) and asks to become freed by singing his Thiruppugazh with devotion. It applies the Siddhanta term for the descent of grace to Murugan himself.
Both call the courtesan's body a mire (அளறு) into which men sink; the Kural's word also means hell, and 574 asks to be taken by the Lord so as not to sink there.
audit_text_issue: Last two lines of 574's praise nearly repeat each other (வழியருளின் பேறு காட்டி)

note: Both counter desire by naming the body's openings and their seepage: the Naladiyar's pot oozing filth from nine holes, 574's rotting, cloth-stopped hole. The Naladiyar calls the lover a fool; 574 asks for rescue.
audit_text_issue: 574's text has obscure lines (இறைவைகொளுங் கூவல், சீலை தீற்று) and the last two praise lines nearly repeat each other.

note: Both make the woman's eye Death: the Kural's lover cannot tell if her look is Death, an eye or a doe, while 578 calls the eye-corners Yama's messengers in a confession it was saved from.

Both say rites and recitation do not yield the truth: Tirumular's men perform many rites and recite hymns yet wither without understanding; 573 doubts that japa, fire-offerings and Agamic learning passed down by gurus can be a refuge without Siva's own gift.

Both define Sivayoga. Tirumular makes it knowing the conscient and non-conscient and becoming one's own light; 575 makes it seeing every element, scripture, letter and god abide as one form, and adds that the malas must go first.

27 asks to see clearly how to leave the embrace and reach the feet; 582 vows to remember the feet even asleep on the breasts after union, so devotion is placed inside desire rather than after it, if the vow is not read as hyperbole.

The Thiruppugazh song asks to hold daily in thought (நாளு நினைவது) Murugan's form counted part by part: faces, twelve arms (ஈராறு தோளு), two feet, consorts, vel and peacock. The Tirumanthiram verse counts Sadasiva's five faces, fifteen eyes and ten hands and ends with that Lord entering and filling the heart (நெஞ்சு புகுந்து நிறைந்து). Both use the counted iconic form as the content of meditation, for different gods.

Both songs confess the same misuse of the poet's art: 569 calls himself the one who sang poems of every kind from foot to hair (பாதாதி கேசமாக வகைவகை கவிபாடும்) on women who price their breasts, and 1150 the poet who wandered singing women from foot to head (பாதாதி கேசம் அளவும் பாடும் கவிஞனாய்). Read together they show the head-to-foot description of women as a named genre the poet repents of, in both cases alongside the term பசு பாசம.

569 confesses having sung women from foot to hair (பாதாதி கேசமாக ... கவிபாடும்). 572, in the same set of Viralimalai songs, is itself such a catalogue, from bathed hair (குந்தளமும்) to anklets (பரிபுர ... பதமும்), turned at the end into a plea that the delusion end. The pairing shows the poet using the confessed genre inside the devotional song.

The Thiruppugazh song asks for the experience of samadhi in which the mind dissolves (மநோலய சமாதி அநுபூதி). The Tirumanthiram verse describes the samadhi in which the mind melts and becomes Siva (சித்தம் உருக்கிச் சிவமாம் சமாதி) and whose bliss does not leave. Both define samadhi by the dissolving of mind, one as a request, the other as a report of its fruit.

571 asks whether, not fixing his mind on the transcendent, he will go with longing for gifts (தராசையுற்று அடைவேனோ) to faithless, averted men of chaff-like fame (துரால்புகழ் ... பராமுக துரோகரை). 306 asks not to perish in vain like bards who seek out the wealth of deceitful misers and call them Pari and Kari. Both set the court poet's begging against praise of Murugan; 306 makes plain the bardic trade that 571's dense compounds name.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 571's compounds are hard to divide and may be garbled (e.g. செர்ருபமி).

note: 572 recalls in its praise that at Vayalur Murugan appeared before the poet and told him to sing the rare great Thiruppugazh so that delusion and mala might end (வயலியில் ... அரிய பெரிய திருப்புகழ் விளம்பு). The second song of the book likewise names the grace that told him to sing Thiruppugazh (திருப்புகழ் ... செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை), at Seyppathi, usually taken as Vayalur. The two are the book's own accounts of its commission; 572 adds its purpose, the ending of மயல் and மலம்.

575 asks to gain the path of Sivayoga in the line of the teaching guru (உபதேச குருபர சம்ப்ரதாயமொடு ஏயும் நெறி). 573 asks whether knowledge handed on by gurus one after another, with japa, fire offerings and breath restraint, can be a refuge (தஞ்சமாமோ), and says it would be so only if Siva gave it (தழலாடி ... ஞான சித்தி தருமாகில்). Read together, 573 puts a condition on the guru-lineage 575 trusts: the teaching avails when the Lord gives it; this depends on the uncertain reading of தரியாத போதகத்தர்.

The Thiruppugazh song asks whether, before youth turns to age (இளமை கிழம்படு முன்), he will come to know and gain the feet. The Tirumanthiram verse says youth wears away and is gone, so hold to Nandi while life is still in you (உயிருள்ள போதே). Both make the passing of youth the reason for turning to the Lord now; the song asks it from inside the pleasures it describes.

576 asks to reach the feet before youth becomes age. The Naladiyar verse pictures the man who fails to: speech failing, leaning on a staff, teeth gone, still with eyes set on desire in the house, with no path to safety (ஏம நெறிபடருமாறு இல்லையே). The Naladiyar shows the end the song's urgency is meant to avoid: desire outliving youth with no way out.

Among its names for courtesans the Thiruppugazh song calls them women who quarrel bitterly when not given (ஈயாத போதில் அறப் பிணக்கிகள்) and who sell their breasts (விலைத் தனத்தியர்). The Naladiyar verse says their love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both make payment the condition of the courtesan's affection, and the song asks on that ground whether a bond (உறவு) with them is fitting.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 580 has corrupt glyphs (மாயா செர்ருப, வா஡ண ரி஡ணரென்).

note: The Thiruppugazh song, its singer unlearned in Vedas and Agamas, asks for the teaching of knowledge beyond the six sixes (ஆறாறு மீதில் ஞானோபதேசம்). The Tirumanthiram verse reports that to one who did not know the nature of the six sixes (ஆறாறின் தன்மை அறியாது இருந்தேனுக்கு) Nandi made it known and stood beyond them. The same term, ஆறாறு, gives the request in one and its fulfilment through the guru in the other.

The Thiruppugazh song asks on what day Murugan will run to him as guard (காவல் என விரைய ஓடி) so that Yama's messengers (இயமதூதர்) do not bind his legs with rope and drag him. The Tirumanthiram verse says there is no fighting the life's departure, but for one who thinks of the Lord, Death's messengers (நமன் தூதர்) will not come near to burn. Both place the Lord between the devotee and Death's servants at the hour of death; the Tirumanthiram's reading is uncertain in its last lines.

Both confess the court poet's begging: 579 praised the man who never gives as Kubera, 589 sang correct Tamil verse to iron-hearted men who show no pity. Both make this, not only desire, a reason he did not seek the Lord.

The Kural says nothing degrades the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow; 589 shows that degradation in the poet himself, trembling and cringing as he sings for gifts, and asks whether such a tongue can gain love for the Lord.

The song asks to be one with the devotees who lay their speech, knowledge, life and feeling as a garland on the lotus feet (உரையையும் அறிவையும் உயிரையும் உணர்வையும் உன்பாத கஞ்ச மலர்மீதே ... புனைதர). Tirumular describes Nandi taking the disciple's body, wealth and life with poured water and setting his feet on him (உடல்பொருள் ஆவி உதகத்தாற் கொண்டு ... நொடியின் அடிவைத்து). The same total giving of the self appears in the Tirumanthiram as a guru's rite of taking and in the song as the devotee's own garland at the feet.

In 589 the poet confesses he sang paltry poems, correct by the rules of Tamil grammar, to iron-hearted patrons who show no pity (இரங்கார்க் கியற்றண் டமிழ்நூலின் உடம்பாட் டுடன்பாட் டியம்பா ... புன்கவிபாடி), driven by hunger. In 613 the same trade is seen from outside: poets who praise men as the dark cloud riding Garuda, slip in their names and steal from old sayings (அவர்பெயர் செருகி ... திருடி ஒருபடி நெருடி). The later song turns the earlier personal confession into a portrait of the patron-poet's craft.

The song asks for the teaching that turns him back (விலக்கும் போதகம்) and for the Lord to say 'do not fear' so that he gives up the evil his mind plans (விடற்கு அஞ்சேல் என அருள்வாயே). Tirumular says the goddess who gives the means rooted out danger from his heart, held craving down and said 'fear not' (அவாவை அடக்கிவைத்து அஞ்சல் என்றாளே). The song asks for exactly what the Tirumanthiram verse reports as done: the word of reassurance coming together with the curbing of desire.
audit_text_issue: 1108 lines 2-3 (சுவா, சுழி) are uncertain.

note: The song names the courtesan who shows her breasts to many (கொங்கை நோக்கப் பலர்க்குங் காட்டி) and calls her life a trade (தொழில் பண்டாட்டம்). The Kural says those of refined understanding will not plunge into the base charms of those whose goodness belongs to everyone (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). The Kural's பொதுநலம், beauty held in common, is what the song shows in action, and the song asks Murugan for the knowledge the Kural assumes the wise already have.

Both songs name disease caught from courtesans as the literal consequence of the pleasure: 592 says that leaping into union with women named by their price (கோல விலை மாதர்) he has taken diseases (கலிய நோய்கள் கொண்டே), and 461 shows the man who paid wandering with swelling sores and festering eyes until onlookers cover their eyes (கண்டவர்க்குக் கண் புதைப்ப). Read together they show the disease motif is a recurring warning in the courtesan songs, in 592 tied to birth and in 461 to public shame.

The praise says Murugan explained to Sambhu the nature of the tvam-pada (சம்புவுக்குத் தொம்பதத்துப் பண்பு உரைத்து). Tirumular names the three padas of the Vedantic sentence, tat-pada, tvam-pada and asi-pada (தற்பதம் தொம்பதம் தானாம் அசிபதம்), as the soul, the Supreme and Siva within turiya. The pairing shows that the Vedantic 'thou' already had a Saiva reading in Tamil, and that the song makes it the content of Murugan's lesson to Siva in place of the usual meaning of Om.

In its refrain the song lists what the courtesans show, among them false pity and agreement of heart (வஞ்சத் திரக்கங் காட்டுவர் நெஞ்சிற் பொருத்தங் காட்டுவர்). The Kural says the weak-hearted touch the shoulders of women who join with them while tending other things in their hearts (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணிப் புணர்பவர்). Both locate the deceit in a heart that is shown as one thing and holds another; the song's காட்டுவர் makes the Kural's divided heart into a performance.

The song's clearest phrase is that, leaving the support of truth for the support of the false (மெய்ச்சார்வு அற்றே பொய்ச்சார்வு உற்றே), he cannot leave the sea of births. The Kural says a wretched birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருளான் ஆம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). Both make the mistaking of false for true the cause of birth, the song as a confession and the Kural as a general law.

The song asks that the birth full of the evil of malam end and that he reach high heaven (மலத்தின் தீமை கூடிய பிறப்புந் தீர ... உயர் சுவர்க்கஞ் சேர). Tirumular says those freed of the five malams become Siva, while those still in the malams' darkness are the kind that go from earth to heaven and hell (பாரின்கண் விண்நரகம் புகும் பான்மையர்). On the reading that the song names heaven as the goal after malam ends, the two conflict: for Tirumular heaven belongs to the round of the bound, not to its end; both verses are uncertain in places.

The song pictures courtesans who call to anyone at all and dance along the street (யாவராயினும் நத்தி அழைப்பவர் தெருவூடே). The Naladiyar says such women, whatever believable words they speak, belong to no one but their own bodies (யார்க்கும் தமரல்லர் தம்உடம்பினார்). The two halves fit: those who call everyone are kin to no one, and the song adds that this drowns the man in maya and births of malam.

In 28 the poet asks that Death not call him and praises Murugan as the one who spoke sweet Tamil to delight the sage of Pothiyai (பொதியவரை முநிவனக மகிழ ... இனியதமிழ் பகர்வோனே). In 598 he asks not to draw near Death nor be born on earth, and to be given the honey-nectar of the knowledge of virtuous Agastya (சீலஅகத்திய ஞான தேனமுதைத் தருவாயே). The later song asks for himself what the earlier one says Murugan gave the sage, and makes that knowledge the remedy against Death and birth.
Both thank Murugan for the grace of being told to sing the Thiruppugazh (செப்பென); 2 lists what the song must hold, and 602 already hears it recited by devotees in all four directions.

The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; 603 confesses exactly that folly, living as if a bubble-like life with wife, sons and house would stand for a crore of aeons.
Both see life as a bubble (புற்புதம்). The Naladiyar praises those who see it so and resolve to end their wandering; 603 confesses that he knows the image and still lives as if it lasted.
8 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's men strike and end his fear; 605 turns the same hour into a battle the servant wins with Murugan's grace, and asks him to come and watch.

The praise calls Murugan the true word of the right path of reasoning that establishes the tattvas, forty-eight and forty-eight (தத்வ நாற்பத்தெட்டு நாற்பத்தெட்டு மேற்றுத் ... சத்ய வாக்யப் பெருமாளே), that is ninety-six. Tirumular says the ninety-six are called common to all, while the thirty-six are the tattvas of the Saivas (தொண்ணூறோடு ஆறும் பொதுஎன்பர் ... ஆறாறு அருஞ்சைவர் தத்துவம்). The Tirumanthiram places the song's count as the shared reckoning of all schools, beside a narrower Saiva count of thirty-six.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 601: கொத்து நூற்றுப் பத்து நாட்ட unclear.

note: The poet says he will never forget the grace that set even him, a small servant, to sing the Thiruppugazh (திருப்புகழைச் சிறிது அடியேனுஞ் செப்பென வைத்து ... அநுக்ரகம் மறவேனே). Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (என்னைநன் றாக இறைவன் படைத்தனன் தன்னைநன் றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யு மாறே). Both poets present their own Tamil work as appointed by the god, not chosen.

The song asks Murugan to come and watch the day when his stammering servant, who worships the two feet, fights with his grace and cruel Death and his army fall (கொடிய மறலியு மவனது கடகமு மடிய ... நினதருள் கொடுபொரு மமர்காண). The Kural says that for those who have gained the strength of austerity even leaping past Death becomes possible (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). Both let a human being overcome Death; the Kural grants it to the strength of tapas, the song to the servant fighting with the Lord's grace.

The poet says he gave the jasmine-smiling women whatever they wanted and gave them gold, and they said there was nothing and went (இட்டு பொன்னை இல்லை யெனஏகி), leaving him to think of his own lack (இன்மை உள்ளி). The Naladiyar says the harlot's love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). The song is the confession of a man who lived out the Naladiyar's comparison.

The song asks for the bliss of one's own form that stands as the ancient first, one, then two kinds, the three gunas, the four Vedas, the five senses and the six limbs (தொல்லைமுதல் தானொன்று மெல்லியிரு பேதங்கள் சொல்லுகுண மூ ... புலனோ ரைந்து ... ஆறங்கம்). Tirumular's opening verse counts the Lord the same way: one, two with grace, within three, knowing four, conquering five, spread as six (ஒன்றவன் தானே இரண்டவன் இன்னருள் ... ஆறு விரிந்தனன்). Both use the counting ladder to say the one becomes all the numbered categories; the song makes that whole ladder the state it asks to be given.

The praise tells Daksha's sacrifice through the punished gods: the moon's body worn, the sun's teeth knocked out, Agni's hand cut off, Brahma's head fallen, Saraswati's nose slipping (சோமன் மேனியுந் தேய ... விதிதலை வீழ நன்பாரதியு மூக்கு நழுவிட). Tirumular's verse lists the same losses, head, face, nose, hand and shoulder, of Hari, Brahma, Daksha, the sun, the moon and Agni (சிரமுக நாசி சிறந்தகை தோள்தான்), as the fate of the good without Hara's grace. The song keeps the list as story, and Tirumular draws the lesson.
The Kural names double-hearted women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom fortune has left; 609 opens its list with gamblers and money-loving women side by side and adds disease.

The poet confesses that he wandered without knowing the full Siva Agamas (பூரணசிவாகமங்கள் அறியாதே), thinking only of women. Tirumular says the Siva Agamas the Lord gives by grace are numberless, and that he keeps their meaning in mind and praises it (அண்ணல் அருளால் அருளும் சிவாகமம் ... எண்ணிநின் றப்பொருள் ஏத்துவன் நானே). Set together, the Agamas are for Tirumular the grace he holds and for Arunagiri a knowledge whose lack he counts among his faults.

15 confesses that the poet himself begged from patrons, praising them as clouds in giving; 613 looks at the same trade from outside, at poets who praise men as the cloud-dark Vishnu and steal verses, and disowns their way.

614 quotes the women's own coaxing words (இங்கே வருக, இனிய இதழ் தந்தேன்) and says they then strip a man of wealth and life alike (பொருள் உயிர்கள் ... பறிகொளும்). Kural 911 puts the harm in the same place: the sweet speech (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்) of those who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்). The song dramatises the speech the couplet warns against.

615 asks for the meaning Murugan told Siva, drawn from the ancient Veda so that disputes end (பழமறை கொண்டே தர்க்கங்கள் அற). Tirumanthiram 51 says the wise left argument and debate (தர்க்க வாதத்தை விட்டு) and gained release by reciting the Veda. Both set the Veda's meaning against தர்க்கம், as what ends it.

Among its petitions 616 asks for a thought beyond dusk and day (அந்தி பகல் அற்ற நினைவு) and a way to the moon-space (சந்திர வெளி). Tirumanthiram 1856 stays in the place where night and day are not (இராப்பகல் அற்ற இடத்தே) and drinks bliss at the Lord's feet. The shared phrase names the same state beyond the alternation of day and night, asked for in one and claimed in the other.

617 rebukes its own mind for not melting at song, at hearing, or at the sight of Death's road (பாட்டில் உருகிலை கேட்டும் உருகிலை), and turns it to Murugan. Tirumanthiram 1486 makes the melting of the unmelting heart (கசியாத நெஞ்சம் கசியக் கசிவித்து) part of the true path itself. The song is the complaint of a heart still unmelted; the verse names what the path does to it.

619 counts wife and children (மனைவி மகவான கடலலை) with women and wealth as one sea in which he sinks and wanders. Naladiyar 130 tells the heart that will not let go of the home bond and pines for its children (மனைப்பாசம் கைவிடாய் மக்கட்கென்று ஏங்கி) that only good done goes with the soul. Both put family attachment, not only lust, among the bonds.

620 describes price-women (விலைமாதர்) who talk of kinship (முறை பேசி) while looking for prosperous houses (வாழ்ந்த மனை தேடி). Kural 912 names the same move: women who weigh the gain and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்), and tells the man to weigh them in return. The song's scene is the couplet's charge acted out.

622 calls the body a hut that is the senses' shirt (இந்திரிய சட்டைக் குரம்பை) and vows not to forget the feet even when it perishes. Tirumanthiram 312 uses the same word for the body, the hut that does not stay (நில்லாக் குரம்பை), and says those who think it lasting cannot see the Lord. 622 is the right response to the fact 312 states.

622 vows that even at the moment the body perishes (குரம்பை அழி பொழுதினிலும்) he will not forget the dancing feet (மறந்திடேனே). Tirumanthiram 176, on the plainest reading, says that when life leaves the body there is no way to fight, but Death's messengers do not come near one who thinks of the Lord (அண்ணலை எண்ணும்). Both make remembrance at the death-hour the defence; 176's construction is uncertain.
Both give the courtesan's vow of oneness and show it false: the Naladiyar's woman swore never to part, like gem and thread, and turned away; 626's women swear 'you are me and I am you' without shame.
8 asks Murugan to come when Death's servants strike; 625 shows those same servants trembling at his vel, so the fear of the plea is answered in the praise.

Both are love-sickness told with the moon, Kama's arrows and the cuckoo; 14 names the speaker as a deceiver longing for women, while 628 leaves its speaker unnamed and ends on Valli at Murugan's chest.

624 calls the women's eyes Death coming with its fortress and pressing into battle (வருமறலி அரணமொடு முடுகு சமர் விழியிணைகள்). Kural 1083 has the man say he never knew what Death was until now: it is a woman's grace with great battling eyes (கூற்றென்பதனை ... பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Death, war and eyes join in both; the Kural's lover is astonished, while the song makes the image a confession.

625's praise has Yama's servants trembling and asking 'what shall we do?' (எமபடரும் என் செய்வோம் என நடுநடுநடுங்க) before the vel. Tirumanthiram 2050 says the guru drove off the band of Death's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்) from his devotees. In both the Lord's power reaches the agents of death themselves.

627 says desire for young women's carp eyes takes a man down the false great road that multiplies the tangle of birth (பிறவி தரும் சிக்கு அது பெருகும் பொய்ப் பெருவழி). Naladiyar 378 says those who mean to reach the right path (செந்நெறிச் சேர்தும் என்பார்) will not embrace such women. Both frame lust as a road that leads away from the true one.

629 lists among what feeds his net of desire the moon that burns like sun, the flute and the blame of women (நார்மாதர் வசையாலும்). Kural 1147 says the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water of this sickness (ஊரவர் கெளவை எருவாக). Both make blame and gossip feed the longing they mean to shame; 629 turns the convention into its own state.
Both picture the poet laughed at by his own: in 610 wife, town and kin mock him, in 631 mother, kin and clan laugh as disease wastes his body; both answer by asking to be drawn to the Lord.

630's praise has the First One dancing the pure dance with Durga beside him and Kali with trident beating time (சூல காளி ... தாள ஓசை). Tirumanthiram 2746 says he danced with Kali (காளியோடு ஆடி) and goes on dancing in the hall. Both set Kali in Siva's dance; 630 makes her a partner keeping time, the reading of the line being unsure.
audit_text_issue: 630 dance line syntax uncertain.

note: 631 says that after the women make him cringe like a dog, disease comes and mother, kin and clan all laugh as his body wastes (தாய் தமர் குலத்தர் யாவரும் நகைக்கவே). Naladiyar 377 says those fooled into taking such women's love as their own get laughter from many (பலரால் நகை). Both end the courtesan's story in public ridicule.
Both describe women who take the wealth from a man's hand once he is caught; the Naladiyar adds that he is laughed at, 633 that his very strength of mind is destroyed.
Both confess the humiliation of pleading before patrons; 15 tells the flattery, 632 says he can no longer bear to plead his poverty to base and cruel men after women took his wealth.
The Kural says only those who join the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; 634 asks in the same image whether he will swim the long wave of birth and reach the pure feet.

632 says that after losing his wealth to women he can no longer bear to plead poverty before base and cruel men (பதகர் கொடியவாளிடத்திலே மிக வறுமை புகல்வதே ... இனி முடியாதே). Naladiyar 78 says even when starving, do not tell your need to those without courtesy (பண்பிலார்க்கு அற்றம் அறிய உரையற்க). The song is the shame the quatrain forbids, felt from inside.

635 calls the body an illusion like lightning at night, and not even that (அல்லில் நேரும் மின் அதுதானும் அல்லதாகிய உடல்). Naladiyar 8 says the wealth of the petty appears like lightning from a black cloud at night (எல்லில் ... மின்னுப்போல்) and vanishes. The same night-lightning is used for wealth in one and the body in the other, and 635 ranks the body below it.

Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, wounded by Kama's flowers and burned by the moon, and plead with him for her: 337 asks for his garland, 645 that he come and give her life, adding the tears she weeps as pearls through the night.

The Kural's woman hears the cowherd's flute as the herald of a burning evening and a weapon that kills; in 647 the cowherds' bamboo flute is one of the evening torments, with the sea and the moon, of a girl sick for Murugan.
Both place sayujya past the ordinary states of consciousness: Tirumular calls it reaching the state beyond waking and becoming Siva; 643 sets it above turiya and beyond every path and sect.
audit_text_issue: 643 has a garble, சுகசெர்ருபத்தை for சுகசொரூபத்தை.

note: 637 confesses seeking gifts (பரிசில் தேடி) by calling graceless patrons Meru, the seasonal rain cloud and the wish-tree (மேரு ... பருவ மேக மே தாரு). Tirumular tells the reader to seek (நாடுமின்) the king of the gods, who becomes great wealth like the rain-bearing cloud (பெயற்கொண்டல் போலப் பெருஞ்செல்வம்). The cloud the poet wasted on misers is, in the Tirumanthiram, the Lord's own figure, and seeking is aimed at the right giver.

638 counts the householder's needs, cloth (துகில்), food (கனபானம்), water and clothes, a woman and a house, and says the life goes in vain (உயிர் அவமே போம்). Tirumular's list is the same kind, cloth, rice, oil, necklace, marriage thread and bangles (கூறையும் சோறும் ... வளையலும்), and those who fix on them sink into the pit (ஆறைக் குழியில் அழுந்துகின்றாரே). Both make the household a list of wants and the list itself the trap.

638 begins its list of wants with the body, cloth, food and medicine for its sickness (மெய் உறுநோயை ஒழிக்கப் பரிகாரம்), and ends whirling in the mountain of births (பவகிரிக்குள் சுழல்வேனை). The Kural says that for those set on cutting off birth even the body is too much (உடம்பும் மிகை), so what other ties should they keep? The song shows how the body's needs multiply into a household, the case the Kural cuts off at the root.

639 names Murugan by a single epithet, the one who straightened the Pandya's hump (வழுதி கூன் நிமிர்த்த). 666 tells the whole story: he smeared the holy ash on the Pandya (வழுதி மேல் திருநீறே பூசி), the hump straightened, the leaf went against the stream and the Jains were uprooted. Together they show Sambandar's Madurai miracle claimed as Murugan's own deed, in brief and in full.
audit_text_issue: 666 has a few corrupt glyphs.

note: The Naladiyar says those who mean to reach the right way (செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென்பார்) do not embrace the breasts of women who go their own way. 641 says such women bring under passion's power (ராகத்தின் வசமாக) even those already walking the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga (சரியைக்ரியை யோகத்தின் வழிவருக்கு). Read together, the song limits the Naladiyar's confidence: being on the path does not by itself keep one away.

642 tells Siva's burning of the cities as a story in short verbs: he laughed and burned them (சிரித்தார் எரித்தார்), then flayed the elephant and burned Madana. Tirumular says fools say only that he destroyed the three cities (முப்புரம் செற்றனன் என்பர்கள் மூடர்கள்); the three cities are the work of the three impurities (மும்மல காரியம்). The Tirumanthiram supplies the inward reading of the deed the song narrates.

643 asks for a reality that those of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga cannot reach and the divisions of sects cannot approach (சமயபேதத்தினுக்கு அணுகொணா). 907, at Vayalur, asks not to perish in the sectarians' rules nor even in the chariyai, kiriyai and yoga disciplines (சரியைக்ரியா யோக நியமத்தின் மாயாது), but to be given unwavering jnana. Both songs set the Saiva paths themselves below the goal, which reads as the book's settled view, not one song's flourish.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 643: சுகசெர்ரு பத்தை is garbled (likely சுகசொரூபத்தை).

note: 644, on one division, asks whether the lustful man caught in women will forget even the feet that made him forget desire (ஆசையை மறப்பித்த கால்கள்). The Kural tells the reader to cling to the clinging of the one who has none, in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). Both make holding the Lord the means by which desire is undone; the song's fear is losing that hold. The division of the song's line is uncertain.

646 says those who live in women's power, who wander without thinking of great austerity (மாதவம் எணாமல்), and who do not recite and bow will shine in hell's fire. Tirumular says those who practise false austerity also enter hell (பொய்த்தவஞ் செய்வார் புகுவர் நரகத்து), and that austerity holds only by true knowledge. The Tirumanthiram adds a condition the song leaves out: neglecting tapas leads to hell, but so does tapas without jnana.

648 pictures Yama's messengers (நமனுடைய தூதர்) coming with the palm leaf, abusing, cutting and putting the man on the stake, and begs Murugan to come quickly at that hour. Tirumular states as done what the song begs for: the guru kept away the band of Yama's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்) from his devotees and ended the sorrow of birth. The plea and the assurance use the same figure.

In 648 Yama's men seize the sinner by the waist-cloth before abusing him, cut his flesh and lay him on the stake. In Tirumular's verse on meat-eating, Yama's messengers (இயமன்றன் தூதுவர்) seize the eaters in sight of all, fling them on their backs into fire-mouthed hell and break them. Both draw the messengers as torturers, not only summoners, which places the song's deathbed scene in the imagery of hell.

649 follows a man through women's arts to the bed and then to disease, lying pale, hungry and thirsty on a mat (நோய்பிணி கிடத்து பாய்மிசை வெளுத்து). Tirumular says that with the yoga by which the bindu does not leave, even the joining of two bodies is Siva's pleasure, while fools embrace women without ending infatuation (மோகங் கெட முயங்கார் மூடர்). The pairing limits the song's verdict: the ruin it shows is the fool's union taken in infatuation (மால்கொடு), not union as such, on Tirumular's account.

650 asks the god to let him cross over by telling him in verse (உனைக் கவிக்குள்ளாய்ச் சொலிக் கடைத்தேறவே) and names Murugan as the meaning in the poems of sages and Tamil poets. Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே), as the answer to repeated birth. Both make composing the god in verse the poet's way out of birth.

Both trace the embryo growing through the sizes of a seed, palm fruit and coconut and slipping head down into the world, a formula the book repeats; 520 goes on to virtue forgotten and a stinking body, 652 to the women who ruin the grown child.
Both make the ten months in the womb the start of bondage: Tirumular's form grows mingled with maya, and 652's child, grown by the way of deeds, ends among women.

651 confesses he never wore the true holy ash (மெய்த்திரு நீறிடா இருவினையேனை) and asks Murugan to smear it on him and let him see the red feet. Tirumular says those who wear the armour-ash gladly lose their deeds (தங்கா வினைகள்), reach the Siva state and join the beautiful feet (திருவடி சேர்வரே). The song's plea follows the Tirumanthiram's sequence exactly: ash, deeds ended, the feet.

Both use the wood-apple swallowed by the elephant, whole outside and empty within. In 653 it is the poet's body (வேழம் உண்ட விளாகனி அதுபோல மேனி) hollowed by delusion; in Tirumular Siva swallows soul, turiya and world like that fruit (கரியுண் விளவின் கனிபோல்). The same image is a ruin in the song and the Lord's taking-in in the Tirumanthiram.

654, on one reading, says living by tasting the letter சி is Sivajnana and falling as the letter ம draws near is great maya. Tirumular's subtle five-letter verse removes நம as impurity (நம்மலம் எல்லாம் ஒழித்திட்டு) so that Sivajnana yoga is attained and சிவாய alone is chanted. The Tirumanthiram makes explicit the scheme the song's letters seem to assume, with ம on the side of bondage and சி on the side of knowledge.

655 asks for the jnana to bow at the feet of those who hold Murugan's feet in mind (நினைவுறு கருத்தர் தாள்கள் பணியவும்). Tirumular calls the ash-wearing devotees gods walking on earth (அடியார் நிகழ் தேவர்கள்) and says those who honour them as the Lord himself have no karma. Both put the devotee in the Lord's place as the object of worship.

Both define the giver by his shame at the word 'none': the Kural's man of good family does not utter the misery of 'I have nothing' and gives without refusing, and 662 names those ashamed to say 'there is none', who do not refuse from what they have, using the same word for misery (எவ்வம்).
The Kural calls the palmyra horse the only defence of those who suffer in love; 664 has Murugan himself, infatuated in Valli's field, mount it, the god taking the lover's last resort.
audit_text_issue: Several phrases of 664 (வாராய்பதி காதங் காதரை ஒன்முரும்) are obscure or corrupt.

note: 656 asks that, with 'mine' gone (எனது அற), he gain the feet and be told the word that marks the bound of silence. The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. Both make the end of 'mine' the condition of the highest gain, the Kural as renunciation, the song as reaching the feet.

657 asks whether the golden feet can be gained other than by words that make all the world know Murugan's emblems (அகிலமும் உணர மொழிதரு மொழியின் அல்லது). The Kural says the two dark deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise (பொருள்சேர் புகழ் புரிந்தார்). Both make proclaiming the Lord the working means, not ornament; the song adds that his own teaching is beyond words (நிர்வசன ப்ரசங்க).

658 asks Murugan to accept, adorning his red feet, a garland of clear verse with fragrant flowers (தெள்ளு கவிமாலை கடிமலர்). Tirumular, having nothing to show the Lord morning and evening, offers the song that cools the heart as the oblation (உள்ளம் குளிர்விக்கும் பாட்டவி). Both make the song itself the offering.

659 asks whether his heart will not learn, while life remains in the world (உலகுயிர் உள்ள பொழுதே), to say that Murugan is Uma's son. The Kural says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). Both set the deadline at the end of life; for the song the deed to be done before it is speech itself, praise.

660 tells how, putting wealth by the handful into a deceitful woman's hand (கள்ள முள்ள ... கையில் அள்ளி பொருள் ஈய), his gems, grain, silver, learning and wealthy kin all vanished. The Kural says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the company of those whom Fortune has left (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The song is a narrative of the Kural's verdict, with learning and kin lost alongside wealth.

661 calls Murugan true to the true and false to the false (மெய்யர் மெய்ய பொய்யர் பொய்ய). Tirumular's horse of salvation, traditionally the breath, gives a hold to the true and leaps and throws the false (மெய்யர்க்குப் பற்றுக்கொடுக்கும் ... பொய்யரைத் துள்ளி விழுத்திடும்). The same pairing of மெய்யர் and பொய்யர் describes a means of release that answers each person according to his truth; in the song that answers the woman's deceit.

663 asks for a joyous play that is neither being nor non-being (உள்ளதும் இலாது அல்லது) and for the teaching that melts the heart. Tirumular says the Lord becomes what is and what is not yet is neither (இல்லதும் உள்ளதுமாய் அன்றாம்), far beyond whatever is said, but becomes life of life when understood. The song asks for the state the Tirumanthiram describes, in the same terms.
audit_text_issue: 663's மல்லதவிரோத division is uncertain.

note: Both take the body apart into its stuff, skin, flesh, blood and bone: the Naladiyar to ask which part is the desired woman, 665 to show the hut the life lives in before it asks for the strength to praise.

665 fears that when its time of speed comes the life, like a fierce elephant (வெங்கனல் உயிர் வேழம்), will run loose along the paths of the senses. The Kural praises one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்), the goad implying the senses as elephants. The Kural answers with firmness; the song asks instead for the strength to recite 'Vel, Kanda'.

Both make the courtesan's welcome depend on the gift: the Naladiyar's women send away even Mal if his hand is empty, and 666's women show delight to the man who gives much and drive off one who does not.
audit_text_issue: 666 has two corrupt glyphs (ஊறல்கள், வேலூர்).

note: 653 gives Sambandar's defeat of the Jains as one epithet of Murugan; 666 tells the whole Madurai episode, the ash on the king, the hump straightened, the leaf against the current, as Murugan's deed.

The song's courtesans show delight when big givers come (அதிகராய்ப் பொருள் ஈவார் நேர்படில் ரசனை காட்டிகள்) and drive off those who give nothing even after union. The Kural's women weigh the gain first and only then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). Both say the warmth is measured to the gift; the Kural draws the rule (keep away), the song gives the scene.
audit_text_issue: 666 has corrupt glyphs (ஊறல்கள், வேலூர்).

note: The poet asks, after his infatuation with the women, for grace to worship daily with keen truthfulness (கூர்வாய்மை கொண்டு இறைஞ்ச). Tirumular says the Lord of the anklets is hard to see except by right thought and truthful speech (நினைவதும் வாய்மை மொழிவதும் அல்லால்), and only those who see him can truly praise him. Both make truthfulness the condition of real worship, not an addition to it.

Both make a single handful of food for the hungry the measure of dharma; 671 confesses the poet did not give even that one handful (ஒருபிடி) while he spent himself on courtesans, where Tirumular sets it as what anyone can do.

The faithful wife of the Naladiyar wonders how women who embrace many men's chests for gain (பொருள்நசையால் பன்மார்பு சேர்ந்தொழுகுவார்) manage it every day. The song shows exactly how: one man on the bed, one circling the door, one rushing in the street, set against each other (ஒருவரை ... ஒருவரை ... ஒருவரை), all thought fitting as a living (உயிர்பிழைப்பது). The song answers the wife's question with the courtesan's method and motive.

The poet confesses a mind that will not let go of desire (ஆசை விட மனம் ஒவ்வாத பதகன்) and asks Murugan to think of ruling even him. Tirumular says that even if those who praise Hara come wrapped in maya (மாயகம் சூழ்ந்து வரவல்லராகிலும்), the Lord becomes one with them. Both hold that delusion still clinging is no bar to being taken by the Lord; the Tirumanthiram verse is obscure in its second line, so the agreement rests on its third and fourth.

The poet asks for the feet that the disputants of the five sects, roaring like the sea, do not know (சமய பஞ்ச பாதகர் அறியாத), feet seen in solitude (தனிமை கண்ட). Tirumular says the six sects standing in the assembly do not see the God standing in the body (ஆயத்துள் நின்ற ... காயத்துள் நின்ற கடவுளைக் காண்கிலர்). Both set the sects' public contest against an inward, solitary seeing.

Here the poet asks to cast off the five elements as impurity (மலமிது என்று போட) and reach a formless stage that does not even speak of 'the world' (உலகமென்று பேச அறியாத உருவமொன்றிலாத பருவம்). At Nimbapuram he asks for the one release that knows neither the five elements nor the four inner faculties nor night and day, with no end, middle or beginning (அந்தநடு ஆதி ஒன்றுமிலதான). The two songs define the goal the same way, by negation of the elements and of form.

Both confess the poet's trade of singing to patrons who do not deserve it; 358 quotes the begging speech, 677 asks only whether he must go on giving endless songs to sinners blind to the Lord's protection.

The Kural says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an afflicting spirit (அணங்கு) to those without discerning understanding. The song's women are illusion-and-song charmers (மயமாயங் கீதவிநோதிகள்) who fall on deluded lovers (மருளாருங் காதலர் மேல்விழு) and feed them a ghoul's food (பேயமுது). Both name the deception and place the danger in the lover's lack of discernment, the song turning the Kural's spirit into a ghoulish meal.
audit_text_issue: 673's compound epithets are hard to divide.

note: The Kural compares the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்தொழிய). The song calls the body a mean nest (புன்கூடு) where the life dwells, with fierce Death already packed inside it (பொங்காவெங் கூற்றம் பொதிதரு), and asks for the feet before that life is taken. The nest image is shared; the song adds that Death lives in the nest from the start.

The song lays out the body's making from earth, water, wind, fire and sky, the ten senses and organs and the four inner instruments, showing Pati and the bond (பசுபதி பாசங் காட்டி), and then asks to be shown the supreme state (பரகதி). Tirumular says the Lord fashions the body and lays out the range from earth upward so that the bond of the soul may leave (பசுபாசம் நீங்கிட). Both treat the tattva-built body as the setting in which the bond is shown and loosened.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are flagged uncertain; 675's சுவமதி and புகல்வழி நாலைந்து are unclear.

note: Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னைநன் றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யு மாறே). The poet, before Death's messenger throws the noose, asks to be ruled by the command 'sing the supreme praise in expansive Tamil' (விரிதமிழால் அம் கூர்த்த பரபுகழ் பாடு என்று ஆட்கொள்). Tirumular states his calling as already given; Arunagiri asks for it as the form his rescue should take.

Both set vultures on the body to answer its admirers: the Naladiyar shows them tearing at the stinking cart once its axle breaks, 679 calls the living body the hut they will feed on and makes it the reason to stop carrying it from town to town.

Tirumular asks what it matters if crows carry off the nest (காக்கை கவரிலென்) once the dancer who lived in the skin bag has left. The song calls the body, burning on the long pyre, already apportioned to crows, dogs, vultures and ghouls (காக்கைக்கு நாய் கழுகு பேய்க்கு அக்கமான உடல்). The same scavengers are named; Tirumular uses them to show the corpse no longer matters, the song to drive the plea for the gift of song before that end.

The Kural asks whether the life, lodging in the body as in a shelter (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு), has found no home of its own (புக்கில்). The song pictures the body as a hut (குரம்பை) carried from town to town and asks to drive out the five senses and enter the house and rejoice (வீட்டிற் புகுந்திருந்து மகிழ்வேனோ), where வீடு is also release. The song names the home the Kural says the life has not yet found.

Tirumular says the six sects did not see the Lord; be clear, settle, and then enter the house without wavering (மாறுதல் இன்றி மனைபுகலாமே). The song asks to stop wandering from town to town and enter the house (வீட்டிற் புகுந்திருந்து). Both figure release as entering a house after restless movement, Tirumular's wandering being among sects and the poet's among towns and others' wealth.

The Kural says craving is the seed that brings unceasing birth to all beings (அவாஎன்ப ... தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). The song says that through the women's eyes, breasts and waist the poet, without support, takes body after body (அநேகம் காயம்) and asks when that time will end. The song applies the Kural's general rule to the poet's own desire for women.
audit_text_issue: 680's middle plea is hard to divide.

note: At Swamimalai the poet tells how Murugan delighted in Keeran's poems of true speech and taught him grammar (வளவாய்மை சொற்ப்ரபந்தம் உள கீரனுக்கு உகந்து ... இலக்கணங்கள் இயல்போதி), and asks grace on his own mean words. At Thiruverkadu he makes the same Keeran the precedent for his plea: as you rescued Keeran (கீரரை ஆர்ப்பாய்), give me one word (ஒர்சொல் அருள்வாயே). The two songs show Keeran's story used as the warrant for the poet's own gift of speech.
audit_text_issue: 681 has a corrupt glyph in வேதபுரீசுரர்.

note: Both warn that the courtesan's sweet words serve her wish for wealth; 683 shows the words in action, the talk of old intimacy leading to the house where the wealth is plundered.

The poet, calling himself without understanding (அறிவில்லியாம் அடியேன்), asks anxiously whether grace will leave him long in the house of darkness (நெடுநாள் இருள் இல்லிலே இடுமோ, அருளில்லையோ). Tirumular says the soul born and dying through folly (பேதைமையாலே) finds its many darknesses go at the ripe season for joining Siva's grace (சிவனருள் சேர்பருவத்து), once it has renounced. Tirumular names the condition and timing the poet's questions leave open.
audit_text_issue: 682 has several garbled words (குணவல்வா, பரிசெல்ரவி, மோடமடர்).

note: The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from the hand, then lies down like a balking ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு சேமாபோல் குப்புறூஉம்). The song's women give their lips while they plunder the wealth (கனிவாய் அதரந்தரு நாளிலே பொருள் சூறைகள் கொண்டு), then fall silent and pick quarrels (மோனமாய் ... சண்டைகள்). Both give the same three-step cycle of sweetness, taking and turning away.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). The song asks not to fall into the women's snare (கண்ணியில் விழாமல்) but to be held within the snare of knowledge of the feet (பதஞான கண்ணியிலுளாக). Both answer a binding with a better binding rather than with none.

Tirumular asks what causes people to gain grace and answers that they change their deluded minds (மருளுற்ற சிந்தையை மாற்றி) and praise the red feet. The poet, deluded by women (மருள் உள்ளி), asks for the very mind able to honour the feet as a gift (அடிபேண ... மனது அருளாயோ). On the reading that Tirumular's காரணம் makes the change of mind the soul's own prior act, the two put grace and the changed mind in opposite order.

The Naladiyar says those who take a worthless woman's love as their own will be laughed at by many (பெறுபவே தாமாம் பலரால் நகை). The poet, sunk in love-making, asks for knowledge before the world mocks him every way (உலகோர்கள் ... நகைகள் கூறி) as a madman reciting Kama's arts. Both make public laughter the end of infatuation; the song turns it into the reason to seek knowledge now.

Tirumular says the First removes darkness, carries one past countless births (எண்ணில் பிறவி கடத்தி) and grants grace so that it never leaves. The poet asks that, gaining the grace of the light of compassion (கருணைப்பிரகாச உனது அருளுற்றிட), he not be born again in a woman's womb (கருவிற் பிறவாதபடி) and reach the Siva-state. Both make grace the agent that ends birth.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1516: மருள்நீங்கா வானவர் கோன் and புலம்பயல் look corrupt.

note: Both are akam songs in another voice built from the classical torments of the lovesick girl, the moon and Kama's arrows; 24 is the mother's lament for her daughter, 693 is the girl's own plea that the god come to her bed.

689 asks whether he too must die (மடிவேனோ), stopped by eyes that rise like spears (அயிலொத்தெழும் இருவிழி), nectar speech and mountain breasts. Naladiyar 44 refuses that very comparison, calling those who liken eyes to a spear (வேல்) blind, petty men, and sees the eye as a palm fruit scooped out once its water is drained (நுங்குசூன் றிட்டன்ன). On the literal reading they disagree about what a woman's eye is: a killing weapon to the poet, a hollow socket to the ascetic, who walks on where the poet is stopped.

Among what the poet lacks, 691 lists dwelling in the silence where speech ends (வசன மறவுறு மவுனமொடு உறைகிலி), and its praise names A, U and M (அகர உகர ... மகர). Tirumanthiram 2844 joins the same two things: in the form of speechless silence (உரையற்ற ஆனந்த மோன சொரூபம்) A merges and becomes U and M, an inner light. Tirumular describes the state that 691 confesses it has not reached.

692 asks whether he should follow the gait of the price-women (விலைமானார்) and fall dazed into the pit called desire (மோகம் என்ற படுகுழியிலே மயங்கி விழலாமோ). Kural 919 makes the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும்). Both picture the courtesan's trade as a hole a man sinks into; the Kural names the sinker base, the song asks it of the poet himself.

693, in a woman's voice, asks not to waste each night seeking the palmyra horse (வனிதை மடல் நாடி நித்த நலியாதே) but that Murugan come to her bed. Kural 1136 is the lover who even at midnight (யாமத்தும்) thinks of riding the madal. The pairing shows the Thiruppugazh giving the madal, a man's resort in the Kural, to a girl who longs for the god.

695 sets the poet's wandering with the worldly (உலகோரொடு திரிவேன்) against being joined to the devotees who worship (உன் அடியாராய் வழிபாடுறுவாரொடு), and asks for that day. Kural 460 says there is no greater help than good company and nothing brings more affliction than bad company (நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை). The song applies the Kural's rule on company to devotion, the good company being the devotees.

Tirumanthiram 1637 says that those still in the round of birth (பவத்திடையாளர்) who come to the people of tapas and hear and serve them may come face to face with Nandi. 695 asks for the day when grace joins him to those who worship as devotees (அடியாராய் வழிபாடுறுவாரொடு). Both make the company of devotees the road to the Lord; Tirumular states the fruit, 695 asks to be admitted.

The praise of 696 is a litany of the Goddess's names, பரை அபிநவை சிவை சாம்பவி ... பயிரவி திரிபுரை ... மோகினி. Tirumanthiram 1051 is a string of her names in the Tripura chakra, நின்ற திரிபுரை நீளும் புராதனி குன்றலில் மோகினி. Both praise Sakti by a bare list of names, Tripurai and Mohini in each; in 696 the list follows a long scene of lovemaking.
audit_text_issue: TM 1051's மாதிருக்கும் சிகை and நாற்கால் கரீடணி are obscure, possibly corrupt.

note: 699 asks to think daily of the feet whose anklets cry out a hundred crore Vedas (நாத சதகோடி மறை ஓலமிடு நூபுரம்). Tirumanthiram 898 makes the paired feet the eight letters and the paired anklets (கழலிணை) fifty-one and seven thousand, the letters and the mantras. Both hear scripture in the Lord's anklets: 699 as their sound, Tirumular as a count of letters.

Both set marriage and the household inside the march to the burning ground: the Naladiyar mocks the man who sees the corpse carried yet marries and thinks there is joy here, and 700 lists embracing women and bearing the household's burden between crawling and burning.

700 runs a life in plural past verbs, பிறந்தனர் கிடந்தனர் இருந்தனர் தவழ்ந்தனர் நடந்தனர், on to இறந்தனர் and the burning. Naladiyar 29 compresses a death into the report நின்றான் இருந்தான் கிடந்தான் ... சென்றான். Both tell a life as a run of verbs of posture to show how fast it passes; the Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good at once (இன்னினியே), 700 asks to end the birth itself.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 700 has a corrupt glyph in வயலு¡ரா.

note: Both tell the courtesan's cycle to its end, the man welcomed while his wealth lasts and then beaten and driven out; 702 adds the bargaining at the start and the new man taken up afterwards.
audit_text_issue: 33's praise has the garbled word மண்டுநநருர்.

note: 701 lists the price-women's charms one by one, among them the voice like the yazh (யாழ்தரு கீத மென்குரல்), and ends in their feigned feelings (விலைமாதர் பாவகங்கள்) in which he sinks. Kural 911 says the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth and not love bring harm. The song spreads into a catalogue the charm the Kural names in one item, and both rest on the pretence.

702 tells the courtesan's cycle: fixing the price, the bed, then snatching the wealth (உள பொருள் பறித்து), quarrelling and beating the man away (கலகமிட்டு அவர் அகல அடித்தபின்). Naladiyar 377 has the same turn: she licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from his hand (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks like a buffalo, and the man who thought her love his is laughed at. 702 adds what the Naladiyar leaves out, the new man taken up with new stories.

Twin songs in one metre: both walk a life from the womb through childhood, women and the hunt for wealth, and both end in the same plea for love that reaches the feet before one falls into hell. 704 dwells longer on infancy (the birth rite, crawling), 703 on youth and roaming.
audit_text_issue: 703 line 4 is garbled (பாழவெளநேரகெய் தாம).

note: Both condemn the man who begrudges another's giving: the Kural says his kin will be left without food or clothing, and 707 puts him among those who fall into Yama's pit.
The Kural says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; 707 lists those who forget the good done them among the brutes who fall into Yama's pit, giving that 'no escape' a place.

Both make the stilled and turned breath the end of dying: Tirumular says that when breath stays with the mind there is no birth or death, and 709 asks that, with the breath turned into the skull and samadhi gained, the endless dying cease.

Both songs trace one life from the womb to ruin: 195 from rolling in blood in a woman's body (உதிரமதிலே உருண்டு) through sixteen years to the women's nets and the wealth lost, 703 from the first day in the mother's body (ஆதிமுதல் நாளில் என்றன் தாயுடலில்) through youth, women and the search for wealth (பொருள்தேடி). 195 asks grace to rule him, 703 asks for love (அன்பு) that reaches the feet before hell; the pairing shows the life-confession as a set form in distant parts of the book.
audit_text_issue: 703 line 4 'பாழவெளநேரகெய் தாமல்' is corrupt (likely பாழ் நரகு எய்தாமல்).

note: 705 names among the girl's torments the flute with its seven-note holes (ஏழோசைத் தொளையாலே), beside Kama's fragrant arrows. Kural 1228 calls the herdsman's flute a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). Both turn the flute's music into a weapon against the lovesick; in 705 the bamboo (வேய்) is named in a run of rhyming words that is hard to divide.

706 asks Murugan to come lest the girl perish from the sea's roar, the slander the women speak each day (நாளும் வஞ்சியர் உற்று உரைக்கும் வசை) and the moon that burns like poison. Kural 1147 says the town's gossip (ஊரவர் கௌவை) is the manure on which this sickness grows. Both make gossip feed the love-sickness rather than shame it away; the song can only ask the god to end it by coming.

708 pictures the kin who gather weeping (சூழ்துற்றார் துற்றழுவாரும்), Yama with trident and noose, the bier and the fire (பாடைக் கூடத் தீயில்). Tirumanthiram 157 follows the wailing kin, wives and children only to the edge of the town (ஊர்த்துறைக் காலே ஒழிவர்), then the wood, the fire and the bath. Tirumular shows how far the kin go; 708 turns the same scene into a plea to be set at the golden feet (பொற்பாதத்தே வைத்தருள்வாயே).

710 shows the whole performance of feigned infatuation (மாமயல் உடைத்தார் போலவும்): messengers by the hundred, the embrace, betel bitten halfway, all to snatch the man's wealth (நீள்பொருள் பறிப்பார்). Kural 913 calls the embrace of women of wealth false (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்), like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The Kural judges the embrace; the song shows the staging that makes it false.

713 opens by naming Murugan the sun that destroys the darkness of anava (ஆணவ திமிரமே அரி சூரிய) in the poet's dark mind. Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas end before the sun appears (சூரியன் தோற்றமுன் அற்ற மலங்களே), as the sunstone burns cotton only in the sun's presence. Both use the sun's coming as the figure for the bond removed, in Tirumular the guru, in 713 Murugan.

713 praises Murugan as the lord of the six sects and their gods (சமய மாறிரு தேவத சமய நாயக), worshipped by all worlds and all Vedas. Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six sects did not see him, and he is not the thing the six sects hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). On the reading that 713 makes the Lord the object the sects reach, the two disagree; if 713 means only that he rules over them, the gap narrows.

714 asks for the knowing that knows within knowing (அறிவுள் அறியும் அறிவு) so as to know the feet that all the seekers, knowing and knowing, do not know (அறிய அறிய அறியாத அடிகள்). Tirumanthiram 2224 turns the same verb over (அறியாத வற்றை அறிவான் அறிவான் ... யார் அறிவாரே) to say the knower who knows without knowing is beyond being known. Both make the play on அறி the argument: ordinary knowing does not reach the goal, and another kind is needed.

715 lists the gross body as skin, bone, pus, nerves, rheum and phlegm rolled into a lump (தோல் எலும்பு சீ நரம்பு பீளை ... கோழை), which the poet carries and wastes in. Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews and skin (குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும்) and asks which of them is the woman. The same inventory of the body cures desire for another's body in the Naladiyar and turns the poet against his own body in 715.

716 confesses that he ran over the earth seeking wealth until his heart withered (பொருள்தேடி ஓடி எய்த்து உளம்வாடி) and made a crore of songs giving names to what only feeds ruin. Tirumanthiram 269 warns not to wither (புலராமல்) praising small-minded men for wealth, but to praise the Lord with a single aim. On the reading that 716's songs praised patrons, the song is the confession of the life Tirumular warns against.

717's praise names the Lord who came into the assembly with a bond (சாதனங்கொடு), was called a madman (பித்தா), and claimed faultless Sundarar for his own (தாழ்வில் சுந்தரனைத் தான் ஒற்றிகொள்). 1101 names Siva who came with love to break Sundarar's bonds and took him as his servant (தொண்டன் என்று அன்று கொண்டிடும்). Both songs of desire for women close on the story of service claimed by the Lord, set beside the poet's own bondage to women.

Both make the Lord's feet the way across the sea of births: the Kural says only those who join his feet swim it, and 718 calls the twin lotus feet a raft (புணை) to be grasped instead of the leaking body.
audit_text_issue: 718: உதிதாம்பரத்தை line obscure.

note: 718 calls the body a hut of the senses made of skin and holes from which blood drains (குருதி வடி தொளைத் தொக்கு இந்த்ரியக் குரம்பை) and asks not to take it as everything. Naladiyar 42 sees the same body as full of holes under a skin covering (தோல்போர்வை மேலும் தொளைபலவாய்) that hides its falsity. Both make skin and openings the body's truth; the Naladiyar asks for a changed view, the song for the feet as a raft away from it.

719 describes the teaching Murugan gave Siva by its effect: speech ended, action died, the mind loosened (உரைமாளச் செயல்மாண்டு சித்தம் அவிழ). Tirumanthiram 1896 defines silence as speech and mind both still (வாக்கு மனமும் இரண்டும் மவுனமாம்), not the tongue alone. The song's upadesa produces exactly the double stilling the Tirumanthiram calls மவுனம், which the poet then asks for himself.

720 asks to leave house, sons, wealth and town together with the delusion of 'I and mine' (யானெனதென்று) and be taken into the expanse of silence. Kural 346 says one who cuts the pride of saying I and mine (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. The song uses the Kural's very pair and names what replaces it: மோன தடம்.

721 says the vel that crushed the demons was thrown so that the poet's two deeds might turn to dust (அடியேன் இருவினை தூள்பட அயில் ஏவிய). Kural 5 says both deeds (இருவினையும்) do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise. The song turns the Kural's general promise into a weapon: the same இருவினை are not merely kept off but shattered by Murugan's vel.

Both see the courtesan's sweetness as aimed at a man's money: the Kural warns that such women's sweet words bring harm, and 723 shows the flattery on the bed with the hand already reaching for the purse.

722 begins by asking to stop babbling scriptures noisily (கலகலெனச் சில கலைகள் பிதற்றுவது) without saying even a little about Murugan. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the pure one's feet (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்). Both judge learning by whether it turns to the Lord; the song makes it the first thing to renounce, before hell and rebirth.

723 counts among its sufferings that the world says 'chi, chi' (உலகத்தவர் சிச்சியெனத் திரி) at the man who trades in courtesans. Naladiyar 377 says those who think a courtesan's love their own, while she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Both name public contempt, not only lost money, as the price.

726 asks that the lotus feet which opened the rare way of silence (அரிய மோன வழி திறந்த நளின பாதம்) never leave his mind. Tirumanthiram 1892 has the seeker fixed in the speech of silence (மோன மொழியில் பதிவித்து) and saved at Nandi's holy feet (நந்தி திருவடி மீதுய்ய). Both join silence and the feet: the feet open the way of silence, and silence ends at the feet.

727 names the women as harlots trading love for money (வேசி என்பவர், காதலின் பொருள் மேவின) and asks instead to worship desiring the good path to Siva's bliss (சிவபோக நல் நூல் நெறி). Naladiyar 378 says those who mean to reach the right path (செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென் பார்) do not embrace such women. Both set the courtesan's bed against the path, and the song names that path as Siva's bliss.

Both use the courtesan's being common to all as the charge: the Kural's women 'whose goodness belongs to everyone' (பொதுநலத்தார்) and 730's பொதுவிகள். The Kural says the wise don't plunge in; 730 is the confession of one who did.
The Kural's women weigh the profit and then speak of virtue; 731's women have minds set on the coin and lying speech. Both make the calculation the mark of the courtesan.

Tirumular says that for those who hold Nandi in love there is no caste; 731 asks that the lowness of being sunk in caste and clan end when he reaches the feet. Both place caste among what falls away at release.

728 asks whether, though vowed as a hereditary servant, his life must swing like the beam of a balance (துலையலை மாறு போலுயிர் சுழல்வேனோ) between that vow and the women. Kural 118 praises the worthy for being like a balance that levels itself and leans to no side (சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல்). The same instrument is the Kural's figure of steadiness and the song's figure of a soul that cannot settle.

729 says the women are as if Death himself had put on a woman's festive form to seize young men's lives (உயர் காலன் பெண் தனக்கு உள கோலாகலம்). In Kural 1083 the lover says he never knew Death before and now knows it, in a woman's grace and warring eyes (கூற்றென் பதனை இனியறிந்தேன் பெண்டகையால்). The Kural's lover's hyperbole becomes in the song a literal warning, with Death as the one in disguise.

730 calls the women plunderers who sing their love to the measure of the money (பொருளளவு ஆசைப் பாடிகள்) and belong to all. Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends with the oil (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure the love exactly by the coin; the Naladiyar adds the image of the lamp going out.

In 732 the courtesan flatters the client that if one looks for his equal even Kadamban, Murugan, falls short (ஒப்பார் உனக்கீடு பார்க்கிற் கடம்பன் மட்டோ). Naladiyar 373 says such women would send away even the red-eyed Mal whom the gods worship if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன் றில்லாரை). The Naladiyar states the hidden condition of the flattery: the client is a god only while he pays.

733 lists the women's eyes as sharper than a spear (பார்வையாமிகு கூரயில்) among the parts that draw the poet into infatuation, and asks to be freed of it. Naladiyar 44 refuses those who call eyes lilies, carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேலென்று) and sees the eye as a scooped palm fruit. The song keeps the poets' simile and prays against its pull; the Naladiyar dismantles the simile itself.

Both make silence the door of release: Tirumular says release comes to those to whom silence has come and all speech ends, and 734 asks for the house of silence (மோன வீடு) beyond the mind, where nothing else is spoken.

Tirumular gives form and formlessness and the thirty-six tattvas to Shakti and Siva; 736 gives the same pairs, form and formless, difference and non-difference, bindu and nada, to Murugan and ends 'the one is you'.

736 calls the one that cannot be seen both form and formless (உருவோடு அருவது) and says it comes before the embodied and speaks as one of them (காயமானவர் எதிரே அவரென வந்துபேசி), ending ஒன்று நீயே. Tirumanthiram 2481 says the Lord becomes formless, form and form-formless (அருவாய் உருவாய் அருவுரு வாகி) and comes as guru (குருவாய் வரும்). Both pass from the threefold nature to the Lord appearing as a human teacher; the song says that one is Murugan.

Both ask to be set among the Lord's devotees as the way out of the round of births: 722 asks to be counted in the throng of servants, 738 to have those who think of Murugan as companions so as not to drown in the sea of seven births.

737 calls Murugan the poet of honour whose verses filled as the Lady on the left of Kailasa's lord wished (கயிலைமலைக் கிழவன் இடக் குமரி விருப்பொடு கருதக் கவி நிறையப் பெறும்). 542 says his mouth smells of the nectar that welled from the first Goddess's breast (பரைமுலையின் ஊறி எழும் அமிர்தம்) and names him the wise one of Kazhi. 542 makes plain the Sambandar story that 737 only touches: the poet's gift comes from the Goddess.
audit_text_issue: 542 has a corrupt glyph in முலையினு஡றி.

note: 738 asks that, in the company of those who think of Murugan (உனை நினைபவர் துணைகொள), he not be lost in the sea of seven births (எழு பிறவியெனு உவரியினிடை கெடாது). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song keeps the sea and adds the devotees' company as the means of crossing.

In 739 the lover asks whether the night as long as an aeon (ஊழி இரவு) must be spent burned by the moon, Kama's bow and the beating sea. Kural 1169 says these long nights (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruel man himself. Both make the lengthened night the separated lover's torment; the song addresses it to Murugan.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives before any scheme to avert it; 742 cites the same elders' word and grants it (தகவாம் அது), yet asks for the Lord's grace to free him from what fate brings. Not a tension, since the poet does not deny the saying: grace is set beside fate as the one thing no human scheme is.
audit_text_issue: Several lines of 742 are hard to split, as the marker notes.

note: 742 fears the hour when the body is burned with rising smoke, becomes food for hell, and kin stand at the door with sinking hearts (தலைக்கடை போய் எதிர் உளமாழ்கி). Tirumanthiram 145 has the town wail, call the man a corpse, burn him and bathe and forget him (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both stage the death scene with the mourners; the Tirumanthiram ends on their forgetting, the song on the poet's plea to escape by grace.
Both are love-sickness songs with the stock torments of moon, Kama's arrows and night or evening, sung to Murugan in a lover's voice rather than as the poet's confession.
audit_text_issue: 739's படியொதான் and the place name திருவர்முர் look corrupt (திருவாமூர்).

note: In 743 the speaker says that by the evening, Kama's arrows, the cuckoo and the fire-pouring moon her life grows faint (ஆவிதளர்வுற்று வாடும்). Kural 1221 tells the evening it is not evening but the hour that eats the life of those once wed (மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). Both make the evening hour a threat to the lover's life itself.

Both turn the plea into a yogic programme, breath, the sun's path, the sky and the dance in 744; muladhara, the three mandalas, bindu and nada and the central pillar in 762; and both praise Murugan as the saint who sent the Jains to the stake.

744 describes an ascent where breath is stopped and sent by the sun's path into the sky (பருதி வழிப்பட விடல் ககனத்தொடு) until all is Siva, then melting in the golden hall where the dance is done (கனக சபைக்குளில் உருகி). Tirumanthiram 2747 maps the channels onto the land, sushumna rising through the Tillai forest (திலைவனத் ... ஏறும் கழுமுனை), and calls these Siva's ground. Both place the dancing hall of Tillai at the end of the yogic channel.
audit_text_issue: 744's last plea line does not split with certainty.

note: 744 calls Murugan the poet who set the Jains on stakes in rows (அமணர் உடல்களை நிரையில் கழுக்களில் உறவிடு சித்திர புலவன்). 751 says at Madurai he sent the Jains to the stake (மதுரையில் அமணரை உயிர்கழு தெறிபட). Both give Sambandar's Madurai deed to Murugan, 751 naming the city.
audit_text_issue: 744 last plea line uncertain

note: Both see the body as a vessel of filth with nine openings; the Naladiyar uses it to mock the man who praises a woman's arms, 745 to confess the poet's own frame and ask, before thought fails, for teaching.

745 lists the body as fat, blood, nerves, flesh, gut, bone and skin packed row on row (நிணமொடு குருதி நரம்பு ... தசைகுடல் ... எலும்பு தோல்). Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews and skin and asks which of these is the woman. The same anatomy serves the Naladiyar against desire and the song as the frame of the poet's confession.

745 asks Murugan to come and make the Upanishad clear before his heart's thought perishes (என்னெஞ்சு தான் நினைவு அழியாமுன்). Kural 335 says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both set a deadline at death's first sign: the Kural for good deeds, the song for receiving teaching.
Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons in verse for gifts, likening men to gods (Vishnu of the milk sea here, clouds in giving in 15), and ask to be turned from it.

747 gives thanks that Murugan showed his anklet feet so that the poet's anava impurity was dried away (சரணக்கழல் காட்டி என் ஆணவ மலம் அற்றிட வாட்டிய). Tirumanthiram 113 says the Lord set his cool feet on the poet's head, showed bliss to the eye and cut away the verdigris (தண்ணின்ற தாளைத் தலைக்காவல் ... காட்டிக் களிம்பு அறுத்தான்). Both make the shown feet the act of grace that removes the soul's root impurity, and both speak as thanksgiving for what has already been done.

747 calls the goddess the power in the foot that struck Death (சிவபத்தினி கூற்றினை மோதிய பதசத்தினி). 756 likewise names her as the one who burned Death (கூற்றுவனைக் காய்ந்த அபிராமி), in a song that pleads that Death not come near. Both credit the conquest of Death to the goddess at Siva's side, the left foot of the Kalan story being hers.

748 confesses that, not reckoning that life may end in a moment (மாத்திரை யாகிலும் ... வாழ்க்கையை நீடென மதியாமல்), he flattered fools as if each were Vishnu to get gold. Naladiyar 302 asks whether it is wrong to go hungry rather than eat by degrading deeds, since death and rebirth take only the instant of a blink (விழித்து இமைக்கும் மாத்திரை). Both set the brevity of life against self-abasement for a living; the song is the confession of the man the quatrain warns.

748 names Murugan as the goal of those who have left all six systems and stilled the mind (சாத்திரம் ஆறையும் நீத்த மனோலய சாத்தியர் மேவிய பதம்). 941 says 'enough, enough' to the clamour of the six faiths and their arts of knowledge (சட்கோல சமயிகள் ... சண்டைக்குள் கேள்வி அலம் அலம்) and asks for the highest state. Both place release beyond the six systems rather than in any one of them.
audit_text_issue: 941 has encoding glitches (¡£பர், வயலு¡ரா)

note: 15 confesses praising patrons as Tamil's refuge; 749 lists the patrons, fools, misers, gamblers, and the result, the poet ruined and lying in the fire of poverty.
The Kural says nothing is more shameful to the tongue than begging; 749 confesses a tongue spent praising unworthy men and a life left in poverty.

749 pictures the poet, after singing fine Tamil to unworthy patrons, lying on the fire of poverty and writhing like a long worm (வறுமையாகிய தீயின்மேல் கிடந்து நெளியும் நீள்புழு). Kural 1049 says one may even sleep in fire, but in poverty one cannot close the eyes at all (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் நிரப்பினுள் யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). Both measure poverty against lying in fire; the couplet rates poverty the worse, and the song makes poverty itself the fire.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 749 has corrupt glyphs (¡£னர், லு¡டு).

note: Both picture old age by faltering steps, the staff and fallen teeth; the Naladiyar faults the old man still clinging to desire, 752 asks to be freed from the birth that brings such an end.
Both tie the courtesan's favour to money: the Naladiyar says a rich oil-presser is sugar to her, 750 that she strips of wealth the men she kisses.

750 dwells on the women's voices, like the yaazh, the parrot and the cuckoo, and calls them women with a price who strip wealth from those who kiss them (விலைமாதர் ... பொருள் பறிப்பார்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love bring a man harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The song lavishes on the sweetness of the voice what the couplet says is its danger.

751 praises Murugan as the one who at Madurai sent the Jains to the stake (மதுரையில் அமணரை உயிர்கழு தெறிபட ... விடுவோனே). 762 likewise addresses him as the one who put on ash so that the Jains who refused it died on the stake (வெண்பொடி இடாத வெஞ்சமணர் மாள வெங்கழுவில் ஏறும்). Both credit Murugan with Sambandar's Madurai contest, the book's identification of the two.

752 ends its portrait of old age, staff in hand, with the old man left standing outside (வெளிநிற்கும் விதம்).
