Naladiyar 326 says one who did no good before old age will be told 'sit outside, go' in his own house even by the maidservant (புறத்திரு போகு என்னும் இன்னாச்சொல்). Both see old age as being put out of one's own house; the quatrain draws a lesson to do good early, while the song asks to be freed from the birth that leads there.

752 asks whether a day will come when Murugan frees him from the birth that brings old age and disease (இடர்பெற்ற ஜனனத்தை விடுவித்து உன் அருள் வைப்பது ஒருநாளே). Tirumanthiram 2974 speaks as one for whom it has happened: Nandi cut away disease, old age and the counted reckoning (பிணி மூப்பு அறுத்து எண்ணும் கணக்கு அறுத்து). The pairing sets the plea against the testimony of its answer.

753 says the experience (அநுபூதி) shines only to those who, both kinds of deeds ended, sleep with awareness (இருவினையற உணர்வொடு தூங்குவார்க்கே விளங்கும்). Tirumanthiram 129 says that in sleep they saw Sivaloka, Siva-yoga and Siva-bhoga within themselves, and asks how that state could be told (தூங்கிக் கண்டார் ... நிலை சொல்வது எவ்வாறே). Both name the waking sleep of the knower as where the experience is found; the song adds the condition that deeds have ceased and asks to be told by Murugan's word what the verse says cannot be told.

754 asks for the release that knows neither the elements, the inner faculties, nor dusk and day (அந்தி பகல் யாதும் அறியாத). Tirumanthiram 1134 places the goal in the place where there is neither night nor day (இரவும் பகலும் இலாத இடத்தே), where one sleeps in grace and does not age. Both mark the highest state by the absence of night and day; the song reaches it by singing Murugan's feet, the verse by seeking the goddess.

754 asks for the release beyond night and day and for the delight of Tamil to sing Murugan's feet (அந்தி பகல் யாதும் அறியாத ... வண்டமிழ் விநோதம் அருள்வாயே). 616, in a distant chapter, asks in the same breath for a thought beyond night and day (அந்தி பகல் அற்ற நினைவு) and a mind to praise Murugan in Tamil. Both pair the state beyond night and day with Tamil praise as its way.

Both set the Lord against Death's servants at the hour of death; Tirumular says they will not harm those who think of the Lord, 756 confesses a life without that love and asks Murugan to keep Kalan away.
The Naladiyar says the harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; 757 shows the moment, the woman leaving the bed because the cash and cloth are not enough.

757 quotes the women's welcome and then shows them, just before bed, finding the cash and cloth not enough and going off in spite (காசு ஆடை வாவியும் போதாமை தீமை கொண்டே போம்). Naladiyar 372 tells of the woman who swore to leap from the peak with her lover but, there being no gold, showed a pain in her feet and would not come on (காணம் இன்மையான் ... கால் கால்நோய் காட்டி). Both catch the moment when the money falls short and the promised love is withdrawn on a pretext.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 757: opening words (பணம் பாஷாணம், மால் கடந்தே போம்) are hard to construe.

note: 758 describes women who melt the heart by arts of stealth, cruelly snatch what a man had saved (முன் கருதி வைத்த வைப்பவை ... தறுகணில் பறித்து) and then embrace him. Naladiyar 377 says the woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from his hand, and then lies down like a balking ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி அவர் கைப்பொருள் கொண்டு). Both show tenderness used as the means of taking a man's money.

758 addresses Murugan as the four-Veda child of Kochai to whom the Lord gave the pearl palanquin (கொச்சையில் சதுர்வேதச் சிறுவ ... நித்திலச் சிவிகையைக் கொடுத்து). 1326 says he was born at Kazhumalam and drank Uma's milk as master of the three Tamils (உமை இரு முலைப்பால் அருந்தி ... கழுமலத்து உதித்தனை). Kochai and Kazhumalam are both names of Sirkazhi; both songs give Sambandar's life to Murugan.

759 says the women's glance is spear, sword, Kama's arrows and the messenger Death sends (நமன் விடு தூதும்). Kural 1083 has the lover say he never knew what Death was and now knows it: a woman's large, warring eyes (பண்டறியேன் கூற்றென்பதனை இனி அறிந்தேன்). Both make the woman's eye Death; the couplet says it in wonder, the song in warning against women who want money.
The Kural names double-minded women with liquor and gambling as the company of those whom fortune has left; 761 calls the women குடிகேடிகள், ruiners of families.

761 calls the women changers who join men in many ways and snatch their money (பணம் எத்தப் பறிகாரிகள் மாறிகள் விதம் எத்தக் கொடு மேவிகள்). Naladiyar 375 likens them to the eel that shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish (மலங்கன்ன செய்கை மகளிர்), embraced by the dull-witted. Both charge the women with double dealing; the quatrain gives it an image, the song a list of names.
Both picture the yogi running up the central staff to the head through the three mandalas; Tirumular promises the body will last an aeon, 762 hopes for the light of a hundred crore moons.
audit_text_issue: 762 has corrupt characters (நலு¡ர).

note: The Naladiyar says courtesans would bow to Mal himself yet send away a man with nothing in his hand; 763 shows them handing the ruined man a begging bowl and staff.

763 says the women, once the gold is gone, hand a man the begging bowl and staff, say 'go', and even give poison (கஞ்சுளியும் தடியும் ஈந்து போ என நஞ்சை இடும்). Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and a rich oil-presser sugar (காணம் இலாதார் கடுவனையர் ... அக்காரம் அன்னார்). Poison belongs to the same reckoning in both: the moneyless man is poison to them in the quatrain, and in the song they give him poison.

The Naladiyar's kings who rode elephants under moon-white umbrellas were carried off and spoken of as dead; 774 gives the same royal splendour, walls, singers and chowries, and asks only whether it ends as a handful of ash.

Both are laments in another's voice for a girl sick with love for Murugan, worn down by the moon, the south wind and the evening; 772 is a bare eight lines, 24 adds the mother's question about bearing daughters.

The lovesick girl of 764 lists the evening's attackers, among them அசைவன விடைமணி, the swinging bells of the bulls coming home. Kural 1228 makes the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) the envoy of the burning evening and a killing weapon (கொல்லும் படை). In both a pastoral sound of homecoming cattle, harmless in itself, becomes an arm of the evening against the parted woman.

765 lists the fools (மூடர்) who do not cry அரகரா, wear the holy ash, anoint the feet or learn the books, and leaves them rolling in the seven hells (நரகேழில் புரள). Tirumanthiram 264 asks those who do not praise the Supreme (பரமனை ஏத்தார்), give or tend groves whether they will stand in hell (நரகத்தில் நிற்றிரோ). Both name the neglected acts of worship one by one and end in hell; Tirumular adds giving to the list.

766 calls the body ஊசற் சுடு நாறு குரம்பை, a stinking hut, and confesses he loved this rubbish-body (கூளச் சடம் ஈதை உகந்து). Tirumanthiram 312 addresses those who think நில்லாக் குரம்பை, the perishing hut, is lasting. The same word குரம்பை carries the same error in both: the poet confesses it, Tirumular diagnoses it as want of learning.

767 describes women who run many trades (பல வாணிபம்), will not give a moment without money (பணமே ஒரு காசு இடை செய்யார) and are deceivers (சற்பனை காரர்). Kural 913 calls the embrace of பொருட்பெண்டிர், women for wealth, a பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், a false embrace. Both make the courtesan's love a trade and its show a falsehood; the poet adds that he is the sinner caught in it and asks how to reach the shore.

768 confesses singing rambling verses (கவிபாடிக் கச்சா பிச்சா) to men blind with drink, lust and anger and wearing himself out for a mean gain. 245 tells the same trade: seeking out the rich, singing them quick verses (ஆசுகவி) that their fame is like Meru, and being told 'come tomorrow'. Read together the two songs give the patron-poet's shame from both ends, the worthlessness of the patrons and the refusal of the reward.
audit_text_issue: 768's compressed syllables make much of the plea uncertain.

note: 769 is a thanksgiving: drawn by women's eyes and lips, the poet was given by grace the sight of the anklet-bound feet (விழி அருள் தந்த பேரருள்), and vows கனவிலும் நனவிலும் மறவேனே. 912 also confesses the women and thanks Murugan who took him in a dream (கனவில் ஆள்) so that he would not fall into the womb, vowing மறவேனே. Both songs turn the usual plea into thanks for grace already given, with the vow of never forgetting as their close.
audit_text_issue: 912 has garbled characters ('க¨ல்முடுஞ்', 'சா¡£செ').

note: In 770 the women flare up if no gold is given now (செம்பொன் இங்கினி இலையெனில் மிகுதியும் முனிவாகி) and quarrel that a month has passed without a gift. In Naladiyar 372 the woman who swore to leap from the peak with her lover holds back at the edge, showing a pain in her feet, because he has no money (காணம் இன்மையான்). Both show the courtesan's love ending at the empty purse, one in open anger, the other in a feigned excuse.

Kural 920 names double-minded women, drink and dice as the company of those whom Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார்). 770 asks that the courtesans and the cruel poverty (கொடு மிடிமை) both leave him, poverty being what the women's thefts have left. The Kural puts loss of fortune before the company; the song shows the company producing the poverty.

771 lists Murugan's grace, victory, குணம் and his love for Valli and closes with the vow மறவேனே, I will not forget. In Kural 1125 the lover says he would recall the woman's குணம் if he ever forgot, but he does not know how to forget (மறப்பறியேன்). The devotee's vow and the lover's boast use the same claim, unbroken remembrance of the beloved's qualities.

773 asks Murugan to see how he stands ashamed (வெட்கி நிற்பது) after singing rich verses to rubbish men, calling them wish-trees (கற்பதாரு) and suns of the three worlds. Kural 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு) than asking, even water for a cow. The song shows the degradation the Kural names: the tongue's shame lies not only in asking but in the flattery the asking requires.
audit_text_issue: 773 opening has a garbled glyph ('தெற்கிலு¡ தை') and uncertain split.

note: 774 sets out the royal life, mansions, singers, chowries, garlands, sandal, and asks whether this body should become ஒருபிடி சாம்பல், a handful of ash. Tirumanthiram 155 shows the man leaving his honey-haired wife, wealth and house (மாடும் மனையும்) for the bier and the common burning ground (பொதுவூர் புறஞ்சுடுகாடு). Both weigh the household's splendour against the cremation that ends it.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 155 line 4 (மதுவூர வாங்கியே) looks corrupt.

note: 776 names the women for a price (விலைமாதர்) among other insults நரகச் சிற்சாடிப் பீடிகள், pits of hell. Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the அளறு, hell or mire, in which worthless men sink. Both make the courtesan herself the hell, not merely a road to it.
audit_text_issue: 776 phrase நரகச்சிற் சாடிப் பீடிகள் hard to construe

note: 739 is a love song of moon, Kama's bow and sea, whose praise names Murugan as the one who makes Death show his back (காலன் முதுகை விரிக்கும்). 777 begins with the same torments (நிலவாலே, ரதிபதி ... கணையாலே) but carries them into the last day when Yama comes to strike (கடைநாளில் அணுகி நமன் எற்ற), asking Murugan then to come and embrace. What 739 keeps apart, love-sickness in the plea and Death in the praise, 777 joins in one request.

Among the habits of the women in 778 is இருநிதி இலரைத் தூர நீக்கவும், sending far away those without wealth. Naladiyar 373 says such women would send away even red-eyed Mal, worshipped by the gods, if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன்று இல்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). The same dismissal of the moneyless, which the Naladiyar sharpens by making the visitor a god.

Tirumular's bindu in the root centre is raised by fire past the throat and becomes cool nectar at the moon; 783 asks Murugan for the same path, root fire through the six supports to the moon's honeyed nectar, as a gift of grace rather than a discipline.
audit_text_issue: 783 has corrupt glyphs (§வ்ளுர்) and several hard-to-divide runs in the first half.

note: 779 asks whether the poet, like a thing of wood (மரத்துறை போல்), must perish covered by மலத்திருள், the darkness of mala. Tirumanthiram 2337 says those freed of the five malas become Siva, while those not at one remain in the ஐம்மல இருள். The song's fear is the second state of Tirumular's verse, given by the poet about himself.
audit_text_issue: 779's text is very short and opens with a stray split (உ ரத்துறை, உ னைச்சிறி).

note: 780 asks how many crores of bodies he has left (எத்தனை கோடி கோடி விட்டுடல்) and what is still to come. 493 says his births outnumber the sands of the seven seas and that the vultures, fire, Yama and Brahma who handle each body are worn out. Both songs open by counting the bodies already left and ask for the feet to end the count; 493 turns it wry, 780 into disgust (சீசீ).

In 781 the courtesans speak for themselves: வாரும் முற்பணம் தாரும் இட்டமென, come, give the money first, then as you please. Kural 912 describes women who weigh the gain first (பயன்தூக்கி) and then speak of their good nature, and tells the man to weigh them in turn. The song gives in their own words the order the Kural describes: payment first, pleasantness after.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 781's ladder image (ஏணி வைத்து) is unclear.

note: 782 asks that the deeds be burnt by the vel and that the poet, among devotees, have a mind like Murugan's own (உனைப் போல் சிந்தையாக). Tirumanthiram 1011 describes the state where the self becomes He and He becomes the self (தான் அவனாக அவனே தான் ஆயிட), the knower becoming Siva. The song asks for likeness of mind; the Tirumanthiram carries it to identity.
audit_text_issue: 782's line on Siva and the crores of women is obscure.

note: 783 raises the fire from the root centre through the six supports and asks to be fed the moon's honeyed nectar (சந்திர ... தேனமுது ஊட்டி). 94 asks for the day of the root yoga (மூலபர யோகம்) when the breath goes through the fire to the moon where இன்ப அமுது ஊறல் wells and then to the space above. The two songs give the same yogic ladder, root, fire, moon, nectar, as the plea, far apart in the book.
audit_text_issue: 783 has corrupt glyphs (§வ்ளுர்) and 94 has 'லு஡டு', 'ஊ஡றும்'-type encoding glitches

note: 784 ends the courtesan's bed in disease: having sunk in their breasts and sweated on the bed, must he wander in a sea of colic and many diseases (சூலை பல நோய்கள் கடலாடி)? Tirumanthiram 263 says cough, wasting, phlegm and fever belong to those who do not do dharma (தருமம் செய்யாதவர்). The song applies to one case what Tirumular states as a rule, disease as the fruit of conduct.

Tirumular reads the Kadavur story as yoga: the fire at the root turned upward with the breath burns Death. 786, sung at Kadavur, asks for exactly this ascent, breath held, darkness burnt and the space above entered, with the kicking of Death in its praise.
audit_text_issue: 786 has a corrupt glyph (அழ லு¡டெ).

note: The Naladiyar's vultures tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks; 785 makes the fallen body a packed meal that vultures and crows greet as their food, the end that adorning it as if it were Kama ignores.
audit_text_issue: 785's sense is flagged uncertain; several phrases are hard to divide.

note: 785 pictures the day the body falls, when vultures and crows hail it as a packed meal (பொதி சோறு ... கழுகாகம் போற்றி நமக்கிரை), and asks Murugan to come on the peacock at that hour. Tirumanthiram 167 asks what it matters if crows carry off the nest (காக்கை கவரில் என்) once the dancer has left it. Tirumular dismisses the corpse; the song marks the moment of its fall as the time for grace.

787 asks whether, free of delusion for the women who pluck wealth without measure, he will sing உனைத் திருப்புகழ். 263 refuses ornaments, elephants and silks and asks to be given the திருப்புகழ் that rests in Murugan's feet. In both songs the book names itself as what the poet asks for in place of worldly getting.

788 says Murugan removed 'our mala' and bade 'sing' (எமது மலத்தைக் களைந்து பாடென அருள), then praised the verse. Tirumanthiram 81 says the Lord made me well so that I would render him well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). Both poets present their own poetry as the purpose the Lord gave them.

2 vows never to forget the grace by which Murugan told him to sing (திருப்புகழ் ... செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை). 788 tells the same call, adding that the removal of mala came first and that Murugan praised what was sung (இயல்கவி மெச்சிட்டு). Two tellings of the poet's commission, at the book's start and in Mayuram.

789 asks not to wander asking who on this earth gives generously (த்யாகம் ஈபவர் யாரென்று அலையாதே). Naladiyar 306 asks why anyone, with a mind racked by desire, should go begging of strangers (ஏதிலவரை இரவு) when poverty can be ended by asking of oneself. Both refuse the round of patrons; the Naladiyar's cure is inward consent to hardship, the song's is the feet.

790 names phlegm, fever, chill and wind (ஈளை சுரம் குளிர் வாதம்) and asks to live instead in மூலம் எனும் சிவயோக பதம். Tirumanthiram 727 says practice at evening, noon and dawn removes phlegm, wind and bile and destroys greying and wrinkles. Both set yoga against the humours' diseases; Tirumular promises bodily cure, the song asks for a state beyond the burning body.

791 sets two seas side by side: the life whirling in the waves of the sea (வாரிதி அலையூடே சுழலும் எனதுயிர்) and the ocean of silent supreme bliss (மவுன பரமசுக ... உததி) into which it asks to sink. Kural 10 has the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்) that only those who reach the Lord's feet can swim. The Kural's way out of the sea is to cross it; the song's is to sink into another sea.
audit_text_issue: 791's சுகோம கோததி is hard to divide.

note: The Naladiyar's harlots' love ends when the hand is empty, as the lamp's light ends with the oil; 797 shows the same end acted out, the man twisted round, kicked and abused once his wealth is gone.

Both are pleas in another's voice for a lovesick girl, worn by the flower bed and by women's blame, asking Murugan for his garland; 798 adds the neighbours' slander and asks for the kadamba garland by name.

The fragrant flower bed (மருக்குலாவிய மலரணை) is in 797 the bed where Murugan embraces Valli and in 798 the bed that burns the girl who longs for him; the two songs share the kura tree and the vel in their closing lines.

792 counts among its wasted years having learned useless arts without grasping a little of their meaning (சவலைக் கலை கற்று அதனிற் பொருள் சற்று அறியாதே). Naladiyar 135 gives the reason this is ruinous: learning has no shore and the learner's days are few (கல்வி கரையில கற்பவர் நாள்சில), so one must choose like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water. The quatrain supplies the rule whose breach 792 confesses.

793 opens on the voice of a man who boasts 'which poet matches me in verse and music' (எனக்கு இயலுக்கு இசைக்கு எதிர் எப்புலவோர்) and takes on turban, rings and betel bag in lordly style, and sets this vanity among the things that mire him in the puddle of birth. 935 lists the same court poet's honours, crown, whisks, the title கவிராஜ, but uses them as the argument for refusing to praise unworthy men (பஞ்ச பாதகரைப் புகழ் செயலாமோ). The poet's pride is a snare in one song and a ground for refusal in the other.

794 asks Murugan for a list of gifts that begins with the meaning of the three Tamils (பகரு முத்தமிழ்ப் பொருள்) and ends with the strength of praise (புகழ் பலத்தினைத் தரவேணும்). Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யு மாறே). Tirumular states as done what Arunagiri still asks for: Tamil praise as the purpose for which the poet is made.

795 catalogues the body as the five elements (படி புனல் நெருப்பு அடல் பவனம் வெளி), the states (அவத்தை), the three gunas, diseases and the fluids, to confess the life he bears in it. Tirumanthiram 2146 gives the doctrinal count behind such a list: elements, senses, malas, gunas and the adharas make up the ninety-six instruments of the first state (ஆதி அவத்தைக் கருவி தொண்ணூற்றாறே). The pairing shows the poet's list drawing on the Siddhanta tally of tattvas, mixed with the body's fluids.

796 confesses seeking many useless arts without grasping the one fruit (பலசவலைக் கலைதேடி ஒருபயனைத் தெளியாது) and asks, before death, to seek the lotus feet. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not worship the good feet (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). Both name the feet as the one fruit (பயன்) that learning exists for; the song is the Kural's question answered as a confession.
audit_text_issue: 796 has garbles (பிதற் றிடுலொக ...... மு முடர், திருப்புழோத).

note: 797 shows the courtesan coaxing with sweet words until the money reaches her, then, when the wealth ends, twisting round to kick and abuse (பொருள்தீரின் முறுக்கியே உதை கொடு வசை உரைதரு). Naladiyar 377 has her lick like a wild cow, take the wealth from his hands, then balk like a stubborn ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி ... சேமாபோல் குப்புறூஉம்). Both turn on the same reversal, fondness while the wealth is in hand and a physical turning away after it.

798, in a girl's voice, asks Murugan to send his kadamba garland so that the mother who raised her will not speak blame (வளர்த்த தாய் தமர் வசையது மொழியாதே) and the neighbours will not slander her (அயலவர் பழியாதே). Kural 1147 names the same two voices as what feeds the lovesickness: the town's gossip its manure and the mother's word its water (ஊரவர் கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). The song asks the god to stop exactly what in the Kural makes the sickness grow.

799 heaps names on the courtesans, among them women with weeping hearts (அழு மனத்திகள்) and those who take young men's wealth (இளைஞர்கள் பொருள் பறித்த). Naladiyar 372 tells one such scene: the woman who vowed to leap from the peak with him, finding he had no gold, showed a pain in her feet and wept (காற்கால்நோய் காட்டிக் கலுழ்ந்து). The quatrain gives the story behind the poet's one-word epithet for tears used as a feint.

800 speaks of the body that wears out and becomes fine ash in the fire, and of not grasping that flaw (நூண்சாம்பல் பட்டுவிடு ... உணராமே). 812 says of proud kings that, burnt among their kin, they become a handful of ash and do not know it (ஒரு பிடிசாம்பல் பட்டது அறிகிலர்). The two songs share the phrase and the charge: the fault is not dying but failing to know one will become ash, and in 812 even kings fail.
audit_text_issue: 800's word division is uncertain (e.g. செர்ந்தூன்று, நூண்).

note: 801 asks Murugan to come one day on the peacock and give his feet, and praises him as the one who came that day with love (அன்று அன்பொடு வருவோனே) so that a devotee who called him 'Kandan, Guha, my guru' might be saved. 810 is that coming told in the first person: the Lord taught, fed him Tamil, led him through light and nada, and came lovingly on the radiant peacock (அன்பொடு கதிர்தோகைப் பரி மேற்கொளும் செயல் மறவேனே). What 801 asks for and attributes to an unnamed devotee, 810 remembers as done to the poet.

804 asks to be rid of the babble of praising the world (உலகப் புகழ்ப் புலம்பு கலி அற்று) and to speak the praise that is rightfully Murugan's (உன் உரிமைப் புகழ்), and its praise tells how Vishnu saved the elephant from the crocodile. 292 quotes the patron-poem it renounces, in which a poor man was likened even to the god who helped in the crocodile pool (முதலை மடுவினில் அதவிய புயல்). The same story is spent on a patron in one song and kept for the god's own praise in the other.

805 says that when the term written by Brahma is reached, men run to the hot burning ground and the body falls and is burnt (ஓடி வெஞ்சுடுங் காடணைந்து சுட வீழ்கி வெந்து), and asks when this trouble ends. Tirumanthiram 145 follows the same procession: the town wails, calls him a corpse, carries him to the burning ground, burns him and bathes and forgets (சூரையங் காட்டிடைக் கொண்டுபோய்ச் சுட்டிட்டு). Tirumular ends on the mourners' forgetting, the song on the poet's plea to be done with it.

807 describes women who play the loving true form to everyone (எவரையும் அன்புடை மெய்க் கோலராக) and take the coins the day is worth, and asks to sing Murugan and enter release instead of falling into their net. Kural 915 says those whose knowledge is refined will not touch the base charms of women whose goodness is common to all (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). The song's 'with everyone' is the Kural's பொதுநலம, and both set understanding or devotion as what keeps a man out.

808 praises the Goddess as the one who keeps charity at all times with two measures of paddy (இரு நாழி நெல்லால் அறம் எப்பொதும் பகிர்வாள்), and asks to melt calling Murugan her son. 1130, in a string of epithets for her, names the same deed: she who guarded dharma with two measures (இருநாழி படிகொடு அறம் காத்த). The two songs, far apart in the book, confirm the poet knew the story of the Goddess's two measures of grain.

809 asks that Death, fiery-eyed with noose and trident on his buffalo, not come near (சமனார் ... அணுகாதே) and that true knowledge (மெய்ஞானம்) and love of Siva be given. Tirumular says that if Yama comes he will strike him with the sword of knowledge (நமன்வரின் ஞானவாள் கொண்டே எறிவன்). The knowledge 809 asks for is the weapon Tirumular claims to hold, so the plea and the boast describe the same remedy from either side.

810 recalls how the Lord led him through the teaching, the light of the kala (கலை சோதிக் கதிர்), nada and the whorl until he entered the open space (வெளியாகப் புக). Tirumular says that by gracious Nandi he knew the space and the light in its middle, and beyond that knows nothing (வெளியை அறிந்து வெளியின் நடுவே ஒளியை ... செழுநந்தியாலே). Both tell a guru-led passage through light to space in the first person; Arunagiri adds Tamil and nada to the stages.
audit_text_issue: TM 839 உளிமுறியாமே is obscure, with a variant.

note: 811 asks Murugan to destroy the pettiness of sect that says 'this is mine' (இன்னது எனக்கு என்னும் மதப் புன்மை) and give a life that cannot be named as 'this' (இன்னது எனப்படா வாழ்க்கை). Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him, for he is not the thing the six sects hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). Both deny that the goal can be the possession of a sect; the song puts it as a life beyond naming.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 811: word division throughout is uncertain because of the alliteration.

note: Both use kings to show impermanence: the Naladiyar's commanders on elephants under the royal umbrella fall when their deeds turn, and 812's lords of elephant armies and conquered directions end as a handful of ash; 812 adds that they never thought to worship.

812 portrays kings who rule armies and swell with pride on cushions, until, among their kin, they are burnt to a handful of ash. Tirumanthiram 153 shows the land's lord mounting for the last time the burning-ground palanquin, people following and drums in front (காட்டுச் சிவிகையொன்று ஏறி). Both make the king the case of impermanence; Tirumular keeps the royal procession for the funeral, and the song adds the charge that they did not think to worship the feet.

813 asks that, rather than wander in the courtesans' net, the darkness of maya burn away as the root fire rises with the inner nada (சங்கோதை நாதமொடு கூடி ... மூல அழல் வீச) and the teaching is spoken in his ear. Tirumanthiram 1937 calls the Siva-yogi one who turns from the women he sees, kindles the fire and lays waste the eye's desire by joining it at the root (அழல்மூட்டிப் ... மூலத்தே சேர்க்கின்ற யோகி). Both set the fire raised at the root against desire for women; the song asks for it as a gift through a guru.

814 asks whether, caught in the courtesans' net, he will fade like an elephant fallen into a pit (வலைபட்டு உழைத்து குழி உற்ற அத்தியென மங்குவேனா). Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). Both picture the man not as seduced but as sunk in a hole he cannot climb out of.

Both name the body's nine openings and the filth inside a skin covering: the Naladiyar's fool praises a pot that seeps from nine holes, and 815 calls the body a hut with nine gates, its filth sloshing under the skin.

Tirumular says that if the body perishes the life perishes before knowledge is won, so he learned the means of nurturing the body; 815 calls the same effort, many medicines and yogas tried on a body that bursts quicker than a bubble, an anguish to be given up for the Lord's feet. The tension holds if 815's yogas are read as practices for preserving the body, as the context of அவாவி suggests.

815, after picturing the body as a hut of nine gates that perishes faster than a bubble, says he kept trying worthless medicines and many yogas for it until his mind cried 'enough' (சாரமில் அவுடதமும் பல யோகமும் முயலா நின்று அலமரு சிந்தை). 355 asks not to become the foolish yogi who, thinking the impermanent flesh will last, holds the breath and withers eating herbs (அனித்தமான ஊன் நாளும் இருப்பதாகவே ... மூலி புசித்து வாடும் அசட்டு யோகி). The two songs, far apart, reject the same project of preserving the body by herbs and breath.

The Kural defines justice as investigating and showing favour to no one; the praise in 821 tells of the Chola king who heard the cow's bell and drove the chariot over his own son, the extreme case of 'no one' including one's own child.

Both open with பாலோ தேனோ, the string of sweet questions: in 818 they are a lullaby's endearments for a child, in 822 a lover's praise of a woman's speech, which the song then turns into questions about the inner light.
audit_text_issue: 818 line with பே¡£யாதே is damaged.

note: 816 asks whether it is right that the poet's days go in vain (நாயேன் வாணாள் வீணே போகத் தகுமோ) without singing the vel or falling at the feet. Kural 38 says that letting no day fall away unused (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) by doing good blocks the road of one's days (வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்). The song takes the Kural's measure of a life by its days and confesses the opposite case, with praise of Murugan as the good the days lacked.

817, in a lovesick girl's voice, says her mother has turned against her (மாதா மாறானாள்) and the town's slander is heard (கோளே கேள்), while the north wind cuts like a saw. Kural 1147 says this sickness grows with the town's talk as manure and the mother's word as water (ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). Both set the same pair, town gossip and the mother's anger, around the parted girl's longing; the Kural states plainly that they feed it.

819 asks for the feet of great knowledge (மாஞானக் கழல் தாராய்) as a treasure. Tirumanthiram 1598 repeats திருவடி ஞானம் four times: it makes one Siva, frees from the prison of mala and is itself release. The four-line song asks for exactly what the Tirumanthiram names, the feet understood as knowledge, and the Tirumanthiram spells out what that gift does.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 819 has corrupt glyphs (ந¨டுழி, எருரில்).

note: 820 says the women's long, proud eyes (மதர்விழி) are nets, and that they come so that men's lifetimes end (மனிதர் வாணாள் அடங்க வருவார்). Kural 1083 says the man never knew what Death was and now knows it: a woman's grace with large, warring eyes (கூற்றென்பதனை இனியறிந்தேன் ... பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both make the woman's eye a form of Death; the Kural speaks in the lover's wonder, the song in the penitent's fear.

821 hopes for a day when, with infatuation gone, tears flow and the heart melts (விழியினிர் இழிவர இதயம் உருகி) and he reaches the two feet. Tirumanthiram 2778 says those who see the holy dance shed tears of grace and their faint heart melts (துளிக்கும் அருட் கண்ணீர் சோர்நெஞ்சு உருக்கும்) as nectar wells up. Both name the same bodily sign, falling tears and a melting heart, as the mark of grace received; the song asks for what the Tirumanthiram reports.
audit_text_issue: 821 has corrupt glyphs (மடலு¡டே, எழு¦பொருள்).

note: 822 turns the lover's questions into the seeker's: is the light growing within me I or you (எனது அகம் வளர் ஒளி நானோ நீயோ), is that place a land or release; the song leaves it a question. Tirumanthiram 1441 says that searching out 'I' and 'He' (நானென்றும் தானென்றும் நாடி) the speaker reached the state where they are not two and can no longer speak of them. The Tirumanthiram answers the question the song only asks.
audit_text_issue: 822's last line (சூழ்சீ ரர்ருர்) looks corrupted for ஆரூர்.

note: 822 questions a woman's speech, eyes and face in a string of alternatives (மொழி பாலோ தேனோ, விழி வேலோ கோலோ, முகம் பானோ நிலவோ). Kural 1081 has the lover ask whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman (அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ ... மாதர்கொல்), his heart reeling. The song uses the Kural's form of bewildered questions, then reuses the same form for the soul's questions about the inner light.

823 confesses wasting the illusory body and precious days on women and asks Murugan to give initiation so he may stand on the path (நெறி நிற்க நீ தீக்ஷை தரவேணும்). Tirumanthiram 1845 names what initiation does: samaya initiation purifies mala and one's own acting ceases (சமைய மலசுத்தி தன்செயல் அற்றிடும்), followed by mantra and kala purification. The Tirumanthiram gives the content of the rite the song asks for as its cure.

Tirumular says that for those whom silence reaches, release and the powers come and all speech ends in a mute word; 824 makes that silent word the guru's teaching, a sword that drives off Death's servants.

824 asks for the sword of teaching in the silent word (மோன உரையில் உபதேச வாளை) so that body, life and the wandering heart melt. Tirumanthiram 2648 says the guru told him the one thing beyond telling (உரையற்ற தொன்றை உரைத்தான்), cut off craving for the arts and entered him. Both describe a teaching that is spoken yet wordless and that cuts; the Tirumanthiram reports its effect, the song asks for it as a weapon against Yama's servants.

825 describes the price-women (விலைமகள்) who befriend a man struck speechless to seize all his wealth and think others' wealth their own. Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man, out of love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song acts out the Kural's distinction between love and wealth in a scene of seizure.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 825's வெகுளியின்கண் நின்று இழிதொழில் is obscure.

note: The Kural begs every beggar not to beg from those who hide what they have; 827 is the confession of a poet who did just that, flattering misers to end his poverty, and turns to the Lord's feet instead.
audit_text_issue: 827 has a corrupt glyph in ரக்ஷ¢க்.

note: 826's courtesans spread their hands and say 'put down everything in your hand' (கையில் உற்ற பொருட்கள் யாவையும் வை எனக் கை விரிக்கும்). Naladiyar 373 says that even Vishnu, if he had nothing in his hand to give (தம் கைக்குக் கொடுப்பது ஒன்றில்லாரை), would be sent away by them with folded hands. Both make the hand the measure of welcome: the song shows the open hand demanding, the Naladiyar the folded hand dismissing.

827 confesses flattering drunken misers to end the misery of poverty (என் பாடு கூறிடும் மிடி தீர) before clinging to Murugan's feet. Kural 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness that thinks to end poverty's misery by begging (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம் என்னும் வன்மை). The song is the Kural's case told from inside: the begging poem quoted, then repented.

Both repent of patron praise: 827 quotes the flattery, calling a miser the kalpaka tree that protects poets, and 828 lists its inversions, the dumb called famous, fools capable and the base lords, with the patron set beside cloud and kalpaka tree.

828 repents of calling fools capable and base men lords (மூடரைச் சமர்த்தர் என்றும் ஊனரைப் பிரபுக்கள் என்றும்) in fine Tamil poems out of countless wants, and asks to worship Murugan instead. Tirumanthiram 269 says not to wither praising petty-minded men for their wealth (புல்லறிவாளரைப் போற்றிப் புலராமல்) but to praise the Lord. The Tirumanthiram's command is the song's repentance, with the same turn from patron to God.

829 says that even if he wanders thirsting for union with dancing women (கலவி தாகம் உண்டு உழல்கினும்) he will not forget the feet. Naladiyar 378 says those who mean to reach the right path will not embrace such women's breasts (தடமுலை சேராரே செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென் பார்). On the reading that 829 lets desire and devotion run together, the two disagree about whether the path survives the embrace.
audit_text_issue: 829: line 21 garbled (தந்த்முல).

note: 830 confesses not thinking the body will fall (விழுதாது எனவே கருதாது உடலை) while Lokayata ruled his mind, and asks for an undying boon. Tirumanthiram 312 addresses those who feel this perishing hut is permanent (நில்லாக் குரம்பை நிலையென்று உணர்வீர்காள்) and says the Lord is not seen in such hearts. Both name the mistake of taking the body as lasting; the song ties it to the materialist school by name.
Both build a woman's charms as questions (மொழி பாலோ தேனோ, விழி வேலோ; சேலோ வேலோ, பாலோ பாகோ). In 822 the questions are turned to the inner light; in 834 they lead to shame and to the Lord's mark.
audit_text_issue: 834 lines 19-21 have garbled shrine names (ராலு¡ர், §வ்ளுர்).

note: 831 asks whether, quarrelling and embracing women again and again, he will wander having given up penance (தவம் அற்க விடுத்து உழல்வேனோ). Kural 266 says those who do tavam do their own work and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). The song places the poet on the Kural's wrong side, with the doubled verbs (சருவிச் சருவித் தழுவித் தழுவி) showing the futile repetition.

832 says the poet grieves as his five senses run (ஓங்கும் ஐம்புலன் ஓட) after pleasure and asks Murugan to rule him by speaking Om. Kural 24 says one who guards the five with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the higher world. Where the Kural's goad is the man's own firmness, the song looks for it outside, in the guru's pranava.
audit_text_issue: ஓம்பை றும் looks damaged.

note: 833 says that craving union with women (கலவிக்குள் உளம் நச்சி) he lost his wealth and fell into poverty and ruin (வளமற்று மிடிபட்டு மடிபட்டு). Kural 920 says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the company of those Fortune has left (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The song tells as a sequence what the Kural states as a sign: desire first, then the loss of திரு.

834 questions the women's features in pairs of alternatives, among them whether their eyes are fish or vel (அக்கண் இணைக்கு இணை சேலோ வேலோ). Kural 1085 asks of a girl's look whether it is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both use the same questioning form for the eye, with a weapon among the answers; the song makes the questions part of the craving it asks to be freed from.
audit_text_issue: Shrine names in 834 lines 19-21 are damaged.

note: 835 asks Murugan to come on the peacock, enter his mind (சிந்தை அங்கு உளம் புகுந்து) and tell him to praise, understand and bow to the red feet. Tirumanthiram 290 says the Lord came unhindered and entered the heart (மறிப்பறியாது வந்து உள்ளம் புகுந்தான்), and the speaker learned a learning that surpasses. Both join the Lord's entry into the mind with instruction; the Tirumanthiram reports the learning, the song asks for the command.

Both credit the poet's singing to Murugan's own teaching: in 2 Murugan told him to sing the Thiruppugazh; in 837 he 'became guru and made me speak this', which the poet wonders at as the fruit of some former day.
audit_text_issue: Song 2 has a corrupt word in the offering list (தன஧முலம்)

note: 836 calls the price-women deceivers even while they lie on the bed (அணைமீதில் துயில் பொழுதே தெட்டிகள்). Kural 913 says the false embrace of women of wealth (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both locate the deceit in the embrace itself, the place where trust would be greatest; the Kural gives it its grim image.

837 marvels that Murugan is the Veda, cloud and rain, sun and moon and stars, space and light (முகிலாய் மழையாய் ... பருதியாய் மதியாய் ... வெளியாய் ஒளியாய்) and became the poet's guru. Tirumanthiram 10 says he himself bears the earth and is the sky, fire, sun and moon, the rain-pouring lady, mountain and sea (தானே ... ஞாயிறும் திங்களும் தானே மழைபொழி தையலுமாய்). The song applies to Murugan the litany of pervasion the Tirumanthiram opens with, adding scripture and dharma to the elements.

Both picture the courtesan whose mind is with another man while she embraces this one; the Naladiyar marvels that men still don't see it, and 838 says she leaves the lover of many days as soon as another brings more wealth.
audit_text_issue: 838's opening lines are hard to divide; the marker flagged them.

note: 838 calls the poet a fool who rejoices that house, wife, kin and abundant wealth are permanent (மனை துணைவியர் தமர் பொருள் பெருத்த வாழ்விது சதமென மகிழ்வுறும் அசட்டன்). Kural 331 calls the paltry understanding that takes what does not last for what lasts (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும் புல்லறிவாண்மை) the lowest. The song's அசட்டன் is the Kural's புல்லறிவு, named in household terms.

838 speaks of common women who, though the young man who joined them first is still there, go to another if they find more wealth (வேறொரு பெயர் தமதிடமது துவட்சியே பெறில் அவருடன் மருவிடு). Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser with earned wealth is sugar. Both say the measure of such love is wealth alone; the song's reading of its opening lines is tentative.

The two songs share their last lines and their Rama praise; 840 asks for the feet that end maya, while 841 only asks whether it must lose its tapas, so the pair shows one shrine-formula carrying two pleas.
audit_text_issue: 841 has a corrupt glyph in வ¨ல்முழ்கி; 840 in அள§முசத்.

note: 839 confesses not having thought of the Lord as a companion (துணை) in his karmic bond, disease and lust, and so wandering daily in griefs, and asks for thought of the red feet. Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety cannot be removed except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one (தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது). The song is the Kural's claim seen from the side of one who has not yet reached the feet.

840 asks for the grace of feet like the young sun's rays (வால ரவிக் கிரணங்கள் ஆமென உற்ற பதங்கள்) so that maya is ended. Tirumanthiram 2001 says the darkness of bond and ignorance vanished through Siva's light of knowledge, as thick darkness leaves at dawn (அருணோதயம் துன்றிருள் நீங்குதல் போல). Both picture release as sunrise dispelling darkness; the song puts the dawn in the feet.

841 asks whether, plunging into a sea of pleasure, giving up all conduct and losing the tapas that brings clarity (சீலம் அனைத்தும் ஒழிந்து ... தேறு தவத்தை இழந்து), he must wander. Naladiyar 57 calls blessed those who keep their vows (விரதங்கள்) and guard good conduct (நல்லொழுக்கம்) when unbearable troubles come to break them. The Naladiyar fears pain as what breaks vows; the song confesses that pleasure did it.

842 asks that before his body falls into Death's tongue like a frog into a snake's mouth (காலனது நா அரவ வாயிலிடு தேரையென) he be granted to say once 'Muruga Vel' among devotees. Kural 335 says good deeds must be done at once, before the hiccup comes and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both set a deadline at the tongue; the song's one good deed is a single utterance of the name.

Both list the body's stuff, blood, flesh, fat, bone and marrow; the Tirumanthiram counts it as the perishing adjunct of the soul, while 843 makes it a house of earth and water the soul moves into and must watch rot.

843 pictures the body as a house of earth and water built of blood, marrow, bone, flesh, guts and nerves (எலும்பு ... நாடி புனைந்திட்டு இருக்கும் மண்சல வீடு) that the soul enters. Tirumanthiram 461 says the Lord wove bones, bound them with nerves and made a house of red flesh (செம்பால் இறைச்சி திருந்த மனைசெய்து) for the seat of life. The same image of the body as a house of bone and nerve serves the Tirumanthiram as wonder at the maker and the song as disgust at its decay.

843 has the soul enter and live in the body's house (வீடு புகுந்திட்டு அதில் மேவி) until it becomes a corpse. Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has not found a home of its own. Both make the body a house the soul only occupies; the Kural's question about a lasting home is the one the song's ending (சடமாமோ) leaves open.

844 asks whether Murugan will now give his holy feet so that the poet may cross the great sea of birth (கருப்பெருங் கடலது கடக்க உன் திருவடிகளைத் தரும்). Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்) and others cannot. The song's plea uses the Kural's image and its condition, the feet, almost word for word.

845 asks for grace so that the memory of a night of union (நினைவு நெஞ்சினின்று அற) and the longing to see those faces leave his heart. Kural 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because even remembering it (உள்ளினும்) gives a joy that does not end. On the reading that both speak of the same remembered union, the Kural prizes the memory as joy and the song asks for it to be erased as bondage.
Both recall the moment Murugan told the poet to sing the Thiruppugazh; 846 adds that he called him as one taking refuge and gave him the experience of release first.
The Naladiyar says the courtesan's love ends when the man's money ends; 846 goes further, that no amount, thousands of thousands of gold coins, ever satisfies her.

847 pictures the round of births as mothers multiplying: one mother, two mothers, many crores of them (ஒருதாய் இருதாய் பலகோடியதாய்), this one becoming that one. Naladiyar 15 has each mother leave to seek her own mother, so that the world goes on mother-seeking-mother (தாய்த்தாய்க்கொண்டு ஏகும்). Both make the chain of mothers the figure of endless birth; the Naladiyar reads it as pitiable impermanence, while the song asks to break it by saying 'Muruga' once.
audit_text_issue: 847 prints ஓருதா for ஒருதா (twice).

note: Both confess praising unworthy men as the kalpaka tree and as Arjuna to get money; 848 sets that trade beside the courtesans as two forms of one failure to praise Murugan.

848 confesses that, to end his poverty, he went to cruel men of the earth (கடுத்த துற்சன மகாதகர்) and set them in verse as a kalpaka king and an Arjuna, and now asks not to be worn out by that fancy. Naladiyar 301 asks whether men of clear understanding (தெருண்ட அறிவினவர்) would follow the self-deluded rich who think the poor live only through them. The song is the confession of one who did what the Naladiyar says the clear-minded will not do, and it adds the false praise as the price of following.

849 calls the poet a low man who will not hear the counsel told him (உரைத்த புத்திகள் கேளா நீசன்) and a fool who does not grasp the true thing in his own mind (உளத்தில் மெய்ப்பொருள் ஓரா மூடன்). Kural 848 describes the man who neither does what he is told nor understands for himself (ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான்தேறான்), whose life is a disease until it departs. The song applies the Kural's double failure to itself, and asks for the feet so that the old sayings become felt knowledge.
audit_text_issue: Typo மெயப்பொரு for மெய்ப்பொரு in 849.

note: Both promise to keep Murugan in mind even while sunk in women's pleasure; 153 says he will never forget, 855 names what he will hold, the feet, the twelve arms and the chest.

850 says the street women's first thought is 'is there money?' (பணம் உண்டென தவலம்படு நினைவு), and that their sweet talk changes the minds and deeds of those who see them. Kural 912 tells the reader to weigh the women who weigh the profit and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்), and keep away. Both put the reckoning of gain before the sweet speech; the song adds that the women's maya is a sorrow only the Lord can end.

851 asks that, calling 'Siva Siva' with a heart become clear (சிவசிவ என்று தெளிவுறு நெஞ்சு), he be given the dancing anklets, while his two deeds fear and mala fades. Tirumanthiram 2715 says those who do not come to clarity by saying Siva Siva are mutes (சிவசிவ என்றே தெளிகிலர் ஊமர்), and that for those who stand in that clarity Siva Siva becomes grace. Both tie the repeated name to clarity (தெளிவு) and to grace, in the same words.

852 asks the Lord to grant the nectar of mantra and jnana teaching (அமுத மந்திர ஞானோபதேசமும் அருளி) and then the anklet feet (கழலார் கழல் அருள்வாயே). Tirumanthiram 2429 reports that the Lord told him the mantra that cannot be spoken (உரைசெய்யா மந்திரம் சொன்னான்) and that he stands wearing the anklet feet (கழலிணை சூடி நின்றேனே). What the song asks for in order, mantra then feet, the Tirumanthiram reports received in the same order.

853 asks not to waste away in hell (மங்கி நரகத்தில் மெலியாமல்) after mischief with women, but to be given the mind to worship the feet (வந்தனைசெய் புத்தி). Tirumanthiram 165 says those who do not worship the form of the konrai-wearer lie in the seventh hell crying as their entrails burn (தொழாமல் ... ஏழா நரகிற் கிடப்பர்). Both make the failure to worship the road to hell; the song asks for the very worship whose absence the Tirumanthiram punishes.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 165: மாயன் is ambiguous.

note: 854 asks that the fragrant lotus feet come always to him (சந்ததமும் வந்திரும் பரிமளப் பங்கய பதங்கள்) so that his cruel deeds, anxiety and mala perish (கொடுவினைச் சஞ்சல மலங்கெடும்படி). Tirumanthiram 967 says the Lord himself comes (தலைவனும் போந்திடும்) to remove the grief of clinging deeds (சார்ந்த வினைத்துயர் போக) for one who keeps to his name without tiring. Both have the Lord come to the devotee, not the devotee go to him, and both name the removal of deeds as the purpose of the coming.

856 asks, instead of wandering under the street women's sway, to know the wisdom of speaking of the Lord and to pour out rhythmic Tamil fit to sing him (நிகர் சந்தத் தமிழ் சொரிந்து பாடவும் அருள்தாராய்). Tirumanthiram 81 says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யுமாறே). Both make Tamil song the purpose for which grace is given to the poet; the Tirumanthiram states it as done, the song asks for it.

857 asks the Lord to hand over the unfading good thing with a word, 'here, take it, the wonder' (மங்கா நற்பொருள் இந்தா அற்புதம் என்றே இப்படி அருள்வாயே). Tirumanthiram 123 gives thanks in a chain of 'he gave' (அளித்தான்): the truth that he is all the world, the feet that dance in the hall, the open space of grace. The song asks for the truth as a direct gift; the Tirumanthiram lists what that gift turned out to contain.
Both begin the body as a drop like dew on a blade of grass; the Tirumanthiram follows the drop through the body's elements, 858 follows it through a whole life to the cremation fire.
Both trace life from a dewlike drop to death; 508 ends asking whether the sorrow will never end, 858 asks for a union in which 'you and I' become one.
Both name as remedy the sharing of even a millet grain (தினையளவு); in 23 it is drawn from the fear of death, in 860 it stands with singing and tapas among the poet's omissions.

859 credits Kumaraguru with the debate in which the Jains played on the stakes (அமணர் கழுவில் விளையாட வாது படை கருது குமரகுருநாத). 865 praises Murugan for taking those who imprisoned the loving ascetics of the Lord and setting them on the stake, while vultures pecked (கழு நெஞ்சிலே ஏற). Both give Murugan the impaling of the enemies of Saiva devotees, the Sambandar story in 859 named as Jains, in 865 as asuras.

860 confesses three omissions: he never went to sing the Lord's praise calmly, never shared even a millet grain's worth (பகிர ஒரு தினையளவு பண்புகொண்டு அண்டிலன), and never thought of the vow of walking in tapas. Tirumanthiram 264 rebukes those who do not praise the Supreme (பரமனை ஏத்தார), do not give even a little to beggars (ஈதலை யாயினும் ஈயார்), and do not tend groves, and asks if they will stand in hell. The song makes the Tirumanthiram's charge a first-person confession, with praise and the smallest gift heading both lists.

861 calls the poet one who does not melt like wax (மெழுகென உருகாவனார்), tangled in mala and maya, and asks the Lord to come and give Siva-jnana teaching. Tirumanthiram 272 says that no fierce penance reaches the gem, only those who melt with love and soften within (அன்போடு உருகி அகங்குழைவார்க்கு அன்றி). Both make melting the condition; the song counts its absence among the poet's faults and asks grace to supply what he cannot.

862 says the poet's life is caught in the net of a union he enjoys even in dreams (கனவிலும் நுகர்தரு கலவியின் வலையிடை) and is perishing there (உயிர் தட்டுப்பட்டு அழிகின்றதோ). Kural 1213 has the woman say her life lasts because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace when she is awake (கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). The same dream-union that keeps the Kural's lover alive is, for the song, the net in which life is lost.

The Kural names God only as the one of eight qualities, whose feet the head must bow to; 863 takes the same epithet, எண்குணமுற்றோன், and places that Lord dancing in a hall within, to be seen in yogic vision.

Both picture old age with failing speech, lost teeth and a staff; the Naladiyar faults the old man who still stays in the house eyeing desire, while 868 adds the household's scorn and asks for the feet that end birth.

863 asks for the grace to see the Lord of eight qualities dancing in the jewelled hall (எந்தை நடித்தாடும் மணிச்சபையூடே) and to bathe in the sea of nectar (அமுதக் கடல் மூழ்கி). Tirumanthiram 2778 says that for all who see the holy dance (திருக்கூத்துக் கண்டவர்க்கு) the heart melts and the nectar of bliss wells up within (ஆனந்தத்து அமுதூறும் உள்ளத்தே). Both join the seeing of the dance to the flood of nectar; the song asks for the sight whose fruit the Tirumanthiram describes.
audit_text_issue: 863: the line on கந்த எழுத்து is hard to divide.

note: 866 reduces the dancing women to their soiled skin (பங்கமார் தொக்கு) and asks not to sink in it but to win the Lord's love through Tamil. Naladiyar 42 says the body is handsome only through the skin that covers its falsity (தோல்போர்வை ... பொய்ம்மறைக்கும்) and should be seen as a bag turned inside out. Both name the skin as the whole of the attraction; the Naladiyar argues it, the song states it in two words and turns to song.
audit_text_issue: 866 line 7 has a stray character (குஞ்சா£).

note: 867 asks to rise at dawn, recite the Lord's names and gain the grace for his eyes to see the space of knowledge (ஞானவெளி கண்கள் காண). Tirumanthiram 600 says that one who looks fully at the light in the eye and stays merged finds the sky-way opening until the open space is seen (வெளி கண்டிட). Both make the open space (வெளி) the thing the eyes come to see; the Tirumanthiram reaches it by a yogic gaze, the song by daily naming.

868 pictures old age: black hair whitening, teeth falling, the back bent and a stick shaking in the hand (ஒர் தடி கை நடுங்கப் பிடித்திடும்), and asks when he will reach the feet. Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come (நரைவரும் என்றெண்ணி), renounced in childhood, while those who delighted in youth will rise painfully leaning on a staff (கோல் ஊன்றி). Both make the grey hair and the staff the end that should turn one early; the Naladiyar warns, the song speaks from inside that end.

869 describes the body of phlegm, guts and rheum that falls to dust, and asks to be freed from cherishing it with earrings, ornaments and clothes (கடுக்கனும் சில பூடணம் ஆடைகள்). Naladiyar 43 asks whether chewing spices, filling the head with flowers and putting on a false finery (பொய்க்கோலம்) can remove the foulness the great saw and abandoned. Both set adornment against the body's filth as useless; the song asks for Sivayoga and jnana to end the cherishing.
Both ask not to escape the women but to keep Murugan in mind amid them; 870 widens it to every state, union, sleep and talk, and asks for the knowledge to recite him.
audit_text_issue: 870 has a garbled glyph (§ல்முழ்கி); 855 has புண்டா£கம்.

note: 870 tells how a child chanting 'Nama Narayanaya' was asked by his raging father where his god was, and Vishnu burst from the pillar as a lion and tore Hiranya's chest with his claws (உகிர் புதைய இரணியனை மார்பீறி). 872 tells the same from the pillar Hiranya struck (கனகன் அங்கையினால் அறை தூணிடை), adding that the Man-Lion drank his blood like nectar. The two songs between them give the Narasimha story whole, the child's chant in one and the blood in the other, both in praise of Murugan's uncle.

871 says that, ruined by women, the poet wanders called wicked, troublesome, mad and fallen (துட்டனெனக் கட்டனெனப் பித்தனெனப் ப்ரட்டனென). Tirumanthiram 2984 says people call him a madman (பித்தன் இவனென்று பேசுகின்றாரே) because he cries out at not seeing the Father. The same public name பித்தன் falls on one for his lust and on the other for his longing for God; the song asks to be moved from the first kind to the second, among the devotees.

872 counts the mind with sky, wind, fire, water and earth as what makes up the one body (மனமெனும் பொருள் ... கூடியதோர் உடல்), in which he wanders in pleasure and sorrow, and asks to conquer that mind (மதியை வென்று). Tirumanthiram 459 says that once the body compounded of many things is settled, the mind sinks into a stupor mixed with maya (மாயங் கலந்த மனோலயம்). Both place the mind's bondage in its being mixed into the body; the song asks for the victory over it that the Tirumanthiram's account makes necessary.

The Kural counts the man who heaps up wealth and does not use it as already dead; 873 puts those who hoarded and buried without giving (ஈயாது தேடிப் புதைத்த) among the wicked bound for the lowest births. Both condemn wealth withheld, the Kural as a life wasted, 873 as a sin with a sequel.
audit_text_issue: Encoding glitch in வயலு¡ரா

note: 873 ends its list of the wicked with those who hoard and bury wealth without giving (ஈயாது தேடிப் புதைத்த துட்டர்கள்) and says they will wander in the lowest births, like dogs (கடைப்பிறப்பினில் உழல்வாரே). Kural 1002 says the delusion of clinging without giving (ஈயாது இவறும் மருள்) brings an unworthy birth (மாணாப் பிறப்பு). Both name the same fault and the same punishment, a low next birth for the one who does not give.
audit_text_issue: 873's middle lines on ப்ராரத்த துக்கம் are hard to divide; not relevant to the link.

note: Tirumular says anyone can give God a green leaf; 874 asks to worship with one flower or leaf if not many flowers. Both make the smallest offering enough, Tirumular as a duty open to all, 874 as a plea that love, not abundance, will be accepted.

875 praises Murugan as the hero who confounds and cuts down the fools who tell lies, heap up wealth and frighten simple people to make their living (அபகடம் உரைத்து அத்தம் மெத்தப் படைத்து உலகில் எளியரை மருட்டி). Kural 659 says all that is taken with tears leaves with tears (அழக் கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம்). The Kural states the law that such wealth departs; the song gives its enforcement to the Lord, who strikes the deceivers themselves.

The Kural's lover asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe, and finds it all three; 876 asks the same question through a dozen guesses, Death (மறலி) and the deer (மான்) among them. The Kural's doubt is a lover's wonder; in 876 it ends by calling such women demons to be avoided.
audit_text_issue: Parts of 876's praise are obscure.

note: 876 runs through the stock likenesses of a woman's eyes, the vel (வடிவேலோ), the red lily (செங்கழுநீரோ), the kayal and kendai fish, and asks whether kinship with women whose eyes plunder can be. Naladiyar 44 names the same set, lily, darting carp and spear (குவளை பொருகயல் வேல்), only to refuse them: an eye is a scooped-out palm fruit (நுங்கு சூன்றிட்டன்ன). Both reject the woman's eye; the Naladiyar strips the simile away, while 876 keeps every simile and reads each one as a weapon.

877 asks Murugan to be angry with him like a mother and speak one teaching (கோபித்துத் தாயென நீ ஒரு போதத்தைப் பேச) so that by that grace he gains the feet. Kural 795 tells one to seek the friendship of those who can speak till one weeps and rebuke (அழச்சொல்லி அல்லது இடித்து) and teach what is proper. The value the Kural places on a friend who rebukes is what the poet asks of his god: a grace that corrects rather than only comforts.

878 asks when his mind's attachment to the false union (பொய்க்கலவி) with women who seal and sell their breasts (முத்திரையிட்ட தனத்தை விற்பவர்) will end. Kural 913 calls the embrace of women of wealth false (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) and likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The song's பொய்க்கலவி is the Kural's பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், and both tie the falsehood to the sale.

Both picture the old man walking unsteadily on a staff after a life of desire; the Naladiyar says those still set on desire then have no way to safety, while 881 asks the golden feet even so, even if he is born again.

In 372, at Arunai, the poet asks not to spend day and night praising women in set comparisons but to be told by grace to think daily (அநுதினம் நினை) of Murugan's procession on the peacock. 879 does what 372 asks: it turns the same descriptive craft on Murugan's crowned six faces, shoulders, vel and anklets and his daily dance (தினந்தோறு நடிப்பது), and asks whether he would tell of anything else (புகல்வேனோ). The pairing shows the confession of 372 and its remedy, praise redirected to the god's form.

880 names women who quote a price (அரைப்பணம் கூறு விலையினர்), whose love falls short with anyone (குறைப்படுங் காதல் குனகிகள்) and who seek money every day (பொருட்டினந் தேடு கபடிகள்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of bangled women who desire wealth, not from love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring harm. The song lists in detail the trade the Kural defines in one line: love absent, money sought.

882 has the women recite the texts of Kama (வேளின் நூல்களை கற்ற விளம்பவும்) as they make love, and calls the delusion a calamity (மோக விபத்து). 370, at Arunai, has the women's carp eyes speak the scripture of Rati's lord (ரதிபதி சுருதி மொழிவன). In both songs love is given a learned text, the god Kama's scripture, so that the seduction is presented as an art taught and recited, not a passing impulse.

883 asks whether grace will not come as a visible form (விம்பமதாய் அருள் அருளாதோ) so that he can reach the feet instead of wandering in women's maya. Tirumanthiram 1584 says release and the knowledge that ends delusion cannot be known unless the Lord takes form and gives grace (நாதன் உருவாய் அருளாவிடில் ஓர ஒண்ணாதே). On the reading of விம்பம் as form, the song's plea is the Tirumanthiram's doctrine of the guru, said as a request.

884 asks Murugan, to end this conjuror's delusion (இந்த்ரசால இப்ப்ரமை தீர), to call him 'come here' and give the true substance that is everywhere (எங்குமான மெய்ப்பொருள் தாராய்). Tirumanthiram 1821 names grace a wide place and the true thing a refuge (பொருளது என்ற புகலிடம்), reached when the one who entered the mind to remove delusion (மருளது நீங்க) is grasped. Both set the real (பொருள்) against delusion and make the Lord's entering or calling the means.

886 asks, instead of nearing the courtesans, to think on the lotus feet and sing in calm joy the Thiruppugazh he sang before at Arunai (முன் அருணை நாடதில் ஓது திருப்புகழ் தணிய ஓகையில் ஓத எனக்கருள் புரிவாயே). Tirumanthiram 81 says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறு). Both poets treat their own song-making as the Lord's gift, and Tirumular and Arunagiri each name their work as the purpose of grace.

887 confesses that he talks to women in doubting comparisons, hair a raining cloud or darkness, eyes swords or does, breasts a mountain, and suffers in a sea of illusion. 372 asks not to spend day and night praising women with hair as darkness that fights the clouds (முகிலை யிகல்பொரு முழுவிருள் குழலென), face as moon, eyes as arrows. The two songs, far apart in the book, make the same confession about the love-poet's similes, and 887's remedy is the praise jnanis sing, called itself release (பரவு நீள்புகழே அது ஆம் மிகு பரம வீடு).

888 asks that the cravings of food, union and maya end (ஊண் புணர்ச்சியுமாயா வாதனை தீர்ந்து) and that Murugan give the conduct of true knowledge (மெய்ஞ்ஞான ஆசாரம்). Tirumanthiram 556 sets out such a conduct: purity, compassion, little food (ஊண் சுருக்கம்), forbearance, truth, and seeing lust for what it is (காமம் ... எனக் காண்பவை). The song names the conduct in a phrase as a gift; the Tirumanthiram spells it out as rules, beginning with the same two cravings, food and lust.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 888 has several corrupt glyphs (க்¡£டா, ¡£பகிரண்ட்ருபா).

note: 889 describes sleeping in the beloved's embrace and vows that even so sleeping he will not forget Murugan's feet (துயில்கினும் உனதடி மறவேனே). Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed god is sweeter than sleep on the soft arms of the one you love (மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்). Both set the sleep of love beside the divine: the Kural lover weighs heaven against it, while the poet keeps the god's feet within it.

890 says the price-women serve men rice with a drug mixed in (இடும் மருந்தொடு சோற்றையே இடு விலைமாதர்). 987 says the courtesans feed men herbal potions (மருத்துப் பச்சிலை தீற்று). Two songs far apart in the book bring the same particular charge, love-medicine, beyond the usual complaint of deceit, which shows it as a recurring item in Arunagiri's picture of the trade.

892 asks that the five senses, the two old deeds and diseases burn to ash like cotton (பஞ்செனஎரிந்து பொடியங்கமாகி) when Murugan comes and gives his feet. Tirumanthiram 117 says the sunstone burns the cotton around it only in the sun's presence (சூரியன் சந்நிதியிற் சுடுமாறு), and so the malas end when the Lord appears. Both use burning cotton for impurity destroyed at once, and both make the destruction wait on the Lord's coming.

Both name the scavengers that will eat the body, foxes, dogs, ghouls and vultures, with owls in 894 and flies, ants and crows in 898; 894 uses them to end its catalogue of disease, 898 to shame those who still swagger in palanquins.
audit_text_issue: 898 has corrupt characters in line 4 (§ர்¡லெ).

note: 893 asks whether he will wander, sinking daily in the mud (சேறுதனில் நித்தம் மூழ்கி) of the price-women and pouring away his days. Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which base men sink (ஆழும்). The song takes the Kural's image of the mire, and adds the daily repetition and the wasted days.

894 calls the body a house Brahma built of blood, brain, flesh, skin and pus that stinks through nine gates (நவத்துவாரம் நாறும்), a puppet of disease to be eaten by foxes and dogs. Naladiyar 47 calls it a pot oozing filth from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்), which the fool addresses with love's epithets because of its dark skin. Both make the nine openings the proof of the body's foulness; the Naladiyar aims at desire, while 894 aims at the wish to carry the body in vain.

The Naladiyar's man sees kin wailing over a corpse carried to the burning ground and still marries believing there is joy here; 895 follows the mourners home from the pyre, where Kama soon sets them laughing again. Both find the same forgetting at the edge of the burning ground.

895 follows the funeral rite by rite and then the mourners, who bathe in water, go home and lose their grief (மருவுபுனல் முழுகி மனை புக்குத் துக்கமறு). Tirumanthiram 145 ends the same way: they burn him, bathe in water and stop thinking of him (நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both make the bath the point where memory of the dead ends; 895 goes on to show desire taking the mourners again.

The Kural says pain perishes when even the names of desire, anger and delusion perish; 896 asks to remove the three faults (முக்குற்றம்) as the first step toward the shoreless sea of release. The link depends on reading முக்குற்றம் as the Kural's three.

896 asks to remove the three faults and, by the knowledge gained in serving the freed who know themselves (தனையுணர் முத்தர்க்கு அடிமைப்பட்டு இலகிய அறிவாலே), see the Real and enter release. Tirumanthiram 1678 describes those of the Siva garb as free of delusion, escaped from carp-eyed women, being themselves among those free of desire (தயலற்றவரோடும் தாமே தாமாகி). The Tirumanthiram describes the freed company; the song asks to serve it and names that service as the road to knowledge.

897 asks whether Murugan will not, as father and mother melt and embrace the child who leaps toward them (தந்தை தாய் உற்றுருகி வந்து சேயைத் தழுவல்), come to him crying for jnana. Tirumanthiram 2627 says the poet called his Lord as a calf calls, and the Lord sought him out and entered his body (நாடிவந்து உள்புகுந்தானே). Both picture grace as the parent who comes running to the child's cry; the Tirumanthiram reports it as done, the song asks for it.

Kural 37 says there is no need to state what virtue is: look at the palanquin's bearer and its rider (சிவிகை பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை), taking the rider's place as merit's fruit. 898 shows the rider in his palanquin (தண்டிகையில்) with chowries and horns, but opens with the body that flies, ants, foxes and crows will eat, and calls the pride arrogance like a rutting elephant's. Read together, the song limits the Kural's lesson: the rank may be the fruit of past virtue, but the one who rides is carrying a corpse to be.
audit_text_issue: 898 line 4 has corrupt characters (§ர்¡லெ).

note: Kural 335 says good deeds must be done before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 899 pictures the same last stage, cough, swollen belly, sense fading, and asks Murugan to come on the peacock and give his feet before life goes (உயிர்போமுன்). Both fix the deadline at the body's last failing; the Kural puts the work on the person, the song puts it on the god.

Both set aside the quarrelling sects and ask instead for one wordless certainty, 339 for the true form filled with silence, 907 for jnana that does not waver; 907 goes further and names the Saiva paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga among the places to be lost.

The Tirumanthiram assigns chariyai, kiriyai, yoga and jnana each to its own people, with the siddhas reaching Siva-jnana at the top. 907 keeps the order but treats the first three as traps rather than steps, asking to be given jnana without perishing in them.

Both songs are built on the refrain அலமலம், 'enough, enough'. 368 sweeps away women, patron-poetry and the sects; 908 the body itself, food, bed, wife, children and kin, keeping only kinship with those who think of the Lord.
The Kural says the good remember through seven births those who wiped away their distress; 911 makes the same vow, never to forget, toward the Lord who cut away the stain of desire and gave jnana.

Both credit Murugan with Sambandar's victory over the Jains: 913 names Sirkazhi, the Kaundinya clan and the leaf that survived the fire; 920 the leaf that swam against the current, the eight thousand impaled Jains and the Pandya king and queen.
audit_text_issue: 913 has garbled glyphs in the last line (வயலு¡ ரியலு¡ர்); 920 has ஞான தீக்ஷ¢த, பூவா ளுருறை.

note: 900 calls the poet an ignorant poor man (சிலது அறியா ஏழை) and asks to receive உன் பதி பசு பாச உபதேசம், the teaching of the triad. Tirumanthiram 115, in its chapter on உபதேசம், gives that teaching: பசு and பாசம் are beginningless like பதி, cannot go and reach it, and do not remain when பதி draws near. The pairing shows what content the Thiruppugazh's plea assumes.

900 asks to be taught பதி பசு பாசம்; 925 asks to leave பசு பாசம் and be brought into the contemplation of the பூரண நிட்கள பதி and into அநுபூதி. The two Murugan songs take the same triad from instruction to experience.

Two Vayalur songs on one plan: a long lovemaking scene, a plea for Siva-knowledge (902 அபரிமித சிவ அறிவு, 917 சிவ தத்வ ப்ரசித்தி and the sea of mukti), and a battle in drum syllables. They share whole phrases, கழுத்தொடு கை கட்டிப் பிணித்து இறுகி in 902 and கழுத்தொடு கை ஒக்கப் பிணித்து இறுகி in 917, and both credit Murugan as teacher, of the mukti path to Siva in 902 and of Tamil to Agastya in 917; 917 adds the judgment that union is a small pleasure.
audit_text_issue: 917 has stray characters (ரக்ஷ¢த்து, §முழ்கி).

note: 903 calls the courtesans இனிய நயமொழி பழகிகள், practised in sweet pleasing speech, who join fools to get their money (மடையர் பொருள்பெற மருவிகள்). Kural 911 says the இன்சொல் of women who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), brings harm. The Thiruppugazh's rhyming abuse makes the same charge: the sweet word is the instrument of the money-seeking.

904 piles up என்னால், 'by me', born, dying, praising, walking, enjoying, and ends இங்கு நான் ஆர், 'who am I here?', turning to the lord who gave him கர்ணாமிர்தப் பதம், a word sweet to the ear. Tirumanthiram 2323 says அறிகின்ற என்னை அறியாது இருந்தேன், until Nandi graced him saying அறிகின்றாய் நீ, and he knew himself the knower. The Tirumanthiram supplies an answer, given as a guru's word, to the question 904 leaves open.

905 calls the poet's sorrow ஒருநாள் பிரிவதும் அரிதாய்ச் சுழல்படும் ஒழியாத் துயர், a whirling grief in which even one day's parting is hard to bear. Kural 1269 says ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் செல்லும் for those who wait for a distant lover's return. The Thiruppugazh borrows the parted lover's measure of a single day, but names it as the bondage to be escaped (தவிரேனோ).

908 begins its அலமல ('enough') list with the body of blood, worms and flesh, then sets aside wife, children, kin and every tie but those who think of the Lord. Kural 345 says that for those set on cutting off birth உடம்பும் மிகை, even the body is excess, so why further ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). Both reason from the body outward to every other bond.

909 confesses the friendship that grows with women he does not think enemies (பகையே என நினையாது உற நண்பு கூரும்). Kural 882 warns: do not fear foes like swords, fear கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு, ties with enemies who seem kin. The Thiruppugazh applies the Kural's statecraft warning about the enemy within to desire.

910 asks for the dancing feet that even the faultless Veda cannot find (ஆசிலாத மறைக்கும் தேடொணாத) to be given எனக்கு இன்று, to me today. Tirumanthiram 578 says that by drawing the mind within one may see இன்று இங்கே the one பழமறை தேடி, whom the ancient Veda sought everywhere. Both set the Veda's failed search against a present, personal finding; Tirumular reaches it by withdrawal of the senses, 910 by asking for grace.

912 thanks the lord who took him as his servant in a dream (கனவில் ஆள் சுவாமீ), so that he would not fall into the womb but sing and serve. Kural 1213 has the parted woman live because she sees in dreams (கனவினால் காண்டலின்) the man who gives no grace awake. The dream in which the beloved comes becomes, in the Thiruppugazh, the place where the god's grace was given.
audit_text_issue: 912's line on Indra's thunderbolt and elephant is partly corrupt.

note: Two songs from the poet's own story, each ending மறவேனே: 911 recalls the Lord calling 'வா' at Viralimalai and giving the nectar of jnana, 912 the Lord taking him in a dream (கனவில் ஆள்) so that he not fall into the womb. Both are thanks for grace already given, not pleas, and both make the answer a vow of memory.
audit_text_issue: 912's Indra/elephant line is partly corrupt.

note: 914 shows the courtesan swearing her price (விலை ஈதே கடிய சத்தியமாம்) and turning harsh (கடுகடுத்திடுவார்) when the money given runs out, and asks whether having joined them is not enough. Naladiyar 378 says such women are sweet while a man is deceived and become harsh as a ram's horn (தகர்கோடாம்) once they have had their fill, and those who seek the right way do not embrace them. Both mark the same turn from sweetness to harshness when the payment ends.
Two Vayalur songs on the one refrain காட்டி, 'showing': in both the courtesans show their bodies and arts to deceive, and 915 turns the same verb on Murugan, who shows jnana.
audit_text_issue: Both have corrupt glyphs in வயலு¡ரா; 901 in மயிலு¡ர்தி.

note: 916 gives most of its praise to the Goddess's names: காளி திரிபுரை அந்தரி சுந்தரி நீலி கவுரி ... அம்பிகை. Tirumanthiram 1046 lists திரிபுரை சுந்தரி அந்தரி ... மனோன்மனி and says the one great one stands as many by these names. The same run of names, Tripurai, Sundari, Antari, serves Tirumular's doctrine of Shakti's forms and the Thiruppugazh's praise of Murugan's mother.

After describing union as an experience one cannot leave for a moment, 917 judges புணரும் இது சிறு சுகம் and asks when it will reach the sea of release, முத்திச் சிவக் கடல். Tirumanthiram 2091 laments those who stand in காமத் தொழில், a pleasure that soon runs out (தீர வருவது), and forget மாதவன் இன்பம், the joy of the great ascetic. Both measure sexual pleasure against a greater bliss and find it small.

918 says the courtesans make the wealth in the lustful man's hand their kin (கைப்பொருள் உறவாகி) and put a price on anyone's heart (யாரையும் நெஞ்சை விலைப்படுத்திடு). Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison, while even an oil-presser who has earned wealth is sugar (அக்காரம்). Both say the man himself does not count, only what he holds.

919 asks Murugan to speak the word (அருள் உரையாதோ) that raises the poet, a low sinner, to the high state in the assembly of devotees great in devotion (பத்திமை சால் அடியார் சபை). Tirumanthiram 547 describes going with the devotees of the Lord's devotees into his city, where those at the gate made him known and the cry went up உடையான் வருக. Tirumular narrates as done the admission among devotees by the Lord's word that 919 asks for.

Both make Murugan the saint who cured the Pandya's hunch and sent the Jains to the stake; 306 sets it against court poetry, 920 against the courtesans, and adds the leaf against the current and the queen who lived on at Alavai.

921 describes women's waists and hill-like breasts that spin the poet about (சுழற்றி) and asks for yoga to grow and the body whirling in disease (உழல் ஆக்கை) to be removed, so that the Lord sits in his breast. Tirumanthiram 2141 has desire rising at the leaf-slender waist and the mind sunk at the breast, carrying a lightning-brief body about, while the mind made firm stands before Siva. Both make the woman's body set one wandering and a steadied inner discipline the way to the Lord's presence.

922 asks that its த்ரிவித கரணங்கள், the three instruments of mind, speech and body, approach Murugan's red feet, free of ties (தொந்தம் அற்று). Tirumanthiram 2612 says strong karma kindles through மன வாக்கு காயம் and does not last when they stand straight. The Tirumanthiram supplies the reason the three instruments matter; the Thiruppugazh turns them toward the feet.

Both take kings riding elephants under the white umbrella as the case that proves death spares no one; the Naladiyar says they too were carried off, 928 that in their music and pride they never know the death Brahma has written.
audit_text_issue: 928 has a corrupt glyph in வயலு¡ர்க்குக.

note: 923 asks to be made wise and settled and given சிவஞான பரயோகம். Tirumanthiram 2712 says that when the impurity is removed, by the power of the Lord's grace தீதில் சிவஞான யோகமே சித்திக்கும். The same compound names the goal in both, and both make it a gift of grace (அருள்வாயே, இறையருள் சத்தியால்).
