After its lovemaking scene, 924 says the Lord's lotus feet with anklets and his golden shoulders with vetchi flowers dance in the poet's eyes (என் நயனத்தில் உற்று நடமிடும்). Kural 1126 has the woman say her lover does not leave her eyes (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார்) and is not hurt when she blinks. The beloved living in the eyes is given in 924 to the god, in place of the women the song describes.
audit_text_issue: 924 has garbled characters (மி¨ச்முழ்கி).

note: 925 asks the Lord to bring the poet (அடைவித்து அருள்வாயே), leaving பசு பாசம், into the contemplation of the Pati known by knowledge. Tirumanthiram 115 says பதியினைச் சென்று அணுகா பசு பாசம், pasu and pasam cannot go to the Pati, but பதி அணுகில் they do not remain. Both make the reaching the Lord's act, not the soul's.

926 asks to be joined by any means to the Lord's devotees (எத்திற் கொடு நின் அடியாரொடும் உய்த்திட்டு) and so given high jnana and the life of the holy feet. Tirumanthiram 1644 says no tapas is needed to make the mind Siva if one has kinship (உறவு) with those whose minds have joined Siva's bliss. Both make the company of devotees the means.

927 describes the tight embrace (கட்ட முயக்கு) with nail-marks on the neck in which words stop and life faints, and asks for a disciplined contemplation having left that experience. Kural 1108 says the embrace (முயக்கு) so close that no breeze can pass between is sweet to lovers. The same close embrace is the Kural's sweetness and the Thiruppugazh's thing to be left behind.

929 vows never to forget, night and day (இராப்பகல் மறவேனே), the forms in which Murugan stands at Vayali and at Vanji. Kural 1207 has the parted woman ask what would become of her if she forgot, since she knows no forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்). The lover's vow of unbroken memory becomes the devotee's vow toward a shrine form.
audit_text_issue: 929 line துவயலி நின்றன வ்யாத்தமும் looks garbled.

note: The song sets the poet against devotees who worship even the servants of devotees as the Lord (அடியவர் அடியவர் அடிமையும் ... நிகரென வழிபடு) and lists what he lacks. Tirumanthiram 2624 speaks from inside that chain, servant to the servants of the servants (அடியார் அடியார் அடியார்க்கு அடிமை), and says the Lord took him as his own for it. The pair shows the servitude the poet confesses he lacks and what the Tirumanthiram says it yields.

The song calls Murugan the one seen by his servants and not to be found by the stubborn (தொண்டரால் காணப் பெறுவோனே, மிண்டரால் காணக் கிடையானே). Tirumanthiram 1804 says the Lord entered the heart of his servant by grace and is not seen, though within, by those without grace (அகம்புகுந்தும் தெரியான் அருள் இல்லோர்க்கு). Both make seeing the Lord depend on the servant's state, not on his nearness.

The song asks whether, instead of drowning in the sea of births made by the two deeds (இருவினைப் பிறவிக் கடல் மூழ்கி), the poet will reach the goal by grace. Kural 10 uses the same sea (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்) and says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim it. The hymn's plea assumes the Kural's rule and asks grace to be on the right side of it.

Both songs describe the pull of women as a needle drawn to a magnet: ஊசி காந்தத்து உறவென வீழ்ந்து here, காந்தமொடு ஊசியென at Chidambaram. The figure makes desire a force the poet does not choose, and in both it is set before a plea for the feet. It is rare in the book, which makes the pairing worth noting.
audit_text_issue: 933 has a garbled glyph in வயலு¡ரா; 501 is clean.

note: Both lament a girl sick with love for Murugan in another's voice, wounded by the moon, the wind and a bird's call; 934 adds the lone flute and ends asking the god to come and embrace her.

In 934 the moon throws fire, the wind strikes and the cuckoo calls, and the singer speaks for a girl wasting with love for Murugan. In 948 the same evening machinery (கோகிலம் அழைக்க, the breeze as chariot, the moon as garland) is Kama's army marching on the poet himself. The akam convention given to the girl in one song is taken by the poet in his own voice in the other.
audit_text_issue: 948 flagged uncertain.

note: Both refuse the bard's flattery of base patrons: 306 mocks calling a miser Pari or Kari, 935 calling sinners the equal of the twenty-one ancient patrons, after listing the poet's own honours.

Both songs end their account of women not with a plea for release but with a vow: even serving women (மங்கையர்க்கு ஆளாகி ஏவல் செய்திடினும்) in 936, even sinking into courtesans' beds (பாயலின் மூழ்கினும்) in 944, the poet will not forget the feet (மறவேனே). The pair shows a distinct form of the confession, one that keeps devotion beside the habit rather than asking to be freed from it.

Both take the coming of grey hair as the reason to turn now: the Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood knowing old age will come, and 940 asks for service at the feet while youth lasts, before the hair whitens like a crane.

Both turn from the uproar of the six faiths and the arts of argument: 941 says 'enough' even to Siva's mantra and yantra lore and asks for the highest state, 951 asks to leave the attachment to argument and know the knowledge that cannot be pointed to.
audit_text_issue: Encoding glitches (சுக் ¡£பர், வயலு¡ரா)

note: The song lists what women's eyes do, among them putting Yama's soldiers to flight (எமபடர் படைகெட்டோட நாடுவ) and torturing life (உயிர்வதை நயனம்). Kural 1083 says the man never knew Death until now, and it is the woman's warring eyes (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). The Kural makes the eyes Death; the song makes them stronger than Death's army, and turns the image toward a plea for the feet.

Both Kongu songs bring Sundarar's stories into Murugan's praise: 940 names Paravai in the pain of separation and the true messenger who hurried to her (பரவையொடு ... மெய்த்தூதர்), and 947 the thousand gold coins for the woman of Kamalalayam and the Lord coming as helper (சகாயன்) to the tired singer. In both the Lord serves his devotee, which is the reverse of the humble service (குற்றேவல் அடிமை) 940 asks to be given.
audit_text_issue: 940's Paravai lines and 947's first half are hard to construe.

note: The song says enough (அலமலம்) even to hearing the mantra and darshana lore of the Saiva texts Siva taught the sages, and asks for the highest state instead. Tirumanthiram 51 says the wise left argument (தர்க்க வாதத்தை விட்டு) and gained release by reciting the Veda. Both reject disputation, but on the reading that 941 sets scripture itself aside as a path, the two disagree on whether reciting scripture brings release.

The song calls Murugan hard for the six faiths to see (சடுசமயங் காண்டற்கு அரியானே). Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six faiths did not see him and he is not what they hold (ஆறு சமயமும் கண்டவர் கண்டிலர்). The hymn's epithet is the Tirumanthiram's teaching in a phrase.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 942: சவதமொடுந் தாண்டித் தக்ருர்வாய் is garbled.

note: The song asks that penance and japa ripen the poet for the feet (தவசெபமும் தீண்டிக் கனிவாகி). Tirumanthiram 1632 says tapas is needed to reach knowledge but not once the samadhi of knowledge is held (தவம்வேண்டு ஞானம் தலைபட வேண்டில்). It places the song's means as a stage that falls away at the goal.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 942 line 5 (சவதமொடுந் தாண்டித் தக்ருர்வாய்) garbled; Tirumanthiram 1632 line 3 probably corrupt.

note: Both meet Death's messengers by turning to the Lord in time: the Tirumanthiram says that for one who thinks of the Lord the messengers will not even think of burning him, and 945 asks for the feet before the messengers with noose and trident seize him.

Both draw old age in the same order, grey hair, failing eyes and teeth, phlegm and cough, then the family's contempt: in 945 kin mock, in 955 the wife reviles and all call him unclean, and both ask for grace at the hour that follows.
audit_text_issue: 945 has நீனைத்தினந் (likely நினைத்தினம்).

note: The song asks Murugan to become the true guru so that the poet neither dies nor is born (இறவாமல் பிறவாமல்). Tirumanthiram 2585 says the Lord he never forgot set him here so that he would not die and be born again (இறந்து பிறவாமல் ஈங்கு வைத்தானே). What the hymn asks for, the Tirumanthiram reports as granted, in nearly the same words.

Both make evening the hour when love's sickness is fullest: the Kural's woman says it buds in the morning and opens at evening; 948 gives that hour to the poet himself and arms it as Kama's army of breeze, moon, cuckoo and sea.

The song praises the true guru (சற்குரு) whose teaching in an instant takes Siva-yogis past the thirty-six tattvas (ஆறாறு தத்துவ மேல்) to the supportless state. Tirumanthiram 2049 says the true guru, giving his feet, brings the soul beyond the tattvas (தத்துவாதீதத்து) and quells its bonds. Both make passing the tattvas the guru's gift, and the hymn ends on the feet as the Tirumanthiram does.

The song asks for one word (ஓர் வாக்கு) whose rule is the soul's knowledge, to cure the disease that does not end. Tirumanthiram 302 says those who hear Siva's word become gods and that hearing the word that bears fruit is the real hold (பயன்பணி கேட்பது பற்றது). The hymn asks for the fruitful word the Tirumanthiram describes.
audit_text_issue: 949 has a broken shrine name (§ப்ருர்).

note: The song holds up taught yogis but asks above all that the poet's desires truly end (இச்சையானவை நேரே தீர), with town and name. Tirumanthiram 2613 says talk of breath and needle is useless; cut desire and attachment (ஆசையும் அன்பும் அறுமின்) and the Lord's place is easy to reach. Both put the end of desire, not yogic technique, at the centre.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 950's heading and closing line show encoding damage (§ப்ருர், பர்ரு ராசூழ்).

note: The song asks to leave the arts of disputation (தர்க்கப் பலகலை) and the quarrels of the six sects and know the knowledge that has no mark (குறியாத அறிவை அறிந்து). Tirumanthiram 2517 says the one who conquers the senses ends dispute quickly (பிணக்கறுவந்து) and knows the Pure One as one. Both make the end of argument the condition of the knowing.
audit_text_issue: 951 அரவியிடந் தப்பி obscure

note: Both describe the courtesan's charm as calculated: the Kural's women weigh the profit before speaking of their virtue, and in 952 they name the price and learn their arts of deceit.

The song rests its plea on there being no other giver: if Murugan does not grant the boon, who else will (வரம் தராவிடில் பிறர் எவர் தருவாரே). Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one (தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான்). The hymn's plea is the Kural's claim spoken by one in need of it.
Both name Murugan's command to sing the Thiruppugazh: 2 remembers the grace of being told to sing, and 954 adds that the command came with lordship, poetic gift and a guru's authority.

Both picture the old man whose teeth are gone and whose body is scorned; the Naladiyar faults him for keeping his eyes on desire still, while 955 lists the decay and asks only for grace at the hour of death.
audit_text_issue: Encoding glitch at the start of 955 (உ ரைத்த)

note: Both make the courtesan's embrace an embrace of a corpse, but in opposite directions: in the Kural the man who embraces her holds a stranger's corpse in a dark room; in 959 the women, looking only at money, will embrace even a corpse.
1 says only that Ganapati first wrote on the first mountain; 956 tells the story fully, that he wrote the Bharata with one tusk on Meru when he was asked.

967 recasts the book's opening song almost formula by formula, the three-eyed Lord's chant of the seed of release, the thirty-three gods, the arrow at the ten heads and the chariot driven by the green-cloud Vishnu, and names the treasure sought as Sivam in devotees' hearts.
Both fault the courtesan's double dealing: the Naladiyar's eel shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish, and 966's women talk as if on a man's side while hooking him for his wealth.

956 asks whether love will not melt all his bones (நெக்கு என்பெலாம் உருகு அன்பு) as he names Murugan's feet, crown and faces. Tirumular says that even making one's bones the firewood (என்பே விறகா) and frying one's flesh reaches nothing, and only those who melt with love (அன்போடு உருகி அகங்குழைவார்) reach the gem. The song takes up the Tirumanthiram's measure, bones and melting love, and turns the ascetic's burnt bones into bones that melt in devotion.

956 marvels at the jnana Murugan gave, in which the clamour of the quarrelling sects (சிலுகிடு சமயப் பங்கவாதிகள் கதறிய வெகுசொல்) fell silent along with the arts and the senses. Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him (ஆறு சமயமும் கண்டவர் கண்டிலர்) and urges clarity and settling. Both put the knowledge of God past the sects' disputes; the song reports it as a gift received.
audit_text_issue: 956 has 'புண்டா£க', an encoding glitch

note: 959 says the courtesans call men while weighing their property (அழைப்பர் ஆஸ்திகள் கருதுவர்), look only at money and drive a man off when he is finished. Kural 912 tells one to weigh and avoid women who weigh the profit and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The song shows the weighing in action, the festival calls and the potions; the Kural gives the rule that the man should weigh them in return.

962 traces the chase after women into roaming for money, hiding and becoming a thief, then a man of darkness (திருடனாகி ... திமிரனாகி), and asks instead for clear jnana (தெளியும் ஞானம்). Kural 287 calls stealth a dark knowledge (களவென்னும் காரறிவாண்மை) absent in those who love measure. The song places theft on the same scale of dark and clear knowing and shows desire as the road to it.

964 asks that, having crossed the sea of desire (ஆசைக் கடலேறி) and bathed in the sea of jnana, he be given the life of knowledge of the Lord (பதிஞான வாழ்வு). Kural 370 says that giving up craving, never filled by nature (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா), at once gives an unchanging nature (பேரா இயற்கை). The Kural states the exchange; the song names what the unchanging state is, a life in knowledge of Pati.

965 asks for kindness to living beings as a kind of understanding (பூதத் தயவான போதம்), with truth and discipline as its ground. Kural 249 says that virtue done without kindness is like a man without clarity seeing the truth (தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்றால்). Both tie compassion to knowing: the Kural makes the lack of one like the lack of the other, and the song asks for them as one gift.
audit_text_issue: Song 965's first word (நீதத்துவம்) is of uncertain split.

note: 966 lists the courtesans who coax and speak as if on a man's side (குனகிகள் பக்ஷம் போல பேசிகள்) and hook men by desire of wealth (பொருளாசைக் கொளுவிகள்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song's 'as if on your side' is the Kural's sweet word without love, named from the man's experience of it.
Both tie the courtesan's company to money: the Naladiyar's love lasts as long as a lamp's oil, and 970 ends with the wealth sought now wasted and no goal left.

968 asks to stand apart from the work (தொழில் வேறுபட நின்று) of the five senses, which stand like hunters, and the four inner instruments, and so understand. Tirumular says the ignorant cry 'curb the five', that curbing them makes one inert, and that he learned the knowledge that does not curb them (அஞ்சும் அடக்கா அறிவு). The song's remedy is the same kind: not suppression of the senses but a knowing that stands apart from their work.

Both speak for a girl in love with Murugan who wastes at evening under Kama's arrows and the wind; 24 is her mother's lament against the anril bird, the south wind and the crescent, while 974 blames the north wind and asks the god to come today.

972 describes lovemaking and asks that at that very moment (மூழ்குற்றிடு போது) Murugan show his faces, peacock and anklet feet. 870, also after a full scene of union, asks that even while sunk in it (கலவிதனில் மூழ்கி ஆழுகினும்), asleep or talking, he be given the knowledge to recite Murugan's arms, feet and faces. Both songs ask not to escape the embrace but to have Murugan present inside it, an unusual plea in a book that mostly asks to be freed from women.

973 asks that he not, desiring women's shoulders (மடவார் தோள் விரும்பி), cross the bounds (வரம்பு கடந்து) and waste away. Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders (மென்தோள்) of women who keep no bounds (வரைவிலா) the mire where base men sink. The song turns the Kural's women without bounds into the man who crosses his own.

974, for a lovesick girl, says the evening and the north wind's thrown fire (வாடை எறிந்த அனல்) have worn her thin before her lover comes. Kural 1228 has the woman say the herdsman's flute is a messenger for the fire-like evening (அழல்போலும் மாலை) and a weapon that kills. Both make evening a burning, and give it a companion that carries the fire, the wind in the song and the flute in the Kural.

975 calls the courtesans those who raise a man up and let the ladder fall (ஏறிட்டிட்டு ஏணியை வீழ்விடு). Naladiyar 372 tells of the woman who swore to leap with him from the peak and, at the peak, having no gold from him, showed a pain in her feet and would not come (மேற்காணம் இன்மையான் மேவாது ஒழிந்தாள்). Both picture the bargain as a climb that she abandons at the top when the money ends.

976 asks for the life that is not heard in the Veda (வேதத்திற் கேள்வி யிலாதது) and not seen by understanding (போதத்திற் காண வொணாதது), naming it only by negations. Tirumular says the Veda and conduct end in kalanta and the great one is beyond speech, word and feeling (பேசா உரையுணர்வற்ற). Both describe the goal as what lies past the Veda and past the mind that knows.

977 compares women's nail-scored breasts to the written palm leaf of poets of elaborate verse (வித்தார கவித்திறத்தினர் பட்டோலை நிகர்த்து). 979 rehearses the stock comparisons of women's breasts and then confesses the base trade (இழிதொழில்) of making such praise-songs for patrons. The two songs show the poet's own craft turned on desire, first as a simile, then as the thing he wants to give up.

Both take the death of kings as the proof of impermanence: the Naladiyar's kings under moon-white umbrellas are carried off, and 978's sword-bearing kings reach the burning ground in a moment; 978 draws from it the renunciant's resolve to end birth.
audit_text_issue: 978's last plea lines are hard to divide.

note: 979 asks when he will drop the base trade of praise-songs made to please patrons and live doing chariyai and kiriyai (சரியை கிரியைசெய்து உயிர்வாழ்வேன்). Tirumular lists what that service is: lighting lamps, gathering flowers, smearing and sweeping the floor, praising, holding the bell, bathing the image (தளிதொழில்). Set together, the poet's service of patrons is to be replaced by service of the temple, a work the Tirumanthiram spells out.
audit_text_issue: 1502 opening garbled ('தீப miடல்').

note: 980 says the courtesans demand the coins named and, when the money is not in hand, drive the man out midway (காசு கேட்டது கைப்பற்றா இடை காதி ஓட்டி). Naladiyar 373 says that even if he were Mal worshipped by the gods, they would send off a man with nothing in his hand to give (தங்கைக்கு கொடுப்பதொன்று இல்லாரை), bowing as they did it. Both make the empty hand the end of welcome; the Naladiyar adds the mock courtesy of the dismissal.
Both follow the corpse from the wailing and the drums to the fire; the Naladiyar ends with the dying carrying the dead, 981 with the ash and a prayer not to be born again.

981 follows the dead body: the townsfolk gather and wail till they tire (ஊரார் குவித்து ... அழுதோய), carry it before it stinks and set it in the fire till it is ash, and asks not to seek this birth again. Tirumular has the whole town gather and wail (ஊரெலாம் கூடி ஒலிக்க அழுதிட்டு), call him a corpse, burn him and bathe and forget. The scene is the same step by step; Tirumular ends with the mourners' forgetting, the song with a prayer against rebirth.
audit_text_issue: Glyph corruption in 981 line 1 (லு¡தாரி).

note: 982 asks to sing Murugan's praise and so gain Siva's state, the great open space of knowledge (ஞானப் பெருவெளி) and the nectar of refuge. Tirumular lists what the guru gave: the truth that he is the world, the world unknown to gods, the dancing feet, and the open space of grace in great bliss (பேரின்பத்து அருள்வெளி). Both name the goal as a vast open space reached through grace, in a stepwise list of gifts.

Both show the man whose speech fails and who walks with a staff; the Naladiyar's old man still keeps his eyes on desire, while 983 traces the whole road from the price-women of youth to the staff and a catalogue of diseases.

983 runs through a life from youth, trade and price-women to wrinkled skin, grey hair and walking with a stick (தடியோடு திரி), then a list of diseases. Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood knowing grey hair comes (நரைவரும் என்றெண்ணி), while those who delighted in youth will rise painfully leaning on a staff (கோல் ஊன்றி). The song fills in the life the Naladiyar warns of, stage by stage, down to the staff.

984 asks whether honey or the syrup of cane can match union (தேனோ கருப்பிலெழு பாகோ இதற்கிணைகள் ஏதோ) and then calls its endless repetition a mud-bath of sorrow (சேறாடல் பெற்ற துயர்). Kural 1121 has the lover say her mouth's moisture is milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன் கலந்தற்றே). The song uses the same sweetness of love's poetry, and then judges it as mire.
audit_text_issue: Glyph corruption in 984 (லு¡டே).

note: Both lead the yogi through the sushumna to a light within; Tirumular's eight-petalled flower holds maya's city, and 985 names the nectar of Sivayoga in the sushumna of the sky as the state it asks Murugan to give.

985 names the fifty-one letters (ஐம்பந்தொரு அக்ஷரம்) as the beginning of all worlds, rivers and cosmic eggs, among the marks of the reality it asks to know. Tirumular counts the paths of the cosmos: thirty-six tattvas, mantras, fifty-one letters (வன்னம் ஐம்பான் ஒன்று), two hundred and twenty-four worlds. Both take the fifty-one letters as one of the stuffs of the world, the Tirumanthiram in a technical count, the song in a hymn.

Thiruppugazh 986 asks for the signs of devotion themselves: melting (உருகியும்), eyes brimming (விழிபுனல் தேக்கிட), love growing night and day (இராப்பகல்), faltering speech and weeping again and again (அழுதழுது). Tirumanthiram 2980 reports the same state as already reached: அன்புள் உருகி அழுவன் அரற்றுவன், என்பும் உருக இராப்பகல் ஏத்துவன். The pairing shows the bhakti the song prays for is the state the Tirumanthiram names as the mark of those who have joined the Lord.

Kural 71 says no bolt can shut in love, since the small tears of the loving (ஆர்வலர் புன்கணீர்) proclaim it. Thiruppugazh 986 turns the tears into the thing prayed for, eyes brimming (விழிபுனல் தேக்கிட) with love growing ever more (அன்பு மேன்மேல்). The Kural treats tears as the sign of love; the song asks for the sign as the gift.

The Kural's women weigh the profit before they speak of virtue; 987 makes the weighing literal, the courtesans assaying the gold they take and counting the hours before the quarrel that ends the bargain.

Thiruppugazh 987 describes courtesans who hug a man's neck, take the wealth from his hand (கைப்பொருள் கழற்றி), count the hours and pick a quarrel to drive him off (கணக்கிட்டுப் பொழுதேற்றி வைத்தொரு பிணக்கிட்டு). Naladiyar 377 gives the same sequence in animal images: the woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth in his hand (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), then balks like an ox. Both make the turn come exactly when the money has been taken.
Both are akam songs for a girl in love with Murugan, burned by Kama's arrows and the night, that ask him to come to her now.
audit_text_issue: 988's tight syllables are hard to divide; reading is conjectural.

note: Thiruppugazh 989 places Death hidden in the sky (விண்மேல் நமன் கரந்து) while the body wastes and the heirs quarrel. Naladiyar 20 warns that merciless Death roams looking for his men and bids the reader keep his stealth in mind (அதன் கள்ளம் கடைப்பிடித்தல் நன்று). Both picture Death as concealed and watching, the Naladiyar to urge provision in time, the song to ask Murugan to come before life goes.

Kural 1121 says the moisture at the white teeth of the soft-spoken girl (வாலெயிறு ஊறிய நீர்) is like milk mixed with honey. Thiruppugazh 990 uses the same ஊறல் twice: the poet wanders in the ஊறல் of the sinful body, while Murugan drinks the ஊறல் of Valli's mouth (வாயில் ஊறல் குடித்து) to end her longing. The Kural's lover's praise is given to the god, while the same word in the plea names what the poet must escape.

Twin songs with one refrain: both set the pomp of riding elephants and horses as a king, and pleasure with women, against the supreme truth (பரமார்த்தம்) never grasped, and both name Murugan as Siva's teacher.
audit_text_issue: Several Sanskrit words in 995's praise are corrupt.

note: In 979 the poet longs to leave praise-poetry for a life of chariyai and kiriyai; in 1004 those who call chariyai and kiriyai penance are among the half-knowers whose path he asks to leave for the experience beyond deeds and malas. The two fit as stages, not as a contradiction.

Both set the quarrels of the sects against knowing the light within: Tirumular says that for one who reaches it there is no quarrel at all, and 1004 asks to leave the quarrelling sectarians for an experience where 'mine' and 'yours' cease.

Both stand the lover of pleasure beside the funeral: the Naladiyar's drum answers the man who sees the corpse carried yet thinks there is joy here, and 1001 asks at the drum and the burning ground whether that is sweet.

Both measure the failure to give by a millet grain: 23 asks to share even a grain of millet before Death's summons, and 1006 opens its self-condemnation with having not a millet-grain's thought of sharing.

Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் ... இறைவன் அடிசேராதார்). Thiruppugazh 992 fears that, not falling at the lotus feet (பாத வாரிஜத்தில் விழாதே), he will drown in the great ocean of seven births (மகோததி ஏழ்பிறப்பினில் மூழ்கா). It is the Kural's image and claim, stated as the poet's own danger, with the feet reached by the litany of praise.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 992 has several corrupt glyphs (ஜ¨முத, புண்டா£கா, கி¡£டா).

note: Kural 266 says those who do tapas do their own work, and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Thiruppugazh 993 charges itself with exactly that pair: a demon of desire (ஆசாப சாசனை, ஆசாப ஈனனை) and a ruin who never sought the gain of tapas (ஊதியத் தவம் நாடாத கேடனை). The self-condemnation reads as the Kural's 'others' speaking of themselves.

Tirumanthiram 168 says that before favour, king, elephants, chariots and wealth (அருளும் அரசனும் ஆனையம் தேரும் பொருளும்) pass to others, joining the true wealth while life lasts is the great tapas. Thiruppugazh 995 confesses missing that truth, that guarding the soul is the highest state (ஆவி காப்பது மேற்பதம்), while wandering on elephants and horses with armies (ஆனை மேற் பரி மேற் பல சேனை), and asks whether the body must go so. The song is the Tirumanthiram's warning spoken too late.
audit_text_issue: 995's praise has corrupt Sanskrit words (தீ¨க்ஷப ¡£¨க்ஷகள்).

note: Tirumanthiram 1 opens with Siva as one and then two, three and on (ஒன்றவன் தானே இரண்டவன்). Thiruppugazh 996 quotes the guru's word it failed to grasp as Siva being one and many (ஏகமாய்ப் பலவாய்ச் சிவபோகமாய்), the same creed in compact form. The song places at its centre, as the truth missed through royal pride, the claim the Tirumanthiram puts first.

Kural 1084 says the girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றத்தால்). Thiruppugazh 997 has the women's kayal eyes plunder life like a spear (ஆருயிர் சூறை கொண்டிடு வேல்போலே). The Kural's lover is overwhelmed by one girl's look; the song takes the same life-taking eye as a danger that sets fate's sorrow whirling.

Tirumanthiram 2528 says the gathered flower has eight petals (ஒருங்கிய பூவுமோர் எட்டிதழ்), with the city of maya inside, and the light is reached through the sushumna. Thiruppugazh 998 begins with a lotus of eight petals (நாலிரண்டு இதழாலே கோலிய ஞால முண்டகம்) with the yogic mantra of the mooladhara and a seat above, where Murugan sits. The song's syntax is a long list and the reading is tentative, but both set an eight-petalled lotus in the body as a yogic seat.

Tirumanthiram 88 tells how Brahma and Vishnu, seeking Siva's foot and crown (அடிமுடி காண்பார் அயன்மால்), did not see his form. Thiruppugazh 999 retells it, the fire hard to find for Brahma of the Vedas and Vishnu of the bird (தெரிவரிதான ... செந்தழல்), and then makes that unmeasured Siva praise Murugan as great guru (மாக்குருநாதன் எனும்படி போற்றிட). The Tirumanthiram's proof of Siva's height becomes the measure of Murugan's.

Kural 261 says bearing what pain comes and causing no pain to living beings is the form of tapas (அற்றே தவத்திற் குரு). Thiruppugazh 1000 calls singing Murugan's valour in the Valli story so that all the land knows, and seeking his feet, the rare tapas (அருந்தவம் வாய்ப்பதும் ஒருநாளே). On the reading that the Kural's definition is exhaustive, the two disagree about what tapas is.

Tirumanthiram 145 has the town wail, take away the dead man's name and call him corpse (பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு), carry him to the burning ground and forget him. Thiruppugazh 1001 has the mourners fondle and weep and then one call out to take away the old corpse (முதுபிணம் எடும் என), with a drum, on the walk to the burning ground. The song adds the question இனிதோ தான், turning the lover's 'sweet' back on that scene.

Thiruppugazh 1 worships the elephant-faced god who holds fruit, appam, aval and puffed rice (கைத்தல நிறைகனி அப்பமொடு அவல்பொரி) and whose devotees' deeds flee. Thiruppugazh 1002 lays out the same offerings, aval, puffed rice, fruits, before the great-bellied elephant, then confesses it has not bowed to the one who comes after him (பிறகு வரும் ஒரு முருக) and that its cruel deeds have not ended. The first song's Ganapati worship becomes here the half-finished rite whose failure is confessed.

Naladiyar 377 says those fooled into taking a worthless woman's love as their own will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Thiruppugazh 1003 reports that outcome from inside: after seeking the courtesans, his kin and all people call him fool, witless and low-born (அசடன் அறிவிலி இழிகுலன் இவன் என இனமும் மனிதருள் அனைவரும் உரைசெய). The song gives the Naladiyar's public ridicule as the poet's own shame.

Kural 915 says those whose knowledge is refined by good intellect will not plunge into the base charms of women whose favours are common (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). Thiruppugazh 1003 confesses the converse: seeking the courtesans, he never learned or tried to follow the words of the great virtuous ones (பெரிய குணதரர் உரைசெய்த மொழிவகை ... பயிலவு முயலவு மறியாத). Both tie the plunge to want of the knowledge that teaching gives.

Kural 322 sets sharing one's food and sustaining many lives (பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல்) at the head of all the virtues the authors gathered. Thiruppugazh 1006 opens its long list of lacks with that one: not a millet-grain's thought of sharing (பகிர நினைவொரு தினையளவிலுமிலி), then without compassion. The self-accusation follows the Kural's order of virtues.
audit_text_issue: 1006 has broken lines (உ கிரினுதி, உ ரக) from spacing in the edition.

note: 1007 vows that whether he sinks, rises or tosses in the ocean of passion (அநுராக உததியதனிடை விழுகினும் எழுகினும் உழலுகினும்) he will not forget the feet as his life's help; 1010 asks whether a day will come when he forgets that ruinous karma of union (பாழ்படும் அருவினை அற மறந்து) and then lives thinking of the feet. On the reading that 1010 makes forgetting the passion the condition for remembering the feet, the two disagree on whether remembrance can live inside the passion or only after it.

1008 likens women with spear eyes to நடுவன், Yama, who strikes young men without pause (இடைவிடாது எறு நடுவனும் என); Kural 1083's man says he never knew Death (கூற்று) before and now knows it in a woman's grace and warring eyes. Both name the beloved's look as Death itself; the Kural says it in wonder, the song in fear of capsizing in the sea of fate.

1011 lists what the rival sects say the ultimate is (உரைதரு பரசமயங்கள் ஓதுவது: form, formless, light, space, pillar of the worlds) and asks to see the thing itself and rest in silence (அது பொருள் கண்டு மோனமொடு உணர்வுற); Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six sects did not see him, he is not what they hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்), so become clear and settle. Both put the reality past the sects' definitions and reach it by a settled, silent clarity; the song's syntax is uncertain on how far it rejects the definitions.

Kural 1084 says the girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்); 1012 makes the same eyes the poison that rose when the gods churned the sea (இமையவர் பற்றிக் கடைந்த அன்றெழு நஞ்சுபோலே), stronger than Kama's five arrows. The song enlarges the Kural's life-eating look into the world-threatening halahala.

1013 shows women, once Kama stands before them, burned by the white crescent like the undersea fire (கொளுந்து வெண்பிறை வடவை எறிக்க), the bees' song and the Malaya breeze wounding the body; Naladiyar 392 hears the rain-clouds' thunder as a funeral drum for women without their companion. In both, the ordinary beauties of nature turn into instruments of pain for the lovesick woman.

Naladiyar 29 says the body lasts like water on a grass tip, so do virtuous deeds now before people say he was gone with his kin wailing (கேள் அலற); 1014 pictures the kin wailing, the palm-wood pyre and Death tying the life, and asks before then (உடன்றுபோமுன்) to learn in the discipline of those who think of Murugan as the giver of the goal. Both use the wailing at death to say 'act before'; the Naladiyar asks for அறவினை, the song for learning in the devotees' company.

1015 asks whether, when Yama's host drags him to hell, the fragrant holy feet, the eternal tattva within release (திருவடி முத்திக்குட்படு நித்யத் தத்துவம்), will not come; Tirumanthiram 1598 says knowledge of the holy feet frees from the prison of impurity and is itself release (திருவடி ஞானமே திண்சித்தி முத்தியே). Both identify the feet with release rather than treat them as a way to it.

1016 says that siddhas, gods, codes of dharma, Puranas and Vedas cannot know the Lord, whose form is the knowledge beyond both knowing and not knowing (அறிவும் அறியாமையும் கடந்த அறிவு திருமேனி); Tirumanthiram 2362 says when one passes beyond knowledge and ignorance and becomes knowledge (அறிவு அறியாமை கடந்து அறிவானால்), that is the true way. The same phrase names the goal in both; the song makes it the Lord's very body.

Kural 1131's lover says that for one who suffers in love there is no safeguard but the palmyra horse (மடல்); 1017's praise has Murugan himself, bowing at the hunter girl's feet and wandering unseen in the millet field, resolve to mount the new madal (புதியமடல் ஏறவும் துணிந்த). The song gives the Kural's desperate lover's last resort to the god.

1018 describes women who show eyes, hair and arms, ask for coins through a broker and stand in the street like peacocks (தெருவினில் மயில்போலே நிற்பார்); Naladiyar 354 says the other kind, unlike household women, show off their charms themselves like a fresh flood (புதுப்பெருக்கம் போலத் தம் பெண்ணீர்மை காட்டி). Both mark the courtesan by self-display; the song adds the broker and the price.

Naladiyar 55 tells the heart that youth has passed to no purpose and disease and old age are coming now (கொன்னே கழிந்தன்று இளமையும்), so set out on the good path; 1019 traces the same life in stages, youth robbed by sly-eyed women, middle age bound by kin's rope, then coughing and losing breath to the pyre, and asks for the day he escapes this forest of a body (மெய்க்காட்டைத் தவிர்வதும் ஒருநாளே). The song spells out the wasted span the Naladiyar sums up in a line.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1019 has a corrupt glyph (று஡ர்த்த).

note: 1020 describes women who praise a man lavishly for money (பொருட்கு மிகத் துதித்து இளகி) before their elaborate lovemaking; Kural 911 warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring harm. Both locate the danger in the flattery bought by money.

Tirumanthiram 81 says the Lord made the poet well so that he would render him well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே), against the waste of being born again; 1021 asks to be set where he reaches the lotus feet with the taste of Tamil and ends death (தமிழ்ச்சுவையிட்டு இறப்பற எய்த்திட). Both make Tamil song the means by which the poet's birth is redeemed.

Tirumular asks what men gain by arguing when time slips away, since arguers cannot bow at the Stainless one's feet; 1028 sends those who learn books to quarrel to Death's town with those who do not melt for the Lord.
The Naladiyar's hoarder who neither enjoys nor gives dies mocked by his own wealth; 1028 adds that such men, who seek money and live without giving, go to Death's town.

Two songs of the same refrain-set turn on disease: 1025 asks for the feet at the hour when humoral disease brings death, 1027 lists diseases at length and asks to be kept from them and set in release.

1023 describes women who price their breasts and sell love's pleasure on camphor beds to the measure of the coins (முலையை விலை கூறிக் காசுக்கு அளவே); Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends with the oil (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both say the love is exactly as long as the money.

Kural 1085 asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ); 1023 has kohl eyes that surpass Yama in killing (யமனை அட மீறிச் சீறும் மைக்கண் விழிவலை). The song takes the Kural's riddle as settled and puts it to work in the courtesan's net.

1026 names Murugan the great life of devotees who think of him with song, music and dance (பாடலிசை மிக்க ஆடல்கொடு பத்தியோடு நினை பத்தர்); Tirumanthiram 1816 says that dancing, singing, weeping and crying out he found Siva's great nature (ஆடியும் பாடியும் அழுதும் அரற்றியும்). Both make the body's song and dance the way devotion reaches God.

1029 asks whether the girl should waste away under Kama's arrows, the roaring sea, the cuckoo and her own mother's harsh enmity (மாதாவின் வார்மைப் பகை); Kural 1147's woman says her sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water (அன்னைசொல் நீராக). In both the mother's scolding feeds the love-sickness it means to check.

1030 confesses that while great craving remains he cannot speak truth (பேரவா அறா வாய்மை பேசற்கு அறியாமே); Kural 364 says purity is the absence of craving and it comes by wanting truth (அவாவின்மை ... வாஅய்மை வேண்ட வரும்). Both bind craving and truthfulness together, the Kural as a rule, the song as self-accusation.

1030 regrets learning books whose noise never ends (ஆரவாரம் மாறாத நூல் கற்று); Naladiyar 256 says the learned hold back while others talk, as dry palm leaves rattle and the green leaf is silent. Both treat noisy learning as the mark of learning gone dry.

Kural 1110's lover says closeness to the woman is like knowledge, each union showing how little was known before (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்றால்), a delight that keeps renewing; 1031 confesses he is never sated (தணியாமல்) by lips that taste ever new (புதிதாய) like fresh cane juice and asks instead for the meaning no one can find. The same endless freshness of desire is joy in the Kural and the obstacle to the true meaning in the song.

1033 asks to hold the feet that are his town, his mother and his kin (ஊர்பெற்ற தாய் சுற்றமாய் உற்ற தாள்); Tirumanthiram 2644 says the Lord rare even for the gods is on this path like father, mother and kin (தந்தை தாய் கேளி யான் ஒக்கும்). Both give God the place of the family one leaves behind.

Kural 340 asks whether the life, a lodger in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்), has no home of its own; 1034 calls the body a hut of skin, bone and flesh (குடிலூடே) where life dwells until the trident-bearer comes to seize it. Both picture the body as a temporary shelter the life must leave; the song asks for devotion before the eviction.
audit_text_issue: 1034 has garbled glyphs ('குடிலு஡டே').

note: 1035 asks to worship the feet of those who praise Murugan's name (உன் நாமம் புகழ்பவர் பாதம் தொழ); Tirumanthiram 1829 says washing and sprinkling the feet of those high in true knowledge is release (பதத்தைச் சுத்தமதாக விளக்கித் தெளிக்கவே முத்தியாம்). The Tirumanthiram gives the worship of devotees' feet the status of release that the song asks for as grace.

1036 asks for the good yoga by which the little life that runs out in its count of breaths, six hundred, a thousand and twenty thousand, may be turned back (ஓடுஞ் சிறுவுயிர் மீளும்படி நல யோகம்); 355 asks not to become a foolish yogi who holds the breath so it does not leave the nostrils (நாசி அடைதல் அந வாயு ஓடாத வகை சாதித்து). On the reading that 355 rejects breath-retention as such, the two disagree; 355 may reject it only when done to keep the impermanent flesh.
audit_text_issue: 1036 breath count uncertain.

note: 1036 counts the breaths by which the life runs out (அறுநூறும் பதினுறழ் நூறும் பதினிருபது நூறும், the 21,600 of a day) and asks for the yoga that turns it back; Tirumanthiram 2149 says fools do not know that by turning back the ajapa breath (அசபையை மாற்றி) the body that has taken form will not perish. Both make the reversal of the breath the remedy for the life running out.

Both follow the funeral to its end: the kin burn the body and then bathe in the water (நீரினில் மூழ்கி; போதா நீருடே போய் மூழ்கா). The Tirumanthiram adds that they stop thinking of the dead; 1041 says they act as strangers.
audit_text_issue: A line of 1041's praise is corrupt (தீயு ஧ட்முள்).

note: The Tirumanthiram teaches that if the breath stays still with the mind there is no birth or death; 1044 rejects the yogi who thinks turning back the breath gives liberation but lacks grace, and asks instead for the feet. The point of difference depends on reading 1044 as faulting yoga without grace, not breath control as such.
audit_text_issue: 1044 praise: வா஡ணச corrupt.

note: The song asks that the poet not enter the womb's path again (வாழுங் கருவழி மருவாதே) and asks for Murugan's paired anklets (உன் கழலிணை பெறுவேனோ). Tirumanthiram 1597 reports the result: the guru set his feet on the poet's head (திருவடி வைத்தென் சிரத்து) so that the womb's path drained away (கருவழி வாற்றிட). The same word கருவழி ties the plea to the Tirumanthiram's account of the feet ending it.

The song names the liberation it has not reached as 'I become you and you become I' (நானே நீயாய் நீயே நானாய்), which the Vedas' meanings cannot search out. Tirumanthiram 1788 states the same goal as experience: on nearing him there is no separate 'I' or 'you' (நானென நீயென வேறில்லை), as flesh and the life in it stand together. Both make the end of the I-you division the mark of release.

The song uses the words நானே நீயாய் நீயே நானாய் for non-dual liberation. In song 626 the same formula is the courtesans' shameless oath, நீயே நானே என்றொரு சத்தியம், sworn to any man for money. The poet uses one phrase for the highest union and for the falsest, which shows how he sets bought love against union with the Lord.

The song repeats the stock comparisons poets give patrons (வேளே போல்வாய், மாலே போல்வாய், காரே போல்வாய்) and regrets carrying them in vain (வீணே) to men who neither fit the praise nor give. Naladiyar 219 judges abuse better than praise of qualities a man does not have (இல்ல புகழ்தலின் வைதலே நன்று). The Naladiyar gives the moral rule; the song confesses breaking it.

This song regrets praise wasted on patrons in the stock comparisons of patronage poetry (வேளே போல்வாய் ... காரே போல்வாய்). Song 1062 makes the same confession about love poetry, the 'is it sword, vel, carp or deer?' questions (வாளோ வேலோ சேலோ மானோ) sung to courtesans, ending கவி பாடா நாயேன். Together they show the poet treating his own craft, spent on patrons or on women, as the thing to repent.

Naladiyar 26 says that once the dancer has left the skin bag (தோற்பை), it does not matter what is done with the body. The song takes the body's end, the hut of sinew, skin and water (நாரால் தோல் நீரால்) becoming a place for dogs and ghouls, as a deadline and asks for the strength to sing the feet before then (நாய்பேய் சூழ்கைக்கு இடமாமுன் ... தாள் பாடு ஆண்மைத் திறல் தாராய்). The Naladiyar's indifference to the corpse becomes in the song a reason to act while the body still serves.
audit_text_issue: 1040's praise lines பர்ழு டேவா னூடே பர்ரு டேயூர் are garbled.

note: This song asks Murugan to rule him by speaking as teacher, scripting the words he wants to hear (வாராய் பேதாய் கேளாய்) that point to the unchanging flame of wisdom. Song 1058 speaks after such a word: it marvels at the word of grace that killed the five senses and turned death away (கருணை வார்த்தை இருந்தவாறு என்). The pair moves from asking for the guru's word to wondering at its effect.
audit_text_issue: 1042's word divisions in this clipped metre are doubtful.

note: Tirumanthiram 1823 maps the temple onto the person: the heart is the great temple, the body the shrine, the soul the linga (உள்ளம் பெருங்கோயில் ... சீவன் சிவலிங்கம்). The song takes the inward temple one step further: the temple is silence that no one can measure (அரிய மோனமே கோயில்), the flowers are the joy of knowledge, and the worship goes to a Siva-form beyond Vedas, words and action. Both move worship inside; the song places it beyond even the heart, in silence.

The song calls its inward worship in the temple of silence the great worship (மாபூசை புரிவேனே). Tirumanthiram 1852 gives the same name to worship in the place where sun and moon do not shine (இலங்காத் தலத்திடை வந்தித்தல் நந்திக்கு மாபூசை) and sends outer worship to the asuras. Both keep the word மாபூசை for worship beyond outward rite.

The song rejects the yogi who thinks the breath, if turned back (வாயு அடைய மீளில் வீடாகும் என நாடி), gives release but who has no grace (அருள் பெறா), and asks to melt into the feet. Tirumanthiram 1854 also turns breath and mind back at the root, then sets the body aside and enters the Pure One's grace (புனிதன் அருள்தனில் புக்கிருந்து) before its worship is complete. Both make grace, not breath alone, the step that finishes the practice.

The song lists the yogic steps: the breath held, the fire kindled at the root (மூல ... அனல் மூள), nectar drunk, and the climb that strikes Yama (எமனை மோதி). Tirumanthiram 345 tells of Siva at Kadavur turning the fire at the root opening upward (மூலத் துவாரத்து மூளும் ஒருவனை) and burning Death (காலனைக் காய்ந்து) in the yoga of fire. The song applies to the practitioner the Death-defeating yoga the Tirumanthiram finds in the Kadavur story.
audit_text_issue: 1045 has a corrupt line (அமுத பான ஧ம்முல).

note: In Kural 1133 the lover says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palmyra horse lovers ride (காமுற்றார் ஏறும் மடல்). The song says women's eyes make even sleepless gods and Vedic ascetics free of infatuation resolve to mount it (துறவரான பேர் யாரும் மடலேறத் துணியுமாறு). The Kural's private loss of shame becomes in the song a power that undoes renunciation, and the poet asks for a way out.

The song asks what Murugan's form is: the form with parts (சகளமோ), the bud of the six supports, the support-less, or the formless (நிராகார வடிவேயோ). Tirumanthiram 1763 answers that the supreme Siva takes form, formlessness and form-with-formlessness together (உருவும் அருவும் உருவோடு அருவும்) and stands as guru to souls. The Tirumanthiram's 'all three' answers the song's 'which one?'.

The song asks for grace to sing the feet with love before Death, sent by Yama with noose and trident (ஏமனால் ஏவி விடு காலன் கொடிய பாசம்), arrives. Tirumanthiram 176 says there is no fighting the life's departure, but if one thinks of the Lord (அண்ணலை எண்ணும்) Death's messengers will not even think of harming one. The Tirumanthiram supplies the promise behind the song's plea.

Tirumanthiram 2217 describes the teacher passing from turiya to turiya-atita (சென்று துரியாதீதத்தே) and there becoming the stainless Supreme, so the states beyond turiya lead to the goal. The song says the abode of supreme wisdom is not reached above turiya (துரிய மீது சாராது) and is followed by no one. The conflict holds if சாராது means that no state beyond turiya reaches it; if it means only that turiya itself falls short, the two agree.

The song calls Murugan one who cannot be touched or seen directly (தொட அடாது ... வடிவு காண வாராது), other than all and yet knowledge itself (வேறாகி அறிவாகி). Tirumanthiram 3035 says he is awareness and life and the senses (உணர்வும் அவனே) yet cannot be reached by thought (எண்ணலும் ஆகான்). Both hold together the Lord's being the knowing in us and his being beyond its reach.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1050 has a stray ** after எதிர்கூற and garbled lines in the praise (கடுவி டாக ளர்ருப நடவி நோத தாடாளர்).

note: This song says the Lord entered the body and taught 'you and I' (நீ நானும் என நேர்மை நூல் கூறி). Song 1038 names liberation 'I become you and you become I' (நானே நீயாய் நீயே நானாய்). The split of 1050 is uncertain, but read together the formula is the teaching given in 1050 and the state sought in 1038.
audit_text_issue: 1050 has a stray ** in the source line; 1038 has ஡ for ஊ.

note: In 1042 the poet asks to hear the guru say 'do not play in the filth of desire and infatuation for women' (மானார் மோகத்துடன் ஆசை மாசூடு ஆடாது) and to turn within. In 1051, after describing lovemaking, he vows that even as infatuation grows he will not forget the feet (மால் கூரினும் உன் நீப சீர்பாதம் மறவேனே). On the reading that 1051 accepts infatuation alongside remembrance, the two songs disagree on whether devotion requires leaving desire.
audit_text_issue: 1051 has encoding damage (஡ for ஊ in மாரனேறு஡தை, இலவிலு஡று; பி஧ல்முழ்க).

note: Both close with the same question, பரம ஞான வீடு ஏது புகல்வாயே. 1049 defines that abode by what cannot touch it; 1054 sets it against the rotting body and against rituals performed for show.

Both see the body as a bubble that forms and bursts (the Naladiyar's மொக்குள், 1054's குமிழி); the Naladiyar praises those who see it so and resolve to end birth, and 1054 confesses cherishing it anyway.
Both say nothing goes with a person at death; the Naladiyar names deeds as the one thing that does, while 1066 lists wealth, servants and wife that do not and turns to praising the feet.

The song builds a cosmic dance verb by verb: Adisesha, Meru, Kali, Siva, ghosts, Sarasvati, Brahma, the gods and the moon all dance (ஆட), and then Murugan with his peacock (மயிலும் ஆடி நீ ஆடி வரவேணும்). Tirumanthiram 2789 builds the same chain, tattvas, Sadasiva, mind, Shakti and the world dancing (ஆட) until the Father dances the dance of bliss. Both use the repeated ஆட to make the god's dance the last step of a world already dancing.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1053: கேர்டுதி is corrupt.

note: The song makes the end of the quarrels of all creeds' debaters (சகல சமய தார்க்கிகர் கலகம் ஒழிய) the first step toward worship of the feet and a knowledge beyond turiya. Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six sects did not see him and he is not what they hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்), then calls for clarity. Both set the arguments of the creeds aside before the Lord can be reached.

The song pictures daughter, wife and mother's kin wailing inside and outside the house (புறமும் ஆர்த்திட) as Yama's men close in, and asks for grace to praise the anklets before then. Tirumanthiram 157 follows the same wailing kin, wives and children (ஆர்த்தெழு சுற்றமும் பெண்டிரும் மக்களும்) only to the edge of the town, where they turn back and burn him. Both show the kin's outcry as unable to go further, which is why the song turns to the feet.

Naladiyar 35 says those who took the body's fruit early, as one takes jaggery from the cane, feel no distress when Death comes (கூற்றம் வருங்கால் பரிவதிலர்). The song asks for the flawless truth so that the mind may ripen and praise the feet (மதியும் மூத்து உனது அடிகள் ஏத்திட) before Death's men come to fight for the hut of bones and disease. Both make the use of the body before Death the answer to Death.

The song marvels at the word of grace that killed the five senses and the instruments and turned death away (புலன் ஐந்தும் மாயக் கரணம் மாய்த்து எனை மரணம் மாற்றிய கருணை வார்த்தை). Tirumanthiram 134 says those who feel beyond words what the teacher speaks (ஆரியன் செப்பும் உரையற்று உணர்வோர்) mix with the shoreless light when the body falls. Both make the guru's spoken word the means of passing beyond the senses and death.

The song lists the poet's failures: he does not fall at the feet, nor even at the feet of those who fall at them (வீழ்வார் கால் மீதினும் வீழேன்), and does not give even bran to those who ask. Tirumanthiram 1857 joins those two failures: what is given to the walking temple, the devotee (நடமாடக் கோயில்), reaches the god in the temple of images. The Tirumanthiram shows why neglect of devotees and of giving is neglect of the Lord.

Naladiyar 91 says those who give gladly what they can even when they have little (இல்லா விடத்தும் இயைந்த அளவினால்) will not find the door of that world shut. The song confesses not giving even a handful of bran (தவிடின் ஆர்ப் பதம் எனினும்) to those who ask, and calls this dying without having lived. The measure is the same in both: giving is judged by what one could give, however little.

The song lists the Lord as sun, moon, earth, sky, water, fire, wind, the stars and the days, the Vedas and the light beyond them, and above them Sivam (மேலே சிவமான தொலைவிலாப் பொருள்). Tirumanthiram 2671 says the yogic god is earth, water, fire, air and sky (மண்ணு நீரனல் காலொடு வானுமாய்) and that his form is beyond even the sky. Both name the Lord as the elements and then place him beyond them.
audit_text_issue: The line naming Krishna is corrupt (஧த்ருர் கோமான்).

note: The song asks Murugan to come on the day of the funeral journey into Death's town and say to Death 'go' and to the poet 'return'. Tirumanthiram 2050 says the true guru set his feet on his devotees' heads and kept away the band of Yama's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்). The Tirumanthiram states as done what the song asks for.
audit_text_issue: 1061 பா஡ண corrupt; plea line uncertain

note: The song opens the funeral with drums sounding (படு பறைகள் ஆர்த்தெழ) and the household crying. Naladiyar 24 counts the drum beats, once, again, and at the third the corpse is covered and the fire lifted (முக்காலைக் கொட்டினுள்), the dying carrying the dead. The Naladiyar takes the drums as proof that no one escapes; the song uses the same scene to ask Murugan to turn Death back.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1061 has a corrupt word பா஡ண.

note: The song confesses the love poetry the poet made for courtesans: are their eyes sword or vel, their hair cloud or forest, their mouths milk or nectar (பாலோ தேனோ பாகோ வானோர் அமுதேயோ). Naladiyar 41 mocks the 'worthies' who cry 'O fair, lovely girl' (மாக்கேழ் மடநல்லாய் என்றரற்றும் சான்றவர்) without seeing that the body is a flimsy dwelling. The Naladiyar names the blindness the song confesses in its own praise-verses.

The song calls the poet's life a mound the water never climbs (நீர் ஏறாதோர் மேடாய்) where weeds spring up from what falls in deeds (வினையூடே விழுவினால் களை எழும்). Tirumanthiram 1695 also pictures deeds as weeds (விழலார் விறலாம் வினை) and says they go when the Lord takes his seat in a purified mind. The song gives the barren field; the Tirumanthiram gives the clearing it asks for.

The song says lust, through women's eyes, drew the poet with delight into the rotting hut that runs with blood (குருதி ஒழுகி அழுகும் அவல குடிலை இனிது புகலாலே). Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen vultures tear at the stinking cart (முடைச்சாகாடு) once its axle breaks. Both set desire's delight against the body that rots.

The song quotes people who promise the nectar drink, the wish-cow and the magic pill (அமிர்த சுரபானம் சுரபி குளிகை) and in return ask for curd, rice and gold, and asks for a day free of that trickery (விரகு). Tirumanthiram 2045 calls false gurus those who have looked over mantra, yoga and release but turn blind for the sake of food (ஊண்பொருட்டு அந்தகர் ஆவோர்). The song gives the practice in the street that the Tirumanthiram names in principle.
Tirumular says Nandi set his holy feet on his head and so drained the path to the womb; 1078 asks Murugan to set his feet on the poet's head in friendship, the same act of the guru's grace.
Both songs give the kin's words at death, 'take it quickly' (கடுகென எடும், எடும் எடு), and the body laid in the fire at the burning ground.

The song pictures sons, father and wife crowding round and wailing (மண்டி அலறி) as Death's noose falls, and asks for Murugan's red-gold feet as a pillar to hold (தம்பம் உனது செம்பொன் அடிகள்). Tirumanthiram 144 says that when the house of the body falls the women and children who ate from it do not follow (பின்செலார்), and only the vow and knowledge go with the dead. The hymn names the support the Tirumanthiram says kin cannot give.

The song traces the body from the womb to a wheezing, pitiable old age (பழசாய் இரைப்பொடு ... விருத்த பரிதாபம்) and asks that before he dies (மடியாமுன்) he be given a life of saying 'Muruga'. Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood, while those who delighted in youth rise later leaning on a staff. Both turn the certainty of old age into a reason to act before it; the hymn's act is a name, the Naladiyar's renunciation.

The poet babbles the books of learning (கலைநூல் பிதற்றி) while his black hair turns white without understanding, and asks to be taught true knowledge. Naladiyar 52 says the best reflect on old age and death and do their real work, and none are more foolish than those who prattle (பிதற்றும்) on grammar and astrology. Both use the same verb for learning recited without the knowledge that matters, set against greying.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1069 has a corrupt glyph in வழ஧முடி.

note: The knowledge the poet asks for is the one praised by the pure brahmins who plunge into the fire rite at the set times and do not die (இறவாத சுத்த மறையோர்). Tirumanthiram 215 says the brahmins who make the oblation (ஆகுதி வேட்கும் அருமறை அந்தணர்) reach the true path by their own understanding (தாம் அறிவாலே). Both treat the fire rite as joined to knowledge, which is what the hymn says its book-learning lacked.

The poet confesses he has no love that swells and melts the heart (பெருக்க நெஞ்சு உவந்து உருக்கும் அன்பு இலன), only angry, insolent speech. Tirumanthiram 272 says that even burning one's bones for firewood will not reach the gem except for those who melt with love and soften within (அன்போடு உருகி அகம் குழைவார்க்கு அன்றி). The hymn's self-accusation names exactly the condition the Tirumanthiram makes the only way.

The song lists house, prattling children, kin, wives, youth and lands, asks not to delight in them as lasting, and asks to worship Murugan with a shining lamp (விளங்கு தீபம் கொண்டு உனை வழிபட). Tirumanthiram 212 says the kin who cling and follow are worse than one's deeds, and that before life goes one should light the lamp of awareness (உணர்விளக்கு ஏற்றி). Both answer the pull of kin with a lamp; the hymn's is a lamp of worship, the Tirumanthiram's one of awareness.

The poet trusted that the wife he joined and his sons would not falter (கலங்கிடார் என்று), took pleasure in the world, and fell into misery. Naladiyar 25 mocks the man who sees kin wailing as a corpse is carried off and still marries, saying there is joy here (உண்டு உண்டு), and the funeral drum answers him. The hymn is the confession of the man the Naladiyar mocks.

The poet relied on wife and sons never failing him. Tirumanthiram 150 says the wife who married with sweet talk, her love sated (நேசம் தெவிட்டி), stops thinking of him, weeps as is fitting on the bier and burns the bond in fire. It gives the limit of the trust the hymn regrets.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 150: வாசந்தி in line 1 is obscure.

note: The song calls Murugan the guru whom Siva approached (குருநாதா) and asks that Death's messengers with their noose and rope not torment him (பாசம் கயிறொடு தூதுவர் நலியாதே). Tirumanthiram 2050 says the guru kept away the band of Yama's messengers (நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்) and ended the sorrow of birth. Both give the guru, not the god as such, the power to turn back Death's messengers.

The singer asks whether Kama's arrows may strike the young girl who lies with pallor (பசலையொடு அணையும்). Kural 1183 has the woman say he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in return (நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து). The hymn sets the classical pallor of love inside a frame of praise, with Murugan as the absent lover.

The poet describes women adorned with civet, agil, sandal, pearls and gems, with blue-lily eyes and nectar speech, in whose beds he melts helplessly (அவர் வசம் உருகி அழியும்). Naladiyar 47 says the fool praises 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' to a pot seeping filth from nine openings because its covering of skin dazzles his eyes (கருந்தோலால் கண் விளக்கப்பட்டு). The Naladiyar names what the adornment the hymn lingers on covers.

Here the women and the union with them drive out the knowledge of hereditary service (வழிவழி அடிமை எனும் அறிவு அகல). In song 728 the poet, having said 'I am yours by descent' (உன் வழிவழியான் எனா), asks whether his life must still swing like a balance beam among deceiving women. Both set the claim of hereditary servitude against the pull of women, and 728 supports reading 1077 as a complaint that the knowledge has been driven out.

The song shows kin saying 'take it quickly', dropping their attachment to the body (உடற்பற்று அற்று), going to the burning ground and laying it in the fire by rule. Tirumanthiram 145 has the town wail, take away his name and call him a corpse, burn him in the burning ground, bathe and stop thinking of him (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both stress how fast the kin's attachment ends, which is why the poet turns to Murugan to burn his troubles instead.

The poet speaks of eating women's spittle and throwing away the capital in his hand (கையில் முதலைக் களைந்து). Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure the courtesan's favour by what is in the hand; the hymn speaks from after the hand is empty.
Both list the body's gut, fat, blood and flesh (குடர், கொழு, குருதி, தடி) to undo desire; the Naladiyar asks which part is the garlanded woman, 1093 shows women perfuming and adorning that same body.
Tirumular says the six sects do not see the God within the body; 1094 calls the crore of rival faiths blind to the one Thing.

The Kural says not asking even from glad givers is ten million times better; 1092 shows the poet who begged from patrons who gave nothing, and seeks the end of that poverty not in better patrons but in the one Thing.
In 1078 the poet says he has escaped the crumbling other faiths; 1094 says why: they are blind to the one Thing.

Sunk in the sea of lust that grows from dark delusion (கருமயல்), the poet sought fish-eyed women as if they were the real thing, or wealth (பொருள் என நாடி), until the last day. Kural 351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes what is not the thing for the thing (பொருள் அல்லவற்றைப் பொருள் என்று). The hymn is a case of the error the Kural names, with Death's noose as its end.

The song sees blood and semen join in the bag of skin and gut (குருதியிலே சுக்கிலம் அது கூடி), with earth, sky, wind and fire, so that the body rises in an illusory birth (மாயப் பிறவி), and asks not to wander in it. Tirumanthiram 460 says that in the womb maya joins her brood to the soul (கர்ப்பத்துக் கேவல மாயாள் கிளைகூட்ட) and karma takes hold. The Tirumanthiram gives the doctrine behind the hymn's word மாய for the birth it describes.

The poet melts over doe-eyed women whose eyes are like strife-making swords with poison set in them (விடம் எலாம் வைத்த கலகவாள் ஒத்த விழி). Kural 1084 says the eyes of the artless girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்). Both make the eye a killer; the Kural's lover admires it, while the poet asks to be saved from it by the wisdom of the feet.

After listing the women's lily-like kohl eyes (குவளையேர் மைக்கண்), ear-rings, gait, hair, breasts and speech, the poet asks, 'should I give my mind to these?' (சித்தம் விடலாமோ). Naladiyar 44 asks, 'shall I give way' (கவற்ற விடுவேனோ) when men call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears, and answers that an eye is like a scooped-out palm fruit. Both refuse the catalogue with the same kind of rhetorical question; the hymn answers it with a catalogue of the god's names.

Instead of the women's anklets crying for refuge, the poet asks to be granted to chant 'nama, refuge' (நமசரண் என்று ஓத) to Murugan. Tirumanthiram 1850 tells the reader to long for the Lord morning, noon and evening and to sow his name with 'nama' (நம என்று நாமத்தை விச்சுமின்). Both make the name joined to 'nama' the act of surrender.
audit_text_issue: 1086 compounds hard to divide.

note: In a mother's voice the singer lists what wastes her daughter: Kama's flower arrows, the bees' humming, the sea's waves and roar, and the moon that burns like the sun (கலைமதி அங்காயும் வெயில்). Kural 1228 says the herdsman's flute becomes a messenger of the burning evening (அழல்போலும் மாலை) and a weapon that kills. Both turn gentle sights and sounds into weapons against the separated lover, the stock torments of akam carried into the hymn.

The song sees the body as blood, water, skin, gut and bone (குருதி சலம் தோலும் குடலுடன் என்பாலும்) holding a life of delusion and lust until Death takes it. Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin (குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும்) and asks which part is the garlanded woman. The same inventory serves the Naladiyar against desire and the hymn as a prelude to death.

Everyone at home says 'take it' of the body, weeps at the burning ground and lights the fire at its head (எரிய எரிமூட்டி). Tirumanthiram 157 has the wailing kin turn back at the town's edge, pile the wood and light the fire (விறகிட்டு எரிமூட்டி), then plunge into the water. Both stage the same cremation step by step; the hymn asks to see the anklet feet before it comes.

Before his kin are struck with grief (உறவின் முறையோர்க்கும் உறுதுயரம் வாய்த்து) and the body is burned, the poet asks for a mind that praises Murugan's feet with longing (வேட்கை). Tirumanthiram 152 ends the body's collapse with the loving ones weeping and going away (அன்புடையார்கள் அழுது அகன்றார்களே). The kin's love ends at the pyre; the hymn asks for a love that is turned to the feet before it.

The poet describes union with women in detail, then calls it the cruelty and deceit of women who give union (கலவி தரு மகளிர் கொடுமை எனும் உறு கபடம்) and asks not to lose his mind in it. Kural 913 says the false embrace of women who sell themselves (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both judge the embrace itself as a lie.

After confessing years of piling titles on patrons in song, the poet asks for the one Thing where speech and mind cease (மொழி ஒழிய மனம் ஒழிய ஒரு பொருள்). Tirumanthiram 1896 says silence is when speech and mind are both still (வாக்கு மனமும் இரண்டும் மவுனமாம்), and silent speech alone is only muteness. The pairing shows the hymn's remedy for wasted praise is not mere silence but the stilling of both.

The women's eyes are made as if Death and Kama had joined to worship slaughter (வதை பழக மறலி விறல் மதனன் வழிபடுதும் என), to take young men's lives. Kural 1085 asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both put Death in the woman's eye; the Kural's lover marvels, the poet calls himself the blind man it has caught.

The praise tells of the elephant who is offered puffed rice, aval, lentils and the three fruits and who writes the whole story of the Kurus with his tusk on the northern peak as the sage speaks (முனி பகர வட சிகரி மிசை ... எழுதும் ஒரு களிறு). The first song of the book praises Ganesha with fruit, appam, aval and puffed rice in hand, who first wrote on the first mountain (முற்படு கிரிதனில் முற்பட எழுதிய). The two share the scribe on the mountain and the offerings, though song 1 makes what he wrote the three Tamils.

The poet describes lovemaking at length and vows that even when lost in passion he will not forget Murugan's feet (அவசமுறுகினும் அடிகள் மறவேனே). Kural 1125 has the lover say he would recall her qualities if he forgot, but he does not know forgetting (மறப்பின் மறப்பறியேன்). The lover's inability to forget is moved from the beloved to the god's feet, and kept even inside another love.

Both follow the dead man to the pyre and the mourners' plunge into the water (நீர்த்தலை மூழ்குவர்; அலைநீரிற் புக்கு முழுகா). Tirumular calls the mourners people without justice, who forget once they have bathed; 1110 lets the bath end their grief and asks for a life of praise before that day.

The Thiruppugazh pictures the body as a tree whose roots are the two deeds (இருவினைகள் வேர்பிடித்து) in the soil of seven births, ripening the fruit of death, and asks for teaching before it falls. The Tirumanthiram names the same two, merit and sin (புண்ணிய பாவம் இரண்டு), and tells the knower to cut both at the root (வேர்அறத்) and seek the Lord beyond them. The song draws out the whole tree that grows from those roots; the Tirumanthiram verse says where the axe goes.

The Thiruppugazh shows women who price their breasts (முலையைவிலை கூறிவிற்று), lead a man into a fine house and onto a flowered bed (வடிவதிக வீடுபுக்கு மலரணையின் மீதிருத்தி), melt his heart and seize what wealth there is. The Kural says the false embrace of women who sell themselves (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both say the paid embrace is empty; the song gives the setting the women stage, and the Kural replaces the bright room and flowered bed with a dark room and a corpse.

In the Thiruppugazh the women tell their lover that while body and life are one there is no yours and mine (உடலுயிரதாயிருக்க உனதெனதெனாமறிக்கை), and the poet calls this a deceit (தோதகம்) and asks for teaching to end it. The Kural's lover says sincerely that his bond with the girl is that of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்னமற் றன்ன). The same figure of body and life is a vow of love in the Kural and a seller's line in the song.

The Thiruppugazh's women swear they cannot bear to be apart for a moment (ஒருபொழுதொணாது), and the poet names their union a deceit. The Naladiyar recalls the woman who said, like the anril birds, 'we will never part from you' (நித்தலும் நம்மைப் பிரியலம்) and then turned away like a ram's horn. Both treat the paid woman's vow of never parting as the snare itself.

The Thiruppugazh speaks of women who seek only money (தனந்தனை நாடி), offer refuge with sweet words knowing their own deceit, and measure out their love falsely (நின்றளந்தும் சளங்கொண்டிடும்). The Kural describes women who weigh the gain and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்) and tells a man to weigh them in turn and keep away. The song's measuring and the Kural's weighing name the same calculation behind the sweet words.

The Thiruppugazh describes lovemaking as falling into a sea of pleasure (இன்பவாரியில் விழுஞ் சிந்தையேன்) and asks how such a mind will ever reach the shore (கரைசேர்வேன்). In the Kural the woman says the sea of love surely exists (காமக் கடல்மன்னும் உண்டே) but there is no safe raft to cross it (ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்). Both make desire a sea with no crossing; the Kural's lovesick woman wants to reach her lover, and the poet wants to get out of desire itself.

The Thiruppugazh pictures lovers entwined like anril birds until two hearts become one (அன்றில்போல் உளமிரண்டொன்றுமாய்), and asks to pass beyond the deeds those women bind him in. The Naladiyar quotes a paid woman who promised never to part, like the anril birds that never separate (புணர்பிரியா அன்றிலும்போல்), and then left. The anril, the bird of unbroken union, appears in both books inside the courtesan's embrace, and both poets look past it.

The Thiruppugazh lists the women's eyes as Kalakuta poison, cruel Death's form and Kama's arrows (கண் காளகூடம் கொடுங் கால்ருபம் பொரும் காமபாணம்), and asks whether his swinging senses will ever stop without saying 'Om namo Kanda'. The Kural's man asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both see death in a woman's eyes; the Kural says it in wonder, the song as a danger it wants a mantra against.

The Thiruppugazh asks not to be worn down by dog-like disputants (நாயொப்பவர்) who call good words evil (நற்சொலைத் தீதெனா) and argue against those who come to true austerity. The Naladiyar says that when the guileless explain virtue, the crooked do not hear it, just as the tanner's dog that chews leather cannot take the taste of milk-rice (குணுங்கர்நாய் பாற்சோற்றின் செவ்வி கொளல்தேற்றாது). Both use the dog for one who cannot receive good words.

The Thiruppugazh asks Murugan to end the nights of pleasure and give instead the bliss of silence and the dissolving of the mind (மவுனபஞ்சர மனோலயசுகம்). The Tirumanthiram teaches that mind and breath go together and that for those who rejoice within the abiding mind, the dissolving of mind (மனோலயம்) comes within it. The song asks for the state by name; the Tirumanthiram verse says how that dissolving is reached through the breath.

The Thiruppugazh describes women whose sword eyes, sharper than the vel, make war on young men's lives (இளைஞராவியை வளைந்தமர்செய் வாள்விழியர்) while their hearts hold deceit. The Kural's man says he never knew what Death was until now: it is a woman's grace with large eyes that make war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both see the woman's eyes as a battle that takes a man's life; the song adds that the eyes serve a deceit aimed at his wealth.

The Thiruppugazh calls the body a hut filled with disease and evil (நோய்தீமை இட்டகுடில்) whose binding will come undone when Death's messenger comes, and asks Murugan to think of him before life is lost. The Kural asks whether the life, lodging in the body as a temporary shelter (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு), has found no home of its own. Both make the body a poor lodging for life; the Kural leaves the question open, the song answers it with praise of the Lord.

The Thiruppugazh pictures the funeral: the bier lifted, the mourners calling, then plunging into the water (அலைநீரிற் புக்குமுழுகா) so that their long grief goes. The Tirumanthiram has the town wail, rename the man a corpse, burn him, then bathe in water and stop thinking of him (நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்). Both mark the ritual bath as the moment grief, and memory, are washed away; the song turns from it to ask for praise of the golden feet before that day.

The Thiruppugazh asks to see a lotus that neither water nor earth touches, spreading in length and breadth as a form of light (தாமரை படர்ந்தோடி நீளமகலஞ் சோதிவடிவான). The Tirumanthiram speaks of lotuses in bud which a spreading light opens (மொட்டலர் தாமரை ... சோதி விரிசுடர்). Both place the inner lotus and its light at the height of yogic vision; the Tirumanthiram verse is obscure, so the pairing rests on the image.

Both count the tattvas as thirty, thirty and thirty-six (முப்பதும் முப்பதும் முப்பத்தறுவரும்; முப்பதும் ஆறாறும் முப்பதும்). Tirumular has them flee when the body-temple falls; 1112 asks for a silence that is other than all of them, reached before death.
audit_text_issue: 1112 line 5 has a corrupt word (வா஡ணச, probably வாரிச).

note: Both describe the ascent through the body's centres (ஆதார சோதனை; சக்ர சடாதாரம் முட்டவும் மீதேறி) to a state in which the senses and inner instruments stop working (புலன் கரணம் புத்தி சாதாரணங் கெட்டான்; சொற்கரணாதீதம்).
audit_text_issue: Corrupt glyph in 1112 line 5 (வா஡ணச, likely வாரிச)

note: Both say that wife, children and goods do not follow the dead. Tirumular names what does go along, vows and knowledge; 1115 asks for the mind to praise the Lord's feet.
audit_text_issue: 1115 lines 5-6 hard to construe, possibly corrupt

note: In both the kin who surround the dead turn back and leave him. 1117 draws the question 'who is kin then?', which its praise answers with Murugan.

1105 confesses praising patrons as the rain cloud, the parijata tree and Meru; 1125 shows who those patrons are, deceitful, loveless and bound for hell, and names the same kind of praise, as Vishnu, Kama or the gods' tree, as the waste of a life.
The Naladiyar says even the starving should not tell their need to men without courtesy; 1125 confesses doing exactly that, going in verse to the cruel and loveless, and asks to be stopped.

The Thiruppugazh asks that before the fixed day when Death sends his messenger with torment (ஒருதூதேவு நெட்டளவாம் வாதை அணுகாமுன்), his heart may melt and he may live chanting Murugan's feet. The Tirumanthiram says the guru set his feet on his devotees' heads and kept away the band of Yama's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்). The song's plea and the Tirumanthiram's statement meet: the feet are what keep Death's messengers off.

The Thiruppugazh pictures the dying man as a bird caught in the snare of the tattvas' workings, giving up its life (ஒட்டில்பட்ட குருகு சத்துவிட்டப்படி), and asks Murugan to come with his devotees at that hour. The Kural says the bond of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்தொழியப் புள்பறந்தற்றே). Both picture death through a bird; in the Kural the bird goes free of its shell, in the song it struggles in a trap and needs a rescuer.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1114: ஒட்டில் uncertain.

note: The Thiruppugazh lists children, wife, kin, money in boxes, gems and servants, all of whom grieve and turn back at the pyre, and asks for the day he no longer melts for what is false (பொய்க்குமெய்க்குச் செயலுமுருகாதே). The Tirumanthiram has the dead man leave behind his wife, his wealth and his house (குழலியும் மாடும் மனையும்), taken to the common burning ground and left. Both name wife, wealth and house as what stays behind; the song draws the lesson that the heart should melt for the Lord's feet instead.
audit_text_issue: 1115's pyre lines are hard to construe.

note: The Thiruppugazh begins with the body of the five elements (பூதக்காயம்) and confesses that he wanders pretending like those who make a show of devotion (நிற்பாரைப்போல அப்பாவித்து), asking for knowledge beyond the bond. The Kural says the five elements laugh within (பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்) at the concealed conduct of a deceitful mind. Both set the pretender's show against the five elements of his own body; the Kural has them mock him, and the song makes the same body the ground of his confession.
audit_text_issue: 1116's word divisions are uncertain throughout.

note: The Thiruppugazh pictures Yama's men binding him with the noose and dragging him off while kin and parents say 'we won't keep you, go' (ஒட்டோம் விட்டுக் கழியீர்), and asks who will be his kin at that time. The Tirumanthiram says that when life leaves the body there is no way to fight it, but think of the Lord and Death's messengers will not even think of burning you (அண்ணலை எண்ணும்). The Tirumanthiram answers the song's question: the Lord thought of is the only ally at that hour.
