The Thiruppugazh confesses seeking wealth like a merchant, like one after honey (செட்டாகத் தேனைப்போல), and singing a few songs to men newly come into fortune. The Naladiyar says people cling to the wealthy and will not leave them though they give nothing, like ants circling a pot of ghee they cannot reach. Both show the seeker hovering round the rich for a sweetness he may never get.

The Thiruppugazh describes consorting with women whose devotion is for silk and palm-leaf earrings, and himself stumbling about in full view of foes and friends in the neighbourhood (ஒட்டார் நட்டார் வட்டாரத்தே ... தடுமாறும்). The Naladiyar says those fooled into taking a paid woman's love as theirs, who take wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Both add public shame to the cost of such love.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1119 is clipped and hard to read.

note: The Thiruppugazh pictures the body as a torn, leaking hut (பைப்பீறற் கூரை) and himself running to every land seeking its food (இரைதேடி) until worn out. The Naladiyar says the foulness of the body is always strengthened by the work of eating (உண்டி வினையுள் உறைக்கும்), and finery cannot hide it. Both see the body as a thing endlessly fed and never made sound.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1120's numerical opening is unclear.

note: The Thiruppugazh confesses that for women who speak false talk of pleasure he went mad taking their lies for truth (பொய்க்கே மெய்க்கே பித்தாகி) and ran to every direction and island for money for their hands. The Naladiyar says some trust the words such women speak to be believed (தேறா மொழிந்த மொழிகேட்டுத் தேறி) and take them for their own, though they belong to no one. Both put the ruin in the man's taking false words as true.

The Thiruppugazh describes women who pass off false love as true and press for coins into their hand (காசுக்கே கைக்குத்திடு மாதர்). The Naladiyar says the friendship of harlots is like a lamp's light: as the light ends when the oil runs out, their love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure such love by the hand, the song by what it demands and the Naladiyar by when it stops.

The Thiruppugazh confesses that he sought food all over the earth and praised unkind, thieving men with words of desire (சோரர்க்கே வித்து ஆசைச் சொற்களை ஓதி), and asks for good words to sing Murugan's feet. The Naladiyar calls the lowest way of life following, out of desire for wealth (பொருள்நசையால்), people who do not recognise one's worth. The song confesses living that lowest way and asks to leave it.

Among the names of the silent mantra the Thiruppugazh asks to be taught is the atom within the atom (சிறிய அணுவையணுவின்), beyond impurity, mind and the three qualities. The Tirumanthiram calls the first Lord the atom within the atom (அணுவில் அணுவினை ஆதிப் பிரானை), approached only by those who can divide it a thousandfold. Both name the supreme as the subtlest thing, and in the song it is what Murugan taught Siva in silence.

The Thiruppugazh's praise is a litany of the goddess's names, Varahi, Kapali, Malini, Mahamayi, Yamalai, Kali, Uma, Narani (நாரணி) and more, whose son is Visakha. The Tirumanthiram lists Tripura, Sundari, Antari, Narani (நாரணி), Isi and Manonmani and says by these the great one stands as many (வருபலவாய் நிற்கும்). Both use the string of names to show one Sakti in many forms.

Both put the faithless woman beside liquor and make her the mark of lost fortune: the Kural's women, drink and dice are the company of those Fortune has left; 1141 calls the drinking courtesans themselves மூதேவிகள், Misfortune, who bring poverty.

Both picture the wailing kin at the funeral. Tirumular's kin turn back at the edge of town and leave the dead man to the fire; 1140 lets the kin wail and asks that Murugan come at that moment with his devotees, so that the dead man is not left alone.
Both stage the deathbed, the kin who lament and leave, and Yama's coming. 1131 asks only to praise Murugan before the end; 1140 asks him to arrive at the funeral itself and fight Death's army.

1127 asks not to be bewildered (மருளாதே) by the pomp of worship, invocations, mantras and sacrificial fuel, but to stand where 'you and I' fall away (நீ நான் அற வேறின்றி நிற்க). Tirumanthiram 1008, closing a chapter on worship, says four times that those given to the Stainless One, the Siva-yogis and the searchers do not want ritual work (வேண்டார்கள் கன்மம்). Both set the ritual apparatus below a union beyond it; the song asks for it, the Tirumanthiram states who has it.

1128's courtesans name a price (விலைகூறி) and stay only if they get a share of the wealth (பொருள் கூறாகப் பெறில் நிற்கவும்), speaking false friendship. Kural 911 warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring harm. The song shows the bargain the Kural names in one line.

1128 calls the courtesans' offer கூடா நட்பு, friendship that does not join, after which they bring ruin and leave (கேடா விட்டகல்). Kural 821, in the chapter titled கூடாநட்பு, says the friendship of those close without inner consent is an anvil to strike on once the chance comes. The song moves the Kural's false-friend pattern into the courtesan's trade, using its very name.

1129 vows never to forget (மறவேனே) that Murugan made him sing the wondrous Thiruppugazh with honey in every direction (அற்புதத் திருப்புகழ் தேனூற ஓதி). Song 2, near the book's opening, likewise ends 'I will not forget' the grace that told him to sing the Thiruppugazh (திருப்புகழ் ... செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை மறவேனே). The book names itself at both ends in the same vow of gratitude; 1129 adds what the gift freed him from, the three impurities and three qualities.
audit_text_issue: Song 2 has a corrupt word in the offering list (தன஧முலம்).

note: 1130's women bargain the price (விலைபேசி) and snatch whatever wealth comes (வருபொருள் கண்டு ஏற்கவே பறிக்கும்) while calling a man in with sweet looks. Kural 912 names women who weigh the profit and then speak of their own good nature (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்) and says to weigh them and keep away. The song is the scene; the Kural adds the advice the song turns into a plea.

1131 has kin and sons lament with many words and then go (சொல் பல கத்திட்டு ... அவர் ஏக) before Yama drags the life away. Tirumanthiram 152, on the body's impermanence, ends with the loving ones weeping and leaving (அன்புடையார்கள் அழுது அகன்றார்களே) as the nine gates shut. Both make the kin's departure the last beat of a death; the song uses it as the moment to ask to praise Murugan first.

Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot swim the great sea of birth (இறைவன் அடிசேராதார்). 1132 narrows the sea to the eddying pool of coupling (சுழி மிதுன வாவியில் புகுந்து முழுகி) and asks for the good, imperishable feet (அழியா மன் நல் பதங்கள்) so as not to drown. The song applies the Kural's image to the poet's own drowning in lust.

Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come (நரைவரும் என்றெண்ணி), renounced in childhood, while those who delighted in youth rise later leaning on a staff. 1133 is the life Naladiyar warns of told from inside: years spent on the burning belly, then grey hair (நரைகளும் பெரிதாயே), the name 'old man' (கிழவன் என்றொரு பேர்), faltering steps, and the question whether he will perish without reaching the Dancer's raised foot.
audit_text_issue: 1133 has corrupt words in the praise (மா஡ண, ஧ட்மு).

note: Tirumanthiram 620 teaches that mind and breath move together, so the dissolving of mind (மனோலயம்) comes within the stilled mind. 1134 asks for the same மனோலயம் by another road, by sinking in the dust of Murugan's feet (சீர்பாத தூளியின் முழுகி). The same goal is reached through breath-yoga in one and through devotion in the other.

Kural 1085's man asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). 1136 opens with the same questioning list, vel or carp or sword or flower, a messenger sent by Yama, a deer or poison (எமன்விடு தூதோ மானோ விடமீதோ). The Kural's wonder becomes in the song the poet's record of the praise that ruined him.
audit_text_issue: 1136: plea lines do not split securely.

note: Kural 173 says those who want the other joy will not do wrong out of desire for the small joy (சிற்றின்பம் வெஃகி). 1137 grants that the pleasure of union is slight (சுகம் அற்பமாகினும்) and still says he cannot, cannot leave it (விடவோ இயலாது இயலாதே), so he asks for release as a gift. The song adds the condition the Kural leaves out: knowing the joy is small does not by itself free a man from it.
audit_text_issue: 1137 has corrupt words (e.g. தத஧முழ்கி).

note: 1137 admits that though the pleasure is small he cannot give it up (விடவோ இயலாது இயலாதே); 1206 says the embrace cannot be left by him alone (தமியேனால் தவிரொணாது) and asks for the young feet. Two songs in different chapters make the same rare admission, that the poet's own will is not enough and the leaving must be given.
audit_text_issue: 1137 has two corrupt words.

note: 1139 counts among the base those who shout down rivals with many quarrelsome books and rise by winning (கலகக் கலை நூல் பல கொண்டு எதிர் கதறி ... வென்று உயர் கயவர்). Naladiyar 313 mocks men who itch to rise and debate on the strength of a word (சுனைத்தெழுதல் காமுறுவர்) without grasping the power of learning. Both treat learning used for contest as a failure of learning.
Both make the courtesan's love last as long as the man's money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out when the oil ends; in 1154 the wealth in his hand is gone and everyone drives him off with 'chi, chi'.

The Kural says smallness adorns itself in self-praise; 1155 gives the examples, the coward praising his valour and the miser calling himself Dharmaputra, and then applies the charge to the poet himself.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them; 1155 mocks men of base lineage (இழிகுலத்தர்) for claiming a high one, which treats birth-rank as real. The conflict holds if இழிகுலத்தர் is read literally as low caste rather than as a term of abuse for base men.
Both send to hell those who give nothing to the one who begs. Tirumular adds those who do not praise the Lord or tend groves; 1146 adds those who do not pay their teacher.
Both put in deep hell those who speak ill of the Lord's devotees. Tirumular means Siva's devotees; 1146 names the servants of both Siva and Vishnu (ஈசர் விஷ்ணுவை சேவைசெய்வோர்).

1143 calls the body a raw clay pot with eight openings and one (எட்டுடன் ஒரு தொளை ... பசு மட்கலம்) soaked in deeds and disease; Naladiyar 47 calls it a pot (கும்பம்) seeping from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்) that the fool praises for its skin. Naladiyar uses the pot to cure desire; the song uses it to ask for the knowledge beyond the tattvas.

1144's courtesans, once the wealth in his hand is gone, say 'no shame? go, go now, call the others' (வெட்கமிலை நட ஏகும் ஏகும் இனி மற்றவரை அழையும்). Naladiyar 373 says such women would bow and send away even red-eyed Mal if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன்று இல்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). The song gives the dismissal in the women's own words.

Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in a corner of the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்) has no home of its own. 1145 calls the body a hut (குரம்பை) worn out in the pit of union and asks when, leaving it (விட்டு அகன்று), he will reach Murugan's lotus feet. The song names the home the Kural's question leaves open.
audit_text_issue: 1145: one line has a lost/garbled run (; ந்த்ரகோபம்).

note: 1148 asks that, lust subsiding, he reach the blissful state practised in the cage of silence (மவுன பஞ்சரம் பயில் தரும் சுக பதம்) and abide in grace. Tirumanthiram 1611 says that for those to whom silence has come (மோனம் கைவந்தோர்க்கு) release too comes to hand. Both make silence the threshold of release.

1149 speaks of the One the clamouring arts cannot point to and the warring sects cannot reach (பதறிய சமயிகள் எட்டாப் பேரொளி), found only by letting go of everything. Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six sects did not see him and he is not what the six sects hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). Both place the goal outside the sects; the song adds renunciation as the way, the Tirumanthiram clarity.

64 scorns those who sit singing a few poor poems (புன்கவி சில பாடி) about a lovesick girl and do not know to praise Senthil. 1150 confesses that he was himself such a poet, wandering as one who sang women's bodies from foot to head (பாதாதி கேசம் அளவும் பாடும் கவிஞனாய்த் திரிவேனை). The charge of the early song becomes the poet's own self-accusation.
audit_text_issue: 1150 flagged uncertain.

note: 1150 confesses he was a poet who sang women from foot to head (பாதாதிகேசம்); two songs later, 1152 runs through hair, brow, ears, eyes, lips, teeth, breasts, gait, waist and feet in one catalogue (குழற்கு ... அடிக்கும்) before asking that his heart not weaken. 1152 performs the genre 1150 names as a fault, and turns it into a plea.
audit_text_issue: 1150's ஆசாரவீன சமயம் and மூகம் தனிற் பிறந்து are uncertain.

note: 1150 counts among his faults that he took this passing life as lasting (மாதேச வாழ்வை நிலையென்றே). Kural 331 calls exactly this, taking what does not last as lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்), the lowest kind of understanding. The song lists the Kural's verdict as one item in a confession.

1151 confesses he sees no way to end his passion and no companion to help (ஒழிக்க ஓர் வகை காணேன் உறுந்துணை ஒன்று காணேன்). Kural 1164's woman says the sea of love is there but no raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்), which commentators read as having no helper. Both name the lack of a helper out of desire; the song then finds it in Murugan, who himself longed for Valli.
audit_text_issue: 1151 மாயான் unclear

note: 1152 asks Murugan to grant the meaning he told Agastya (அகத்தியனொடு உரைத்த பொருள்); 598 asks for the honey-nectar of the virtuous Agastya's knowledge (சீல அகத்திய ஞான தேனமுது). Both ask for the teaching Murugan gave Agastya, 598 as escape from death and birth, 1152 as the cure for a heart weakened by a woman's body.

Both hear the funeral drum and see the corpse covered. The Naladiyar counts the beats with detachment and ends 'the dying carry the dead'; 1158 is the dead man's own view of his mourners, and turns the scene into a plea for the feet at that hour.
audit_text_issue: 1158: பிண்முடச் likely corrupt for பிணமூட; mourners' lines hard to split.

note: Both tell a life in one breath from the embryo in the womb. 9 stops at youth, women and disease; 1163 goes on to the stick, the bed, Death and the pyre, and so asks not for grace but for an end to birth.
audit_text_issue: 1163 has a corrupt glyph in சிறைவை஢ட.

note: Both show an old man with failing speech or teeth and a staff whose eyes are still on desire. The Naladiyar says such a man has no way to safety; 1166 is the old man's own confession and still hopes his mind will turn to song.
Both put good deeds before the body fails: the Kural before the hiccup stops the tongue, 1167 before the day the wife spits and life slips away. 1167 joins dharma to bowing before Murugan.
audit_text_issue: 1167 has a garbled glyph (ருத஧முழ்க).

note: Both name Vishnu as the god who followed after a poet's song (பாவலோர்கள் பாடல் கண்டு ஏகும் மால், வண்டமிழ் பயில்வோர் பின் திரிகின்றவன்): a repeated formula for the uncle.

Tirumular 1446 matches the four paths to four kinds of men and lets only the last, the siddhas, reach Siva-knowledge (சித்தர் சிவஞானஞ் சென்றெய்துவோர்). 1157 sets those infatuated with the first three (சரியை கிரியை மக யோக மோகிகள்) among those who chase the truth and cannot know it. The song keeps the ranking but adds a limit: a path held with infatuation (மோகம்) does not reach, and what it asks for instead is melting (உருகி) among devotees.

The Kural says that for those whose delusion is gone (மருள்நீங்கி) and whose sight is clear, darkness leaves (இருள்நீங்கி) and joy comes. 1159 asks that darkness not cover (இருள் மூடாவகை) a mind caught in delusion (மோகாதி) and the senses, and that knowledge rise like dawn (நிற்குண ஞானோதய). The song turns the Kural's statement into a plea, with delusion, darkness and clear knowledge in the same order.
audit_text_issue: 1159's opening syntax is unclear.

note: The Kural asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ), since it has all three. 1160 also measures women's eyes against three things: it says they beat the carp (சேலை அடர்த்து), have more of poison (ஆலம் மிகுத்து) and are fiercer than the deer (உழையைச் சீறு). The Kural's lover wonders at the look; the song makes the same comparison into arrows (விழிக் கணை) and asks to put that desire far away (ஆசையினைத் தூரவிடுத்து).

Both name the love-drug among the paid women's tricks: 1161 opens with சொக்குப்பொடி and wealth taken by cunning (கைப்பொருளைக் கெத்தில் பற்றி), and 1183 has பொடிமாயம், a drug that burns the belly (உதரம் எரிதர மருத்திட்டு). 1161 asks for the wonder that cuts attachment (பற்றற); 1183 asks to be taken out of that union. Drugging, beyond robbery, is a detail the courtesan songs rarely give, and here two neighbouring songs share it.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1161: திக்குக்கெட்டு ஒட்டுச் சிட்டென பட்டத்துற is obscure.

note: 1162 asks that the poet, calling himself a dog (நாயினன்), become one who wears the feet as a crown (சீர்பாத சேகரன்). 1175 gives the same title to Murugan himself, who wears the anklet feet of the hunter girl (கிராதை நூபுர ... பத்மபாத சேகர). Put together, they show the devotee's posture of wearing the feet given to the god in his love for Valli.

Tirumular's town wails, takes away the man's name and calls him a corpse (பேரினை நீக்கிப் பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு), carries him to the burning ground, burns him and bathes and forgets. 1163 ends a whole life the same way: sons and kin, worn out, call it a corpse (பிணமெனவே), say 'lift it, lift it' (எடுமெடுமின்) and burn it on the pyre (சுடலைமிசை எரியினிட). Tirumular stops at the mourners' forgetting; the song uses the scene to ask that birth itself end (செனனமிது தவிர).

The Naladiyar's wife feels shy each time her husband embraces her and wonders how women who embrace many men for gain (பொருள்நசையால் பன்மார்பு சேர்ந்து) do it every day (எஞ்ஞான்றும்). 1164 describes those women from the cheated man's side: daily they make love (தினம் ... புணர்ந்திட்டு), daily they cheat and seize his goods as if collecting a debt (தினம் தெட்டிக் கடன்பற்றிக் கொளும் மாதர்). The wife cannot imagine that daily trade; the song says what it costs the man, and asks for the feet so that he may gain Sivam.

Both lay the five letters on the body: Tirumular puts ந at the feet, ம at the navel, சி and வ at the shoulders and ய as the light above. 1165 has ந the two feet (நகரம் இருபாதமாகி), ம the belly, சி the chest, வ the mouth and ய the crown, then adds the அ and உ of Om. The two schemes agree on the feet, belly and crown and differ over the shoulders and mouth, so the body-mantra was not fixed in a single form.
audit_text_issue: 1165 நதிமுடிய சாரமாகி likely corrupt for யகாரம்; second half's syntax uncertain.

note: In Tirumular the women who once wanted the speaker like sugarcane juice now find him bitter kaanjiram fruit (கரும்பொத்துக் காஞ்சிரங் காயுமொத்தேனே). 1167's old man is seen by his wife, who spits (மனையாள் கண்டு உமிழ்ந்து), while others scold. In both, the women's turning away marks old age; Tirumular stops at the change, and the song asks to do fruitful dharma (பயன்கொள் தருமம்) before that day.

The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்) and those who do not cannot. 1168 pictures births rising like the seven seas (திரை ஏழே போல் எழு பிறவி மாக்கடல்) and asks Murugan to end his weariness in it, give him his feet to wear (உனது தாளே சூடி) and lift him into the assembly of devotees. The song keeps the Kural's sea and feet and adds the devotees' company (அடியார் வாழ் சபை) as the place reached.

Tirumular says the true guru kept away the band of Death's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்) and ended the sorrow of birth. 1169 shows those messengers (ஏமதூதர்) at work, crushing the body like sugarcane in the mill (ஆலைமீதிலே கரும்பு எனவே) while the women of the house weep, and asks Murugan to see it and come (கண்டு வருவாயே). What Tirumular states as done, the song asks for at the very hour.

Tirumular says the Lord who made birth for joy shut it in the bond of sorrow, fastening skin and flesh to bone (என்பிற் கொளுவி ... தோல் தசை) until it runs to its end. 1170 builds the body from water, bone and skin (நீரும் என்பு தோலினாலும்), born of the parents' desire, running through youth and lust until Yama throws his noose (பாசம் வீச), and asks whether this illusion (மாயம்) will end. Tirumular gives the binding to the Lord's concealment, while the song gives it to the parents' desire and ends it with Yama.
audit_text_issue: 432: தோற்றசை read as தோல் தசை; sense uncertain.

note: Tirumular says the six sects are like six roads to one great city, and those who argue 'this is good, that is bad' are dogs barking at a hill. 1171 says the quarrelling six sects (கலகச் செற்றச் சட்சமயிகள்) cannot state or grasp (புகலற்குப் பற்றற்கு அரியது) the teaching Murugan gave Siva. Both blame the quarrel, not the sects as such; the song adds that the teaching itself lies beyond the arguers.

Both make the palmyra horse the end point of love's suffering. In the Kural it is the lover's only strength; in 1174 it is what a learned renouncer and yogi is reduced to, and he asks whether fate or grace brought him there.

Both describe the truth that scriptures, practices and debaters cannot reach and call it a great ocean of bliss (மகோததி), and both answer with the feet. 1175 builds the whole plea from negatives; 1157 sets the four Saiva paths themselves among those that fail.
Both build the courtesan's arts on the verb of showing (காட்டுவர், காட்டி). 1183 adds robbery and the love-drug; 1176 turns the verb back on Siva and Murugan, asking to be shown the feet instead.

Both describe women who take all the wealth from a man's hands while he believes in their love. The Naladiyar ends in the town's laughter at the fool; 1183 ends in a plea to be taken out of that union.

Both give Murugan the love-sickness the poet confesses: the south wind and Kama's arrows wound him until he goes to Valli in the millet field. 1181 puts in his mouth the plea to save his life from love's fever.

The Naladiyar's paid women seem sweet while the man is fooled and turn harsh as a ram's horn once they are full (தாமார்ந்த போதே தகர்கோடாம்). 1173's women take the wealth of many and then pick a quarrel to drive them out (பலர் பொருள் கவர்ந்து இடை கலாமிட்டு ஓட்டிகள்), after weeping and rubbing their eyes as if in love (அன்புமுடையாரைப் போல் ... கண்பிசையும்). The song gives the same turn from feigned love to hostility and adds the false tears.

Tirumular's mirror verse says that for those who say the Lord is within and without he is within and without, and for those who say he is neither, he is neither. 1177 asks to know, by awareness in the place where body, breath, faculties and self are lost (யானும் இழந்த இடந்தனில் உணர்வாலே), what all the debaters and sects hold as 'it is' and 'it is not' (ஆமென அன்றென நின்றதை). Tirumular shows the sects finding what they assert; the song asks for that same thing by a knowing that comes only after the self is lost.

The Kural's woman says the sea of love exists and there is no raft to cross it (காமக் கடல் ... ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). 1181 cannot cross the ocean called desire (ஆசை என்கிற பாராவாரம்) and sets beside it a second ocean, of tantra, ritual, Veda and Agama, whose shore he never sees. The song keeps the Kural's sea with no crossing and adds the sea of scripture, which does not save either; only the guru's grace is left.

The Naladiyar says men without money are poison to the paid women, while a man who has worked an oil press is sugar to them if he has wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம் அன்னார்). 1182 calls them dancing girls who soften at the sight of gold (பொன்கண்டு இளகு கூத்திகள்). Both make gold the only thing that moves them; the song adds the poet's own enslavement and asks to praise the hills instead.
audit_text_issue: 1182's list of hills is garbled.

note: Tirumular says that when the body's roof falls, the women and children who ate from it do not follow; only vows and knowledge go with the dead. 1184 is the householder's life of toil for those same dependents, the children to be supported and the wife to be fed (சிறுவரும் ... துணைவியும்), and Brahma's script (வண்போதன் தீட்டும் தொடர்), and asks to praise Kanda before Death takes him at the burning ground. The song is the care Tirumular says will not follow, together with the plea to turn before it ends.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1184: opening phrases (வம்பாருந் தேக்குண் டிட) hard to construe.

note: Both go through the woman part by part. 1185 lists waist, gait, feet, hair, earrings, breasts, lips, eyes, smile and forehead, each ending in -க்கே, and confesses a swoon at every limb (அவயவம் அனைத்தூடினும் அவசமுறு மயல்). The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman (எத்திறத்தாள்). The same catalogue serves the infatuation in the song and its cure in the Naladiyar.

Tirumular names the three impurities, anava, maya and karma, as bran and husk around the sprouting grain, and tells the soul to separate its bonds. 1186 asks for the same three to go: the mind's maya (மனமாயை), the two hard deeds (இருகாழ்வினை) and the old impurity cut at the root (மலம் வேரற). The song names what follows the cutting, the joy of knowledge as experience (ஞான அநுபூதி) and play with the devotees at the feet.
audit_text_issue: 1186 has a garbled word (யற்முதுடை).

note: Both are a mother's lament for a daughter lovesick for Murugan, worn by the moon, the wind and the evening; 24 adds the anril bird, 1189 the gossiping women and the herdsman's flute.
The herdsman's flute as a weapon of evening: the Kural's woman calls it a messenger of the burning dusk that kills, and in 1189 the cowherd's flute is among the things wearing the girl down.
audit_text_issue: 1189 has corrupt characters (லு஡தி).

note: The Naladiyar sketches the old man whose speech fails and teeth fall but who still keeps his eyes on desire; 1194 lists every stage of that decay down to the stench of the sickbed and turns it into a plea for grace at the last moment.

The song piles up walled mansions (மாடம்), gold in the house and many women, then ties the body to the bier (பாடை) and gives the 'doll' to the fire. Tirumanthiram 155 names the same three things left behind, the honey-haired woman, the wealth and the house (குழலியும் மாடும் மனையும்), as the body is set down at the common burning ground. Both make the list of possessions the measure of what the bier strips away.
audit_text_issue: 1187: the line on the hunter girl ends corruptly; 155: மதுவூர வாங்கியே may be corrupt.

note: The song asks for the One that shines when the five elements, the inner instruments and the 'I' all subside (நான் போய் ஒடுங்க அடங்கலும் மாய்ந்தால் விளங்கும் அது ஒன்றினை). Tirumanthiram 135 says that when the five beginning with sound settle back by their own path (சத்த முதல் ஐந்தும் தன்வழித் தான் சாரில்) the conscient joins only the Conscient, flame to flame in pure space. The Thiruppugazh petition asks for exactly the state the Tirumanthiram describes as the end of that subsiding.

The song asks for 'that which was spoken' (மொழிந்ததை) when Siva bowed, a single thing (அது ஒன்று) that appears only when everything else has ceased. Tirumanthiram 2648 says the guru told him 'the one thing beyond telling' (உரையற்ற தொன்றை உரைத்தான்) and cut off the craving for the arts. Both speak of a teaching that is uttered yet lies beyond utterance, with the guru as speaker.

The song says the poet has already reached desirelessness (வேண்டாமை ஒன்றை அடைந்து) and fallen melting at the feet. Kural 362 says that not-being-born comes when one wants not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). The Kural makes வேண்டாமை the means to release; the song treats it as the threshold already crossed, from which only grace remains to be asked.

1190 says that the karma which, while his mind lay degraded among the price-women (விலைமாதர்), still made him think of the six-faced one is something he will never forget (மறவேனே). 1198 says that even while his mind practises the arts of love he will not forget (மறவேனே) the sword in Murugan's hand and his feet. Both songs refuse the usual 'first renounce, then remember' and claim remembrance in the midst of the indulgence itself.

The song asks that, not ruined by women, he be granted to learn and recite Thiruppugazh and the tattva knowledge in threefold Tamil (திருப்புகழ் கற்கவும் ஓதவும் முத்தமிழ் தத்துவ ஞானம்). Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யு மாறே). Tirumular states as accomplished vocation what Arunagiri asks for: that the knowledge of God be given in, and as, Tamil verse.

The song says the women's embrace melts body and life like wax in fire (தீ மெழுகிட்டானதோ), and asks instead for the golden feet where the mind dissolves (மனோலயம்) once craving for the world (புலக அவா) is removed. Tirumanthiram 325, in its chapter against toddy, praises the samadhi where the mind is melted and becomes Siva (சித்தம் உருக்கிச் சிவமாம்) and its pure honey. Both keep the melting and the intoxication but move them from the senses to God.

1194 inventories old age clause by clause: teeth fallen, back bent like a bow (முதுகு வெஞ்சிலை காட்டி வளைந்தது), cough come, speech failing, the stench of filth, then 'now it is a moment, come'. Song 68 runs the same list, teeth loose, back bent (முதுகே வளைய), cough, speech slurring, filth flowing, and ends asking Murugan to come quickly on the peacock. It is a near-repeat of the same song-form across distant chapters, the old-age catalogue closed by a summons.

1194 ends its catalogue of decay with 'now it is a matter of a moment' (நிமிஷம் இங்கினி ஆச்சு) and turns to Murugan. Naladiyar 55 says youth has passed for nothing and disease with old age is coming now (இன்னே பிணியொடு மூப்பும் வருமால்) and calls the heart to set out on the good path. Both make the arrival of old age the last call to turn, one as prayer and one as self-address.

In 1196 the women who loved him weep and fall on him while elders and young ask 'what is left to do, is he dead?' (ஏது கருமம் இவர் சாவு) and carry him off to the burning ground. Tirumanthiram 150 has the wife who married with sweet talk weep 'as is fitting' (அமைய அழுதிட்டு), burn the bond in fire and make the offering. Both show grief at the bier as brief and dutiful, the dead man's ties ending with the rite.

The song asks on what day, before he becomes the work of Mugadi (முகடித் தொழில்), the goddess of misfortune, Murugan will grant him the work of his service (அடிமைத் தொழில்). Kural 617 says Mugadi (மாமுகடி) dwells in sloth and Lakshmi at the feet of the one without sloth. Both set Mugadi against a chosen labour, effort in the Kural and service to God in the song.
audit_text_issue: 1197 ஆகாஎ நாளினில் looks garbled.

note: 1198 describes nights with common women and says that even while his mind practises the arts of love he will not forget (மறவேனே) Murugan's sword and golden feet. Song 153, after its own detailed lovemaking, says that even if he falls into that river of pleasure he will not forget the feet even a little (சிறிது மறவேனே). A near-repeat across distant chapters of the same claim, that remembrance survives within the indulgence.

The song calls Murugan the supreme guru who showed the matted-haired Lord the silent way that the ancient Veda gives (பழய மறை தரும் மவுன வழி). Tirumanthiram 2661 has Nandi, the guru, stand fixed in the high silence (உயர் மோனத்தான்) once the three states and the three turiyas end. In both, the highest teaching a guru gives is silence.

Song 153 states flatly that even fallen into the river of pleasure he will not forget the feet (மறவேனே). 1201, after its own picture of union, asks to be given ways to praise the feet and the vel even in the days when his mind is lost in that passion (மனது அழியும் நாட்களினும் ... ஏத்தும் வகை தரவேணும்). The vow becomes a petition: remembrance in passion is something to be granted, not assumed.
Both picture Yama's palm-leaf summons with drums, the bier and wailing kin; 23 draws the lesson of sharing before it comes, 1215 asks instead for love of the anklets.
Both name the courtesan's want as money, not love: the Kural warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth bring harm, and 1214 calls them women whose minds seek coins.

1203 asks that, as a corpse burns to nothing, his malas with the two diseases die so that he becomes pure space (சுத்த வெளியாகி) and gains release. Tirumanthiram 135 says that in pure space flame joins flame (சுத்த வெளியிற் சுடரிற் சுடர்சேரும்) once the senses settle back. Both name சுத்த வெளி as the state of the freed soul.
audit_text_issue: 1203's first line has a corrupt glyph (பிண஧முடி) and uncertain divisions.

note: 1204 gives the mourners' own words: don't leave the corpse at the threshold, raise the bier before it rots, call the drums, stop the weeping, lift the body (எடுமினி யாக்கையை) before it stinks. Tirumanthiram 145 has the town wail, take away his name and call him a corpse (பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு), burn him, bathe and stop thinking of him. Both show the living hurrying the body out once life has gone.

1205 says that by Brahma's decree he has taken every body again and again, born at the mouth of every womb (யோனி வாய்தொறும்) for aeons he cannot count, and asks not to be born again. Tirumanthiram 185 says the base, after harsh Death has put them in the pit of the womb (கருக்குழி), fall into it again, their bewilderment unending. Both describe rebirth as a repeated fall through the womb.

1205 asks Murugan to grant that he not be born again (இனிப் பிறவாது நீ அருள்புரிவாயே). Kural 362 says that if one must want, one should want non-birth, and it comes when one wants not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). The Kural adds the condition the song leaves to grace: freedom from desire is the way to non-birth.

1206 admits that alone he cannot give up the embrace (தமியேனால் தவிரொணாது) and so asks for Murugan's young feet rich in compassion. Tirumanthiram 1938, on one reading of தானே, says Siva-yoga does not stay without grace and that one who harbours lust lives in fear. Both put grace before one's own effort against desire.

1207 describes women who call young men and draw out a great deal of money (மிக்க காசு இழைத்து), until he is drained, tongue dry, living in fear and shame. Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்), as a lamp's light ends with the oil. The Naladiyar gives the rule; the song is the man inside it, emptied and still asking.

1208 speaks of breasts that rise and plot killing like Death (கூற்றெனக் கொலைசூழும்). In Kural 1083 the man says he never knew what Death (கூற்று) was and now knows it: a woman's grace with war-making eyes. Both name the woman's body as கூற்று, the Kural as a lover's discovery, the song as the wanderer's danger.

1211 calls himself a sinner whose mind never gained the knowledge that says neither 'you' nor 'I' (நீ நான் எனாத அறிவு). Tirumanthiram 1788 describes that state: nearing him there is no difference of 'I' and 'you' (நானென நீயென வேறில்லை), as flesh and the life in it. What the song confesses it lacks, the Tirumanthiram states as attained.
audit_text_issue: 1211 has a corrupt glyph in the opening lines.

note: 1212 asks to set his heart's lotus as the flower, thread love through it, tie it on his tongue and adorn Murugan's feet with a garland of letters (மாத்ருகா புஷ்ப மாலை), with a pure mind as the bee. Tirumanthiram 1823 makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the mouth the gate and the senses the lamps. Both turn the parts of the person into the materials of worship, a garland in one and a temple in the other.

1213 says the women lead a man by their foul-smelling passage (பீறற் சலத்து வழி நாற) and torment him with infatuation. Naladiyar 47 calls the body a pot that seeps filth from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்) and the fool dazzled by its skin. Both answer desire with the body's foulness; the Naladiyar argues it, while the song complains of still being led by it.

The praise of 1214 is a litany of the Goddess: yogi, jnani, Parabrahmi, Neeli, Narani (நாரணி), Abhirami and Manonmani. Tirumanthiram 1046 lists her as Tripura, Sundari, Narani (நாரணி), Isi and Manonmani (மனோன்மனி) and says by these names the great one stands as many. Both songs worship Sakti through a run of names, several of them shared.

1215 asks that, before Yama's servants show the palm leaf and carry off the life (ஓலை காட்டி யமபடர்), he be given the awareness to think with love on the anklets. Tirumanthiram 176 says there is no fighting the life's leaving, but think of the Lord (அண்ணலை எண்ணும்) and Death's messengers will not touch you. The Tirumanthiram gives the promise that the song's request relies on.

Both follow the corpse from the house: the kin strip him or wrap him in torn cloth, light the pyre and then bathe. The Tirumanthiram calls them people without justice; 1227 calls life itself pure falsehood and asks for the state of Siva.

The Kural's women who weigh the profit before they speak match 1231's women who sell love after reckoning the coins in a man's hand (கைக்காசின் அளவறிந்து); 1231 adds the poets who sing such women's bodies.
audit_text_issue: Encoding glitches in the praise (சுக்஡ணவ, தசக்஡ணவ)

note: Both confess the court poet's sin of singing a patron in borrowed praise for gain; 1226 calls the stock comparisons stolen, 1022 the patron undeserving, and both turn the song to the feet.
Tirumular explains salokam, samipam and sarupam as stages gained through chariyai and the paths after it; 1221 names Murugan lord of the devotees of exactly these three, stopping short of sayujyam.
audit_text_issue: 1221 line 10 garbled (அ ளுறித்) and சர்ருப for சாரூப.

note: The song asks that Pati, pasu and pasam be set apart each from each without stain (பதி பசு பாசம் ஆனவை கசடற வேறு வேறு செய்தருள்வாயே). Tirumanthiram 115 says pasu and pasam are beginningless like Pati and cannot reach him, but when Pati draws near they do not remain (பதியணுகில் பசு பாசம் நில்லாவே). The Tirumanthiram gives the doctrine of the three; the song turns it into a plea, asking the Lord to make the approach the soul cannot.

The song asks Murugan to drive off the twofold disease of impurity with Siva's light (இருநோய் மலத்தை சிவ ஒளியால் மிரட்டி) and set his paired feet on the poet's head (முடிமேலே இணைதாள் அளித்து). Tirumanthiram 113 tells the same act as done: the Lord came down, set his cool feet on the head as a guard (தண்ணின்ற தாளைத் தலைக்காவல் முன்வைத்து) and cut away the verdigris (களிம்பறுத்தானே). Feet on the head and the removal of impurity go together in both; the song asks for what Tirumular reports receiving.

The song pictures the mantra as a sword (மந்த்ர வாளால்) that cuts down Yama's servants who come by fate's path for the life (விதிவழியின் உயிர்கவர வருகொடிய யமபடரை வெட்டித் துணித்து). Kural 269 says that for those who have gained the power of austerity even leaping past Death becomes possible (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). Both hold that Death can be overcome by a discipline; the Kural names tapas, the song a mantra which, it says, sects and the sixty-four arts cannot reach.
audit_text_issue: 1222's opening line split is uncertain.

note: The song tells of women who cling with love and then leave without attachment by deceit (அணைந்து பின் பற்றற்று அகல் மாயம்), leaving the heart sore and burning. Naladiyar 376 gives the same turn in one woman: she who promised never to part, like a gem on its thread or the anril birds, has turned away like a fighting ram's horn. The Naladiyar dramatises the promise and its breaking that the song names in a phrase.

Among the poet's faults the song names piling great wealth and eating it without sharing (ஈட்டு மாபொருள் பாத்து உணாது), ending in a body for crows, dogs and jackals. Kural 227 says the fiery disease of hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). The song uses the Kural's own word for sharing to name its absence as a sin that ends in a wasted death.

The song confesses hoarding wealth and eating without sharing (பாத்து உணாது) and ends with the body eaten by crows, dogs, jackals and ghosts (காக்கை நாய் நரி பேய்க்குழாம் உண). Tirumanthiram 250 commands the reverse: look out for others before you eat (பார்த்திருந்து உண்மின்), do not hoard old goods (பழம்பொருள் போற்றன்மின்), and learn from the crow that calls before it eats. The crow appears in both, as the sharer in the Tirumanthiram and as the eater of the hoarder's body in the song.

The poet asks whether he should go about without fear or shame (அச்சக் கூச்சமற்று), called a rake (தூர்த்தன்) by all who hear, infatuated and mad after wealth. Kural 1020 says the movements of those with no shame within are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string (நாணால் உயிர்மருட்டி அற்று). The Kural's judgement on the shameless is applied in the song as a confession by one who sees himself becoming that.

The song tells the funeral step by step: the young men bind the body, wrap it in torn cloth, burn it, and all bathe and go home to sit (சுட்டுக் குளித்து மனை புக்கிட்டு இருப்பர்), then judges that life is pure falsehood. Tirumanthiram 145 has the same sequence: the town wails, calls him a corpse, burns him at the burning ground, bathes and stops thinking of him (சுட்டிட்டு நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). The burning, the bath and the return close both verses; the song adds its plea for release from birth.

The song opens with drums beaten in a throng (கட்டக் கணப்பறைகள் கொட்ட) as the clan binds the body for the burning. Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sounded in the hall for a wedding may that same day sound as funeral drums (மணப்பறை ஆயின அன்றவர்க்கு ஆங்கே பிணப்பறையாய்). The funeral drum is the opening image of both; the Naladiyar sharpens it by setting it against the wedding drum.

The song asks whether the illusion (மாயம்) by which the heart dies in the deceitful love of women will end, and its refrain calls Murugan the one who conquered maya and Vel, the god of love (மாயையும் ... வேளையும் வென்று). Tirumanthiram 346 reads Siva's burning of Kama at Korukkai as an inner yoga: settling the mind, turning back the way of the linga, destroying the work of Kama (காமன் செயலழித்து). The god's victory over Kama, which the song only praises, is in the Tirumanthiram a discipline the yogi performs.
audit_text_issue: 1228 reads யாயையு, emended to மாயையு.

note: The song opens on women who make men take up the begging bowl (கப்பரை கைக்கொள வைப்பவர்), catching young men with kohl and painted faces. Naladiyar 377 says the worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hand (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks, and those who think her love theirs are laughed at. Both make the man's ruin the end of the courtesan's love; the song names its last stage, the bowl.

Among those the poet lives with, the song names women who show their price (விலைகாட்டு ... அரிவைமார்) and liquor (கள்), and asks for the feet while life lasts in a wilting body. Kural 920 puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of those Fortune has left (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The pairing of priced women and drink is the same in both; the song's lines are hard to divide, so its full list is uncertain.
audit_text_issue: 1230's first four lines are clipped and hard to divide.

note: The song sets beside the women who sell love some who learn to make poems on those women's limbs (அவயவங்களைப் பாடு கவி தெரிந்து கற்பார்கள்). Song 1226 confesses the poet's own version of that trade: stealing the old poets' comparisons (பழங் கிளவி பல களவுகொண்டு) and singing them on a patron for gain. Read together they name the misused poem twice, on a woman's body and on a patron, and both turn it to the feet instead.
audit_text_issue: 1231 has encoding damage (சுக்஡ணவ, கடற்று஡ளி, சக்஡ணவ).

note: Tirumular's dead man leaves the honey-haired woman, the wealth and the house and is carried to the common burning ground; 1235 lists wife, servants, clan and gathered wealth and ends with the body in a small old rag at the burning ground.
audit_text_issue: TM 155 line 4 'மதுவூர வாங்கியே' is obscure; 1235's 'அரிடசுடு' looks garbled.

note: Tirumular's sectarians stay inside their sect and never gain the experience free of ego; 1246 asks whether one should speak endlessly as scripture instead of seeking the one cause known by experience (அநுபூதி), having said 'enough' to the sects.

The song asks for the day when, crossing the sea of birth with its deceitful fish and sharks in the boat of true speech (மெய்கள் தோணிப் பிறவி அலைவேலை), he will lay flowers on Murugan and recite his words. Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). The song keeps the Kural's sea and adds a boat, truthful speech, and worship as the crossing.

The poet asks Murugan for the threefold Tamil in his service (நின்பணி தமிழ்த்ரயத்தை அருள்வாயே) so that he may tell the fame of the two feet. Tirumanthiram 81 says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யுமாறே). Both take Tamil verse to be the work the god gives his poet; the song asks for the gift that Tirumular says he was made for.
audit_text_issue: 1234: பேசா is ambiguous.

note: The song asks that before the sorrow called death draws near (மரணம் என்ற துக்கம் அணுகாமுன்), while Death torments him with his deeds, he may stand with untroubled mind thinking of Murugan's feet. Kural 335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல்வாராமுன்). Both set the deadline at the death-throe; the Kural asks for good deeds before it, the song for an untroubled thought of the feet.

The song tells of women who embrace a man close, take his money and then bite his lips again (ஆகம் உற அணைத்து காசை அபகரித்து மீள இதழ் கடிப்பது), and the poet drunk on the poison of desire. Kural 913 calls the false embrace of women who want wealth (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both put the deceit in the embrace itself; the song shows the theft placed between the embraces.
audit_text_issue: The word after மவுலியர்க்கு (சாவியது) is unclear.

note: The song asks Murugan to clear away the pleasure of living with wife and children, praising them in the heart as 'my wealth' (எந்தன் தனங்கள் என்றென்று), and to give his feet. Kural 63 records that people call their children their wealth (தம்பொருள் என்பதம் மக்கள்) and gives the reason, in a chapter praising the getting of children. On the reading that the Kural approves the saying, the song treats as a bond to be cleared the very claim the Kural explains and accepts.

The song calls Murugan the one who dwells in the bodies of devotees who conquered the five senses (ஐந்திந்த்ரியங்கள் வென்று ஒன்றும் அன்பர் அங்கம் பொருந்தும்). Kural 6 says those who stand on the path of the one who quenched the five senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) live long. In the Kural the god is the one who controlled the senses; in the song he lives in the devotee who has.

The song lists, among the attachments of a body of filth and blood, the study of many arts, suffering daily without meaning (கலைபல பிடித்து நித்தம் அலைபடும் அநர்த்தம்). Kural 400 calls learning the imperishable, excellent wealth, beside which other things are not wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி). On the reading that கலை is learning in general, the song counts as a bond what the Kural sets above all possessions; if கலை means only worldly arts the conflict narrows.

The song asks for a way of stillness with a drooping gaze, breath held, the light appearing and Sivayoga stirring the soul (தூங்கிய பார்வையொடு தாங்கிய வாயுவொடு தோன்றிய சோதியொடு சிவயோகம்). Tirumanthiram 605 gives the method: both eyes set on the nose, the breath held within, and those who can rest in absorption (தூங்கவல்லார்க்கு) gain a body without fear. The song's plea follows the Tirumanthiram's stages, gaze, breath and absorption, and names the light as their result.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1240: line 15 seems short of syllables.

note: The song asks to be granted a way of living in idleness (சோம்பினில் வாழும்வகை), the stillness of the one absorbed in Sivayoga. Tirumanthiram 128 says the idle ones (சோம்பர்) dwell and lie in pure space and their awareness is where the Veda ends. Both use 'idleness' for the yogi's rest beyond action, a word otherwise of blame.
audit_text_issue: 1240 line 15 seems short of syllables.

note: The song personifies Siva-knowledge as a lady of the lotus whose union gives Siva-bliss (சிவஞான புண்டரிக மலர்மாது உடன் கலவி சிவபோகம்), set against the common women the poet runs after. Tirumanthiram 1133 speaks of the lady who is knowledge (அறிவான மங்கை), whose grace fills the mind of those who know the knowledge that does not part. Both make knowledge a woman to be joined; the song uses the figure against desire for women.

The song fears the wretchedness of being cast off after he served the women and then stopped giving the money they wanted (காசைக் கொடாத பின்பு சீரற்று). Naladiyar 372 tells of the woman who swore to leap from the peak with her lover but, since he had no gold, pleaded aching feet and left (காணம் இன்மையான் மேவாதொழிந்தாளே). Both show the courtesan's love ending exactly where the money ends.

The poet asks that when Death comes by fate to seek his life he be given the thought to call 'Adi Muruga' (ஆதிமுருகா ... நினைவு தருவாயே), and the praise has Murugan bow at the feet of the guru Om Namasivaya (ஓநமசிவாய குரு பாதம்). Tirumanthiram 2702 says that when Death lays hand on the soul to change its life, it is the five letters that protect (அரணம் கைகூட்டுவது அஞ்செழுத்தாமே). Both make a sacred name the defence at death; the song asks for Murugan's name while bowing to the five letters in its refrain.

The poet, whose desire for gold, land and women does not end and who does crores of sins, fears Death dropping him into the seven hells (நரகேழில் விழுந்தாழ) and asks Murugan to come speaking the word of wisdom (ஞான விளம்போசை) so his sins go. Tirumanthiram 2194 says the soul in which ignorance remains perishes, and if its delusion branches further it reaches the seven hells (ஏழ் நரகத்து). The Tirumanthiram traces the hells to ignorance and delusion; the song asks for wisdom as the remedy.
audit_text_issue: Several words in Thiruppugazh 1244 are corrupt (e.g. ஧வ்முழ்க, லு஡மாசை).

note: The song asks that before the failing time comes for wealth, servants, kin, sons and house (தப்பு நிலைமை அணுகைக்கு வர ... குறுகாமுன்) he be given the thought to melt in devotion and hold the feet daily. Kural 333 says wealth has the nature of not staying, so while you have it do at once what stays (அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both make the passing of wealth a reason for haste; the Kural's lasting deed is in the song devotion to the feet.

Tirumular says people wander off calling this or that the supreme and that going the ordained way stills the mind's 'that or this' (அது இது); 1247 asks to know, without quarrelling with the sects, the Lord beyond he, she and it, this and that.
The Naladiyar's wise see the body as a bubble in pelting rain and resolve to end their wandering; 1252 calls the poet's own life a bubble (புற்புதப் பிராணன்) and asks for the true word instead.
Both are akam laments at dusk with the south wind, the moon, the anril bird and Kama's arrows; 24 is in a mother's voice, 1254 in the girl's own, asking for the hero's garland.

1247 asks to know the Lord who has passed beyond he, she and it in every distance (அவன் இவன் உவன் ... அவள் இவள் உவள் அது இது உது எனும் ஆறு அற்று) and beyond form and the formless. Tirumanthiram 1872 calls the light within the dark neither woman nor man nor neuter (பெண்ணல்ல ஆணல்ல பேடல்ல), unknowable to anyone. Both deny the Lord the categories of gender and grammar; the song adds person and distance, the Tirumanthiram adds that he sees without eyes and hears without ears.

1247 asks to know the Lord without quarrelling (சருவா நின்று) with the many sectarians, ritualists and hair-plucking ascetics. Tirumanthiram 1547, in the chapter on the quarrel of sects, says that if one knows how to gain the light standing within there is no quarrel at all (பிணக்கொன்றும் இல்லை). The song asks for the knowing as the way out of the dispute; the Tirumanthiram states that the dispute ends where that knowing begins.

1248 likens women's breasts to the tusks of a rutting elephant (கடாக் களிற்று உரகோடு), to peaks and to tender coconuts, and confesses wasting nights and days in their net. Kural 1087 says the cloth over a woman's firm breasts is like the face-cloth over a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம்). Both use the elephant in rut for the breast's force; in the Kural the cloth restrains it, in the song nothing does and the poet asks to be set to praise instead.

1249 asks that his two deceitful deeds be destroyed as he plunges and plays in the Sivaganga tank (சிவகங்கை தனில் முழுகி விளையாடி), with Sivam leaping into him. Tirumanthiram 509 says the many holy waters are within the heart, and those who do not bathe there so that deeds are destroyed (வினைகெட) wander over hollow and height with deceitful minds. If Sivaganga is the outer tank of Chidambaram, the song asks for the cleansing the Tirumanthiram says outer waters cannot give; if it is an inner water, as the following possession by Sivam may suggest, the two agree.

1250 names the great maya that looks on the leather bag of the five elements as 'I' (தோற்பை யானாக நோக்கும் மா மாயை) and tends a body that ghosts, vultures, jackals and crows will tear (காக்கை பீறா). Tirumanthiram 167 asks what it matters if crows carry off the nest once the dancer who stood in the skin bag (தோற்பையுள் நின்று ... கூத்தன்) has left it. The Tirumanthiram separates the dweller from the bag; the song names the failure to make that separation as the delusion it cannot end.
audit_text_issue: 1250's line 'வேலோடு வேய்த்த ....... ; ளையோனே' is corrupt.

note: 1250 calls the body a leather bag (தோற்பை) oozing the mire of desire, wrongly taken as oneself, and pictures its tearing by scavengers. Naladiyar 26, in nearly the words of Tirumanthiram 167, asks what it matters whether the body is dragged off with a rope, buried or reviled once the dancer within the skin bag (தோற்பையுள் நின்று) has gone. The ethical and the devotional books share the figure; the song turns it into a confession of still tending the bag.

1251 sets itself against sophist sectarians who rise to argue and plant flag against flag (கொடிக்கொடி எதிர்கூறி), and asks to be wholly the Lord's servant and given the one word that reveals the first principle the Vedas do not know. Tirumanthiram 2515 says there is no need to quarrel (பிணங்கவும் வேண்டாம்): if all agree 'our Lord is the Lord', there love can be had. Both answer the debate of sects by turning from argument to surrender; the song asks for a word, the Tirumanthiram for agreement and love.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1251: first-half verb chain hard to assign.

note: 1252 calls the poet's life a bubble (புற்புதப் பிராணன்) and asks for the true word Murugan gave Siva. Tirumanthiram 2587 sets the body beside a bubble on flowing water (கழிகின்ற நீரிற் குமிழி), a vanishing shadow-man and camphor in flame, and says it goes into the Supreme. The same figure of transience leads the song to ask for teaching and the Tirumanthiram to describe the body's dissolution into the Supreme.

1253 asks, before the fierce ones (likely Death's servants) close in and break his strength (சினமிகுத்த திண்ணர் ... வன்மை சிதையாமுன்), to be given the good of speaking and writing true words of the Lord daily. Tirumanthiram 255 says Death comes in force (வன்மையில் வந்திடும் கூற்றம்) without asking whether one is good, poor or young, and urges good austerity before it. Both race the same violent end; the Tirumanthiram's remedy is tapas, the song's is praise spoken and written.

1256 confesses that his mind went to women and asks whether a day will come when, thinking of the Lord, the books he learned would rejoice (கற்ற நூல் உகக்க). Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the one of pure knowledge (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்). The song applies the Kural's verdict to the poet himself: his learning is shamed until it is turned to the Lord.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1256: syllable lost before ளையோனே.

note: 1257 describes women who enchant with poison eyes, speak many desires (இச்சை பல பேசி) and whose minds crave good wealth (நற்பொருள் அவா மனத்தர்), and asks not to waste away infatuated with them. Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not the man (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song shows the talk and the craving the Kural names, and the daily wasting (நித்தம் மெலியாதே) that is the harm.

1258 has the poet, shown women's bodies, ready to ride the madal (மடலூர) and falling on those who drag out his life, and asks for the lamp of Vedanta to end that darkness. Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard or strength but the palmyra horse (மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). The Kural's last resort of a lover becomes in the song a mark of the rogue's delusion (தூர்த்தன் மோகாந்தகாரம்), answered by a lamp rather than a public plea.

1259 melts like wax in fire (எரியுறு மெழுகென) before women whose carp-eyes fight like weapons (படைபொருவன விழிக் கயல்). Naladiyar 44 refuses to be troubled by men who call eyes lilies, fighting carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேல்), and sees an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The same comparison that the Naladiyar dismantles is the one the song confesses to have yielded to, asking the Lord to end the suffering it brings.

1261 asks for the word of wisdom, rising bliss without 'I' and self (யானொடு தானிலா), that ends his deeds and the beginningless bond. Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. Both make the loss of 'I' the gate to release; the song asks for it as a gift of grace after confessing that he took women's deceit for teaching.
audit_text_issue: 1261: a syllable before ருபார்வை is lost.

note: The Naladiyar's 'he stood, he sat, he lay, and with kin wailing he was gone' urges virtue now; 1265 extends the same list of verbs from birth to corpse (பிறந்தார் கிடந்தார் இருந்தார் தவழ்ந்தார் நடந்தார்) and turns it into a plea for the Lord's 'fear not'.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks where the woman is among them; 1270 calls the body a cage of filth, skin, water and bone, but draws service to the Lord from it rather than disgust at women.
audit_text_issue: 1270's text is largely hard to construe; the marker flagged it.

note: Tirumular rouses the root and joins it to the head through the middle channel to reach the holy feet; 1275 asks for the light above the root centre and the steady gem-light in the middle path.
audit_text_issue: 1275 line 'நநடு ழிதனிலை' is corrupt (doubled syllable, probably நடு வழி).

note: Both set a list of kin against Death's coming: 1266 with Death's rope and a household quarrelling over property, 1267 with Yama on the buffalo and a grief for kin called illusory.
Two vows rather than pleas: 1255 will speak only of the feet whether king or poor, 1276 will not forget them even in the deluded embrace of women.
Both akam laments end with a request for the hero's flowers, his garland in 1254 and kura blossoms in 1268, against Kama's arrows and the sea.

1262 tells how Murugan, seeking Valli, lost his shame (நாணம் அழிந்து), changed form and walked till his feet ached, struck by Kama's arrows. Kural 1133 has a lover say he once had shame and manliness and now has only the madal that lovers ride. The Kural's loss of shame in a man's love is told in the song of the god himself, set against the poet's own confession of desire.
audit_text_issue: 1262 has a line missing its beat marker; a word may be lost.

note: 1263 describes the body as an upright hut (நிமிர் குடில்) with hands and two legs that Brahma builds skilfully, into which life enters and which ends in fire. Tirumanthiram 161 describes it as a dwelling with two posts and one ridge beam (காலும் இரண்டு முகட்டலக் கொன்று), thatched by a craftsman rather than a palm-thatcher. Both read the body as a built house standing on two legs; the Tirumanthiram admires the work, the song stresses it is built of disease and deeds.

1264 asks to know the yogi's joy called Nada-Paraparam that came out of Bindu and the full, causal power (பூரணி காரணி விந்து வெளியான நாத பராபரம்) and so reach the Lord's two feet. Tirumanthiram 708 says supreme bindu, supreme nada, bindu, nada, the sheltering Shakti and Parai are the feet of the Supreme (பரைபரன் பாதமே). The song climbs the series toward the feet; the Tirumanthiram says the series is the feet.

1264 asks to feel the breath of wisdom, see the light and reach the feet of the Lord seated on the lotus where a thousand nadis meet (நாடி ஒராயிரம் வந்த தாமரை). Tirumanthiram 857 says that by rousing the base through the middle channel and joining it with the head, the good reach the holy feet (திருவடி நண்ணி). Both place the feet at the crown, at the end of the channels.

1265 tells a life in verbs: they were born, lay, sat, crawled, walked, weakened and became corpses (பிறந்தார் கிடந்தார் இருந்தார் தவழ்ந்தார் நடந்தார் தளர்ந்து பிணமானார்). Tirumanthiram 2188 uses the same verbs (பிறந்தார் கிடந்தார் ... தவழ்ந்தார் ... நடந்தார் வளர்ந்தார்) for the states of awareness within waking. The child's stages serve one as a march to the burning ground and the other as a map of inner states.

1266 asks, before Death throws his long rope and seizes his life (நெட்டைக் கயிற்றிட்டு வளையாமுன்), to melt with devotion and be given true words to speak of the feet. Kural 335 says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both use the 'before' of death to make the present urgent; the Kural asks for good deeds, the song for words while the tongue still works.

1267 calls the grief for children, mothers, in-laws and wife an illusory grief deeper than the sea (மைத்த வேலைக்கு நெடிது உற்ற மாயத் துயரம்) and asks for the feet so his mind may be stilled. Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and leave wordlessly, as a bird leaves its nesting tree (சேக்கை மரன் ஒழியச் சேண்நீங்கு புள்போல). The Naladiyar shows why the song's grief for kin can be called illusory.

1269's praise says the Lord thinks daily of keeping those who never fail in sweet speech from coming again by the womb (இனிய சொல் மறாத சீலர் கருவழி வராமல்). Kural 98 says sweet speech free of pettiness gives joy in the next life and in this. The song carries the Kural's reward for sweet speech to release from birth.
audit_text_issue: 1269 has garbled words (மிகுமுனருபதானம், க்டுர); Kural 98 shows சிறுமையுவு for சிறுமையுள்.

note: 1270 asks to become the Lord's servant before the breath leaves the cage of filth, skin and bone and father, wife, mother and kin cry out at the burning ground (குலைந்து ஆர்ப்பெழும் காட்டில்). Tirumanthiram 157 has the kin, wives and children who rise up wailing (ஆர்த்தெழு சுற்றமும்) turn back at the town's edge while the body is burned. Both make the wailing kin the sign that they cannot follow; the song draws the plea for service from it.

1271 confesses a mind that thinks a hundred crore sorrows in an instant (மனநூறு கோடி துன்பம் நொடிமீதிலே நினைந்து) and asks for release on the day the body falls. Kural 337 says those who cannot know they will live one moment more think thoughts in the many crores (கருதுப கோடியும் அல்ல பல). The same crores of thought against a moment's life serve the Kural as irony and the song as confession.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1271: விநன்முடி is garbled.

note: 1272 traces a life from conception in passion through the months of the womb, birth, crawling and walking to the harlot's net, and asks whether he must die so. Tirumanthiram 163 compresses the same course: born after three hundred days, married at twelve, perished at seventy, and people do not see the ruin (கேடறியீரே). Both count life by its stages to show its waste; the song fills the stages with its own fault.

1273 likens pearl-hung breasts to an elephant with two tusks thrust forward (இருகோடு முற்பட்ட கரிபோலும்) and says the women's spear eyes cloud his mind. Kural 1087 likens the cloth over a woman's breasts to the face-cloth of a rutting elephant. Both see the breast as an elephant; the song makes it the cause of his whirling grief and asks to worship the feet with many words instead.

1274 calls Murugan the guru who taught old Siva the ending of pati, pasu and pasa (பதி பசு பாசத் தீர்வினை). Tirumanthiram 115 states the doctrine: of pati, pasu and pasa, the last two are beginningless like pati and cannot reach it, but when pati draws near they do not remain. The Tirumanthiram gives the content of the teaching the song credits to Murugan.

1276 says that even if he embraces women and his mind is deluded he will not forget the Lord's feet (மதிமயங்கினும் ... பதங்கள் மறவேனே). 1262, describing the same lovemaking, asks whether he will forget that desire and know the Lord (ஆசை மறந்து உனை உணர்வேனோ). On the reading that 1262 makes forgetting desire the condition of knowing, the two disagree on whether remembrance can live inside desire.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1262: a line lacks its beat marker, possibly a lost word.

note: The same four lines of plea, Kama's arrows, the blue sea, the cuckoo of the grove and 'embrace the deer', with only the epithets changed; the two read as variants of one song.
Both songs end by naming Murugan as Sambandar: 1282 by name and by his child's dance, 1287 by the milk of Uma and the impaling of the Jains, and both credit him with filling the land with Tamil.
The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; 1289 dramatizes those words (laughing talk, soothing care) and ends with the plunder of wealth.

1277 vows that even while two become one body in maya (மாயை படுபோதும்) the poet will not forget Murugan's arms, faces and feet (மறவேனே). Tirumanthiram 2857 says the Lord is himself the union and the sulking (புணரும் அவனே புலவி அவனே). The song keeps remembrance alive inside the embrace; the Tirumanthiram goes further and makes the embrace itself the Lord.

1278 asks, beyond women's embrace and endless births, for the pure great state of silent supreme bliss (ஒரு மவுன பரமசுக சுத்தப் பெரும்பதம்). Tirumanthiram 2844 names the true form as speechless bliss and silence (உரையற்ற ஆனந்த மோன சொரூபம்). Both join silence and bliss as one final state; the Tirumanthiram adds its analysis through the letters of Om.

1279 calls the body the nest where life dwells (ஆவியுறை கூட்டில்) and asks that it be fed the scripture of knowledge instead of women and wealth. Kural 338 likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest (குடம்பை) empty. The Kural uses the nest to show the bird will leave it; the song asks what the bird should be fed while it is still there.
audit_text_issue: 1279's கேணியுற வேட்ட and ஆணியுள வீட்டை are unclear.

note: 1280 asks that the distortion of the gunas run off (குணவிகாரம் ஓட) so that he grows clear and joins the unspeakable supreme form of knowledge. Tirumanthiram 2296 maps sattva, rajas and tamas onto waking, dream and sleep, and says the gunaless state that ends them is stainless turiya (மாய்த்திடும் நிற்குணம் மாசில் துரியமே). The Tirumanthiram supplies the map of the state the song only names as clarity beyond the gunas.

1283 asks not to be born oozing from the womb again (கருப்பற்று ஊறிப் பிறவாதே) and for the experience of the holy golden feet. Tirumanthiram 1597 says that Nandi as guru placed his feet on the poet's head so that the path to the womb was drained away (கருவழி வாற்றிட). What the song asks, the Tirumanthiram reports as done: the feet close the womb-path.
audit_text_issue: Glyph ஡ in 1283 line 1.

note: 1281 asks, among other things, not to grow weary reciting the three Tamils (முத்தமிழை ஓதித் தளராதே), which is hard to read alone. 1284 spells out the danger: not to recite colourful Tamil poems that please deceitful scoundrels (கபட்ட சட்டர்க்கு இதத்த சித்ரத் தமிழ்கள் உரையாதே). Read together, the weariness of 1281 is likely Tamil spent on patrons rather than on the Lord.

1287 asks to leave the vain devotion of the sects (சமய பத்தி வ்ருதா) and seek the worship of Siva at the lotus feet. Tirumanthiram 1534 declares the six sects nothing but waste (அவமல்லதில்லை அறுசமயங்கள்) and bids one cling to Nandi's feet and be saved. Both set the feet against the sects; neither counts Siva-worship itself as a sect.
audit_text_issue: 1534: line breaks uncertain.

note: 1288 asks for a word of the heart that is not settled in the mass of quarrelling scriptures (சருவிய சாத்திரத் திரள்) nor in the six-fold seat, and is hard to gain even by the Vedas. Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six sects did not see him, and he is not the thing they hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). Both place what is sought outside the systems; the Tirumanthiram adds a way, clarity upon clarity (தேறித் தெளிமின்).
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1288: அனிதய வார்த்தை and சடுதிகழ் ஆஸ்பதம் are obscure; the latter may mean the six adharas rather than six systems.

note: 1289 describes women who laugh and talk, tend a man until his mind is soothed, and then plunder his wealth (தனத்தைச் சூறைகொள் மடவார்). Naladiyar 377 has the worthless woman lick like a wild cow, take the wealth from his hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balk like an ox. Both show the same sequence, tender care first and the seizure of wealth after.
Both name 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது) as what must be cut; the Kural promises a world above the gods to whoever cuts them, and 1292 asks the cutting itself as a gift of knowledge.

In both the town's gossip feeds the girl's love-sickness rather than ending it; the Kural makes it manure for the sickness, and 1297 sets the reproach of women beside Kama and the moon as what sinks her in sorrow.
The same frame, the moon, Kama and a question ending -லாமோ, closing on தம்பிரானே; 1290 asks about the girl, 1303 is her own voice and adds the world's reproach.

1292 asks to be given the knowledge in which 'I' and 'mine' are cut away (யான் எனது அற்றிடு போதம்). Tirumanthiram 1556 says those who stay inside their sect, even with the light of Om within, never gain the experience free of the ego (ஆங்காரம் அற்ற அனுபவம்) nor freedom from birth. The Tirumanthiram names what blocks the gift the song asks for.

1293 asks for the experience of the feet (அநுபூதி) and describes it as nectar, sugar and honey (ஆரமுதமான சர்க்கரை தேனே). Tirumanthiram 2940 places the light beyond the turiyas within an experience that speech does not reach (உரையில் அநுபூதி). The same word is given tastes in the song and is put beyond words in the Tirumanthiram, so the song's sweetness is a figure for something it cannot state.

1294 asks, as one who seeks the dance of knowledge (ஞான நிருத்தம்) with a melting that grows daily, for the wealth of experience. Tirumanthiram 2793 says that when pasu and pasa stand apart the Supreme dances everywhere, the dance of knowledge of those in Siva's bliss (சிவானந்தத்தோர் ஞானக் கூத்து). The Tirumanthiram explains what the song's dance of knowledge is: the Lord's dance seen by the freed.

1295 asks to be given the dance, by the path of high austerity (தவத்தின் நெறியாலே) with those established in nishtha as companions. Tirumanthiram 1632 says tapas is needed to reach knowledge but not needed once the samadhi of knowledge is in hand (தவம்வேண்டா ஞான சமாதிகை கூடில்). The Tirumanthiram limits the song's austerity to a means that drops away at the goal.
audit_text_issue: TM 1632 line 3 (மச்ச கசமார்க்கத்தோர்க்கு) looks corrupt.

note: 1299 asks not to enter the river of births with its waves (பிறவியலை யாற்றினில் புகுதாதே) and to be given the vision of Murugan's feet. Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The same pairing, births as water and the feet as the way across, appears in the Kural's opening chapter and in this late song.

1299 calls Murugan the meaning of the scriptures of the six creeds (அறுசமய சாத்திரப் பொருளோனே). Tirumanthiram 1557 says the First Lord moves among the six sects so that they seek his feet (சமயங்கள் ஆறும் தன் தாளிணை நாட). Both place the six creeds under the one Lord rather than against him.

1288 asks for a word not settled in the quarrelling scriptures or the six-fold seat (சருவிய சாத்திரத் திரள்), and 1299 calls Murugan the meaning of the six creeds' scriptures (அறுசமய சாத்திரப் பொருளோனே). Together they hold that the scriptures quarrel as texts yet share one meaning, which is the Lord, reached through the guru's word (குரு வாக்கியப் பொருள்).

1300 asks for the knowledge that cannot be completed by writing on the leaves of books (புத்தகத்து ஏட்டில் தீட்டி முடியாது), revealed by grace. Kural 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own true understanding prevails (உண்மை அறிவே மிகும்). Both put the deciding knowledge outside book-learning; the Kural leaves its source unnamed, and the song names it as grace.

1301 speaks of public women who desire gold (பொன்னை விரும்பிய பொதுமாதர்) and asks Murugan to desire the poet so that the poet may desire him. Kural 911 sets women who desire wealth against those who desire with love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்). The song takes the Kural's contrast between desire for wealth and desire for the person and carries it over to grace.

1302 calls house, children and kin a net of maya (மனைமக்கள் சுற்றம் எனும் மாயா வலை) he cannot cross. Tirumanthiram 1530 says the sects, caught in the bond of house and children (மனைமக்கள் பாசத்தில்), fall writhing into the pit of maya (மாயக் குழி). Both name the household itself as maya's trap, the song as a net and the Tirumanthiram as a pit.

1304 asks not to be born into the deceptive false hut (மாயத் தெற்றிப் பொய்க்குடில்) of the five elements. Kural 340 asks whether the life that lodges in a corner of the body (துச்சில்) has no home of its own. Both see the body as a poor lodging the life does not own; the Kural asks a question, while the song asks to be spared the hut.
The Kural opens with A as first of letters and God as first of the world; 1307 makes Murugan the letter A itself (அகரமுமாகி), and the one above the three gods.
Both turn into a catalogue of shrines; 1306 is wholly the list, while 1313 sets the list after a yogic ascent, as if the outer pilgrimage answered the inner one.
audit_text_issue: Both have corrupt glyphs (஧வ்ளுர், நாவலு஡ர், வயலு஡ரா).

note: The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; 1317 names their lavish lying speech and love set at a price, and adds the brass polished to pass for gold.

The Naladiyar sees the old man with failed speech, a staff and lost teeth still eyeing desire; 1321 gives the same old age in detail, adds the medicines, and draws the remedy not from renunciation but from song and the feet.

The Thiruppugazh hymns Murugan as அயனென ஆகி அரியென ஆகி அரனென ஆகி அவர்மேலாய், becoming Brahma, Vishnu and Hara and standing above them. The Tirumanthiram says of Siva தானே அயன்மால் என நின்று தாபிக்கும், he himself stands as Brahma and Vishnu and establishes things. Both make the highest god the one who becomes the lesser gods; the song adds that he is also above them.

In the Thiruppugazh's long litany of the Goddess whose son Murugan is, the names வயிரவி நீலி stand among Kali, the trident-bearer and Abhirami. The Tirumanthiram's Bhairavi mantra opens with the same pair, நின்ற வயிரவி நீலி நிசாசரி, and bids one proclaim her. The pairing shows Arunagirinathar's Goddess names drawing on the fierce Bhairavi of the Saiva mantra tradition, here made Murugan's mother.

The Thiruppugazh asks Murugan to come performing the dance of knowledge நாரணனும் வேதன் முன்பு தெரியாத, that Narayana and Brahma never knew. The Tirumanthiram tells the story behind the phrase: அடிமுடி காண்பார் அயன்மால் இருவர் படிகண்டிலர், Brahma and Vishnu searched for Siva's foot and crown and did not see his form. The song gives Siva's unseen form to Murugan's dance.

The Thiruppugazh asks for Murugan's ஞான நடம், the dance of knowledge, so that Death does not come near. The Tirumanthiram follows Siva's dance inward, ending in ஞானத்துள் ஆடி முடித்தான், he danced within knowledge and completed it. The Tirumanthiram places the dance inside knowledge; the song asks for that dance to come to the poet as protection from Death.

The Thiruppugazh confesses a heart that wavered for மாது மனையான மைந்தர் சேரு பொருள், wife, house, children and wealth, taking this life as permanent (வாழ்வு சதமாம் இது). The Tirumanthiram mocks people who say of வாழ்வும் மனைவியும் மக்கள் உடன்பிறந்தாரும், 'what limit is there to what is ours?'. Both name the household list and say the error is believing it lasts; the Tirumanthiram's way out is giving, the song's is the feet.

The Naladiyar says a harlot's love is like a lamp's light: விளக்கொளியும் நெய்யற்ற கண்ணே அறுமே, அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும். The Thiruppugazh speaks from after that moment: நீடு பொருள் போன பின்பு பாதகனுமாகி நின்று, when the great wealth had gone he stood a sinner. The song takes the Naladiyar's warning past poverty to guilt, the loss the proverb does not count.

Both songs trace the same yogic ascent from the same root: 1313 begins at நாலு சதுரக் கமலம் and reaches விந்து நாத ஓசை, and 506 begins at நாலுசதுரத்த ... மூலகமலம் and reaches the conch sound of விந்துநாதம். The Pazhamudircholai song asks to go out by the மூல வாசல் into Murugan's light, the Chidambaram song to reach the hall of countless dances; the same map ends at Murugan in one and at Siva's dance in the other.
audit_text_issue: 1313 has garbled characters in the shrine list (e.g. '஧வ்ளுர்', 'நாவலு஡ர்').

note: The Thiruppugazh asks Murugan to give today யோக பேதவகை எட்டும் இதில் ஒட்டும் வகை, the way the eight kinds of yoga join in this ascent. The Tirumanthiram names those eight: இயம நியமமே ... தியானஞ் சமாதி அயமுறும் அட்டாங்கம். The song asks as a gift for what the Tirumanthiram sets out as a practice.
audit_text_issue: 1313's numerical splits (ஆர மூணு பதி, நுறு பத்தினுடன் எட்டு) are unsure.

note: The Tirumanthiram says that in the womb (கர்ப்பத்து) maya joins her brood to the soul, thought arises and karma takes firm hold. The Thiruppugazh tells the life that follows, from கருவாகியெ தாய் உதரத்தினில் உருவாகவெ through nursing to wife, kin and wealth taken as சதமாம் இது, permanent. The Tirumanthiram names the bond made in the womb; the song shows it playing out over a whole life.

The Tirumanthiram holds that if the body perishes the life perishes, so உடம்பை வளர்க்கும் உபாயம் அறிந்தே உடம்பை வளர்த்தேன், knowing the means, I nurtured the body. The Thiruppugazh asks whether one can gain யோக சித்தி by fattening உடல்செய் கோர பாழ் வயிற்றை daily with food, and sets its hope on the feet of knowledge instead. If the question is read as ironic, as its wording suggests, the song denies what the Tirumanthiram affirms: that tending the body is the road to the goal.

The Thiruppugazh seeks the feet of knowledge that dance in உருவிலாத பாழில் வெட்டவெளியில், the formless void, the open space. The Tirumanthiram crosses the void to reach Nandi's feet and rests in கற்பனை உதறிய பாழில், the void that has shaken off even imagining. Both make the பாழ், the empty void, the place where the feet are found rather than a loss.

The Thiruppugazh lists courtesans who நேசித்தாரையும் எத்தி வடிப்பவர், cheat and drain even those who love them. The Naladiyar's worthless woman ஆமாபோல் நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு, licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands, then bolts like a buffalo. Both make the affection itself the means of draining the lover; the Naladiyar adds the ridicule that follows.

The Thiruppugazh asks Murugan to rule him by giving சோதி உணர்கின்ற வாழ்வு சிவம் என்ற சோகம், the 'I am He' that the life knowing the light is Siva. The Tirumanthiram says that to those who say சோகம் on the path of union, சிவமாம் அமலன் சிறந்தனன், the stainless Siva stands forth. The pairing supports reading the song's சோகம் as soham, the meditation of identity with Siva, rather than as grief.

The Thiruppugazh confesses நாதமொடு விந்துவான உடல் கொண்டு நானிலம் அலைந்து திரிவேனே, wandering the earth in a body made of nada and bindu, and asks for சிவம் என்ற சோகம். The Tirumanthiram makes the same link a method: lives come from விந்துவும் நாதமும், and விந்து அடங்க விளையும் சிவோகமே, when bindu is contained Sivoham grows. What the song asks as a gift, the Tirumanthiram makes the fruit of restraining bindu.

The Kural's lover says பண்டறியேன் கூற்றென்பதனை இனியறிந்தேன், he never knew Death before and now knows it, in a woman's battling eyes. The Thiruppugazh calls the women மாய நமனுக்கும் உறவாகி, kin even to Death. The Kural's lover is overwhelmed by desire; the song makes the same identity of woman and Death a warning.

The Kural says பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம் is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The Thiruppugazh lists every display of the courtesans with the refrain காட்டி, showing, and calls them those who உயிரை விலைகொளும், buy a man's life for a price. Both say the embrace is false and paid for; the song makes the price life itself, not wealth alone.

The Kural's lover says he would remember her if he forgot, but மறப்பறியேன், he does not know how to forget. The Thiruppugazh says that even while sunk in love-play, மகிழ்கினும் ... முடிவடிவொடு அங்கை வேலும் மறவேனே, he will not forget Murugan's crowned form and the vel in his hand. The same claim of never forgetting moves from the beloved to the god, and in the song it holds even in the middle of desire.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1322 line 2 has a lacuna ('....... ; ளநீரின்').

note: Both confess the poet's craft spent for wealth: 1092 the praise-songs sung to patrons who gave nothing, 1323 the arts and poems learned and sung while running the streets after money.

The Kural says கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி, learning is the imperishable wealth and nothing else is wealth. The Thiruppugazh confesses that after learning கலைபல நூல்கள் and singing many poems he ran through the streets after பொருளெனும் ஆசை, the desire called wealth. The song limits the Kural's claim: learning is wealth only if it is not spent hunting the other kind.

Both mark the end by the physician giving up (Tirumular's lets go the pulse, 1325's says no remedy will work) while wife and wealth stay behind or wail; Tirumular leaves it there, while 1325 asks for Murugan to come at that hour.
audit_text_issue: 1325 has a broken line marker (....... ;) before யல்தோகை.

note: Tirumular's first verse counts the Lord from one to eight (one, two by grace, within three, knowing four, conquering five); 1326 uses the same counting device through seven to tell Murugan's acts, so the numbers become theology in one and narrative in the other.
audit_text_issue: Some number phrases in 1326 are obscure, as the marker notes.
